paper_title: The puzzle of global Double Field Theory: open problems and the case for a Higher Kaluza-Klein perspective
original_question: Can Double Field Theory recover a general geometric string background, meaning a smooth spacetime manifold equipped with a non-trivial Kalb-Ramond field whose Dixmier-Douady class [H] is nonzero in H3(M, Z), rather than only the restricted cases in which the recovered gerbe is flat or torsion?
self_contained_problem:
Background. In string theory a geometric string background consists of a smooth manifold $M$ equipped with a closed 3-form $H \in \Omega^3(M)$ with integral periods, representing the curvature of a $U(1)$-bundle gerbe whose Dixmier–Douady class $[H] \in H^3(M,\mathbb{Z})$ classifies the gerbe up to isomorphism. The Kalb–Ramond $B$-field is a (local) connective structure on this gerbe; globally, on overlapping patches it is glued by gauge transformations governed by the gerbe data.

Double Field Theory (DFT) is a field theory formulated on a "doubled" space whose local model is $\mathbb{R}^{2d}$ with coordinates $(x^\mu, \tilde x_\mu)$ subject to the strong constraint $\partial^M \otimes \partial_M = 0$, with an $O(d,d)$-invariant generalized metric $\mathcal{H}_{MN}$ encoding the metric $g$ and the $B$-field. Solutions of the strong constraint locally depend on only $d$ of the $2d$ coordinates, recovering an ordinary $d$-dimensional supergravity background $(g, B)$.

Question. Does there exist a globally defined formulation of Double Field Theory that, upon solving the strong constraint, recovers an arbitrary geometric string background $(M, [H])$ with smooth manifold $M$ and topologically non-trivial Kalb–Ramond field having Dixmier–Douady class $[H] \neq 0$ in $H^3(M,\mathbb{Z})$ (in particular, classes that are neither zero nor torsion)? Equivalently, can the patching/glueing data of DFT be extended so that the recovered bundle gerbe is allowed to have arbitrary, non-flat, non-torsion Dixmier–Douady class, rather than only the cases in which the gerbe is flat or torsion?
category_tag: Double Field Theory and bundle gerbes
status_search_result: Recent work on extended/higher geometric formulations of Double Field Theory (e.g., Alfonsi's program on the higher Kaluza–Klein/extended correspondence) discusses this as an unresolved problem: a global DFT geometry that recovers an arbitrary Kalb–Ramond field with non-trivial Dixmier–Douady class is not known. Proposals interpret doubled geometry as an atlas for the higher geometry of bundle gerbes, but a complete construction recovering general non-flat, non-torsion gerbes from DFT remains open.

paper_title: The puzzle of global Double Field Theory: open problems and the case for a Higher Kaluza-Klein perspective
original_question: Can Exceptional Field Theory be formulated as a Higher Kaluza-Klein theory on the total space of the twisted M2/M5-brane bundle gerbe over 11-dimensional super-spacetime?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ denote 11-dimensional super-spacetime, modeled as the super-Minkowski supermanifold (or, more generally, a super-spacetime equipped with the structure required to support 11-dimensional supergravity). Over $X$ there exists a twisted bundle 2-gerbe (the "M2/M5-brane super 2-gerbe") whose underlying super L∞-cocycles are those classifying the M2-brane and M5-brane charges, namely the cocycles
$\mu_{M2} \in H^4(\mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{i}\mathfrak{n}\mathfrak{k}_{10,1|32};\mathbb{R})$ and $\mu_{M5} \in H^7(\mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{i}\mathfrak{n}\mathfrak{k}_{10,1|32};\mathbb{R})$ on 11-dimensional super-Minkowski; let $\mathcal{G} \to X$ denote the total space (in the sense of higher/principal ∞-bundles) of this twisted M2/M5 super 2-gerbe.

A "Higher Kaluza-Klein theory" on the total space of a smooth principal ∞-bundle $\pi:\mathcal{G}\to X$ is, by definition, a theory of an Ehresmann-type higher connection on $\mathcal{G}$ together with an invariant generalized metric on $\mathcal{G}$, whose dimensional reduction along the higher fibers reproduces, on the base $X$, both an ordinary metric and a tower of higher gauge fields with their associated charges and dualities.

Exceptional Field Theory (ExFT) is the U-duality-covariant reformulation of 11-dimensional supergravity in which the metric and the higher form fields ($C_3$, $C_6$, ...) of supergravity are unified into a single generalized geometric object on an "extended" or "exceptional" spacetime, with extra coordinates conjugate to M2- and M5-brane winding modes, subject to a section constraint that locally selects an 11-dimensional slice.

Problem. Prove or disprove the following: there exists a formulation of Exceptional Field Theory as a Higher Kaluza-Klein theory on the total space $\mathcal{G}$ of the twisted M2/M5-brane super 2-gerbe over 11-dimensional super-spacetime $X$, such that
(i) the generalized tangent geometry of ExFT on the exceptional extended space is naturally identified, fiberwise, with the higher tangent geometry of $\mathcal{G}\to X$;
(ii) the section constraint of ExFT corresponds to the higher Ehresmann horizontality condition on $\mathcal{G}$; and
(iii) the dimensional reduction along the higher fibers of $\mathcal{G}$ recovers 11-dimensional supergravity together with its M2- and M5-brane charges and U-duality structure on $X$.
category_tag: Higher gauge theory and exceptional field theory
status_search_result: Subsequent work has carried out this program partially. The Double Field Theory case (T-duality covariant) has been formulated as Higher Kaluza-Klein theory on the total space of the Kalb–Ramond bundle gerbe (Alfonsi, 2020). For the exceptional/U-duality case, the program of formulating Exceptional Field Theory as a higher Kaluza-Klein theory on the M2/M5 super 2-gerbe has been developed in subsequent works ("Extended Field Theories as higher Kaluza-Klein theories", 2021; "Towards an extended/higher correspondence", 2021), establishing the correspondence in significant cases but not yet a complete, fully global construction including all U-duality groups and full supergravity reduction. Hence the problem appears partially solved.

paper_title: The Lieb-Thirring inequalities: recent results and open problems
context_brief: Removing the 1−ε loss in the improved bound
original_question: In the improved orthonormal Lieb-Thirring inequality with a semiclassical main term and an additional gradient-error term, can one remove the prefactor 1−ε in front of the semiclassical term while still keeping a finite constant in front of the gradient correction?
self_contained_problem:
Let $d\ge 1$ and let $(u_j)_{j=1}^N$ be an orthonormal family in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$. Define the one-particle density
$$\rho(x)=\sum_{j=1}^N |u_j(x)|^2,\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^d,$$
and the kinetic energy
$$T[(u_j)]=\sum_{j=1}^N \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}|\nabla u_j(x)|^2\,dx.$$
Let $K_{\rm cl}(d)=\frac{d}{d+2}\bigl(4\pi^2\bigr)\bigl(\Gamma(d/2+1)\bigr)^{-2/d}$ be the semiclassical Lieb–Thirring constant, so that
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\rho(x)^{1+2/d}\,dx$$
is the natural Thomas–Fermi-type density functional appearing in the semiclassical kinetic energy.

It is known that for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ there exists a constant $C(d,\varepsilon)<\infty$ such that, for every orthonormal family as above,
$$T[(u_j)]\;\ge\;(1-\varepsilon)\,K_{\rm cl}(d)\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\rho(x)^{1+2/d}\,dx\;-\;C(d,\varepsilon)\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\bigl|\nabla\sqrt{\rho(x)}\bigr|^2\,dx.$$

Question: Does there exist a finite constant $C(d)<\infty$ such that, for every orthonormal family $(u_j)_{j=1}^N$ in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$,
$$T[(u_j)]\;\ge\;K_{\rm cl}(d)\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\rho(x)^{1+2/d}\,dx\;-\;C(d)\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\bigl|\nabla\sqrt{\rho(x)}\bigr|^2\,dx\,?$$
That is, can the prefactor $(1-\varepsilon)$ in front of the semiclassical term be replaced by $1$ while keeping a finite constant in front of the gradient correction term?
status_search_result: The improved orthonormal Lieb–Thirring inequality with semiclassical constant $(1-\varepsilon)K_{\rm cl}(d)$ and a gradient correction term is established in the literature (Nam, J. Funct. Anal. 2018; with simplified proofs in subsequent works such as the 2023 "simple approach" paper). Whether one can take $\varepsilon=0$ while keeping a finite gradient-term constant is consistently described as an open question; recent surveys on the state of the Lieb–Thirring inequalities (2022–2023) still list this as an open problem, with no published resolution found.

paper_title: The Lieb-Thirring inequalities: recent results and open problems
original_question: In dimension d=1, determine the optimal constant L_{γ,1} for the remaining unresolved range 1/2 < γ < 3/2. Equivalently, decide whether Conjecture 12 is true there, namely whether L_{γ,1} equals the one-particle constant L^(1)_{γ,1} throughout that interval.
self_contained_problem:
For γ ≥ 0 and d ≥ 1, the Lieb–Thirring inequality asserts that there exists a finite constant L_{γ,d} such that, for every real-valued potential V on R^d with V_- = max(-V,0) ∈ L^{γ+d/2}(R^d), the negative eigenvalues λ_1(V) ≤ λ_2(V) ≤ … < 0 of the Schrödinger operator -Δ + V on L^2(R^d) satisfy

  ∑_j |λ_j(V)|^γ ≤ L_{γ,d} ∫_{R^d} V_-(x)^{γ+d/2} dx.

Let L_{γ,d} denote the smallest such constant (the optimal/sharp Lieb–Thirring constant). Define the one-particle constant L^{(1)}_{γ,d} as the value of the analogous ratio when V is restricted to potentials producing exactly one negative eigenvalue; explicitly,

  L^{(1)}_{γ,d} = sup_V |λ_1(V)|^γ / ∫_{R^d} V_-^{γ+d/2} dx,

with the supremum taken over nontrivial V for which -Δ + V has at least one negative eigenvalue. In dimension d = 1 it is known that L_{γ,1} = L^{(1)}_{γ,1} for γ = 1/2 and for all γ ≥ 3/2.

Problem. Determine the optimal constant L_{γ,1} for every γ in the open interval (1/2, 3/2). Equivalently, decide whether

  L_{γ,1} = L^{(1)}_{γ,1}    for all γ ∈ (1/2, 3/2).
status_search_result: The one-dimensional sharp Lieb–Thirring constant for γ ∈ (1/2, 3/2) remains an open problem. The endpoints γ = 1/2 (Hundertmark–Lieb–Thomas) and γ ≥ 3/2 (Lieb–Thirring; with d=1, γ=3/2 going back to Gardner–Greene–Kruskal–Miura giving L_{3/2,1}=3/16) are settled, but no proof or disproof of the conjectured equality L_{γ,1} = L^{(1)}_{γ,1} on the open interval has been published as of recent surveys (2022).

paper_title: The Lieb-Thirring inequalities: recent results and open problems
original_question: For d≥3 and γ=0, determine the optimal constant L_{0,d} in the Cwikel-Lieb-Rozenblum inequality N_≤(-Δ+V) ≤ L_{0,d} ∫_{R^d} V_-(x)^(d/2) dx. In particular, decide whether Conjecture 16 is correct, namely whether L_{0,d} = L_{0,d}^{cl} sup_{L∈N_0} a_L, where a_L = ((L+d-1)! (L+d/2) / L!) / (((L+(d-2)/2)(L+d/2))^(d/2)).
self_contained_problem:
Let $d\geq 3$. For a real-valued potential $V$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $V_-:=\max(-V,0)\in L^{d/2}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, consider the Schrödinger operator $-\Delta+V$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, and let $N_{\le 0}(-\Delta+V)$ denote the number of its non-positive eigenvalues (counted with multiplicity). The Cwikel–Lieb–Rozenblum inequality asserts the existence of a finite constant $L_{0,d}$ such that
$$N_{\le 0}(-\Delta+V)\;\le\; L_{0,d}\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} V_-(x)^{d/2}\,dx$$
for every such $V$. Define the sharp (smallest admissible) constant $L_{0,d}$ as the supremum of the left-hand side divided by the right-hand side over all admissible $V\not\equiv 0$.

Let
$$L_{0,d}^{\mathrm{cl}} \;=\; \frac{1}{(4\pi)^{d/2}\,\Gamma(d/2+1)}$$
denote the semiclassical constant, and for $L\in\mathbb{N}_0=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ define
$$a_L \;=\; \frac{\dfrac{(L+d-1)!}{L!}\bigl(L+\tfrac{d}{2}\bigr)}{\bigl((L+\tfrac{d-2}{2})(L+\tfrac{d}{2})\bigr)^{d/2}}.$$

Determine the value of $L_{0,d}$. In particular, decide whether
$$L_{0,d} \;=\; L_{0,d}^{\mathrm{cl}}\,\sup_{L\in\mathbb{N}_0} a_L.$$
status_search_result: The sharp value of the CLR constant $L_{0,d}$ in dimensions $d\ge 3$ remains open. Recent work (Hundertmark–Kunstmann–Ried–Vugalter, Invent. Math. 2022; Frank–Hundertmark–Jex–Nam and follow-ups, 2024) has improved the best known upper bounds and explicitly solved a variational problem associated with the CLR-type bounds, but the conjectured identification with $L_{0,d}^{\mathrm{cl}}\sup_L a_L$ has not been established.

paper_title: The Lieb-Thirring inequalities: recent results and open problems
original_question: For magnetic Schrödinger operators, determine whether the optimal magnetic Lieb-Thirring constant L^mag_{γ,d} in sum_n |E_n((−i∇+A)^2+V)|^γ ≤ L^mag_{γ,d} ∫_{R^d} V_-(x)^(γ+d/2) dx always coincides with the non-magnetic optimal constant L_{γ,d}.
self_contained_problem:
Let $d\geq 1$ and $\gamma\geq 0$. For a magnetic vector potential $A:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$ (sufficiently regular) and a real-valued potential $V:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ with $V_-:=\max(-V,0)\in L^{\gamma+d/2}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, consider the magnetic Schrödinger operator
$$H_{A,V}=(-i\nabla+A)^2+V$$
acting in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, and let $\{E_n(H_{A,V})\}$ denote its negative eigenvalues (counted with multiplicity).

Define the optimal magnetic Lieb–Thirring constant $L^{\mathrm{mag}}_{\gamma,d}$ as the smallest constant such that
$$\sum_n |E_n(H_{A,V})|^{\gamma} \;\leq\; L^{\mathrm{mag}}_{\gamma,d}\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} V_-(x)^{\gamma+d/2}\,dx$$
holds for all admissible $A$ and $V$. Define the optimal non-magnetic Lieb–Thirring constant $L_{\gamma,d}$ analogously, but only for $A\equiv 0$.

It is known that $L_{\gamma,d}\leq L^{\mathrm{mag}}_{\gamma,d}$. Determine, for each pair $(\gamma,d)$ with $\gamma\geq 0$ and $d\geq 1$ (within the regime where the inequality is meaningful, i.e., $\gamma\geq 1/2$ if $d=1$ and $\gamma>0$ if $d=2$, $\gamma\geq 0$ if $d\geq 3$), whether the equality
$$L^{\mathrm{mag}}_{\gamma,d}=L_{\gamma,d}$$
holds.
status_search_result: The question whether the optimal magnetic Lieb–Thirring constant equals the non-magnetic one appears to remain open. While all currently known explicit upper bounds for the non-magnetic constants extend without change to the magnetic case, no general proof of equality (nor a counterexample) is known.

paper_title: The Lieb-Thirring inequalities: recent results and open problems
original_question: In one dimension, for powers (−Δ)^s with s in (1/2, 3/2), decide whether in the critical case γ = 1 − 1/(2s) the optimal Lieb-Thirring constant equals the corresponding one-particle constant.
self_contained_problem:
Let $s\in(1/2,3/2)$ and consider the fractional Laplacian $(-\Delta)^s$ on $\mathbb{R}$. For a real-valued potential $V$ on $\mathbb{R}$ (say $V_-\in L^{\gamma+1/(2s)}(\mathbb{R})$), let $\{\lambda_j(V)\}_{j\ge 1}$ denote the negative eigenvalues of the Schrödinger-type operator $(-\Delta)^s - V(x)$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$. The Lieb–Thirring inequality at exponent $\gamma\ge 0$ asserts that there is a finite constant $L_{\gamma,s,1}$ such that
$$\sum_j |\lambda_j(V)|^\gamma \;\le\; L_{\gamma,s,1}\,\int_{\mathbb{R}} V(x)_+^{\gamma+\frac{1}{2s}}\,dx,$$
and one writes $L_{\gamma,s,1}^{\mathrm{opt}}$ for the smallest such constant. Define the one-particle (Weyl-type single eigenvalue) constant
$$L^{(1)}_{\gamma,s,1} \;=\; \sup_{V\not\equiv 0}\;\frac{|\lambda_1(V)|^\gamma}{\int_{\mathbb{R}} V_+^{\gamma+\frac{1}{2s}}\,dx},$$
which by definition satisfies $L^{(1)}_{\gamma,s,1}\le L_{\gamma,s,1}^{\mathrm{opt}}$.

Consider the critical exponent $\gamma = 1 - \tfrac{1}{2s}$. Determine whether
$$L_{\gamma,s,1}^{\mathrm{opt}} \;=\; L^{(1)}_{\gamma,s,1}$$

paper_title: The Lieb-Thirring inequalities: recent results and open problems
original_question: Does the bound |E_1(−d^2/dx^2 + V)| + |E_2(−d^2/dx^2 + V)| ≤ L^(1)_{1,1} ∫_R V_-(x)^(3/2) dx hold for every real one-dimensional potential V? Equivalently, resolve the associated isoperimetric 'oval problem' for planar curves.
self_contained_problem:
Let $H = -\dfrac{d^2}{dx^2} + V(x)$ be the one-dimensional Schrödinger operator on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ with a real-valued potential $V$ such that $V_- := \max(-V,0) \in L^{3/2}(\mathbb{R})$. Denote by $E_1(H) \le E_2(H) \le \cdots < 0$ the negative eigenvalues of $H$ (counted with multiplicity), if any. Let
$$L^{(1)}_{1,1} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}} \cdot \frac{3}{4} \cdot \frac{2}{\pi}\cdot \pi = \frac{3}{16}$$
denote the conjectured sharp Lieb–Thirring constant for $\gamma=1$, $d=1$ (so that $L^{(1)}_{1,1}=3/16$, twice the semiclassical constant in $d=1$, $\gamma=1$).

Question: Does the inequality
$$|E_1(H)| + |E_2(H)| \;\le\; L^{(1)}_{1,1} \int_{\mathbb{R}} V_-(x)^{3/2}\,dx \;=\; \frac{3}{16}\int_{\mathbb{R}} V_-(x)^{3/2}\,dx$$
hold for every such potential $V$ (where $|E_2(H)|$ is set to $0$ if $H$ has fewer than two negative eigenvalues)?

Equivalently, establish the following isoperimetric "oval problem": for every smooth closed curve $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ of length $2\pi$, parametrized by arc length $s \in \mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, with (signed) curvature $\kappa(s)$, the lowest eigenvalue $\lambda_1(\Gamma)$ of the operator
$$-\frac{d^2}{ds^2} + \frac{\kappa(s)^2}{4}$$
on $L^2(\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z})$ satisfies $\lambda_1(\Gamma) \ge 1$, with equality for the round circle.

paper_title: The Lieb-Thirring inequalities: recent results and open problems
original_question: For Lieb-Thirring inequalities at positive density, determine the optimal constants L'_{γ,d}, and in particular decide whether they equal the semiclassical constants for γ≥3/2.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. For γ ≥ 0 and d ≥ 1, define the classical (semiclassical) constant
  L^cl_{γ,d} = (4π)^{-d/2} Γ(γ+1) / Γ(γ+1+d/2).

Positive-density Lieb–Thirring inequality. Consider the d-dimensional torus T^d_L = (R/LZ)^d (or, equivalently, the positive-density / periodic setting on R^d). Given a real-valued potential V on T^d_L sufficiently regular and decaying at infinity in the suitable sense, let H = -Δ - V act on L^2(T^d_L), and let {λ_j(H)}_j denote the negative eigenvalues of H below the essential spectrum (relative to the free Laplacian -Δ). It is known that there exists a smallest finite constant L'_{γ,d} > 0 such that the inequality
  Σ_j |λ_j(H)|^γ ≤ L'_{γ,d} ∫ V_+(x)^{γ+d/2} dx
holds for all admissible V, where V_+ = max(V,0). Equivalently, L'_{γ,d} is the sharp constant in the Lieb–Thirring inequality at positive density (the dual one-particle density form).

Problem.
(a) Determine the optimal (smallest possible) value of the constant L'_{γ,d} for every γ ≥ 0 and d ≥ 1.
(b) In particular, decide whether for every γ ≥ 3/2 and every d ≥ 1 one has the equality
  L'_{γ,d} = L^cl_{γ,d},
i.e. whether the sharp positive-density Lieb–Thirring constant equals the semiclassical constant in this range.
status_search_result: The sharp values of the positive-density Lieb–Thirring constants L'_{γ,d} remain unknown. Recent works (Frank–Lewin and others, including the periodic Lieb–Thirring paper of Frank–Gontier, and Nam's improved bound with semiclassical constant plus gradient error term, ~2018–2022) make progress with semiclassical-type lower bounds and error terms but do not determine L'_{γ,d} or settle whether they equal L^cl_{γ,d} for γ ≥ 3/2. The state-of-the-art survey (2022) still lists this as open.

paper_title: The Lieb-Thirring inequalities: recent results and open problems
original_question: Do analogous positive-density Lieb-Thirring inequalities exist for exponents γ<1, especially for γ=0 where the question is tied to bounds on spectral shift functions?
self_contained_problem:
Background. For $\gamma\ge 0$ and a real-valued potential $V$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, the classical Lieb–Thirring inequality asserts that the negative eigenvalues $\{-E_j(V)\}$ of the Schrödinger operator $-\Delta+V$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ satisfy
$$\sum_j E_j(V)^{\gamma}\;\le\; L_{\gamma,d}\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} V_-(x)^{\gamma+d/2}\,dx,$$
where $V_-=\max(-V,0)$, and the inequality holds for $\gamma\ge 1/2$ if $d=1$, $\gamma>0$ if $d=2$, and $\gamma\ge 0$ if $d\ge 3$.

Positive-density setting. Let $\Pi_F$ denote the spectral projector of $-\Delta$ onto the Fermi sea $\{-\Delta\le \mu\}$ at chemical potential $\mu>0$, and consider the perturbed operator $-\Delta+V$. The positive-density Lieb–Thirring inequality (proved for $\gamma\ge 1$) bounds a quantity of the form
$$\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[(-\Delta+V-\mu)_-^{\gamma} - (-\Delta-\mu)_-^{\gamma}\right]$$
by an integral involving an appropriate power of $V_-$ (with constants depending on $\gamma$, $d$, and $\mu$).

Problem. Determine whether analogous positive-density Lieb–Thirring inequalities hold in the regime $\gamma<1$. In particular:

(a) For $0<\gamma<1$, does there exist a constant $C=C(\gamma,d,\mu)$ such that
$$\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[(-\Delta+V-\mu)_-^{\gamma} - (-\Delta-\mu)_-^{\gamma}\right] \;\le\; C\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} V_-(x)^{\gamma+d/2}\,dx$$
(or an appropriate variant involving both $V_-$ and $V_+$) for all sufficiently regular $V$?

(b) For $\gamma=0$, formulate and prove the corresponding bound, which is equivalent (in suitable formulations) to an $L^p$-type bound on the spectral shift function $\xi(\lambda;-\Delta+V,-\Delta)$ at energy $\lambda=\mu>0$ in terms of $\|V_-\|_{L^{d/2}}^{d/2}$ (or a comparable norm of $V$).
status_search_result: The positive-density Lieb–Thirring inequality was established by Frank–Lewin–Lieb–Seiringer (Duke Math. J., 2013) for exponents $\gamma\ge 1$. The extension to $\gamma<1$, and in particular the case $\gamma=0$ tied to $L^p$-bounds on the spectral shift function, is highlighted as an open question in the survey on recent results and open problems concerning Lieb–Thirring inequalities, and no general resolution appears in the subsequent literature retrieved (only partial results in special situations such as $\kappa=0$ in $d\ge 3$).

original_question: For dimensions d≥2, decide whether there exist bounded complex potentials V in L^(γ+d/2)(R^d) for every γ>1/2 such that the non-selfadjoint operator −Δ+V has infinitely many eigenvalues in the lower half-plane accumulating at every point of [0,∞).

Let $d\ge 2$ and let $-\Delta$ denote the Laplacian on $\mathbb{R}^d$. For a (possibly complex-valued) potential $V\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)\cap L^{\gamma+d/2}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, consider the closed non-self-adjoint Schrödinger operator $H=-\Delta+V$ acting in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, defined on the domain of $-\Delta$. Its essential spectrum equals $[0,\infty)$, and its discrete spectrum consists of isolated eigenvalues of finite algebraic multiplicity in $\mathbb{C}\setminus[0,\infty)$.

Determine, for every $\gamma>1/2$, whether there exists a bounded complex-valued potential $V\in L^{\gamma+d/2}(\mathbb{R}^d)\cap L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)$ such that the operator $-\Delta+V$ has infinitely many eigenvalues in the open lower half-plane $\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\operatorname{Im} z<0\}$ which accumulate at every point of $[0,\infty)$.

paper_title: The Interiors of Uranus and Neptune: Current Understanding and Open Questions
original_question: How did Uranus and Neptune form as outer Solar System planets, including whether they formed near their present heliocentric distances or migrated and possibly switched positions, and what formation models can self-consistently reproduce each planet's hydrogen-helium envelope and heavy-element inventory?
self_contained_problem:
Develop and evaluate self-consistent formation models for the two outermost giant planets of the Solar System, Uranus (heliocentric distance ≈ 19.2 AU, mass ≈ 14.5 Earth masses) and Neptune (heliocentric distance ≈ 30.1 AU, mass ≈ 17.1 Earth masses), each of which is composed of a hydrogen–helium envelope (estimated mass between roughly 1 and 4 Earth masses) surrounding a heavy-element-dominated interior (estimated heavy-element mass between roughly 12 and 15 Earth masses). Specifically:

1. Determine whether these planets accreted in situ near their current heliocentric distances or formed at smaller heliocentric distances and subsequently migrated outward to their present orbits, including the possibility that the two planets switched their relative ordering during dynamical evolution.

2. Construct a planetary growth model that, within the lifetime of the protoplanetary gas disk (taken to be of order a few million years), simultaneously and self-consistently reproduces, for each of the two planets, both (a) the final total mass and (b) the observationally inferred ratio of hydrogen–helium envelope mass to heavy-element mass.

A satisfactory solution must couple solid (planetesimal and/or pebble) accretion, gas accretion, disk evolution, and orbital migration in a single self-consistent calculation that yields two planets with the masses, compositions, and orbital architectures of Uranus and Neptune.
status_search_result: The formation of Uranus and Neptune remains an actively debated open problem in planetary science. Recent reviews and modeling studies (e.g., Helled & Fortney 2020 and follow-up works through 2023–2025) continue to state that no formation model has yet self-consistently reproduced the masses, H/He envelope fractions, and heavy-element inventories of both ice giants, and the question of in situ formation versus migration (including position swapping) is unresolved.

paper_title: The Interiors of Uranus and Neptune: Current Understanding and Open Questions
original_question: What are the present compositions and internal structures of Uranus and Neptune: how are hydrogen-helium, water, rock or refractory material, methane, ammonia, and other heavy elements distributed with depth; are the interiors best described by distinct layers or by continuous composition gradients; and which density profiles can fit the planets' measured mass, radius, rotation, and gravity data?
self_contained_problem:
Model a giant planet as a self-gravitating, rotating fluid body in hydrostatic equilibrium, characterized by a spherically- or oblately-symmetric mass density profile ρ(r) (possibly with latitudinal dependence due to rotation) and a depth-dependent composition specifying the local mass fractions of hydrogen–helium, water, rock/refractory material, methane, ammonia, and other heavy elements. Given the following observational constraints for Uranus and (separately) Neptune:

  • total mass M,
  • mean radius R at the 1 bar pressure level,
  • rotation period (and hence angular velocity Ω),
  • the measured low-order even gravitational harmonics J₂ and J₄ (defined by the external gravitational potential expansion U(r,θ) = (GM/r)[1 − Σ_{n≥1} J_{2n}(R/r)^{2n} P_{2n}(cosθ)]),

and using a thermodynamically consistent equation of state P(ρ,T,X) for mixtures of the species above with a prescribed thermal profile (e.g.\ adiabatic in convective regions), determine:

(a) the radial distribution of each chemical component, i.e. the functions X_i(r) for i ∈ {H/He, H₂O, rock, CH₄, NH₃, other heavies};

(b) whether the interior is best represented by a small number of chemically distinct layers separated by sharp boundaries, or by smoothly varying composition gradients (and in the latter case, identify the gradient profiles);

(c) the full set, or a representative family, of density profiles ρ(r) (and associated composition profiles) that simultaneously reproduce the observed M, R, Ω, J₂, and J₄ to within their measurement uncertainties.

Describe and, where possible, quantify the non-uniqueness (degeneracy) of solutions consistent with these constraints.
status_search_result: The composition and internal structure of Uranus and Neptune remain open problems in planetary science. Available gravity, mass, radius, and rotation data are insufficient to uniquely determine interior density and composition profiles; recent modeling work continues to produce multiple, observationally indistinguishable layered and gradient-based structure models, and resolving the degeneracy is a stated motivation for future ice-giant missions.

paper_title: The Interiors of Uranus and Neptune: Current Understanding and Open Questions
original_question: Which parts of Uranus and Neptune are superadiabatic, meaning regions where a steeper-than-adiabatic temperature gradient is needed to drive convective motion, and how do condensable species such as methane, hydrogen sulfide, and water in the middle and deep atmospheres change the temperatures inferred for the deeper interiors?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a giant ice-planet model of Uranus and of Neptune, idealized as a spherically symmetric fluid body in hydrostatic equilibrium with pressure P(r), temperature T(r), density ρ(r), and a mixture of hydrogen, helium, and condensable volatiles (notably methane CH4, hydrogen sulfide H2S, and water H2O). Define the adiabatic temperature gradient ∇_ad = (∂ ln T/∂ ln P)_S and the actual gradient ∇ = d ln T/d ln P. A region is called superadiabatic if ∇ > ∇_ad; in such a region a steeper-than-adiabatic temperature gradient is required to maintain convective heat transport, typically because condensation of a heavy species across a cloud layer increases the mean molecular weight μ with depth and stabilizes the layer against ordinary convection (the Ledoux criterion ∇ > ∇_ad + (φ/δ) ∇_μ, where ∇_μ = d ln μ/d ln P, must be satisfied for convection).

(a) Determine, as a function of radius (or pressure), which layers of Uranus and which layers of Neptune are superadiabatic. In particular, identify all condensation levels of CH4, H2S, and H2O in the middle and deep atmospheres at which a positive jump in mean molecular weight forces ∇ > ∇_ad, and characterize the resulting stably stratified or double-diffusive (semiconvective) layers.

(b) Quantify how the presence of these superadiabatic condensation layers modifies the temperature profile T(r) inferred for the deep interior, relative to the standard fully-adiabatic interior model anchored at the 1-bar level. Specifically, give the increase ΔT_deep in deep-interior temperature as a function of the assumed deep abundances of CH4, H2S, and H2O and of the thicknesses of the corresponding superadiabatic layers, and discuss the consequences for the equation of state, the inferred bulk composition, and the thermal evolution (luminosity) of each planet.
status_search_result: The identification of superadiabatic regions in Uranus and Neptune and the quantitative effect of condensable species (CH4, H2S, H2O) on inferred deep-interior temperatures remains an active open problem in ice-giant interior modeling. Recent work (e.g., Markham & Stevenson, Friedson & Gonzales, Scheibe et al., Vazan & Helled) has explored stably stratified moist layers and superadiabatic gradients but has not produced a definitive layer-by-layer determination, and the topic is highlighted as open in upcoming Uranus-mission science motivations.

paper_title: The Interiors of Uranus and Neptune: Current Understanding and Open Questions
original_question: How are the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune generated: which electrically conducting materials and convective regions exist inside each planet, how much water or other material is required to create an ionic or super-ionic interior, and how can magnetic-field structure and variability constrain the planetary interiors?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a model ice-giant planet consisting of concentric layers of hydrogen, helium, water, ammonia, methane, and rock, in hydrostatic equilibrium under self-gravity, with an equation of state and conductivity profile σ(ρ,T,X) (depending on density ρ, temperature T, and composition X) appropriate to high-pressure mixtures of these constituents. Suppose the planet supports a magnetohydrodynamic dynamo governed by the standard Boussinesq (or anelastic) MHD equations

  ∂_t u + (u·∇)u = −(1/ρ)∇p + ν∇²u − 2Ω×u + (1/μ_0 ρ)(∇×B)×B + buoyancy,
  ∂_t B = ∇×(u×B) + (1/μ_0 σ)∇²B,
  ∇·B = 0,

in a rotating spherical shell, with convection driven by an internal heat flux. The observed surface magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune are strongly non-axisymmetric and non-dipolar, with substantial quadrupole and octupole contributions.

Determine, within this framework:

(a) Which interior regions (specified by radial extent and composition) must be simultaneously electrically conducting and convecting in order to sustain a dynamo producing surface magnetic fields with the observed multipole spectrum and morphology of Uranus and Neptune.

(b) The minimum mass fraction (and corresponding radial distribution) of H₂O required, given current high-pressure equations of state and ab initio conductivity data for ionic and super-ionic water, for the conducting layer to attain magnetic Reynolds numbers Rm = UL/(η) sufficient (Rm ≳ 50) to drive such a dynamo; and whether other candidate constituents (e.g. ionic ammonia, hydrogen–helium mixtures, or rocky/silicate phases at high P,T) can substitute for or supplement water in providing the required conductivity.

(c) What quantitative constraints on the interior density, composition, and convective structure can be inferred from improved measurements of the spatial structure and secular variability of the surface magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune.
status_search_result: The generation mechanism of the non-dipolar magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune, the precise composition and depth of the conducting convective layer, and the minimum required water content remain active open research problems. Thin-shell convective dynamo models (Stanley & Bloxham 2004, 2006) reproduce the observed multipolar morphology qualitatively, but the underlying interior composition is not uniquely determined; recent ab initio studies of super-ionic H₂O, NH₃, and H–C–N–O mixtures continue to refine but have not settled the question. New constraints await a dedicated Uranus or Neptune orbiter mission.

paper_title: The Interiors of Uranus and Neptune: Current Understanding and Open Questions
original_question: What causes Uranus's atmosphere to show only a few visible features while Neptune's atmosphere appears more active and complex with storms and vortices, and how much of that contrast is due to different internal heat fluxes, orbital properties, seasons, or axial tilts?
self_contained_problem:
Uranus and Neptune are similar in mass, radius, and bulk composition, yet observations show that Uranus's visible atmosphere displays very few discrete features, while Neptune's atmosphere exhibits pronounced activity, including storms and large-scale vortices. The two planets differ in several relevant respects: (i) their measured internal (intrinsic) heat fluxes differ by roughly an order of magnitude, with Uranus's intrinsic flux being consistent with zero and Neptune's being substantially positive; (ii) their orbital properties (heliocentric distance and orbital period) are not identical; (iii) their seasonal forcings differ; and (iv) their obliquities (axial tilts) differ dramatically, Uranus being tilted by about 98° versus Neptune's roughly 28°.

Provide a quantitative, physically consistent explanation of the observed contrast in atmospheric activity between Uranus and Neptune. In particular, determine and justify what fraction of this contrast can be attributed individually and jointly to: (a) the difference in internal heat flux, (b) the differences in orbital properties, (c) the differences in seasonal insolation patterns, and (d) the differences in axial tilt. The answer should identify the dominant mechanism (or combination of mechanisms) responsible for Uranus's quiescent appearance relative to Neptune's dynamic atmosphere.
status_search_result: The contrast in atmospheric activity between Uranus and Neptune remains an open problem in planetary science. Recent works (radiative-convective models, 3D cloud-resolving simulations from 2024, and thermal evolution studies) attribute much of the difference to Uranus's much lower internal heat flux, with axial tilt and seasonal forcing as additional contributors, but a fully quantitative attribution among these causes has not been established, and reconciling the perceived bulk similarity of the two planets with their very different intrinsic fluxes is described as a long-standing challenge.

paper_title: The Interiors of Uranus and Neptune: Current Understanding and Open Questions
original_question: How large is the family of interior density structures allowed by the current gravity fields of Uranus and Neptune, including the poorly sampled innermost 30 percent of each planet and the lack of useful sixth-degree gravitational-harmonic constraints?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a rotating, fluid, axially symmetric planet in hydrostatic equilibrium occupying the ball of radius R. Its interior mass distribution is described by a density field ρ(r, μ), where r ∈ [0, R] is the radial coordinate and μ = cos θ is the cosine of the colatitude. The exterior gravitational potential, evaluated outside the planet, admits the multipole expansion

U(r, μ) = (GM/r) [ 1 − Σ_{n≥1} (R/r)^{2n} J_{2n} P_{2n}(μ) ],

where P_{2n} are Legendre polynomials and J_{2n} are the (even) zonal gravitational harmonic coefficients defined by

J_{2n} = − (1/(M R^{2n})) ∫_planet ρ(r', μ') (r')^{2n} P_{2n}(μ') dV'.

Fix the planetary mass M, equatorial radius R, and uniform rotation rate Ω, and suppose ρ is required to be non-negative, monotonically non-increasing in r along each colatitude, and consistent with hydrostatic balance under self-gravity and centrifugal forcing for some barotropic equation of state.

Let J_2^obs and J_4^obs be specified with prescribed observational uncertainty intervals [J_2^obs ± σ_2] and [J_4^obs ± σ_4], while J_6 is treated as essentially unconstrained (its uncertainty interval covering the full physically plausible range). Assume in addition that the radial region 0 ≤ r ≤ 0.3 R contributes negligibly to J_2 and J_4 within their uncertainties, so that the density there is effectively unconstrained by J_2 and J_4.

Problem. Characterise the set

𝒮 = { ρ(r, μ) : ρ satisfies the structural and hydrostatic constraints above, and the J_{2n}[ρ] computed from ρ lie within the prescribed observational intervals for n = 1, 2, with no constraint imposed for n ≥ 3 },

and, in particular, quantify the size (e.g. the range of admissible inner-core masses, central densities, mean molecular-weight profiles, and bulk compositional gradients) of 𝒮 for the rotation rate, mass and radius parameters of Uranus and of Neptune. Equivalently, provide sharp bounds, or a complete parametric description, of all interior density profiles ρ(r, μ) compatible with the present-day measured gravitational harmonics of these two planets.
category_tag: inverse problems for planetary gravity fields
status_search_result: The degeneracy of interior-structure models for Uranus and Neptune given current gravity-field data is widely acknowledged as an open problem in planetary science. Recent reviews and modeling studies emphasize that many distinct density profiles fit the available J_2, J_4 within uncertainties, that the inner ~30% of each planet is essentially unconstrained, and that improved constraints (notably J_6 and higher harmonics, achievable only through future orbiter missions such as a proposed Uranus Probe/Orbiter) are required to reduce this degeneracy. No definitive characterisation of the admissible family has been established.

paper_title: The Interiors of Uranus and Neptune: Current Understanding and Open Questions
original_question: How can detailed atmospheric abundance measurements of giant and intermediate-mass exoplanets, combined with host-star properties and planetary mean densities, clarify the nature of gaseous-rich planets with masses and sizes comparable to Uranus and Neptune?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the class of gaseous-rich exoplanets whose masses and radii lie within the range spanned by Uranus and Neptune (roughly 14–17 Earth masses and 3.9–4.0 Earth radii, with bulk mean densities of order 1.3–1.6 g cm⁻³). For each such planet, suppose one can obtain: (i) detailed atmospheric abundance measurements (mixing ratios of H, He, C, N, O, S and selected heavier species, including metallicities relative to solar and key elemental ratios such as C/O and N/O), (ii) the elemental abundances and metallicity of the host star, and (iii) an accurate planetary mean density derived from independent mass and radius determinations.

Develop a quantitative framework that uses these three categories of observables jointly to constrain the interior structure and bulk composition of such intermediate-mass gaseous planets. Specifically, determine to what extent the combined dataset:

(a) distinguishes among competing interior models (e.g., differentiated rock/ice/H–He envelope models versus compositionally inhomogeneous or fully mixed models),
(b) constrains the bulk heavy-element mass fraction and the partitioning of heavy elements between atmosphere, envelope, and deep interior,
(c) tests whether the atmospheric metal enrichment relative to the host star follows a universal mass–metallicity relation analogous to that suggested for the Solar System giants, and
(d) clarifies the formation pathway (e.g., core accretion with planetesimal vs. pebble delivery, or gravitational instability) of planets in the Uranus/Neptune mass–radius regime.

Formulate the inverse problem precisely, identify the minimal set of observational precisions required for each input quantity to yield non-degenerate constraints on items (a)–(d), and characterize the residual degeneracies that cannot be broken by these data alone.
category_tag: exoplanet atmospheric composition and interior structure
status_search_result: The question is a broad open research direction in planetary science concerning how exoplanet atmospheric abundances, host-star data, and mean densities together constrain interiors of Uranus/Neptune-mass planets. As of 2026 it remains an active area: JWST atmospheric spectra of sub-Neptunes and ice-giant analogs are being analyzed, and no definitive framework yet links these observables uniquely to interior structure. The question is open.

Is the G_f-closure of all achievable effective tensors L* equal to the closure obtained using only multiple-rank laminate microstructures, for every positive integer n?

  (ii) $
abla\cdot J_i=0$ in the periodic sense;
  (iii) the constitutive law $J(x)=L(x)E(x)$ holds a.e.

The effective tensor $L^*$ is the constant tensor characterized by $\langle Jangle = L^*\langle Eangle$, where $\langle\cdotangle$ denotes the average over $\mathbb{T}^2$, taken over all admissible $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$. original_question: For three-dimensional isotropic composites made from two isotropic phases, are all effective conductivity functions sigma*(sigma) realizable by multiple-rank laminate microstructures? If the answer is yes, is it enough to use laminate constructions in which each lamination step is taken only along mutually orthogonal directions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider three-dimensional periodic (or stochastically homogeneous) two-phase composites built from two isotropic linear conductors with scalar conductivities σ₁, σ₂ > 0, occupying volume fractions f and 1−f. For such a composite, the effective (homogenized) conductivity tensor σ* is defined via the standard cell problem for the steady-state conductivity equation ∇·(σ(x)∇u) = 0, and the composite is called isotropic when σ* = σ*·I is a scalar multiple of the identity. Let G(σ₁, σ₂) denote the set ("G-closure") of all pairs (f, σ*) realizable as f ranges over [0,1] and over all microgeometries producing an isotropic effective tensor.

A rank-N laminate is constructed inductively: a rank-1 laminate is a simple layering of the two phases (or of previously constructed laminates) along a single unit direction n₁; a rank-k laminate is obtained by laminating a rank-(k−1) laminate together with one of the pure phases (or another laminate) along a direction n_k, with separation of length scales between successive lamination steps. The laminate is called orthogonal if all lamination directions n_1, …, n_N are mutually orthogonal (so at most three distinct directions are used in three dimensions).

Question: 
(a) Is every isotropic effective conductivity σ* attainable by a two-phase isotropic 3D composite—i.e., every point of G(σ₁, σ₂)—realizable as the effective conductivity of some finite-rank laminate microstructure built from the two phases?
(b) If yes, does it suffice to restrict to orthogonal laminate microstructures, in which all lamination directions are mutually orthogonal?
category_tag: Homogenization and G-closure of conductivity composites
status_search_result: No source was found establishing the full G-closure of 3D two-phase isotropic conductivity composites by (orthogonal) finite-rank laminates. While many extremal points of the G-closure are known to be attainable by multi-rank laminates (Milton, Lurie–Cherkaev, Tartar, etc.), the general realizability question and the sufficiency of mutually orthogonal lamination directions in three dimensions appear to remain unresolved in the literature.

original_question: For isotropic two-phase composites with complex effective permittivity, some known geometries place the effective permittivity on a particular bounding circular arc in the complex plane and can therefore attain maximal absorption in the quasistatic limit. Are there other microgeometries with isotropic effective permittivities whose effective responses also lie on that same arc?
self_contained_problem:
Consider isotropic two-phase composite materials in the quasistatic limit, in which two isotropic homogeneous phases with complex (frequency-dependent) permittivities $\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2 \in \mathbb{C}$ are mixed in prescribed volume fractions $f_1, f_2 \ge 0$ with $f_1+f_2=1$. For any such microgeometry, the effective permittivity $\varepsilon_*$ is a complex scalar (because of isotropy) and is known to lie in a lens-shaped region of the complex plane whose boundary consists of two circular arcs determined by $\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2$ and the volume fractions; one of these arcs is the locus on which the effective absorption $\mathrm{Im}\,\varepsilon_*$ is maximized over isotropic mixtures of the two phases at the prescribed volume fraction. It is known that certain explicit microgeometries (for instance, doubly coated sphere/cylinder assemblages and certain hierarchical laminate constructions) produce isotropic effective permittivities lying exactly on this maximal-absorption bounding arc.

Question: Are there microgeometries, other than these known ones, whose effective permittivities are isotropic and also lie on this same maximal-absorption bounding arc? Equivalently, characterize all isotropic two-phase microstructures whose complex effective permittivity attains a point on this arc.
category_tag: Bounds on effective properties of composites
status_search_result: Recent work (Kern–Miller–Milton, 2020; Deshmukh–Milton, 2025) confirms that the maximal-absorption circular arc is optimal and is attained by doubly coated cylinder assemblages and certain rank-hierarchical laminates. However, no characterization is given of all isotropic microgeometries whose effective permittivities lie on this arc, and the question of whether other essentially different microgeometries achieve the same arc appears to remain open.

context_brief: elastic G-closure with void or rigid phase
original_question: Take a composite formed by mixing an isotropic elastic phase with either a void phase or a rigid phase. Can one completely characterize the resulting G-closure, that is, the full set of effective elasticity tensors obtainable from all such microstructures?
self_contained_problem:
Consider two-phase composite materials in $\mathbb{R}^d$ ($d=2$ or $3$) made by mixing an isotropic linearly elastic phase, with given Lamé moduli (bulk modulus $\kappa>0$ and shear modulus $\mu>0$), with a second phase that is either void (zero stiffness) or rigid (infinite stiffness). For a given volume fraction $\theta\in(0,1)$ of the elastic phase, consider all possible periodic (or, equivalently, all measurable) microstructures and form the set of effective elasticity tensors $C^*$ obtained by homogenization, where $C^*$ is a positive (semi)definite, fully symmetric fourth-order tensor relating average strain to average stress. The G-closure $\mathcal{G}_\theta$ is defined as the closure (in the appropriate $H$-convergence topology) of the set of all such effective tensors realizable as some microstructure varies.

Problem: Provide a complete characterization of the G-closure $\mathcal{G}_\theta$ for the elastic+void mixture, and likewise for the elastic+rigid mixture. That is, give necessary and sufficient conditions on a fourth-order tensor $C^*$ for it to belong to $\mathcal{G}_\theta$, for every volume fraction $\theta\in(0,1)$.
status_search_result: The weak G-closure (sharp bounds on coexistent stress-strain pairs and on effective compliance/energy) is known: Allaire–Kohn (rigid+elastic) and Gibiansky–Cherkaev/Allaire (void+elastic) provided sharp energy bounds and identified extremal microstructures (near-optimal unimodes and pentamodes). However, the full G-closure—a complete characterization of all attainable effective elasticity tensors—remains unresolved in general, particularly in 3D.

context_brief: optimal auxetic objective for fixed c
original_question: Fix c>0. Among isotropic composites made from an elastic phase and void, which microstructures in two and/or three dimensions maximize the quantity mu* - c kappa*, or at least form a sequence of microstructures whose values of mu* - c kappa* converge to the supremum?
self_contained_problem:
Consider linearly elastic two-phase composites in dimension d ∈ {2,3} consisting of an isotropic elastic phase (with prescribed bulk modulus κ > 0 and shear modulus μ > 0) and a void phase (zero stiffness), assembled in arbitrary periodic or, more generally, homogenizable microgeometries with prescribed volume fractions allowed to vary. By homogenization, any such microstructure produces an effective stiffness tensor; restrict attention to those microstructures whose effective behavior is isotropic, characterized by an effective bulk modulus κ* ≥ 0 and an effective shear modulus μ* ≥ 0.

Fix a constant c > 0 and define the functional F(κ*, μ*) = μ* − c κ*. 

(a) Determine the supremum of F over all isotropic elastic-void composites in dimension d (for d = 2 and for d = 3), as a function of c, κ, and μ.

(b) Identify explicit isotropic microstructures attaining this supremum, or, failing attainment, exhibit a sequence of isotropic microstructures whose values of μ* − c κ* converge to the supremum.
status_search_result: The problem of identifying optimal isotropic elastic-void microstructures maximizing μ* − cκ* (a proxy for auxetic behavior with prescribed trade-off between shear and bulk effective moduli) is an active research topic. Numerical and computational studies of optimal auxetic isotropic microstructures with void exist (e.g., topology optimization, TPMS-based designs, homogenization-based recovery), but a rigorous mathematical characterization of optimal microstructures attaining the supremum of μ* − cκ* for arbitrary c > 0, in 2D and 3D, does not appear to be established in the literature. The problem is generally regarded as open.

original_question: When deformations are finite but still small enough that nonlinear geometric effects matter, can one derive bounds that relate the achievable compressive deformations and shear deformations of composites made from an elastic phase and void, rather than relying only on infinitesimal linearized moduli?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a two-phase composite occupying a reference region $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ consisting of an isotropic hyperelastic solid phase and a void (empty) phase. Subject the composite to macroscopically uniform finite (not necessarily infinitesimal) deformations characterized by an average deformation gradient $\bar F$, decomposed via the polar decomposition into stretches and rotations, and expressed through invariants such as a macroscopic compressive (volumetric) deformation $\bar J = \det \bar F$ and a macroscopic shear (deviatoric) deformation. Geometric nonlinearities (large rotations and stretches) are retained, so the response cannot be captured solely by linearized infinitesimal elastic moduli.

Problem: Derive rigorous, microstructure-independent bounds that correlate the simultaneously achievable macroscopic compressive deformations and macroscopic shear deformations of such elastic-and-void composites in the regime of finite (but moderate) deformations. Equivalently, characterize the admissible region in the plane of macroscopic compressive vs. shear deformation invariants, going beyond bounds formulated only on infinitesimal linearized effective moduli.
category_tag: bounds for composites in finite elasticity
status_search_result: A web search did not surface any rigorous bounds correlating finite-deformation compressive and shear responses of elastic-plus-void composites. Available results address related topics (bounds on linearized effective moduli, energy bounds for cavities, void growth around inclusions, shear-band dilation) but none establish the requested finite-deformation correlation bounds. The problem appears still open.

original_question: For isotropic composites made from two isotropic elastic phases, with one phase possibly rigid or void, can one derive bounds on the achievable effective bulk and shear modulus pairs (kappa*,mu*) that improve on the current best-known inequalities, and ultimately determine the optimal bounds exactly?
self_contained_problem:
Consider isotropic composite materials formed by mixing two isotropic linearly elastic phases in prescribed volume fractions f_1 and f_2 = 1 - f_1, where each phase i ∈ {1,2} has bulk modulus κ_i and shear modulus μ_i (with the limiting cases of one phase being rigid, μ_i = κ_i = ∞, or void, μ_i = κ_i = 0, allowed). For any such composite, the homogenized (effective) elasticity tensor is again isotropic and is characterized by an effective bulk modulus κ* and an effective shear modulus μ*. Define the attainable set

  G(f_1; κ_1, μ_1, κ_2, μ_2) = { (κ*, μ*) : (κ*, μ*) is realized by some isotropic two-phase composite with the given phase moduli and phase-1 volume fraction f_1 } ⊂ ℝ_{>0} × ℝ_{>0}.

The classical Hashin–Shtrikman–Walpole inequalities give two-sided bounds on κ* and μ* separately, and partial coupled bounds on the pair (κ*, μ*) are known.

Problem. Derive bounds on the set G(f_1; κ_1, μ_1, κ_2, μ_2) that strictly improve on the currently best-known inequalities relating κ* and μ* simultaneously, and ultimately determine the optimal (sharp, attainable) coupled bounds describing G exactly, including the cases in which one of the phases is rigid or void.
category_tag: Bounds on effective moduli of composites
status_search_result: While the separate Hashin–Shtrikman–Walpole bounds on κ* and μ* are classical and attainable in many regimes, the problem of finding optimal coupled bounds on the pair (κ*, μ*) for two-phase isotropic elastic composites remains open. Subsequent work (e.g., Cherkaev–Gibiansky, Milton, Allaire–Kohn, Liu) has produced partial improvements via translation/quasiconvexification methods and identified extremal microstructures attaining the bulk-modulus or shear-modulus bound separately, but a complete description of the optimal G-closure for two isotropic phases (especially with rigid or void inclusions) has not been established.

paper_title: An update on Weihrauch complexity, and some open questions
original_question: Is the operator b definable from the rest of the Weihrauch-degree structure, in the setting where ⊔ and ⊓ are known to be definable from ≤W, ∗ is definable from 1, ≤W, and ×, ⋄ is definable from 1, ≤W, and ⋆, and → is definable from ⋆ and ≤W?

paper_title: An update on Weihrauch complexity, and some open questions
context_brief: Overt choice on non-Fréchet-Urysohn coPolish spaces
original_question: For overt choice VC_X on non-Fréchet-Urysohn coPolish spaces X, can this principle be classified more precisely than the currently known bounds LPO ≤W VC_X ≤W (isEmpty : \A(N^N) → S)?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions.

A represented space is a pair (X, δ_X) where δ_X is a partial surjection from Baire space N^N onto X. A multivalued function f : ⊆ X ⇒ Y between represented spaces is Weihrauch reducible to g : ⊆ Z ⇒ W, written f ≤_W g, if there are computable functions H, K : ⊆ N^N → N^N such that whenever G is a realizer of g (i.e. G(z) is a name of some w ∈ g(δ_Z(z))), the map p ↦ H(p, G(K(p))) is a realizer of f.

A topological space X is Fréchet–Urysohn if for every A ⊆ X and every x in the closure of A, there is a sequence in A converging to x. A space is coPolish if it is the colimit of an increasing sequence of Polish subspaces with appropriate compatibility (equivalently, a quasi-Polish countably tight cb_0 space arising as a sequential colimit of Polish spaces); examples include the space of polynomials with the colimit topology of finite-dimensional subspaces.

For a represented space X, let A(X) denote the hyperspace of closed subsets represented by enumerations of basic open sets that intersect the set (the "overt" representation). The overt choice principle on X is the multivalued function
  VC_X : ⊆ A(X) ⇒ X,
sending a nonempty closed set A ∈ A(X) to any element of A.

The Weihrauch degree LPO is represented by the limited principle of omniscience
  LPO : N^N → {0,1}, p ↦ 1 if p = 0^ω, else 0.

The principle isEmpty : A(N^N) → S sends a closed subset of Baire space (given by its overt representation) to the Sierpiński-space value 1 if the set is empty and ⊥ otherwise.

It is known that for every non-Fréchet–Urysohn coPolish space X,
  LPO ≤_W VC_X ≤_W (isEmpty : A(N^N) → S).

Problem. Determine, for each non-Fréchet–Urysohn coPolish space X, the precise Weihrauch degree of VC_X. More precisely, give a classification (e.g. in terms of standard Weihrauch degrees or a topological invariant of X) that strictly improves upon the bounds LPO ≤_W VC_X ≤_W (isEmpty : A(N^N) → S).
status_search_result: The de Brecht–Pauly–Schröder work on overt choice (Computability, 2020) establishes the bounds LPO ≤_W VC_X ≤_W isEmpty for non-Fréchet–Urysohn coPolish X and shows VC_X ≡_W LPO on a minimal such space, but no general classification beyond these bounds is reported. No subsequent work resolving the general case was located, so the question appears still open.

paper_title: An update on Weihrauch complexity, and some open questions
original_question: What is the Weihrauch degree of the task that, given a Player I winning strategy in the Wadge game for a function, produces a point of discontinuity of that function? The source further notes that a computable winning strategy is known to imply the existence of a computable point of discontinuity, but it is open whether there is a uniform argument establishing this.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Work in the Baire space $\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}$ with its product topology. For a (partial) function $f:\subseteq \mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}\to\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}$, the Wadge game $G(f)$ is played as follows. In each round, Player I plays one natural number, extending an input sequence $x\in\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}$, while Player II plays either a natural number, extending an output sequence $y\in\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}$, or a "pass" symbol. After $\omega$ rounds, Player II wins if either Player I's sequence $x$ does not lie in $\operatorname{dom}(f)$, or Player II's sequence $y$ is infinite and equals $f(x)$; otherwise Player I wins. It is a classical fact that $f$ is continuous on its domain iff Player II has a winning strategy in $G(f)$, and (in the effective version) Player I has a winning strategy in $G(f)$ iff $f$ is discontinuous at some point of its domain.

Weihrauch reducibility. Given multi-valued partial functions $F,G$ on $\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}$, one says $F\le_{\mathrm W} G$ if there exist computable functionals $H,K$ such that for every $G$-realizer $g$, the map $x\mapsto K(x,g(H(x)))$ is a realizer of $F$. The induced equivalence classes are the Weihrauch degrees.

Problem. Determine the Weihrauch degree of the multi-valued problem
$$\mathsf{WadgeDisc}\;:\;\sigma \;\mapsto\; \{x\in\operatorname{dom}(f_\sigma) : f_\sigma \text{ is discontinuous at } x\},$$
where the input $\sigma$ is (a code of) a Player I winning strategy in the Wadge game for some function $f_\sigma$, and the output is any point at which $f_\sigma$ is discontinuous.

It is known that whenever such a winning strategy is computable, there exists a computable point of discontinuity for $f_\sigma$; the question asks whether this passage is uniformly Weihrauch-computable, and if so to identify its precise Weihrauch degree.
status_search_result: Searches turned up subsequent work on the discontinuity problem and on game characterizations of lower cones in the Weihrauch lattice (Brattka's "The Discontinuity Problem"; Nobrega–Pauly's game characterizations), but none of the located sources explicitly compute the Weihrauch degree of producing a point of discontinuity from a Player I winning strategy in the Wadge game. The question appears to remain open.

paper_title: An update on Weihrauch complexity, and some open questions
context_brief: False statements in extended Weihrauch degrees
original_question: What are examples of interesting extended Weihrauch degrees of false statements, and how do those degrees relate to the usual scaffold of standard Weihrauch degrees?
self_contained_problem:
Background. Weihrauch reducibility compares multi-valued functions on represented spaces: for partial multi-valued functions f, g :⊆ N^N ⇒ N^N, one writes f ≤_W g if there exist computable functions H, K :⊆ N^N → N^N such that, whenever p is a name for an instance of f, K(p) is a name for an instance of g, and whenever q is a name for a g-solution to that instance, H⟨p, q⟩ is a name for an f-solution. The induced equivalence classes are the (standard) Weihrauch degrees, and they form an extensively studied lattice used to calibrate the uniform computational content of mathematical theorems.

Bauer's extended Weihrauch degrees enlarge this structure by representing problems as relations (or predicates) on Baire space rather than as multi-valued functions; in this larger structure one can also assign a degree to "problems" that have no solutions at all, including formal counterparts of false mathematical statements. The standard Weihrauch degrees embed into the extended Weihrauch degrees in a natural way, and the extended structure contains additional degrees corresponding to such empty/false problems.

Problem. Exhibit explicit and mathematically natural examples of extended Weihrauch degrees that arise from false statements (i.e. problems with empty solution set, or that otherwise fail to be realized by any function), and determine how these degrees sit relative to the embedded scaffold of standard Weihrauch degrees: identify their position with respect to standard benchmark degrees (such as the degrees of LPO, LLPO, choice principles C_N, C_{N^N}, WKL, lim, etc.), describe their behaviour under the lattice and algebraic operations (join, meet, product, parallelization, composition), and characterize structural features that distinguish "false" extended Weihrauch degrees from those induced by genuine multi-valued functions.
status_search_result: No source found that resolves this question. Recent work (e.g., a 2025 preprint constructing a topos for extended Weihrauch degrees, and work on instance reducibility) further develops the framework of extended Weihrauch degrees but does not appear to give a classification or natural catalogue of degrees corresponding to false statements relative to the standard Weihrauch scaffold. The question therefore appears to remain open.

paper_title: On an Open Question in Recovering Sturm--Liouville-Type Operators with Delay
original_question: For each degenerate regime of the delayed Sturm-Liouville two-spectra inverse problem in which uniqueness fails, describe the corresponding classes of iso-bispectral potentials: distinct complex-valued L2(0,pi) potentials q satisfying q(x)=0 on (0,a) such that the boundary value problems L_0(a,q) and L_1(a,q) have one and the same pair of spectra.
self_contained_problem:
Let $a\in(0,\pi)$ be a fixed delay parameter, and let $q\in L_2(0,\pi;\mathbb{C})$ be a complex-valued potential satisfying $q(x)=0$ for $x\in(0,a)$. For $j\in\{0,1\}$, let $\mathcal{L}_j(a,q)$ denote the boundary value problem for the functional-differential equation
$$-y''(x)+q(x)\,y(x-a)=\lambda\, y(x),\qquad x\in(0,\pi),$$
(with the convention that $y(x-a)=0$ for $x<a$), under the boundary conditions
$$y'(0)-h\,y(0)=0,\qquad y^{(j)}(\pi)+(-1)^j H\,y(\pi)=0,$$
where $h,H\in\mathbb{C}$ are fixed parameters; denote by $\sigma_j(a,q)$ the spectrum of $\mathcal{L}_j(a,q)$.

Two potentials $q_1,q_2$ (each vanishing on $(0,a)$) are called iso-bispectral if 
$$\sigma_0(a,q_1)=\sigma_0(a,q_2)\quad\text{and}\quad \sigma_1(a,q_1)=\sigma_1(a,q_2).$$
It is known that for $a\in[\pi/2,\pi)$ the pair of spectra $\bigl(\sigma_0(a,q),\sigma_1(a,q)\bigr)$ uniquely determines $q$, while for $a\in(0,\pi/2)$ uniqueness fails: this is the degenerate regime, in which infinite families of distinct iso-bispectral potentials exist.

Problem: For every $a$ in the degenerate regime $(0,\pi/2)$, give a complete description of the class of iso-bispectral potentials, i.e., describe explicitly all complex-valued $q\in L_2(0,\pi)$ with $q|_{(0,a)}=0$ that share a given pair of spectra $\bigl(\sigma_0(a,q),\sigma_1(a,q)\bigr)$.
category_tag: Inverse spectral problems for delay Sturm–Liouville operators
status_search_result: Non-uniqueness in the degenerate regime $a\in(0,\pi/2)$ has been established by constructing infinite families of iso-bispectral potentials: the cases $a\in[2\pi/5,\pi/2)$ and $a\in[\pi/3,2\pi/5)$ were treated first, and the remaining nonlinear case $a\in(0,\pi/3)$ was settled in a 2021 follow-up (arXiv:2102.08149) by Buterin–Vasiliev, again by constructing iso-bispectral families. However, a complete classification (full description of all iso-bispectral potentials) for every degenerate $a$ does not appear to have been achieved; existing results provide explicit infinite families rather than an exhaustive characterization, so the problem of describing the classes is partially solved.

paper_title: On an Open Question in Recovering Sturm--Liouville-Type Operators with Delay
original_question: For Robin-type variants of the delayed Sturm-Liouville inverse spectral problem, where the boundary conditions y(0)=y^(j)(pi)=0 are replaced by y'(0)-h y(0)=y^(j)(pi)=0 with complex h, determine whether an iso-bispectral counterexample analogous to the one constructed for y(0)=y^(j)(pi)=0 can be built, or whether the two spectra continue to determine the potential q uniquely in the corresponding delay ranges.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Sturm–Liouville-type differential equation with constant delay
\[
-y''(x) + q(x)\,y(x-a) = \lambda\, y(x), \qquad x \in (0,\pi),
\]
where the delay parameter satisfies $a \in [\pi/3, \pi)$, the complex-valued potential $q \in L_2(0,\pi)$ is supported on $[a,\pi]$, and $q(x)=0$ for $x\in[0,a)$ (so that the term $q(x)y(x-a)$ is interpreted with $y$ extended appropriately on $(-a,0)$).

For $j\in\{0,1\}$ and a fixed complex number $h\in\mathbb{C}$, let $\sigma_j(q,h)$ denote the spectrum (counted with multiplicity) of the boundary value problem
\[
-y''(x) + q(x)\,y(x-a) = \lambda\, y(x), \qquad y'(0) - h\,y(0) = 0,\quad y^{(j)}(\pi) = 0.
\]
Thus $\sigma_0(q,h)$ corresponds to the boundary condition $y(\pi)=0$ and $\sigma_1(q,h)$ to $y'(\pi)=0$.

Inverse spectral problem. Given $h\in\mathbb{C}$ and the two spectra $\sigma_0(q,h)$ and $\sigma_1(q,h)$, is the potential $q$ uniquely determined?

Question. Decide which of the following holds for $a$ in the range $[\pi/3, 2\pi/5)$ (and, more generally, for the delay ranges in $[\pi/3,\pi)$ where non-uniqueness is known to fail or to hold in the Dirichlet case $y(0)=y^{(j)}(\pi)=0$):

(a) Construct an explicit pair of distinct potentials $q_1,q_2 \in L_2(0,\pi)$ (with the support assumption above) and a value $h\in\mathbb{C}$ such that
\[
\sigma_0(q_1,h) = \sigma_0(q_2,h) \quad\text{and}\quad \sigma_1(q_1,h) = \sigma_1(q_2,h),
\]
i.e., an iso-bispectral counterexample for the Robin-type boundary conditions; or

(b) Prove that, for every $h\in\mathbb{C}$ and every admissible $a$, the pair $(\sigma_0(q,h), \sigma_1(q,h))$ uniquely determines $q$.
category_tag: Inverse spectral problems for delay Sturm–Liouville operators
status_search_result: The Neumann subcase $h=0$ of the Robin-type boundary condition $y'(0)-hy(0)=0$ has been resolved in the negative: a counterexample (an infinite family of iso-bispectral potentials) was constructed for delay $a\in[\pi/3,2\pi/5)$, paralleling the earlier Dirichlet ($y(0)=0$) counterexample. The general Robin case with arbitrary complex $h$ does not appear to have been fully settled; the obstruction noted in the Robin setting (loss of the relation that determines an auxiliary constant from the kernel) means the Dirichlet-style construction does not directly transfer, and uniqueness/non-uniqueness for general $h\neq 0$ remains an outstanding question.

original_question: Assuming the hypergraphic planted clique detection conjecture for fixed integer d ≥ 2, which states that when κ grows strictly slower than N no sequence of polynomial-time tests can distinguish the null model G_d(N, 1/2) from the planted-clique model G_d(N, 1/2, κ) with vanishing total error, can stronger evidence for this conjectured hardness be established for additional algorithmic frameworks beyond the Metropolis and low-degree polynomial methods already analyzed, specifically for classes such as statistical query, sum-of-squares, belief propagation, and approximate message passing?
self_contained_problem:
Fix an integer $d \ge 2$. For a positive integer $N$, let $G_d(N, 1/2)$ denote the null model: a random $d$-uniform hypergraph on vertex set $[N]$ in which every $d$-subset of $[N]$ is included as a hyperedge independently with probability $1/2$. For an integer $\kappa = \kappa(N) \in \{1, \dots, N\}$, let $G_d(N, 1/2, \kappa)$ denote the planted-clique model: first sample a hypergraph as above, then choose a uniformly random subset $K \subseteq [N]$ of size $\kappa$ and add all $d$-subsets of $K$ as hyperedges (so $K$ becomes a $d$-uniform clique). Assume the following Hypergraphic Planted Clique (HPC) detection conjecture: if 
$$\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{\log\kappa}{\log N} \le 1-\tau\quad\text{for some }\tau>0,$$
then for every sequence of polynomial-time (in $N$) tests $\phi_N : \text{hypergraphs on }[N] \to \{0,1\}$, 
$$\liminf_{N\to\infty}\Big(\mathbb{P}_{H_0}(\phi_N(G)=1)+\mathbb{P}_{H_1}(\phi_N(G)=0)\Big) > \tfrac{1}{2},$$
where $H_0$ is $G_d(N,1/2)$ and $H_1$ is $G_d(N,1/2,\kappa)$.

Existing rigorous evidence for this conjecture covers Metropolis-type local algorithms and low-degree polynomial tests. Provide rigorous evidence (in the form of unconditional lower bounds against detection in the regime $\log\kappa/\log N \le 1-\tau$) for the HPC detection conjecture in additional algorithmic frameworks, specifically: 
(i) statistical query (SQ) algorithms,
(ii) sum-of-squares (SOS) semidefinite programming hierarchies,
(iii) belief propagation (BP),
(iv) approximate message passing (AMP).
status_search_result: A search shows substantial work on lower bounds for the standard (graph) planted clique problem in SOS, SQ, and related models (Barak et al., Feldman et al., Hopkins–Steurer, etc.), but evidence for the hypergraphic variant has so far been established only for Metropolis-type and low-degree polynomial algorithms (Luo–Zhang 2020). No published work was found establishing analogous SQ/SOS/BP/AMP lower bounds specifically for the hypergraphic planted clique detection problem, so the challenge appears to remain open.

original_question: Let f be a nonzero function in L1(R), and let Lambda be a nonempty discrete subset of R with bounded density, meaning that sup_x #(Lambda intersect [x, x+1)) < +infinity. Assume that f + Lambda tiles R at level zero. Must Lambda have a uniform density D(Lambda), in the sense that #(Lambda intersect [x, x+r)) = D(Lambda) * r + o(r) as r -> +infinity uniformly in x? Equivalently, if a nonempty bounded-density set Lambda has the Fourier transform of its point-mass measure delta_Lambda vanishing on some open interval, does that force Lambda to have a uniform density?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f \in L^1(\mathbb{R})$ be a nonzero function and let $\Lambda \subset \mathbb{R}$ be a nonempty discrete set of bounded density, that is,
$$\sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} \#\bigl(\Lambda \cap [x, x+1)\bigr) < +\infty.$$
We say that $f + \Lambda$ tiles $\mathbb{R}$ at level zero if
$$\sum_{\lambda \in \Lambda} f(t - \lambda) = 0 \quad \text{for almost every } t \in \mathbb{R},$$
where the series converges absolutely a.e.

The set $\Lambda$ is said to have uniform density $D(\Lambda)$ if there exists a real number $D(\Lambda)$ such that
$$\#\bigl(\Lambda \cap [x, x+r)\bigr) = D(\Lambda)\, r + o(r) \quad \text{as } r \to +\infty,$$
uniformly with respect to $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

Question: Suppose $f + \Lambda$ tiles $\mathbb{R}$ at level zero, with $f$ and $\Lambda$ as above. Must $\Lambda$ possess a uniform density $D(\Lambda)$?

Equivalently (in Fourier-analytic form): if $\Lambda \subset \mathbb{R}$ is nonempty and of bounded density, and the Fourier transform (in the distributional sense) of the measure $\delta_\Lambda = \sum_{\lambda \in \Lambda} \delta_\lambda$ vanishes on some nonempty open interval $(a, b) \subset \mathbb{R}$, does it follow that $\Lambda$ has a uniform density?
category_tag: tilings by translates and Fourier analysis
status_search_result: The problem is presented as an open question in a 2020 survey on tilings of the real line by translates of a function. No subsequent published resolution was found in the search; the question of whether bounded-density level-zero tiling sets must be uniformly distributed (equivalently, whether bounded-density sets whose Fourier transform vanishes on some open interval must have uniform density) appears to remain open.

original_question: Does there exist a measurable set Omega subset R with 0 < mes(Omega) < +infinity such that its indicator function 1_Omega tiles R by translations over a set Lambda subset R that does not have periodic structure, either at level one or, more weakly, at some other integer level w? Here, not having periodic structure means that Lambda cannot be written as a disjoint union of finitely many arithmetic progressions a_j Z + b_j with a_j > 0.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{R}$ be the real line equipped with Lebesgue measure $\operatorname{mes}$. For a measurable set $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}$ with $0<\operatorname{mes}(\Omega)<+\infty$, let $\mathbf{1}_\Omega$ denote its indicator function. Given a discrete set $\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}$ and a positive integer $w$, we say that $\mathbf{1}_\Omega$ tiles $\mathbb{R}$ by translations along $\Lambda$ at level $w$ if
$$\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\mathbf{1}_\Omega(x-\lambda)=w\qquad\text{for almost every }x\in\mathbb{R}.$$
The case $w=1$ corresponds to a partition (modulo measure zero) of $\mathbb{R}$ into translates of $\Omega$.

Say that a set $\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}$ has periodic structure if it can be written as a disjoint union
$$\Lambda=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^{N}\bigl(a_j\mathbb{Z}+b_j\bigr)$$
of finitely many arithmetic progressions, where $a_j>0$ and $b_j\in\mathbb{R}$. Otherwise, $\Lambda$ is said to lack periodic structure.

Question: Does there exist a measurable set $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}$ with $0<\operatorname{mes}(\Omega)<+\infty$, a positive integer $w$, and a translation set $\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}$ lacking periodic structure such that $\mathbf{1}_\Omega$ tiles $\mathbb{R}$ along $\Lambda$ at level $w$? In particular, can this be achieved at level $w=1$?
category_tag: translational tilings of the real line
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in a survey on tilings by translates of a function. Subsequent work (e.g., on periodicity of low-complexity tilings, and counterexamples to the periodic tiling conjecture in higher dimensions by Greenfeld–Tao) has not, to current knowledge, resolved this one-dimensional question for indicator functions of finite-measure sets, which would necessarily be unbounded. No paper found claims a construction or a proof of impossibility on $\mathbb{R}$ at any integer level $w$.

original_question: Let d > 1 and let f be an integrable function on R^d. Suppose f tiles R^d at some level w with a translation set Lambda subset R^d of bounded density, meaning that there exists M > 0 such that #(Lambda intersect (x + B)) <= M for every x in R^d, where B is the open unit ball in R^d. Must there exist a lattice L subset R^d such that f + L is also a tiling, possibly at a different level w'?
self_contained_problem:
Let $d>1$ be an integer. A discrete set $\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ is said to have bounded density if there exists $M>0$ such that $\#(\Lambda\cap(x+B))\le M$ for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$, where $B$ denotes the open unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Given $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and a real number $w$, we say that $f$ tiles $\mathbb{R}^d$ at level $w$ with translation set $\Lambda$ if $\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda} f(x-\lambda)=w$ for almost every $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ (the series converging absolutely a.e.). For a lattice $L\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ (i.e., a discrete subgroup of $\mathbb{R}^d$ of full rank), we write $f+L$ for the tiling by the translates of $f$ along $L$.

Question: Suppose that $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)$ tiles $\mathbb{R}^d$ at some level $w$ with a translation set $\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ of bounded density. Must there exist a lattice $L\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ and a real number $w'$ such that $f$ tiles $\mathbb{R}^d$ at level $w'$ with translation set $L$ (i.e., $f+L$ is a tiling)?
