original_question: For the EKG sequence defined by a_1=1, a_2=2, and for n≥3 taking a_n to be the smallest unused positive integer with gcd(a_n,a_{n-1})≥2, determine the asymptotic structure of the associated 4-regular graphs. In particular, decide whether the observed cone/parabola-type geometry persists for large N and explain why the second eigenvalue stays suspiciously close to 4.
self_contained_problem:
Define the EKG sequence $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ by $a_1 = 1$, $a_2 = 2$, and for every $n \ge 3$, $a_n$ is the smallest positive integer not already appearing among $a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}$ such that $\gcd(a_n, a_{n-1}) \ge 2$. (It is known that this sequence is a permutation of the positive integers.)

For each integer $N \ge 1$, construct a graph $G_N$ as follows. The vertex set is $\{1, 2, \dots, N\}$. Draw an edge between distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ whenever
$$\gcd(a_i, a_j) \ge 2 \quad\text{and}\quad |i - j| \le 2,$$
or, more generally, define $G_N$ to be the natural $4$-regular graph (away from boundary vertices) associated with the EKG sequence in which each vertex $i$ is connected to the indices of the two nearest preceding and two nearest following terms sharing a nontrivial common factor with $a_i$. Embed $G_N$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ using a standard spectral embedding via the eigenvectors corresponding to the smallest nonzero eigenvalues of its (combinatorial) Laplacian.

Let $\lambda_1(G_N) = 4 \ge \lambda_2(G_N) \ge \cdots$ denote the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix of $G_N$.

(a) Determine the limiting geometric structure of the spectral embedding of $G_N$ as $N \to \infty$. In particular, prove or disprove that the embedded vertices asymptotically concentrate on a cone or paraboloid-type surface.

(b) Determine $\lim_{N\to\infty} \lambda_2(G_N)$, and explain rigorously why $\lambda_2(G_N)$ remains extremely close to $4$ for all large $N$ (i.e., bound the spectral gap $4 - \lambda_2(G_N)$ asymptotically).

original_question: For the Recamán sequence defined by a_0=0 and a_n=a_{n-1}-n when that value is positive and has not appeared earlier, and a_n=a_{n-1}+n otherwise, remove repeated values and form the associated 4-regular graphs of initial segments. Give a precise explanation of the extraordinary graph structure that appears after duplicates are removed.
self_contained_problem:
Define the Recamán sequence $(a_n)_{n\ge 0}$ by $a_0 = 0$ and, for $n \ge 1$,
\[ a_n = \begin{cases} a_{n-1} - n & \text{if } a_{n-1} - n > 0 \text{ and } a_{n-1}-n \notin \{a_0,a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}\}, \\ a_{n-1} + n & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]
For each $N \ge 1$, let $S_N$ be the multiset $\{a_0,a_1,\dots,a_N\}$ and let $T_N \subseteq S_N$ be the set obtained by deleting every element of $S_N$ that occurs more than once (i.e., keeping only those values that appear exactly once in the segment). Re-index the retained values in their original order of appearance as $b_0,b_1,\dots,b_{M(N)}$, and form the 4-regular circulant-like graph $G_N$ on vertex set $\{0,1,\dots,M(N)\}$ in which each index $i$ is joined to $i\pm 1$ and $i\pm 2$ (mod $M(N)+1$), with the vertex $i$ embedded in the plane at the point $(i, b_i)$.

Give a precise mathematical description of the large-scale structure exhibited by the family of graphs $\{G_N\}_{N\to\infty}$ (for instance, asymptotic density of retained terms, the distribution of gaps $b_{i+1}-b_i$, recurring geometric patterns of the planar embedding, or any provable self-similarity), formulated as a rigorous statement and proof.
status_search_result: The Recamán sequence (OEIS A005132) is well known and has many empirical observations, but no rigorous theorem characterizing the "extraordinary structure" of graphs obtained from initial segments after removing duplicate values appears in the literature. Even basic conjectures about A005132 (e.g., whether every nonnegative integer eventually appears) remain open, so the more refined structural question is also open.

original_question: For Leroy Quet's sequence defined by a_1=1, a_2=2, and for n≥3 choosing a_n as the smallest unused positive integer such that gcd(a_n,a_{n-1}) differs from gcd(a_{n-1},a_{n-2}), explain why the associated 4-regular graph has the observed nontrivial structure and decide whether that structural behavior continues for arbitrarily large initial segments.
self_contained_problem:
Define a sequence $(a_n)_{n\geq 1}$ of positive integers as follows. Set $a_1=1$ and $a_2=2$. For each $n\geq 3$, let $a_n$ be the smallest positive integer that has not yet appeared among $a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}$ and that satisfies
$$\gcd(a_n,a_{n-1}) \neq \gcd(a_{n-1},a_{n-2}).$$
For each integer $N\geq 1$, build a 4-regular graph $G_N$ on the vertex set $\{a_1,a_2,\dots,a_N\}$ by joining each term to its two immediate predecessors and two immediate successors in the sequence (so vertex $a_n$ is adjacent to $a_{n-2}, a_{n-1}, a_{n+1}, a_{n+2}$ when these exist).

original_question: For the Gray-encoding permutation A006068 obtained by ordering nonnegative integers so that their binary-derivative strings are in lexicographic order, explain rigorously why the associated 4-regular graphs have the striking structure shown in the paper.
self_contained_problem:
For a nonnegative integer $n$ with binary expansion $n = \sum_{i\ge 0} b_i 2^i$ (with $b_i \in \{0,1\}$ and only finitely many nonzero), define its binary derivative to be the infinite string $d(n) = (c_0, c_1, c_2, \ldots)$ where $c_i = b_i \oplus b_{i+1}$ (XOR). Order the nonnegative integers $n_0, n_1, n_2, \ldots$ so that the sequence of strings $d(n_0), d(n_1), d(n_2), \ldots$ is in lexicographic order; the resulting permutation $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, $a(k) = n_k$, agrees with the OEIS sequence A006068 (the inverse Gray code).

Now form the following family of 4-regular graphs $G_N$ for each integer $N \ge 5$: take vertex set $V_N = \{0, 1, \ldots, N-1\}$ and, for each index $k$, connect $k$ to its two nearest neighbors on each side in the sequence $a$, i.e. join $k$ to $k\pm 1$ and $k\pm 2$ modulo $N$ in the ordering induced by $a$ (equivalently, take the 4-regular circulant-like graph defined by the consecutive 4-window structure of the sequence $(a(0), a(1), \ldots, a(N-1))$ when this list is reinterpreted as vertices via $a$).

Prove rigorously that the graphs $G_N$ exhibit the highly structured (non-random) macroscopic geometric pattern empirically observed when they are drawn with a force-directed (spring) layout: namely, identify and prove the precise combinatorial / geometric structure (e.g., number and shape of large-scale "lobes" or self-similar nested clusters, automorphism group, and growth rate of graph-theoretic diameter and bandwidth) of $G_N$ as $N \to \infty$.

original_question: Let A053392 map a decimal integer to the decimal concatenation of the sums of each pair of consecutive digits, and then remove duplicates to obtain A347520. Explain why the associated 4-regular graphs of this de-duplicated digit-concatenation sequence are so striking and highly regular.
self_contained_problem:
Define a map f on positive integers as follows: write n in base 10 as a string of digits d_1 d_2 … d_k (with k ≥ 2), form the sequence of pairwise sums s_i = d_i + d_{i+1} for i = 1, …, k−1, and let f(n) be the integer whose decimal representation is the concatenation of the decimal representations of s_1, s_2, …, s_{k−1} (so each s_i contributes one or two decimal digits). For example, f(9327) = concat(9+3, 3+2, 2+7) = concat(12, 5, 9) = 1259. For 1 ≤ n ≤ 9 (single-digit n), set f(n) = 0.

original_question: Characterize which sequences produce the paper's 'spiral' type of associated 4-regular graph. In particular, make precise the heuristic that spiral graphs arise from consecutive blocks of increasing subsequences, and determine how far the model a(n,k)=exp(k(f(n)-f(k))) captures the full phenomenon after reading the triangular array by rows and removing duplicates.
self_contained_problem:
Construction. Given a finite list of n distinct real numbers x_1, x_2, ..., x_n (an "ordered sequence"), associate to it a 4-regular graph G = (V, E) on n vertices labeled 1, ..., n as follows: connect vertex i (for 2 ≤ i ≤ n−1) to its two left neighbors and two right neighbors in the list when ranked by value, in the natural cyclic manner used to build the so-called "horizontal/vertical-visibility-style" 4-regular graph; equivalently, for each index i let p(i) and q(i) be the indices of the largest j < i with x_j < x_i and with x_j > x_i (respectively), and let r(i), s(i) be the analogous indices on the right side, and connect i to {p(i), q(i), r(i), s(i)} (with boundary conventions making the graph 4-regular).

Empirically, certain input sequences produce drawings of G that look like a "spiral": a long curve that winds around itself in a regular pattern. One source of such examples comes from triangular arrays: given a function a(n,k) defined for 1 ≤ k ≤ n, list the values a(1,1), a(2,1), a(2,2), a(3,1), a(3,2), a(3,3), ... by rows, then delete duplicates while preserving order, and feed the resulting sequence into the construction. In particular, the model a(n,k) = exp(k (f(n) − f(k))) for various functions f produces spiral graphs.

Problem. 
(a) Give a precise characterization of which input sequences (x_1, ..., x_n) give rise to a spiral 4-regular graph under this construction.
(b) In particular, formalize and prove (or refute) the heuristic that spiral graphs arise exactly from sequences that decompose into consecutive blocks of increasing subsequences (specifying the block-length growth required).
(c) Determine the full class of triangular arrays a(n,k) whose row-by-row, duplicate-removed reading produces a spiral graph, and decide to what extent this class is captured by the family a(n,k) = exp(k (f(n) − f(k))) as f ranges over a natural class of functions.
status_search_result: The construction and the spiral phenomenon are introduced in a problem list on graphs from sequences, where the authors explicitly state they do not have a clear characterization and that the full extent of the phenomenon is not currently understood. No subsequent work resolving the characterization was found.

original_question: Do optimal polynomial approximants have further applications in signal processing research?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a Hilbert space of analytic functions on the unit disk $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ in which the monomials $\{z^n\}_{n\ge 0}$ form an orthogonal basis (for example, the Hardy space $H^2$, the Bergman space $A^2$, or a weighted Dirichlet-type space $D_\alpha$ with norm $\|\sum a_n z^n\|_\alpha^2 = \sum_{n\ge 0}(n+1)^\alpha |a_n|^2$). For a function $f\in\mathcal{H}$ that does not vanish identically and a nonnegative integer $n$, the optimal polynomial approximant (opa) of degree $n$ to $1/f$ in $\mathcal{H}$ is the unique polynomial $p_n$ of degree at most $n$ that minimizes
$$\|p f - 1\|_{\mathcal{H}}$$
over all polynomials $p$ of degree at most $n$. These polynomials and their reversed versions arise in connection with cyclicity in $\mathcal{H}$ and, classically, with the design of finite impulse response (FIR) and infinite impulse response (IIR) filters via least-squares inverse polynomial methods.

Problem. Identify and rigorously formulate one or more new applications of optimal polynomial approximants in signal processing — for example, in the design, analysis, or stability of FIR/IIR filters, in deconvolution, prediction, or spectral factorization problems — beyond the classical least-squares inverse FIR design of the 1970s. Specifically, exhibit a signal-processing problem (with a precise model and objective functional) whose solution is given by, or quantitatively controlled by, optimal polynomial approximants in some space $\mathcal{H}$ as above, and prove the corresponding optimality, convergence, or error-bound statement.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open-ended invitation to find further applications of optimal polynomial approximants (opas) in signal processing. A brief search shows continuing mathematical work on opas (cyclicity, zeros, Jacobi matrices) but no widely recognized new signal-processing application beyond the classical least-squares inverse FIR/IIR filter design literature, so the question remains an open research direction.

original_question: Given a function f in a weighted Hardy space H^2_omega such that its polynomial multiples are dense in the space, and given zeta in the unit circle T, is there a sector with vertex at zeta that is devoid of zeros of the optimal polynomial approximants to 1/f? More generally, are there regions or rays that the zeros avoid?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\omega = (\omega_k)_{k\geq 0}$ be a sequence of positive weights, and let $H^2_\omega$ denote the weighted Hardy space of analytic functions $f(z) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty a_k z^k$ on the open unit disk $\mathbb{D}$ with norm $\|f\|_\omega^2 = \sum_{k=0}^\infty |a_k|^2 \omega_k < \infty$. A function $f \in H^2_\omega$ is called cyclic if the set of polynomial multiples $\{p f : p \text{ polynomial}\}$ is dense in $H^2_\omega$. For a non-identically-zero $f \in H^2_\omega$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the $n$-th optimal polynomial approximant of $1/f$ is the polynomial $q_n$ of degree at most $n$ that minimizes $\|p f - 1\|_\omega$ over all polynomials $p$ of degree at most $n$.

Question: Given a cyclic function $f \in H^2_\omega$ and a point $\zeta \in \mathbb{T} = \partial\mathbb{D}$, does there exist an open sector with vertex at $\zeta$ that contains no zeros of any of the optimal polynomial approximants $q_n$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$? More generally, characterize the regions or rays in the complex plane that are avoided by the zeros of the sequence $(q_n)_{n\geq 0}$.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in a 2021 survey on optimal polynomial approximants. Subsequent work (e.g., results on equidistribution of zeros on the unit circle for certain cyclic polynomial generators, and electrostatic/OPUC-based analyses from 2022–2025) has produced partial results in special cases but no general resolution of the sector/zero-avoidance problem for arbitrary cyclic functions in weighted Hardy spaces has been reported. The problem appears to remain open in full generality.

original_question: Let f(z_1, z_2) be a polynomial that does not vanish in the bidisk D^2. Is the optimal polynomial approximant of 1/f in H^2(D^2) zero-free in D^2?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ denote the open unit disk and $\mathbb{D}^2 = \mathbb{D} \times \mathbb{D}$ the open bidisk. Let $H^2(\mathbb{D}^2)$ be the Hardy space of holomorphic functions $g(z_1,z_2) = \sum_{j,k \geq 0} a_{j,k} z_1^j z_2^k$ on $\mathbb{D}^2$ with $\|g\|^2 := \sum_{j,k \geq 0} |a_{j,k}|^2 < \infty$. For a polynomial $f \in \mathbb{C}[z_1,z_2]$ with $f(0,0)\neq 0$ and a nonnegative integer $n$, the optimal polynomial approximant of $1/f$ of degree $n$ in $H^2(\mathbb{D}^2)$ is the unique polynomial $p_n$ of degree at most $n$ (in each variable, or in total degree, fixed once and for all) that minimizes $\|1 - p f\|_{H^2(\mathbb{D}^2)}$ over all such polynomials $p$.

Question: Suppose $f(z_1,z_2)$ is a polynomial that does not vanish in $\mathbb{D}^2$. Is every optimal polynomial approximant $p_n$ of $1/f$ in $H^2(\mathbb{D}^2)$ necessarily zero-free in $\mathbb{D}^2$?

original_question: Suppose f is a polynomial with zeros Z(f) in the complement of the open unit disk D, and let q_n be the n-th optimal polynomial approximant of 1/f in H^2_omega. For which weights {omega_k}_{k in N} is it true that 1 - q_n f converges to 0 uniformly on compact subsets of D \ Z(f)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\{\omega_k\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ be a sequence of positive real weights, and let $H^2_\omega$ denote the Hilbert space of analytic functions $f(z)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty a_k z^k$ on the open unit disk $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ with finite norm
$$\|f\|_\omega^2 = \sum_{k=0}^\infty |a_k|^2 \omega_k < \infty.$$
For $f\in H^2_\omega$ not identically zero and $n\in\mathbb{N}_0$, the $n$-th optimal polynomial approximant of $1/f$ in $H^2_\omega$ is defined as the polynomial $q_n$ of degree at most $n$ that minimizes $\|pf-1\|_\omega$ among all polynomials $p$ of degree at most $n$.

Now suppose $f$ is a polynomial whose zero set $Z(f)$ lies entirely in $\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{D}$ (i.e., all zeros have modulus $\ge 1$), and let $q_n$ be the $n$-th optimal polynomial approximant of $1/f$ in $H^2_\omega$.

Characterize the weight sequences $\{\omega_k\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ for which $1-q_n f \to 0$ uniformly on compact subsets of $\mathbb{D}\setminus Z(f)$ as $n\to\infty$.

paper_title: Notes on open questions within density functional theory (existence of a derivative of the Lieb functional in a restricted sense and non-interacting v-representability)
context_brief: Restricted differentiability of the interacting Lieb functional
original_question: For the interacting Lieb functional FL[n] in density functional theory, can one prove that FL[n] admits a derivative in a restricted or weak sense for every interacting ensemble v-representable density n in the set B, even though FL[n] is nowhere Gateaux differentiable on the full Banach space X? Any such result must identify physically meaningful perturbation directions that preserve particle number and keep perturbed densities inside the admissible density set S, while still making the directional derivative finite and linear on that restricted class.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ be the spatial domain and fix a particle number $N \in \mathbb{N}$. Consider the Banach space
$$X = L^1(\mathbb{R}^3) \cap L^3(\mathbb{R}^3),$$
equipped with the norm $\|n\|_X = \|n\|_{L^1} + \|n\|_{L^3}$, and the admissible set of $N$-particle densities
$$S = \Big\{ n \in X : n \ge 0 \text{ a.e.}, \ \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} n = N, \ \sqrt{n} \in H^1(\mathbb{R}^3) \Big\}.$$
For an electron–electron interaction $\hat{W}$, define the interacting Lieb (constrained-search) functional
$$F_L[n] = \inf\Big\{ \mathrm{Tr}\big(\hat{\Gamma}(\hat{T}+\hat{W})\big) : \hat{\Gamma} \text{ is an } N\text{-particle ensemble density matrix yielding } n \Big\},$$
where $\hat{T}$ denotes the kinetic-energy operator. Let
$$B \subset S$$
be the subset of densities that are interacting ensemble $v$-representable, i.e., densities $n \in S$ that arise as the ground-state density of $\hat{T}+\hat{W}+\sum_i v(x_i)$ for some external potential $v$ in a suitable dual class.

It is known that $F_L$ is convex on $S$ but is nowhere Gâteaux differentiable on $X$ in the usual sense.

Question. Does $F_L$ admit a derivative in some restricted (weak) sense at every $n \in B$? More precisely, does there exist a class $\mathcal{D}_n \subset X$ of admissible perturbation directions $\delta n$ such that:
(i) each $\delta n \in \mathcal{D}_n$ satisfies $\int \delta n = 0$ (particle-number preserving) and $n + t\,\delta n \in S$ for all sufficiently small $t > 0$;
(ii) the one-sided directional derivative
$$D_{\delta n} F_L[n] := \lim_{t \downarrow 0} \frac{F_L[n + t\,\delta n] - F_L[n]}{t}$$
exists and is finite for every $\delta n \in \mathcal{D}_n$;
(iii) the map $\delta n \mapsto D_{\delta n} F_L[n]$ is linear on $\mathcal{D}_n$ and represented by a (Kohn–Sham) potential $v_n$, in the sense that $D_{\delta n} F_L[n] = -\int v_n\, \delta n$ for all $\delta n \in \mathcal{D}_n$;
(iv) the class $\mathcal{D}_n$ is large enough to recover the conclusions normally drawn from Gâteaux differentiability of $F_L$ at $n$ (in particular, applicability to the Kohn–Sham scheme), without imposing further restrictions on $n$ beyond $n \in B$?
category_tag: Density functional theory / Lieb functional differentiability
status_search_result: The question of whether the Lieb functional admits a derivative in a restricted/weak sense at every interacting ensemble v-representable density remains open in general. Lammert (2007) showed the standard proof of Gâteaux differentiability is flawed and that $F_L$ is neither Gâteaux nor Fréchet differentiable in the usual sense; positive results exist only under extra restrictions (e.g. densities bounded away from zero with $L^2$ derivatives), or in special settings such as spinless fermions in one dimension (2025 work by Sutter et al.). No general result removing all restrictions on $B$ has been established.

paper_title: Notes on open questions within density functional theory (existence of a derivative of the Lieb functional in a restricted sense and non-interacting v-representability)
context_brief: Restricted bounded derivative of the Kohn-Sham potential
original_question: Does the Kohn-Sham potential functional vs[ns], defined for non-interacting ensemble v-representable densities ns in Bs, admit a derivative in a restricted sense for every ns in Bs, and is that derivative bounded? The notes identify a positive answer as sufficient to prove the non-interacting v-representability conjecture, but they also note that establishing such a derivative rigorously is difficult, especially in degenerate cases, and that the inverse response kernel χs^-1[vs[ns]] is unbounded.
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Consider the Kohn–Sham (KS) framework of density functional theory in which one considers N-electron systems described by single-particle densities ρ on R^3 with ρ ≥ 0 and ∫ρ = N. A density n_s is said to be non-interacting (pure-state or ensemble) v-representable if there exists a one-body local potential v_s such that n_s arises as the ground-state density of a non-interacting N-electron Hamiltonian H_s = -½Δ + v_s (acting on a Slater determinant or an ensemble of degenerate ground-state determinants). Let B_s denote the set of non-interacting ensemble v-representable densities. By the Hohenberg–Kohn theorem applied to non-interacting systems, the assignment n_s ↦ v_s[n_s] is well defined (up to an additive constant) on B_s, giving the KS potential functional v_s : B_s → (potentials modulo constants).

Let χ_s[v_s[n_s]] denote the static non-interacting density–density linear response operator at the potential v_s[n_s], i.e. the operator giving δn_s in terms of an infinitesimal perturbation δv_s of the KS potential at fixed particle number; let χ_s^{-1}[v_s[n_s]] denote its (formal) inverse on the space of density variations summing to zero.

We say that v_s admits a "derivative in a restricted sense" at n_s ∈ B_s if there exists a linear operator D[n_s], acting on an admissible class of density variations δn (those tangent to B_s, i.e. preserving total particle number and remaining inside B_s to first order), such that
   v_s[n_s + δn] - v_s[n_s] = D[n_s] · δn + o(‖δn‖)
in a suitable norm, modulo additive constants. The operator D[n_s] is said to be bounded if it extends to a bounded linear operator on the relevant Banach space of density variations.

Question. Does the KS potential functional v_s : B_s → potentials admit, at every density n_s ∈ B_s (including degenerate ground-state cases), a derivative in the above restricted sense, and is this derivative bounded? Equivalently, can one rigorously establish such a bounded restricted derivative of v_s[n_s] on B_s, in a way that would imply the non-interacting v-representability conjecture (the statement that every "reasonable" N-electron density is non-interacting ensemble v-representable)?

Note that the natural candidate D[n_s] = -χ_s^{-1}[v_s[n_s]] is in general unbounded, since the eigenvalues α_j of χ_s can approach 0, so a separate argument or alternative construction is required.
status_search_result: The general non-interacting v-representability problem and the existence of a (bounded) derivative of the KS potential functional in a restricted sense remain open. Partial progress has been obtained in restricted settings: a 2025 work treats non-interacting Schrödinger operators with distributional potentials on the one-dimensional torus, showing Hohenberg–Kohn and that the non-interacting Lieb functional is differentiable on the v-representable densities in that setting. No general resolution of the conjecture (covering degenerate cases in R^3) appears in the literature.

original_question: For a br-graph H, let S_H be its switching graph. A k-ary weak near unanimity polymorphism is an idempotent polymorphism phi, for k >= 3, such that phi(x, x, ..., x, y) = phi(x, x, ..., y, x) = ... = phi(y, x, ..., x, x), and it is conservative when phi(v_1, ..., v_k) is always one of the inputs. Calling a polymorphism of S_H semi-conservative when it preserves symmetric lists, is it true that S_H has a semi-conservative weak near unanimity polymorphism if and only if S_H has a conservative weak near unanimity polymorphism?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. A br-graph is a graph in which each vertex is labeled either black or red (so V(H) is partitioned into B(H) ∪ R(H)). A homomorphism between br-graphs preserves both edges and vertex colors. For a br-graph H, define its switching graph S_H as the br-graph with vertex set V(H) × {0,1}, where the edges and color labels are determined by H according to the standard switching construction (so that homomorphisms G → S_H correspond to "switchings" of homomorphisms into H).

Polymorphisms. For k ≥ 1, a k-ary polymorphism of a br-graph G is a homomorphism φ : G^k → G (where G^k is the categorical product in the category of br-graphs). It is idempotent if φ(x, x, …, x) = x for every x ∈ V(G). For k ≥ 3, an idempotent polymorphism φ is a weak near unanimity (WNU) polymorphism if, for all x, y ∈ V(G),
   φ(y, x, x, …, x) = φ(x, y, x, …, x) = ⋯ = φ(x, x, …, x, y).
A polymorphism φ is conservative if φ(v_1, …, v_k) ∈ {v_1, …, v_k} for all choices of v_i.

For the switching graph S_H, a list on S_H is a subset L ⊆ V(S_H) = V(H) × {0,1}. Such a list L is called symmetric if (v, 0) ∈ L ⇔ (v, 1) ∈ L for every v ∈ V(H). A polymorphism φ of S_H is semi-conservative if for every symmetric list L and every (v_1, …, v_k) ∈ L^k one has φ(v_1, …, v_k) ∈ L (equivalently, φ preserves all symmetric lists).

Question. Is it true that, for every br-graph H, the switching graph S_H admits a semi-conservative weak near unanimity polymorphism if and only if S_H admits a conservative weak near unanimity polymorphism?
status_search_result: The question is described as a disproved conservative-collapse question, indicating that the equivalence between having a semi-conservative WNU polymorphism and having a conservative WNU polymorphism on switching graphs S_H fails in general (counterexample exists). General web search did not surface a public independent confirmation, but the contextual labeling indicates the equivalence has been refuted.

original_question: For a given positive integer n, what is the largest possible number K(n) of triangles that can be formed by n straight lines in the plane if only triangles that are nonoverlapping and uncut by any of the lines are counted?
self_contained_problem:
Let n be a positive integer with n ≥ 3, and consider an arrangement of n straight lines in the Euclidean plane R^2. Such an arrangement partitions the plane into open polygonal regions (cells). Call a triangle T admissible for the arrangement if:
(i) the three sides of T lie on three of the n lines, and
(ii) the open interior of T is one of the cells of the arrangement (equivalently, no other line of the arrangement crosses the interior of T, and the interiors of any two such triangles are disjoint).

Define K(n) to be the maximum, over all arrangements of n lines in the plane, of the number of admissible triangles. Determine K(n) as an explicit function of n (or, for each n, determine its exact value).

Known facts that should be respected: Tamura's upper bound K(n) ≤ ⌊n(n−2)/3⌋, and the Clément–Bader strengthening that this bound cannot be attained when n ≡ 0 or 2 (mod 6). The problem is to determine the exact value of K(n) for all n.
status_search_result: The Kobon triangle problem is a long-standing open problem in combinatorial geometry. Tamura's upper bound ⌊n(n−2)/3⌋ is known, and Clément–Bader showed it is not achieved for n ≡ 0, 2 (mod 6). Exact values of K(n) are known for several small n (e.g., n = 3–9, 13, 15, 17, 19, 21, ...), with recent SAT-based work (Savchuk, 2025) confirming the optimum for n = 11. The general formula for K(n) remains unresolved.

original_question: Among all plane regions of width 1 that can be moved through a right-angled hallway of width 1 by continuous rigid motions in the plane, which region has the largest possible area?
self_contained_problem:
Let H ⊂ ℝ² be the L-shaped hallway of unit width formed by the union
  H = {(x,y) : x ≤ 0, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1} ∪ {(x,y) : 0 ≤ x, -x ≤ y ≤ 1 - … } 
more precisely, H = ((-∞, 1] × [0,1]) ∪ ([0,1] × (-∞, 1]), i.e., two perpendicular corridors of width 1 meeting at a right-angled corner.

A "sofa" is any connected planar region S ⊂ ℝ² (not required to be convex) for which there exists a closed interval I ⊂ ℝ and a continuous one-parameter family {Φ_t}_{t ∈ I} of rigid motions of the plane (each Φ_t an orientation-preserving isometry, with t ↦ Φ_t continuous in the usual topology on the group of rigid motions) such that:
  (i) for every t ∈ I, Φ_t(S) ⊂ H;
  (ii) for sufficiently early t the region Φ_t(S) lies entirely in the horizontal corridor (-∞, 1] × [0,1], and for sufficiently late t it lies entirely in the vertical corridor [0,1] × (-∞, 1].

Determine the supremum of the area of S over all such sofas, and exhibit a region attaining it. In particular, decide whether the maximum is achieved by Gerver's region (a specific shape composed of 18 analytic arc pieces with area approximately 2.2195).
status_search_result: In November 2024, Jineon Baek posted a ~119-page preprint claiming a proof that Gerver's sofa (area ≈ 2.2195) is optimal. The result has been widely reported but, as of early 2026, peer review has not been confirmed as complete in the available sources, so the problem is best described as having a recently announced (not yet fully verified) solution.

original_question: For each positive integer n, what is the smallest triangle that can contain n circles of radius 1 without overlap?
self_contained_problem: For each positive integer $n$, determine the triangle of smallest area (equivalently, smallest scale) that contains $n$ pairwise non-overlapping closed disks of radius $1$ in the Euclidean plane. Here "contains" means each disk lies entirely inside the closed triangular region, and "non-overlapping" means the interiors of the disks are disjoint. The triangle is allowed to be arbitrary (not required to be equilateral or isosceles), and one seeks, as a function of $n$, the infimum of the area (or of a chosen size parameter) of a triangle admitting such a packing, together with the configurations achieving the optimum.
status_search_result: For the special case of equilateral triangles, optimal packings of n unit circles are proved only for small n (roughly n ≤ 15), with conjectured optima for n up to about 34; the problem is open in general. For arbitrary triangles the question remains unresolved for general n, with only partial results, bounds, and constant-factor approximation methods (e.g., split packing) known.

original_question: Let F be a known plane region representing a forest. Find a parametrized curve C such that, no matter which point P of F a hiker starts from and no matter which initial direction the hiker faces, every curve congruent to C with initial point P eventually leaves F; among all such guaranteed-escape curves, which one minimizes the worst-case escape time, equivalently the length of the shortest trajectory that guarantees escape?
self_contained_problem:
Let F ⊂ ℝ² be a fixed, known plane region (the "forest"). A parametrized curve C: [0, L] → ℝ² is said to guarantee escape from F if, for every starting point P ∈ F and every rigid motion (translation and rotation) sending the initial point C(0) to P, the resulting congruent image C̃ of C is not entirely contained in F (i.e. C̃ exits F at some parameter value).

Among all parametrized curves C that guarantee escape from F in this sense, determine one that minimizes the arc length L (equivalently, the worst-case time/distance until escape, assuming unit speed). That is, find

  inf { length(C) : C guarantees escape from F },

and exhibit an optimal curve achieving (or approaching) this infimum, for a given forest shape F — and, more ambitiously, give a procedure that produces such an optimal curve for an arbitrary plane region F.
status_search_result: Bellman's lost-in-a-forest problem, posed in 1955–1956, remains open in general. Optimal escape paths are known for a handful of special forest shapes (e.g. infinite strips, half-planes, circles, certain rectangles and some convex regions), but no general solution for arbitrary plane regions has been verified. A 2024 arXiv preprint by Z. Deng proposes a general framework, but it is not established as a community-accepted solution and the problem is still listed as open (e.g. on Wikipedia and related surveys).

original_question: Does every Jordan curve in the plane contain four points that are the vertices of a square? Here a Jordan curve is a simple closed curve, and 'inscribes a square' means that the four vertices of the square lie on the curve, without requiring the whole square to lie inside the region bounded by the curve.
self_contained_problem:
A Jordan curve is a subset of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ that is the image of a continuous injective map from the unit circle $S^1$ into $\mathbb{R}^2$ (equivalently, a simple closed curve). One says that a Jordan curve $C$ inscribes a square if there exist four distinct points $p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4 \in C$ that are the vertices of a (non-degenerate) square in $\mathbb{R}^2$; the square itself is not required to lie in the bounded region enclosed by $C$, only its four vertices must lie on $C$.

Question: Does every Jordan curve in $\mathbb{R}^2$ inscribe a square?
status_search_result: The general inscribed square (Toeplitz) conjecture remains open. Many special cases are known: convex curves, piecewise analytic/smooth curves (Emch and others), and recent work by Greene–Lobb (2020–2024) establishing inscribed rectangles and cyclic quadrilaterals for smooth Jordan curves and progress for Lipschitz curves. The problem for arbitrary continuous Jordan curves has not been resolved.

paper_title: Some open questions on morphological operators and representations in the deep learning era: A personal vision
context_brief: Hybrid MMBB and standard deep-learning pipelines
original_question: Can MMBB networks, whose primitives are lattice-theoretic morphological operators, be combined with standard deep-learning layers such as convolution, downsampling, upsampling, max-pooling, and ReLU to form relevant learnable pipelines?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(L, \wedge, \vee)$ be a complete lattice (e.g., the lattice of grayscale images $L = \mathbb{R}^{H\times W}$ with pointwise order). A *morphological operator* on $L$ is a mapping built from the lattice-theoretic primitives of erosion $\varepsilon_B(f)(x) = \inf_{b\in B} f(x+b)$ and dilation $\delta_B(f)(x) = \sup_{b\in B} f(x+b)$ with structuring element $B$, together with their compositions (opening, closing, etc.). A *Max-Min Basis-Based (MMBB) network* is a feed-forward parametric model whose layers are finite sup-inf (equivalently, max-min) combinations of such morphological primitives, with the structuring elements (and possibly the basis weights) treated as learnable parameters.

A *standard deep-learning layer* refers to one of: a linear convolution layer, a downsampling (strided) layer, an upsampling (e.g., transposed convolution or nearest-neighbor) layer, a max-pooling layer, or a ReLU activation $x \mapsto \max(x,0)$.

Problem. Construct hybrid feed-forward architectures that interleave MMBB layers with standard deep-learning layers (convolution, down/upsampling, max-pooling, ReLU) so that the resulting models:
(i) are end-to-end trainable by gradient-based optimization (with a well-defined notion of subgradient through the sup/inf primitives);
(ii) are universal in some precise approximation-theoretic sense on a class of image-to-image or image-to-label mappings of interest; and
(iii) on at least one standard learning task (e.g., image classification or semantic segmentation) demonstrate a quantifiable advantage—either in parameter efficiency, interpretability, or performance—over a purely convolutional baseline of comparable size.

Formalize the notion of "relevant learnable pipeline," exhibit such a construction, and prove the corresponding approximation and trainability guarantees.
status_search_result: Several recent works construct and train hybrid architectures combining morphological layers (erosion/dilation, max-min) with standard CNN primitives—e.g., hybrid morphological-convolutional networks for medical imaging (Frontiers in AI, 2023), "Deep Morphological Networks" (Pattern Recognition, 2020), and "Training Deep Morphological Neural Networks as Universal Approximators" (2025). These give partial positive answers (working hybrid pipelines, some universal-approximation results). However, a fully general theory matching the MMBB lattice-basis formulation with rigorous approximation and trainability guarantees and consistent empirical advantage is not established, so the question is only partially solved.

paper_title: Some open questions on morphological operators and representations in the deep learning era: A personal vision
original_question: What Lipschitz morphological layers can be introduced into deep neural networks to control their Lipschitz constants and regularity, and can these morphological regularizing layers replace standard nonlinearities such as pooling plus ReLU without degrading network expressiveness?
self_contained_problem:
Background. Mathematical morphology on grayscale images is built from two basic nonlinear operators acting on a function f : R^d → R with respect to a structuring function b : R^d → R ∪ {−∞}: the dilation (f ⊕ b)(x) = sup_{y ∈ R^d} { f(x − y) + b(y) } and the erosion (f ⊖ b)(x) = inf_{y ∈ R^d} { f(x + y) − b(y) }. A flat structuring element on a compact set B ⊂ R^d corresponds to b = 0 on B and −∞ elsewhere, recovering the local sup/inf operators. A map T between normed function spaces is L-Lipschitz if ||T(f) − T(g)|| ≤ L · ||f − g|| for all f, g.

A feed-forward neural network is a composition F = L_n ∘ σ_{n−1} ∘ L_{n−1} ∘ ··· ∘ σ_1 ∘ L_1, where each L_k is an affine (or convolutional) operator and each σ_k is a pointwise nonlinearity (e.g. ReLU x ↦ max(x,0)) possibly followed by a pooling operator (e.g. max-pooling). The Lipschitz constant of F (with respect to specified input/output norms) is bounded above by the product of the Lipschitz constants of its layers, and controls the regularity, robustness and generalization of the network.

Define a "morphological layer" to be any layer M whose action on its input feature maps is given by a finite composition of dilations, erosions, openings (f ↦ (f ⊖ b) ⊕ b), closings (f ↦ (f ⊕ b) ⊖ b), or supremal/infimal convolutions with learnable structuring functions, possibly followed by an affine combination across channels.

Problem. 
(a) Characterize the families of morphological layers M as above for which one can give an explicit, sharp, computable upper bound on the Lipschitz constant Lip(M) (with respect to the L^∞ and L^2 norms on inputs and outputs), in terms of the parameters of the structuring functions; describe in particular which choices of structuring functions and channel-mixing rules guarantee Lip(M) ≤ 1.

(b) Determine whether such "Lipschitz morphological layers" can be inserted into a deep neural network so as to control its overall Lipschitz constant while preserving — or improving — the network's expressive power. Concretely: exhibit, or prove the impossibility of, an architecture in which every standard nonlinearity of the form (max-pooling ∘ ReLU) is replaced by a Lipschitz morphological layer, in such a way that the resulting class of functions is at least as expressive (in a precise approximation-theoretic sense, e.g. universal approximation on compact sets of continuous functions) as the original architecture.
status_search_result: Web searches show extensive ongoing work on (i) Lipschitz regularization of neural networks (spectral normalization, Lipschitz bounds for ReLU/max-pooling) and (ii) morphological neural networks based on learnable dilations/erosions. However, no source was found that provides a complete characterization of Lipschitz morphological layers replacing pooling+ReLU without loss of expressiveness; the question appears to remain an open research direction.

paper_title: Some open questions on morphological operators and representations in the deep learning era: A personal vision
context_brief: Generalized Tailor problem with morphological networks
original_question: How efficiently can the generalized Tailor problem, the problem of decomposing any shape according to a set of templates, be solved by networks inspired by morphological iterative algorithms and group morphology?
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Let $E$ denote a discrete workspace, e.g. $E=\mathbb{Z}^d$, and let $\mathcal{P}(E)$ denote its power set, whose elements are called shapes. Fix a transitive group $G$ acting on $E$ (for instance the translation group, the motion group, or an affine group). For a shape $X\in\mathcal{P}(E)$ and $g\in G$, write $g\cdot X = \{g\cdot x : x\in X\}$.

Given a finite collection of shapes $\mathcal{T}=\{T_1,\dots,T_k\}\subset \mathcal{P}(E)$, called templates, and a target shape $S\in\mathcal{P}(E)$, the Generalized Tailor Problem asks whether $S$ admits a decomposition
$$ S \;=\; \bigsqcup_{i=1}^{N} g_i \cdot T_{j_i}, $$
where $g_1,\dots,g_N\in G$ and $j_1,\dots,j_N\in\{1,\dots,k\}$, and the union is disjoint (a tiling of $S$ by transformed copies of templates from $\mathcal{T}$). The optimization version asks for a decomposition minimizing $N$ or another prescribed cost.

A morphological iterative network is a feed-forward neural architecture whose elementary layers are the standard operators of mathematical morphology — erosion $X\ominus B = \{x : B+x\subseteq X\}$, dilation $X\oplus B = \bigcup_{b\in B}(X+b)$, opening, closing, hit-or-miss transforms — together with their group-morphology generalizations relative to $G$ (where translation is replaced by the action of $G$), and pointwise lattice operations $\cup,\cap$. The depth of such a network is the number of sequential morphological layers, and its size is the total number of structuring elements used.

Question. Determine the optimal asymptotic complexity, in terms of network depth and size, of solving the Generalized Tailor Problem for a family of templates $\mathcal{T}$ and group $G$ by morphological iterative networks. Concretely: provide upper and lower bounds on the minimal depth $D(\mathcal{T},G,n)$ and size $S(\mathcal{T},G,n)$ of a morphological iterative network that, given any input shape $S\subseteq E$ contained in a window of $n$ points, outputs a valid decomposition of $S$ into $G$-transformed copies of templates from $\mathcal{T}$ whenever such a decomposition exists, and reports infeasibility otherwise.
status_search_result: Web searches return material on group morphology and on morphological shape decomposition, but no work providing complexity bounds for solving the Generalized Tailor Problem with morphological-iterative or group-morphology-inspired networks. The question appears to remain open.

paper_title: Some open questions on morphological operators and representations in the deep learning era: A personal vision
context_brief: Learning topological extinction features with reconstruction
original_question: Can persistence or extinction-value features associated with image topology be learned for topological image classification and segmentation by using morphological reconstruction operators, and what architecture should implement the needed iterative reconstruction process, such as a residual architecture, recurrent architecture, or another design?
self_contained_problem:
Background. In mathematical morphology, given a grayscale image $f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ (with $\Omega\subset\mathbb{Z}^2$) and a marker image $g\le f$, the morphological reconstruction by dilation $R_f(g)$ is defined as the limit of the iteration $g_0=g$, $g_{k+1}=(\delta_B(g_k))\wedge f$, where $\delta_B$ is the elementary dilation by a structuring element $B$ and $\wedge$ denotes pointwise minimum; this iteration converges in a finite number of steps to the smallest image $h$ with $g\le h\le f$ that is invariant under $\delta_B(\cdot)\wedge f$. Reconstruction by erosion is defined dually. Using such reconstruction operators one can compute, for every regional maximum (or minimum) $M$ of $f$, its extinction value $\mathrm{ext}(M)$ associated with a measure (volume, dynamics, area), which quantifies the persistence of $M$ under successive morphological filterings; extinction values are closely related to persistent homology of the sublevel/superlevel filtration of $f$ in dimension $0$.

Problem. Design and analyze a trainable deep neural architecture $\mathcal{N}_\theta$, with parameters $\theta$, whose internal computation realizes (or approximates) the iterative morphological reconstruction process $g_{k+1}=(\delta_B(g_k))\wedge f$ with learnable structuring elements / nonlinearities, and whose output produces, for each pixel of an input image $f$, a feature vector encoding the extinction values (equivalently, the $0$-dimensional persistence) of the regional extrema to which it belongs. Specifically:

(a) Prove or disprove that there exists such an architecture for which the learned features are provably consistent estimators of the true extinction values associated with a chosen extinction measure (volume, dynamics, or area), in the sense that as the network depth (number of unrolled reconstruction iterations) tends to infinity the output converges, uniformly on a suitable class of images, to the exact extinction map.

(b) Determine which class of architectures is best suited to implement the unbounded-iteration reconstruction fixed point: a feed-forward residual network of the form $g_{k+1}=g_k+F_\theta(g_k,f)$, a recurrent network sharing weights across iterations, or another design; in particular, characterize necessary and sufficient conditions on $F_\theta$ for the discrete dynamics to converge to $R_f(g)$.

(c) Demonstrate that the resulting persistence/extinction features can be end-to-end trained for topological image classification and semantic segmentation tasks, in the sense that gradients with respect to $\theta$ exist almost everywhere and that minimizing a suitable topological loss based on these features yields segmentations with prescribed Betti numbers.
status_search_result: Related lines of work exist (differentiable persistent-homology losses for segmentation, topology-preserving deep segmentation, and learnable morphological layers), but no published work appears to provide a unified architecture that learns morphological-reconstruction-based extinction/persistence features through an iterative reconstruction module while characterizing the optimal residual vs. recurrent design. The specific question therefore appears to remain open.

paper_title: Some open questions on morphological operators and representations in the deep learning era: A personal vision
original_question: Can architectures based on parametric families of morphological multiscale operators be learned efficiently while giving better interpretability for shape-recognition or texture-recognition tasks, and which parametric structuring functions are most useful in deep learning, such as quadratic functions defined by a shape covariance matrix or convex functions defined by Minkowski addition of oriented segments?
self_contained_problem:
Background. For a grayscale image f : Z^2 → R and a structuring function b : Z^2 → R ∪ {−∞}, the morphological dilation and erosion are defined by
  (f ⊕ b)(x) = sup_{y} { f(x − y) + b(y) },   (f ⊖ b)(x) = inf_{y} { f(x + y) − b(y) }.
Compositions of dilations and erosions at multiple scales (e.g. openings, closings, top-hats, alternating sequential filters) yield morphological multiscale operators. A multiscale architecture is built by stacking such operators, possibly with linear/pointwise layers, where the structuring functions b = b_θ are taken from a parametric family with learnable parameters θ.

Two parametric families of particular interest are:
  (i) Quadratic structuring functions b_Σ(y) = −(1/2) y^T Σ^{−1} y, where Σ is a positive-definite "shape covariance" matrix (so the level sets of b are ellipses);
  (ii) Convex piecewise-linear structuring functions obtained as the Minkowski sum b = s_1 ⊕ ... ⊕ s_k of oriented line segments s_i of given lengths and orientations (so the level sets are zonotopes).

Problem. Design a deep architecture whose layers are parametric morphological multiscale operators of the above type, and address the following:
  1. Provide a training scheme (e.g., suitable smooth surrogates, gradient computations, or initialization strategies) such that the parameters θ of the structuring functions can be learned efficiently from data, with provable or empirically demonstrable convergence and stability.
  2. Determine which of the parametric families (i)–(ii), or other parametric families of structuring functions, lead to the best performance and the most informative parameters (e.g., explicit shape or orientation descriptors) on shape-recognition and texture-recognition tasks, in a way that yields better interpretability than standard convolutional networks.

Specifically: do there exist parametric morphological multiscale architectures that can be trained efficiently and that achieve, on shape- or texture-classification benchmarks, competitive accuracy together with quantifiably improved interpretability of the learned filters as geometric primitives?
status_search_result: Recent literature on morphological neural networks (e.g., works on learnable structuring elements, PConv/Pdilation layers, and deep morphological networks 2021–2025) has explored parametric structuring functions including quadratic/elliptic and convex/zonotopal forms, with progress on differentiable training via smooth approximations. However, no consensus has emerged on which parametric family is most fruitful, and interpretability gains over CNNs on shape/texture tasks remain a topic of active investigation. original_question: For ultrametric convolutional neural networks operating on dendrogram or rooted-tree representations of data, how can the convolution operation be learned efficiently, how should max-pooling and unpooling layers be defined, and are there additional layers specifically useful for this type of neural network?
self_contained_problem:
An ultrametric space is a metric space (X, d) in which the distance d satisfies the strong triangle inequality d(x, z) ≤ max{d(x, y), d(y, z)} for all x, y, z ∈ X. Finite ultrametric spaces are in bijection with rooted trees (dendrograms) whose leaves are the points of X, where the distance between two leaves equals the height of their lowest common ancestor.

Consider data represented as points in a finite ultrametric space, equivalently as leaves of a rooted tree (dendrogram) endowed with a height function on internal nodes. A convolutional neural network operating on such data is called an ultrametric convolutional neural network: each layer takes as input a function f : X → ℝ^c on the leaves (or more generally on the nodes) of an ultrametric/dendrogram structure and outputs another such function, in a way compatible with the hierarchical/ultrametric geometry.

Address the following:

(a) Define a notion of convolution operator on functions over a finite ultrametric space (or its associated dendrogram) which (i) respects the ultrametric/hierarchical structure, (ii) has a finite parameterization that can be learned by gradient-based optimization, and (iii) admits an efficient algorithm (specify its computational complexity in terms of the number of leaves and the depth of the tree).

(b) Define max-pooling and unpooling layers for such networks, in a way consistent with the ultrametric structure: max-pooling should aggregate values along subtrees (e.g., children of an internal node) to produce a function on a coarsened dendrogram, and unpooling should provide a corresponding inverse-like operation suitable for encoder–decoder architectures. State precise definitions and prove that the resulting operators are equivariant or invariant under the appropriate isomorphisms of dendrograms.

(c) Identify additional layer types that are specifically meaningful for ultrametric convolutional neural networks (for example, layers exploiting the lattice of internal nodes, the partial order of subtrees, or non-Archimedean arithmetic) and motivate their usefulness either theoretically or by an explicit construction.

paper_title: Some open questions on morphological operators and representations in the deep learning era: A personal vision
context_brief: Smooth approximations for trainable morphological operators
original_question: Which smooth approximation to max-min-based morphological operators, such as counter-harmonic means or Log-Sum-Exp terms, is most relevant for training hybrid deep-learning networks whose learned nonlinearities may behave either like standard convolutions or like morphological operators?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ be a real-valued signal and let $b:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ be a structuring function. The flat/grey-level morphological dilation and erosion of $f$ by $b$ are defined by
\[
(f\oplus b)(x)=\sup_{y}\bigl(f(x-y)+b(y)\bigr),\qquad (f\ominus b)(x)=\inf_{y}\bigl(f(x+y)-b(y)\bigr),
\]
so that the basic morphological operators are governed by pointwise maxima and minima. Two well-known smooth (differentiable) families of approximations to these max/min operations are:

1. The counter-harmonic mean (CHM) of order $P\in\mathbb{R}$: for a positive weight kernel $w$ and a positive function $f$,
\[
\mathrm{CHM}_P(f;w)(x)=\frac{(w\ast f^{P+1})(x)}{(w\ast f^{P})(x)},
\]
which tends to a dilation as $P\to+\infty$, to an erosion as $P\to-\infty$, and to a standard linear convolution at $P=0$.

2. The Log-Sum-Exp (LSE) approximation with temperature $\beta>0$:
\[
\mathrm{LSE}_\beta(g)(x)=\frac{1}{\beta}\log\!\int e^{\beta\,g(x,y)}\,dy,
\]
which approximates $\sup_y g(x,y)$ as $\beta\to+\infty$ and $\inf_y g(x,y)$ as $\beta\to-\infty$.

Consider hybrid trainable layers in a deep neural network in which a learnable parameter (such as $P$ in CHM, or $\beta$ together with sign parameters in LSE) interpolates between linear convolution and a max-/min-based morphological operator, so that the layer can learn to behave either as a convolution or as a dilation/erosion (or some intermediate operator) depending on the data.

Problem. Determine which of these smooth approximations to max-min-based morphological operators (counter-harmonic means, Log-Sum-Exp, or another candidate family) is most appropriate for training such hybrid deep networks. Specifically, identify a smooth approximation family $\{T_\theta\}_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of morphological operators that simultaneously:
(a) recovers exact dilation, erosion, and ordinary linear convolution as limiting or special values of the parameter $\theta$;
(b) admits gradients with respect to $\theta$ and the input that are numerically stable and well-behaved across these limits;
(c) provably allows gradient-based optimization to converge to genuinely morphological (max/min) regimes when these are optimal for a given learning task;
and prove or rigorously justify the optimality of the chosen family among reasonable alternatives, or show that no such family is uniformly best and characterize the trade-offs.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction concerning the design of trainable smooth morphological layers in deep networks. Subsequent work (e.g. on PConv/Counter-Harmonic layers, LogSumExp morphological networks, and smooth morphological neural networks) has explored both CHM and LSE approximations empirically, but no consensus or rigorous proof has been established identifying a uniquely optimal smooth approximation for hybrid morphological/convolutional learning. The problem therefore appears to remain open.

paper_title: Some open questions on morphological operators and representations in the deep learning era: A personal vision
context_brief: Morphological PDE schemes as neural-network layers
original_question: Which numerical schemes for morphological partial differential equations are relevant for learning morphological operators or other nonlinear layers in deep-learning pipelines, how should the iterative nature of the approximations be handled, and can numerical schemes for morphological PDEs of matrix fields be used to learn nonlinearities for symmetric positive definite matrices or other matrix-valued data in Riemannian deep learning?
self_contained_problem:
Background. In mathematical morphology, the basic operators of flat dilation and erosion of a scalar image $u_0:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ by a structuring element associated with a convex function admit a partial differential equation (PDE) formulation. For example, dilation/erosion by balls of radius $t$ correspond to the Hamilton–Jacobi PDEs
$$\partial_t u = \pm\|\nabla u\|,\qquad u(\cdot,0)=u_0,$$
whose viscosity solutions $u(\cdot,t)$ realize the morphological operator at scale $t$. Solving such PDEs numerically requires specialized upwind, Rouy–Tourin, Osher–Sethian, or high-accuracy predictor–corrector schemes, and the schemes have been extended to fields of symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices $U_0:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathrm{Sym}^+(d)$ by exploiting the eigenstructure of symmetric matrices to define matrix-valued dilation/erosion.

In a deep-learning pipeline, a layer $L_\theta$ is a (typically differentiable) parametric mapping between feature tensors. A morphological layer is one whose forward pass approximates a dilation, erosion, or related nonlinear morphological operator (with learnable structuring function or shape parameters), so that gradients with respect to the parameters can be computed via backpropagation through the discretized PDE solver.

Problem. Address the following three questions.

(a) Identify which numerical schemes for the scalar morphological PDEs (upwind finite-difference, Rouy–Tourin, Engquist–Osher, semi-Lagrangian, predictor–corrector, etc.) are best suited to be embedded as layers $L_\theta$ in a deep network so that:
 (i) the forward pass faithfully approximates a parametric dilation/erosion or other nonlinear morphological operator, and
 (ii) the discrete scheme is differentiable (or admits a tractable subgradient) with respect to both the input feature tensor and the learnable parameters $\theta$ of the structuring function.

(b) Each such scheme is iterative: a target scale $t$ is reached by composing $K=t/\Delta t$ explicit time steps under a CFL-type constraint. Determine how this iterative structure should be handled inside a learnable layer—e.g., by fixing $K$, by using implicit/unrolled iterations, by adaptive time stepping, by deep-equilibrium-style fixed points, or by training-time vs. inference-time scheme switching—so that training is stable and the layer remains expressive.

(c) Let $U:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathrm{Sym}^+(d)$ be an SPD-matrix field and consider matrix-valued morphological PDEs of the form
$$\partial_t U = \pm\,\mathcal{F}(\nabla U),$$
where $\mathcal{F}$ is built from the spectral decomposition of the matrix gradient so as to preserve positive definiteness. Decide whether existing numerical schemes for such matrix-field morphological PDEs can be turned into layers of a Riemannian deep network operating on SPD-valued data (or other structured matrix-valued data) so as to provide nonlinear activations that respect the SPD geometry, and characterize what theoretical guarantees (preservation of positive definiteness, equivariance, stability under the chosen Riemannian metric) such layers can offer.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction. While individual ingredients exist—numerical schemes for scalar and matrix-field morphological PDEs (e.g., Burgeth et al.) and Riemannian SPD networks (Huang & Van Gool and follow-ups such as DreamNet)—no published work appears to combine differentiable morphological-PDE solvers as learnable layers for SPD/matrix-valued Riemannian deep learning, so the combined questions remain open.

paper_title: 25 Open Questions About Vector Bundles and Their Moduli
context_brief: Existence of Ulrich bundles on smooth varieties
original_question: Which smooth projective varieties admit Ulrich bundles? Equivalently, for which smooth projective varieties can one find a vector bundle satisfying the standard Ulrich vanishing and linear-resolution conditions?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X \subset \mathbb{P}^N$ be a smooth projective variety of dimension $n$ over an algebraically closed field, embedded by a very ample line bundle $\mathcal{O}_X(1)$. A coherent sheaf $\mathcal{E}$ on $X$ is called an Ulrich bundle (with respect to $\mathcal{O}_X(1)$) if $\mathcal{E}$ is a locally free sheaf such that 
$$H^i(X, \mathcal{E}(-j)) = 0 \quad \text{for all } i \geq 0 \text{ and } 1 \leq j \leq n.$$
Equivalently, the pushforward of $\mathcal{E}$ under a finite linear projection $X \to \mathbb{P}^n$ is a trivial bundle, and equivalently $\mathcal{E}$ admits a linear resolution over $\mathbb{P}^N$ of the form 
$$0 \to \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^N}(-N+n)^{\oplus a_{N-n}} \to \cdots \to \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^N}(-1)^{\oplus a_1} \to \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^N}^{\oplus a_0} \to \mathcal{E} \to 0.$$

Determine for which smooth projective varieties $X$ (with respect to some, or every, very ample polarization $\mathcal{O}_X(1)$) there exists an Ulrich bundle $\mathcal{E}$ on $X$. In particular, does every smooth projective variety admit, for some very ample embedding, an Ulrich bundle?
status_search_result: The problem of which smooth projective varieties carry Ulrich bundles is widely regarded as open, often referred to as the Eisenbud–Schreyer conjecture (which expects a positive answer). Numerous partial results exist for special classes — varieties of minimal degree, certain surfaces and threefolds via the Serre construction, blow-ups, and varieties with low Picard rank — but the general existence problem remains unresolved as of recent (2024–2025) preprints.

u(E) = v$, and characterize the realizable subset of admissible values.

paper_title: 25 Open Questions About Vector Bundles and Their Moduli
context_brief: Realizing admissible width-height pairs on Z_k
original_question: Let Z_k = Tot(O_{P^1}(-k)). Suppose (w,h) is a pair of admissible local numerical invariants satisfying the bounds of [BGK2, Cor. 2.18], where w and h are the width and height components of the local holomorphic Euler characteristic. Does there exist a vector bundle E on Z_k with (w(E), h(E)) = (w,h)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{P}^1$ denote the complex projective line and let $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(-k)$ be the line bundle of degree $-k$ on $\mathbb{P}^1$ for an integer $k \geq 1$. Let $Z_k = \mathrm{Tot}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(-k))$ be the total space of this line bundle, viewed as a smooth complex surface containing the zero section $\ell \cong \mathbb{P}^1$ with self-intersection $-k$.

For a holomorphic rank-2 vector bundle $E$ on $Z_k$, the local holomorphic Euler characteristic of $E$ along $\ell$ is
$$\chi(\ell, E) := h^0(Z_k, (R^0 \pi_* E)/\pi_* E) + h^0(Z_k, R^1\pi_* E),$$
where $\pi : Z_k \to \mathrm{Spec}\,\Gamma(Z_k,\mathcal{O}_{Z_k})$ is the contraction of $\ell$. This decomposes as a sum of two non-negative integer invariants
$$\chi(\ell, E) = w(E) + h(E),$$
called the width and height of $E$, defined respectively as the lengths of the cokernel of the natural map $\pi_*E \to R^0\pi_* E$ and of $R^1\pi_* E$.

Call a pair of non-negative integers $(w,h)$ \emph{admissible} on $Z_k$ if there exist sharp bounds (the standard bounds for width and height of a rank-2 bundle on $Z_k$ in terms of its splitting type $j$ on $\ell$, namely the inequalities characterising which pairs occur as $(w(E), h(E))$ for some rank-2 bundle on the formal neighbourhood of $\ell$ with given first Chern class).

Question: Given any admissible pair $(w,h)$ on $Z_k$, does there exist a holomorphic rank-2 vector bundle $E$ on $Z_k$ with $w(E) = w$ and $h(E) = h$?

original_question: Is the Atiyah-Jones conjecture true for every irrational complex surface, i.e. does the inclusion of the instanton moduli space of charge k into the corresponding gauge-theoretic configuration space induce isomorphisms in low-degree homology and homotopy in that setting?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth complex projective surface that is irrational (i.e., not birational to $\mathbb{P}^2$). For a compact Lie group $G$ (e.g. $G=SU(2)$), let $M_k(X)$ denote the moduli space of $G$-instantons of charge $k$ on $X$ (anti-self-dual connections on a principal $G$-bundle of second Chern class $k$, modulo gauge), and let $B_k(X)$ denote the corresponding gauge-theoretic configuration space of all connections modulo gauge (equivalently, the classifying space of based gauge transformations of the bundle). There is a natural inclusion $\theta_k : M_k(X) \hookrightarrow B_k(X)$.

The generalized Atiyah–Jones conjecture asserts that, for each fixed integer $q \ge 0$, there exists $k_0(q)$ such that for all $k \ge k_0(q)$ the map $\theta_k$ induces isomorphisms
$$H_q(M_k(X);\mathbb{Z}) \xrightarrow{\cong} H_q(B_k(X);\mathbb{Z}), \qquad \pi_q(M_k(X)) \xrightarrow{\cong} \pi_q(B_k(X)).$$

Question: Does this conjecture hold for every irrational complex surface $X$?
status_search_result: The Atiyah–Jones conjecture has been established for $S^4$ (Boyer–Hurtubise–Mann–Milgram), for ruled surfaces (Hurtubise–Milgram), for rational surfaces (Gasparim and collaborators), and for blown-up surfaces over base cases. No proof is known for irrational complex surfaces in general, and the question is listed as open.

paper_title: Polycyclic Codes Associated with Trinomials: Good Codes and Open Questions
original_question: Suppose C is a polycyclic code over a finite field F_q whose associate trinomial is x^n - a x^i - b, and suppose its generator polynomial g(x) divides x^n - a x^i - b and also satisfies g(x)^2 = x^n - a x^i - b. Must C always be iso-dual, that is, equivalent to its Euclidean dual code?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field and fix integers $n>i\ge 1$ and elements $a,b\in\mathbb{F}_q$ with $b\ne 0$. Consider the trinomial $f(x)=x^n-ax^i-b\in\mathbb{F}_q[x]$ and the quotient ring $R=\mathbb{F}_q[x]/(f(x))$. A polycyclic code $C$ associated with $f(x)$ is an ideal of $R$; equivalently, identifying elements of $R$ with their coefficient vectors in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$, $C$ is an $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear subspace of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ that is closed under the polyshift $(c_0,c_1,\dots,c_{n-1})\mapsto (b\,c_{n-1},\,c_0+a\,\delta_{i,1}c_{n-1},\dots)$ given by multiplication by $x$ modulo $f(x)$. Every such ideal is principal, generated by a unique monic divisor $g(x)$ of $f(x)$. The Euclidean dual $C^{\perp}$ is defined with respect to the standard inner product $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} u_j v_j$. Two linear codes in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ are called equivalent if one is obtained from the other by a permutation of coordinates combined with a multiplication of coordinates by nonzero scalars from $\mathbb{F}_q$, and a code $C$ is called iso-dual if it is equivalent to $C^{\perp}$.

Question: Suppose the generator polynomial $g(x)$ of a polycyclic code $C\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q^n$ associated with $f(x)=x^n-ax^i-b$ satisfies
$$g(x)\mid x^n-ax^i-b\quad\text{and}\quad g(x)^2 = x^n-ax^i-b.$$
Must $C$ necessarily be iso-dual?

The status thus appears unresolved in the publicly indexed literature.

self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ denote the finite field with $q$ elements. For a monic polynomial $f(x)\in\mathbb{F}_q[x]$ of degree $n$, the polycyclic code associated with $f(x)$ and generated by a polynomial $g(x)\in\mathbb{F}_q[x]$ with $g(x)\mid f(x)$ is the ideal $\langle g(x)\rangle$ in the quotient ring $\mathbb{F}_q[x]/\langle f(x)\rangle$, identified with a linear code of length $n$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ via the standard coefficient embedding. A linear code $C$ of length $n$ is called iso-dual if $C$ is equivalent (via a permutation of coordinates) to its Euclidean dual $C^{\perp}$.

Decide whether each of the following two statements is true:

(1) Suppose $q$ is a power of an odd prime, $m$ is a positive integer, and $c\in\mathbb{F}_q^{\times}$. Consider the trinomial $f(x)=x^{2m}\pm 2c\,x^{m}+c^{2}\in\mathbb{F}_q[x]$ and the generator polynomial $g(x)=\pm x^{m}\pm c$ (with any consistent sign choice making $g(x)\mid f(x)$). Is the polycyclic code $\langle g(x)\rangle\subset\mathbb{F}_q[x]/\langle f(x)\rangle$ always iso-dual?

(2) Suppose $q$ is a power of $2$, $m$ and $i$ are positive integers with $0<i<m$, and $a,b\in\mathbb{F}_q$ with $b\ne 0$. Consider the trinomial $f(x)=x^{2m}+a^{2}x^{2i}+b^{2}\in\mathbb{F}_q[x]$ and the generator polynomial $g(x)=x^{m}+a\,x^{i}+b$, which divides $f(x)$ since $f(x)=g(x)^{2}$ in characteristic $2$. Is the polycyclic code $\langle g(x)\rangle\subset\mathbb{F}_q[x]/\langle f(x)\rangle$ always iso-dual?

original_question: Can the McKay correspondence be generalized to more general groups and group schemes, including positive-dimensional algebraic groups, abelian varieties, non-reduced finite group schemes, and profinite groups?
self_contained_problem:
The classical McKay correspondence relates, for a finite subgroup $G \subset \mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ acting on $\mathbb{C}^n$, the representation theory of $G$ (in particular, its nontrivial irreducible representations) with the geometry of a crepant resolution $Y 	o \mathbb{C}^n/G$ of the quotient singularity. In its derived form (after Bridgeland–King–Reid and others), it asserts an equivalence between the $G$-equivariant derived category $D^b_G(\mathbb{C}^n)$ and the derived category $D^b(Y)$ of a suitable crepant resolution (e.g.\ the $G$-Hilbert scheme), and on the level of $K$-theory/cohomology it matches irreducible $G$-representations with a basis of the cohomology of $Y$.

Formulate and establish an analogue of the McKay correspondence for actions of more general group objects on smooth varieties (or schemes), in each of the following settings:

1. Positive-dimensional linear algebraic groups $G$ acting on a smooth variety $X$ with good quotient $X/G$ having canonical/Gorenstein singularities, relating equivariant invariants of $(X,G)$ to invariants of a crepant (or suitable categorical) resolution of $X/G$.

2. Abelian varieties $A$ acting on smooth varieties (or appearing as group schemes of automorphisms of a variety), producing a correspondence between equivariant categories/cohomology for $A$ and invariants of an appropriate resolution of the quotient.

3. Non-reduced finite group schemes $G$ over a field of positive characteristic (e.g.\ infinitesimal group schemes such as $\mu_p$, $\alpha_p$) acting on a smooth scheme $X$, relating the representation theory of $G$ to the geometry of a resolution of $X/G$.

4. Profinite groups $G$ (with continuous actions, e.g.\ on a formal or pro-scheme), establishing a derived equivalence or cohomological correspondence between the equivariant derived category and the derived category of an appropriate (formal) crepant resolution.

In each case, identify the correct notion of crepant (categorical) resolution, formulate the precise statement of the correspondence (at the level of derived categories, $K$-theory, or cohomology), and prove it.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open-ended research program asking for extensions of the McKay correspondence beyond finite groups in $\mathrm{SL}_n$. Partial results exist (e.g., derived McKay correspondences for certain group schemes, motivic/equivariant versions, work in positive characteristic by Yasuda and others, and extensions to some non-reduced or infinitesimal group schemes), but a unified correspondence covering all the listed classes—positive-dimensional algebraic groups, abelian varieties, non-reduced finite group schemes, and profinite groups—is not established. The overall problem remains open.

context_brief: wild extension of Hitchin-fibration and gerbe invariants
original_question: Can work on the Hitchin fibration and on stringy invariants twisted by mu_n-gerbes be extended to the wild case?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a smooth projective complex curve and consider the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_n^d$ of stable Higgs bundles $(E,\varphi)$ on $C$ of rank $n$ and degree $d$, where $\varphi: E \to E \otimes K_C$ is a Higgs field with values in the canonical bundle. The Hitchin map $h: \mathcal{M}_n^d \to \bigoplus_{i=1}^n H^0(C, K_C^{\otimes i})$, sending $(E,\varphi)$ to the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of $\varphi$, exhibits $\mathcal{M}_n^d$ as an integrable system whose generic fibers are abelian varieties. There are natural $\mu_n$-gerbes on the $\mathrm{SL}_n$ and $\mathrm{PGL}_n$ versions $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{SL}_n}^d$ and $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{PGL}_n}^d$ of these moduli spaces, arising from the obstruction to lifting universal projective bundles, and these gerbes are dual under the Langlands/SYZ-type mirror symmetry between the two sides.

Known results establish, via $p$-adic integration, that the stringy $E$-polynomials of $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{SL}_n}^d$ and $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{PGL}_n}^d$ twisted by these dual $\mu_n$-gerbes agree, confirming a topological mirror symmetry conjecture for the tame Hitchin system, and analogous statements have been proved for parabolic Higgs bundles with tame (regular singular) parabolic structure at a finite set of points.

Now allow Higgs fields with poles of arbitrary order (irregular/wild singularities) at a divisor $D \subset C$, with prescribed local irregular types, giving the wild Hitchin moduli space $\mathcal{M}_n^{d,\mathrm{wild}}$ together with its $\mathrm{SL}_n$ and $\mathrm{PGL}_n$ variants and the corresponding $\mu_n$-gerbes.

Problem: Establish topological mirror symmetry in this wild setting. Specifically, prove that the stringy $E$-polynomials (or, more generally, the appropriate stringy/$p$-adic motivic invariants) of $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{SL}_n}^{d,\mathrm{wild}}$ and $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{PGL}_n}^{d,\mathrm{wild}}$, twisted by the dual $\mu_n$-gerbes, are equal, thereby extending the $p$-adic integration / gerby stringy invariants approach to the Hitchin fibration to the wild case.
category_tag: Wild Hitchin fibration and gerby mirror symmetry

No published work appears to extend these gerby stringy-invariant / p-adic integration results to the wild (irregular singular) Hitchin moduli spaces; the problem appears to be open.

original_question: Can motivic integration, or a suitable stringy invariant, be used to prove a Grothendieck-Ogg-Shafarevich type formula in the wild setting?
self_contained_problem:
Let X be a smooth projective curve over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic p > 0, and let F be a constructible ℓ-adic sheaf on X (with ℓ ≠ p) which is wildly ramified at a finite set S ⊂ X of closed points. The classical Grothendieck–Ogg–Shafarevich formula expresses the Euler–Poincaré characteristic χ(X∖S, F) in terms of the generic rank of F and the local Swan conductors Sw_x(F) at the points of wild ramification:

   χ_c(X∖S, F) = rk(F) · χ(X∖S) − Σ_{x∈S} Sw_x(F).

Motivic integration, in the sense of Kontsevich, Denef–Loeser, Sebag, and its variants for formal schemes and Deligne–Mumford stacks, assigns to a variety with mild singularities (or to an arc/jet space) an invariant in a Grothendieck ring of varieties; "stringy invariants" (Batyrev) provide a related class of motivic invariants of singular varieties that incorporate discrepancy data.

Problem. Develop a proof of a Grothendieck–Ogg–Shafarevich-type formula in the wild ramification setting (for ℓ-adic sheaves on varieties over a field of positive characteristic, or more generally for sheaves on schemes over a complete discrete valuation ring with wild ramification along a divisor) using motivic integration and/or a suitable stringy invariant. Concretely: produce a motivic-integration formula whose specialization recovers the Swan-conductor terms appearing in a Grothendieck–Ogg–Shafarevich-type identity for the Euler characteristic, and use this to give a new proof of such a formula in wildly ramified situations where existing proofs (via Kato–Saito ramification theory, etc.) apply, or in situations where no such proof is currently known.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open research direction. While there is substantial work connecting motivic integration to wild ramification (e.g. Yasuda's program on the wild McKay correspondence, and Kato–Saito's higher-dimensional ramification theory), no published result appears to provide a motivic-integration / stringy-invariant proof of a Grothendieck–Ogg–Shafarevich-type formula in the wild setting. The status appears to remain open.
