original_question: Can one explore a version of the McKay correspondence over global fields, especially number fields?
self_contained_problem:
Develop a version of the McKay correspondence in which the base field is a global field, with particular attention to number fields. More precisely, formulate and investigate an analogue of the following picture in the global-arithmetic setting.

Background. Classically, for a finite subgroup $G \subset \mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ acting linearly on $\mathbb{A}^n_{\mathbb{C}}$, the McKay correspondence relates invariants (cohomological, K-theoretic, motivic, or stringy) of the quotient singularity $\mathbb{A}^n_{\mathbb{C}}/G$ and of its crepant resolutions to the representation theory and conjugacy classes of $G$. A motivic/stringy form of the correspondence expresses the stringy motivic invariant of $[\mathbb{A}^n/G]$ as a sum, over conjugacy classes of $G$ (or over $G$-covers of a formal disk), weighted by a certain "age" or "weight" function. Over a non-closed or positive-characteristic base, the wild McKay correspondence (due to Yasuda and others) replaces the sum over conjugacy classes by an integral over the moduli space of $G$-torsors over a punctured formal disk $\mathrm{Spec}\, K((t))$, using a $p$-adic measure, and connects the resulting invariants to mass formulas counting extensions of local fields.

Problem. Let $K$ be a global field (for instance, a number field) and let $G$ be a finite group. Construct a McKay-type correspondence over $K$ that:
(i) defines suitable arithmetic/motivic invariants of the quotient stack $[\mathbb{A}^n_K/G]$ (and of crepant resolutions of $\mathbb{A}^n_K/G$ when they exist),
(ii) expresses these invariants as a global sum or integral over $G$-torsors over $\mathrm{Spec}\, K$ (or over arithmetic curves over $K$), assembling local contributions at all places of $K$ in a manner compatible with the wild McKay correspondence at each completion, and
(iii) relates the resulting global invariants to the asymptotic counting of $G$-extensions of $K$ ordered by discriminant, in the spirit of Malle's conjecture, and to height-zeta-function-type counts on the quotient in the spirit of the Batyrev–Manin program.

Determine to what extent such a correspondence can be defined, prove its existence in significant cases, and clarify its precise relationship with Malle's conjecture on the distribution of number field extensions with prescribed Galois group.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an exploratory open direction. The wild McKay correspondence has been developed over local fields (in particular over $\mathbb{Q}_p$ and equal-characteristic local fields) by Yasuda and collaborators, and is known to connect with mass formulas and to suggest refinements of Malle's conjecture. However, no published global-field version of the McKay correspondence over number fields has been established; the question remains an open research program.

original_question: Can Galois extensions of a number field be counted using a new weight function derived from tuning modules?
self_contained_problem:
Background. Let $K$ be a number field. For a finite group $G$, classical results in arithmetic statistics study the counting function
$$N(K, G; X) = \#\{L/K \text{ Galois extension inside a fixed algebraic closure} : \mathrm{Gal}(L/K) \cong G,\ |N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{d}_{L/K})| \le X\},$$
where $\mathfrak{d}_{L/K}$ is the relative discriminant. More generally, one considers weighted counts of the form
$$N_w(K, G; X) = \sum_{\substack{L/K \text{ Galois} \\ \mathrm{Gal}(L/K)\cong G,\ \mathrm{disc} \le X}} w(L/K),$$
for a weight function $w$ assigned to each Galois extension $L/K$.

Suppose that to every Galois extension $L/K$ with group $G$ one can associate a "tuning module" $T(L/K)$, i.e. a finitely generated module over a suitable arithmetic ring (for instance, a $\mathbb{Z}[G]$-module or an order-module attached to $L/K$) functorially built from $L/K$, and let $w_T(L/K)$ be a numerical invariant extracted from $T(L/K)$ (such as a regulator, an index, or a size of a torsion submodule).

Problem. Define a weight function $w_T$ derived from the tuning modules $T(L/K)$ that produces a meaningful weighted count $N_{w_T}(K, G; X)$ of Galois extensions of $K$, and determine the asymptotic behavior of $N_{w_T}(K, G; X)$ as $X \to \infty$. In particular, exhibit a choice of $w_T$ for which the resulting asymptotic is more tractable, or carries finer arithmetic information, than the standard discriminant-ordered count.
category_tag: arithmetic statistics of number field extensions

Standard literature on counting Galois extensions of number fields uses discriminant or conductor weights and does not address this specific tuning-module weight, suggesting the problem remains open.

context_brief: Global hyperbolicity versus self-adjointness in non-stationary spacetimes
original_question: For a general non-stationary globally hyperbolic spacetime, after conformally rewriting the metric in the form g̃ = -dt² + g̃Σ,ij(t,x) dxi dxj, does global hyperbolicity impose enough geodesic-completeness structure on each spatial slice (Σ_t, g̃Σ_t) to imply essential self-adjointness of the spatial Klein-Gordon or Laplace-type operator L(t)? Equivalently, outside the static, warped-product, and uniformly controlled sliced-space settings already understood in the paper, what precise relation remains between global hyperbolicity of the Lorentzian spacetime and geodesic completeness of the associated Riemannian hypersurfaces?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth, time-oriented, globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold of dimension $n+1$. By choosing a Cauchy temporal function and performing a conformal rescaling, one may write the metric in the form
$$\tilde g \;=\; -dt^{2} + \tilde g_{\Sigma,ij}(t,x)\, dx^{i}dx^{j}, \qquad t\in\mathbb{R},$$
where for each $t\in\mathbb{R}$ the slice $(\Sigma_{t},\tilde g_{\Sigma_{t}})$ is a smooth Riemannian $n$-manifold (with $\Sigma_{t}$ diffeomorphic to a fixed smooth manifold $\Sigma$). For each $t$, let $L(t)$ denote the spatial Klein–Gordon-type operator
$$L(t) \;=\; -\Delta_{\tilde g_{\Sigma_{t}}} + V(t,\cdot),$$
acting on $C_{c}^{\infty}(\Sigma_{t})\subset L^{2}(\Sigma_{t},\mathrm{vol}_{\tilde g_{\Sigma_{t}}})$, with $V$ smooth and (say) bounded below.

Assume one is outside the three already-understood settings:
(i) static spacetimes, (ii) standard warped products $\tilde g = -dt^{2} + f(t)^{2}h(x)$ with $h$ a fixed Riemannian metric on $\Sigma$, and (iii) sliced spaces with uniformly controlled families $\{\tilde g_{\Sigma_{t}}\}_{t}$ (e.g., uniformly equivalent to a fixed complete metric with uniform curvature/derivative bounds).

Question. In this general non-stationary regime, does global hyperbolicity of $(M,g)$ imply that each spatial slice $(\Sigma_{t},\tilde g_{\Sigma_{t}})$ is geodesically complete, and does it imply that $L(t)$ is essentially self-adjoint on $C_{c}^{\infty}(\Sigma_{t})$ for every $t\in\mathbb{R}$? More precisely, determine the exact relationship — in the absence of stationarity, warped-product structure, or uniform slice control — between global hyperbolicity of the Lorentzian manifold $(M,g)$ and geodesic completeness of the Riemannian hypersurfaces $(\Sigma_{t},\tilde g_{\Sigma_{t}})$, and characterize when essential self-adjointness of $L(t)$ follows.
status_search_result: Subsequent work (notably the 2024/2025 paper "Global Hyperbolicity and Self-adjointness," J. Geom. Phys., 2025) extends essential self-adjointness results to additional classes of globally hyperbolic spacetimes via geodesic completeness of Cauchy slices, but only for "various classes" and not for fully general non-stationary spacetimes. The general relation between global hyperbolicity and geodesic completeness of arbitrary Cauchy slices is known to fail in general, and the corresponding self-adjointness question outside the controlled settings remains open.

paper_title: Open Problem: Is There an Online Learning Algorithm That Learns Whenever Online Learning Is Possible?
context_brief: Weak universal online learning characterization by C_w
original_question: In realizable binary online learning with arbitrary measurable target concepts f*: X → {0,1}, say that weak universal online learning is possible under a possibly random instance sequence X if some online learning algorithm has expected total mistakes o(T) through time T for every measurable f*. Let C_w be the family of all possibly random sequences X = {X_t}_{t∈N} such that every disjoint sequence {A_i}_{i∈N} of measurable sets satisfies E[|{i ∈ N : {X_1,...,X_T} intersects A_i}|] = o(T). Is C_w exactly equal to the set of all instance sequences X such that weak universal online learning is possible under X?
self_contained_problem:
Consider realizable binary online learning over a measurable instance space (X, F). Let {X_t}_{t∈N} be a (possibly random) sequence of X-valued random variables, called the instance sequence. An online learning algorithm is a sequence of (possibly randomized, independent of {X_t}) measurable maps f_t : X^{t-1} × {0,1}^{t-1} × X → {0,1}. For a measurable target concept f* : X → {0,1}, the algorithm's expected number of mistakes through time T is

  M_T(f*) = E[ Σ_{t=1}^{T} 1{ f_t(X_1, …, X_{t-1}, f*(X_1), …, f*(X_{t-1}), X_t) ≠ f*(X_t) } ].

The algorithm is called weakly universally consistent under {X_t} if M_T(f*) = o(T) as T → ∞ for every measurable f* : X → {0,1}. Say that weak universal online learning is possible under {X_t} if some online learning algorithm is weakly universally consistent under {X_t}.

Let C_w denote the family of all (possibly random) sequences X = {X_t}_{t∈N} such that, for every disjoint sequence {A_i}_{i∈N} of measurable subsets of X,

  E[ |{ i ∈ N : {X_1, …, X_T} ∩ A_i ≠ ∅ }| ] = o(T)  as T → ∞.

Question: Is C_w exactly equal to the set of all (possibly random) instance sequences X under which weak universal online learning is possible?
status_search_result: A 2022 paper by Blanchard ("Universal Online Learning: an Optimistically Universal Learning Rule", COLT 2022, arXiv:2201.05947) provides a complete characterization of the processes admitting strong and weak universal online learning, and is described as closing the COLT 2021 open problems posed by Hanneke on universal online learning, including the conjectured characterization via C_w.

paper_title: On Global Hyperbolicity of Spacetimes: Topology Meets Functional Analysis
original_question: Let (A, ≺) be a globally hyperbolic partially ordered set, meaning in particular that it carries an interval topology and that its closed intervals [a, b] = {x : a ≼ x ≼ b} are compact in that topology. Does compactness of these intervals by itself force (A, ≺) to be bicontinuous? More specifically, is there an order-theoretic analogue of the spacetime result that compact causal diamonds in the Alexandrov topology imply strong causality in non-compact spacetimes of dimension strictly greater than 2? If such an analogue exists, what should play the role of the condition “dimension strictly greater than 2” for globally hyperbolic posets, and is it possible that no dimension-type restriction is needed in the poset setting even though it is needed for spacetimes?
self_contained_problem:
Let (A, ≺) be a partially ordered set with strict order ≺ and associated reflexive order ≼. For a, b ∈ A, write [a, b] = {x ∈ A : a ≼ x ≼ b}. Equip A with the interval topology, namely the topology generated by the subbasis of sets of the form {x : a ≺ x} and {x : x ≺ b} for a, b ∈ A.

Recall that (A, ≺) is said to be bicontinuous if there is an auxiliary "way-below" relation ≪ on A satisfying the standard interpolation and approximation axioms in both the order ≼ and its opposite, so that for every x ∈ A the set ↟x = {y : x ≪ y} is directed-like and x = sup{y : y ≪ x}, with the analogous properties holding in the opposite order.

Call (A, ≺) a globally hyperbolic poset if every closed interval [a, b] is compact in the interval topology.

Question. Does the compactness of all intervals [a, b] in the interval topology by itself imply that (A, ≺) is bicontinuous? This is the order-theoretic analogue of the spacetime statement that compactness of all closed causal diamonds in the Alexandrov topology implies strong causality of the spacetime, where in the spacetime version the conclusion is known to require the dimension to be strictly greater than 2. If such an analogue holds, identify the order-theoretic condition on (A, ≺) that should play the role of the dimension restriction; in particular, decide whether any such restriction is needed in the purely order-theoretic setting, or whether compactness of intervals alone suffices to force bicontinuity.
category_tag: Globally hyperbolic posets and domain theory
status_search_result: Web search surfaces the foundational works of Martin–Panangaden on globally hyperbolic posets and interval domains, where bicontinuity is typically built into the definition. No source located resolves the specific question of whether compactness of intervals in the interval topology alone forces bicontinuity, nor identifies an order-theoretic analogue of the dimension>2 hypothesis. The status therefore appears unresolved in the available literature.

paper_title: On Global Hyperbolicity of Spacetimes: Topology Meets Functional Analysis
context_brief: Reconstructing spacetime topology from interval domains
original_question: Given the equivalence between the category of globally hyperbolic posets and the category of interval domains, can the topology of a spacetime be reconstructed in a technically rigorous way from the topology of an interval domain? Moreover, since topologies such as the Zeeman fine topology, Göbel’s generalization, and the Hawking–King–McCarthy topology are not metrizable, does that non-metrizability help identify an appropriate spacetime topology other than the manifold topology when interval domains are taken as the underlying order-theoretic model?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. A poset (P, ≤) is called continuous if it carries the standard order-theoretic notions of way-below relation ≪ and approximation, and bicontinuous if both (P, ≤) and its order-dual are continuous. A globally hyperbolic poset is a bicontinuous poset whose interval topology (generated by sets of the form ↑a ∩ ↓b) is locally compact and Hausdorff. The interval domain IP of such a poset is the set of nonempty closed order-intervals [a,b] = {x : a ≤ x ≤ b}, ordered by reverse inclusion, equipped with the Scott topology; this construction yields a category-theoretic equivalence between the category of globally hyperbolic posets (with suitable morphisms) and the category of interval domains.

A globally hyperbolic spacetime (M, g) — i.e. a time-oriented Lorentzian manifold admitting a Cauchy hypersurface — becomes such a poset under the causal order ≤ given by the chronological/causal future. On M one may consider, besides the manifold topology τM, several finer topologies: the Zeeman fine topology τZ, Göbel's generalization τG (extending Zeeman's construction to curved spacetimes), and the Hawking–King–McCarthy (path) topology τHKM. Each of these strictly refines τM and is known to be non-metrizable.

Problem. Let (M, g) be a globally hyperbolic spacetime, viewed as a globally hyperbolic poset, and let IM be its associated interval domain with the Scott topology.

(a) Provide a precise, mathematically rigorous procedure that reconstructs a topology on M from purely order- and domain-theoretic data of IM, and characterize which topologies on M (manifold, Zeeman, Göbel, Hawking–King–McCarthy, or others) can be recovered in this way.

(b) Determine whether the non-metrizability of the topologies τZ, τG, τHKM — together with the order-theoretic and topological structure of the interval domain IM — singles out a canonical "spacetime topology" on M distinct from the manifold topology τM that is intrinsic to the interval-domain model.
status_search_result: Martin and Panangaden established that globally hyperbolic spacetimes form a category equivalent to interval domains and that the manifold topology can be recovered as the interval topology of the causal poset. However, no published work appears to address the rigorous reconstruction of non-manifold spacetime topologies (Zeeman, Göbel, Hawking–King–McCarthy) from interval-domain data, nor whether their non-metrizability picks out a canonical alternative spacetime topology. The question therefore appears to remain open.

original_question: For functions defined on a finite interval, what is the full characterization of one-parameter families of fractional integral operators I^alpha and associated fractional derivative operators D^alpha that satisfy the six desiderata HL1-HL6: linearity of I^alpha and D^alpha, the semigroup law I^alpha1 o I^alpha2 = I^(alpha1+alpha2), the left-inverse identity D^alpha o I^alpha = Id, existence of the limits D^alpha -> D^0 as alpha -> 0 and D^alpha -> D^1 as alpha -> 1, D^0 equal to the identity, and D^1 equal to the first derivative?
self_contained_problem:
Consider functions defined on a finite real interval $[a,b]$. Determine and fully characterize all one-parameter families of linear operators $\{I^{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\ge 0}$ (to be interpreted as fractional integrals) and the associated one-parameter families of linear operators $\{D^{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\ge 0}$ (to be interpreted as fractional derivatives) acting on suitable spaces of functions on $[a,b]$ that simultaneously satisfy the following six desiderata:

(HL1) For every $\alpha\ge 0$, $I^{\alpha}$ is linear.

(HL2) For every $\alpha\ge 0$, $D^{\alpha}$ is linear.

(HL3) Index (semigroup) law: $I^{\alpha_1}\circ I^{\alpha_2}=I^{\alpha_1+\alpha_2}$ for all $\alpha_1,\alpha_2\ge 0$.

(HL4) Left-inverse property: $D^{\alpha}\circ I^{\alpha}=\mathrm{Id}$ for all $\alpha\ge 0$.

(HL5) The limits $\lim_{\alpha\to 0^{+}} D^{\alpha}=D^{0}$ and $\lim_{\alpha\to 1^{-}} D^{\alpha}=D^{1}$ exist (in an appropriate operator topology on the chosen function space).

(HL6) $D^{0}=\mathrm{Id}$ and $D^{1}=\dfrac{d}{dx}$.

Provide a complete description of every such pair of families $(I^{\alpha},D^{\alpha})$ on a finite interval, going beyond the Riemann–Liouville family (which is known to satisfy these desiderata together with stronger additional conditions).
status_search_result: The problem appears to be posed as an open problem in the line of work by Luchko on general fractional integrals and derivatives. While Luchko's 2023 paper "The General Fractional Integrals and Derivatives on a Finite Interval" extends Sonin-kernel-based GFI/GFD to finite intervals and provides families satisfying versions of the desiderata, a full characterization of all one-parameter families on a finite interval satisfying exactly the six Hardy–Littlewood/Hilfer–Luchko desiderata (without strengthening them) does not appear to have been completed; on the half-line a uniqueness-type characterization is known under stronger conditions, and the finite-interval case is presented as an extension/open question.

original_question: What is the general form of fractional integrals and fractional derivatives for functions defined on a finite interval when those operators are required to satisfy the desiderata HL1-HL6 that formalize the expected algebraic and limiting behavior of fractional calculus operators?
self_contained_problem:
Let $[a,b]\subset\mathbb{R}$ be a finite interval and consider, on a suitable space of real- or complex-valued functions defined on $[a,b]$, two one-parameter families of linear operators
$$\{I^{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\ge 0},\qquad \{D^{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\ge 0},$$
which are intended to play the roles of "fractional integral" and "fractional derivative" of order $\alpha$, respectively. Require that these families satisfy the following six desiderata:

(HL1) $I^{0}=D^{0}=\mathrm{Id}$ (the identity operator).

(HL2) $I^{1}$ coincides with the ordinary definite integration operator $f\mapsto \int_{a}^{x} f(t)\,dt$, and $D^{1}$ coincides with the ordinary derivative $\dfrac{d}{dx}$ (on appropriate domains).

(HL3) Index law for the integrals: $I^{\alpha}\,I^{\beta}=I^{\alpha+\beta}$ for all $\alpha,\beta\ge 0$.

(HL4) The derivative is a left inverse of the integral: $D^{\alpha}\,I^{\alpha}=\mathrm{Id}$ for all $\alpha\ge 0$.

(HL5) Continuity (in an appropriate topology) of the families with respect to the order $\alpha$, including the limiting behavior $I^{\alpha}\to\mathrm{Id}$ and $D^{\alpha}\to\mathrm{Id}$ as $\alpha\to 0^{+}$.

(HL6) An appropriate generalized Fundamental Theorem of Fractional Calculus connecting $I^{\alpha}$ and $D^{\alpha}$ on the chosen function spaces.

Problem: Determine the most general form of the operator families $\{I^{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\ge 0}$ and $\{D^{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\ge 0}$ acting on functions defined on the finite interval $[a,b]$ such that all six desiderata (HL1)–(HL6) are satisfied. In particular, characterize the admissible kernels (and the associated function spaces) for which such left- and right-sided fractional integrals and derivatives can be constructed, and exhibit their explicit representation.
category_tag: general fractional calculus on a finite interval
status_search_result: A 2023 paper by Luchko, "The General Fractional Integrals and Derivatives on a Finite Interval" (Mathematics 11(4), 1031), introduces left- and right-sided general fractional integrals and derivatives on a finite interval using Sonine-type kernel sets (Luchko/Kochubei sets) and develops their fundamental theorem, providing a substantial answer to the problem in this kernel-based framework. A fully general classification under all six desiderata HL1–HL6 in maximal generality does not appear to be definitively closed, so the problem is best regarded as partially solved.

original_question: Can the analytical characterization problems for fractional integrals and derivatives be developed in the multidimensional setting for functions defined on R^n, rather than only for one-dimensional domains?
self_contained_problem:
Develop analytical characterizations of fractional integration and fractional differentiation operators for functions of several real variables. Concretely, for a suitable class of functions f : ℝⁿ → ℝ (or ℂ), one considers multidimensional analogues of the Riemann–Liouville/Riesz fractional integrals
  (I^α f)(x) = c(n,α) ∫_{ℝⁿ} |x − y|^{α−n} f(y) dy,  0 < Re α < n,
and the corresponding fractional derivatives D^α (e.g. Riesz, Marchaud, or hypersingular-integral-type derivatives).

Problem: Provide intrinsic analytical characterizations of the ranges and domains of these multidimensional operators. In particular:

(a) Characterize the image I^α(X) of a given function space X ⊂ L^p(ℝⁿ) (or X = L^p, Lipschitz, Hölder, Besov, Sobolev, etc.) by means of explicit conditions on the function itself (such as integrability, smoothness moduli, finite differences, hypersingular integrals, or behavior at infinity), without reference to the operator I^α.

(b) Determine necessary and sufficient analytical conditions on a function g : ℝⁿ → ℝ in order that g = I^α f for some f ∈ X, and analogously characterize when a function lies in the natural domain of D^α.

(c) Establish the multivariate analogues of one-dimensional inversion, composition, and mapping theorems for fractional integrals and derivatives in this characterization framework.

Resolve these characterization problems in the n-dimensional setting for n ≥ 2, paralleling the known one-dimensional theory.
status_search_result: Multidimensional fractional integration (Riesz potentials) and hypersingular-integral characterizations of their ranges on ℝⁿ have been extensively developed, notably in the monograph of Samko–Kilbas–Marichev and in Samko's "Hypersingular Integrals and Their Applications," which give characterizations of Riesz potentials of L^p functions for n ≥ 1 via finite differences and hypersingular integrals. However, complete intrinsic analytical characterizations for general function spaces and for general fractional-derivative-type operators in ℝⁿ remain an active research direction, with many cases still open.

original_question: Given a function kappa in C^-1(0,+infinity), what conditions are necessary and sufficient for kappa to belong to the class Ln of generalized Sonine-kernel pairs satisfying (kappa * k)(t) = 1^{<n>}(t), and how can one derive a representation of the associated kernel k?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C_{-1}(0,+\infty)$ denote the space of functions $f:(0,+\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $f(t)=t^{p}f_1(t)$ for some $p>-1$ and some $f_1\in C[0,+\infty)$, and let $C_{-1,0}(0,+\infty)$ denote the subspace of those with $p>-1$ allowing the exponent to range so that $f$ may be locally integrable but possibly singular at $0$. For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ let 
$$1^{\langle n\rangle}(t)=\frac{t^{n-1}}{(n-1)!},\qquad t>0,$$
and denote by $*$ the Laplace convolution $(f*g)(t)=\int_0^t f(t-\tau)g(\tau)\,d\tau$. Define the class $\mathcal{L}_n$ of generalized Sonine kernel pairs as the set of pairs $(\varkappa,k)$ with $\varkappa\in C_{-1}(0,+\infty)$, $k\in C_{-1,0}(0,+\infty)$ satisfying
$$(\varkappa * k)(t)=1^{\langle n\rangle}(t),\qquad t>0.$$

Problem: Given a function $\varkappa\in C_{-1}(0,+\infty)$, find necessary and sufficient conditions on $\varkappa$ for the existence of a kernel $k\in C_{-1,0}(0,+\infty)$ such that $(\varkappa,k)\in\mathcal{L}_n$, and provide an explicit representation formula for the associated kernel $k$ in terms of $\varkappa$.
category_tag: Generalized Sonine kernels and fractional calculus
status_search_result: A complete intrinsic characterization of $\mathcal{L}_n$ membership for arbitrary $\varkappa\in C_{-1}(0,+\infty)$, together with an explicit formula for the associated kernel $k$, does not appear to be established. Existing work characterizes pairs in $\mathcal{L}_n$ via Laplace transforms ($\widetilde\varkappa(p)\widetilde k(p)=1/p^n$) and constructs examples (power kernels, Bessel-type kernels, and pairs derived from $\mathcal{L}_1$ Sonine pairs), but it is also noted that such constructions do not exhaust $\mathcal{L}_n$. The problem of giving necessary and sufficient conditions plus a representation of $k$ appears to remain open in the general setting.

original_question: Can one develop a theory of general fractional integrals and general fractional derivatives on conventional function spaces beyond the spaces treated in the paper, in particular on L^p spaces and on Holder weighted spaces?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $\kappa:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ be a Sonine kernel, i.e. a locally integrable function for which there exists an associated kernel $k$ such that
$$\int_0^t \kappa(t-\tau)\,k(\tau)\,d\tau = 1, \qquad t>0.$$
For such a pair $(\kappa,k)$, define the general fractional integral (GFI) and the general fractional derivatives (GFD) of Riemann–Liouville and Caputo type, respectively, by
$$(\mathbb{I}_{(\kappa)} f)(t) = \int_0^t \kappa(t-\tau) f(\tau)\,d\tau,$$
$$(\mathbb{D}_{(k)} f)(t) = \frac{d}{dt}\int_0^t k(t-\tau) f(\tau)\,d\tau, \qquad ({}_*\mathbb{D}_{(k)} f)(t) = \int_0^t k(t-\tau) f'(\tau)\,d\tau.$$
Recall the classical weighted Hölder space $H_0^{\lambda,\mu}([a,b])$ (functions $f$ with $(t-a)^\mu f(t)$ Hölder continuous of order $\lambda$ vanishing at $a$) and the Lebesgue spaces $L^p([a,b])$, $1\le p\le\infty$, on which the Riemann–Liouville fractional integrals and derivatives have a well-developed mapping theory.

Problem. Develop a corresponding theory of the general fractional integrals $\mathbb{I}_{(\kappa)}$ and the general fractional derivatives $\mathbb{D}_{(k)}$, ${}_*\mathbb{D}_{(k)}$ with Sonine kernels acting on:
(i) the Lebesgue spaces $L^p([a,b])$, $1\le p\le\infty$;
(ii) the weighted Hölder spaces $H_0^{\lambda,\mu}([a,b])$.

Specifically, identify natural subclasses of Sonine kernels for which $\mathbb{I}_{(\kappa)}$, $\mathbb{D}_{(k)}$, and ${}_*\mathbb{D}_{(k)}$ are bounded operators on these spaces, characterize their ranges, establish the corresponding fundamental theorems of general fractional calculus in this functional-analytic setting, and obtain mapping properties that parallel the classical Hardy–Littlewood and Hölder-space theorems for the Riemann–Liouville operators.
category_tag: general fractional calculus on function spaces
status_search_result: Recent surveys on general fractional integrals/derivatives with Sonine kernels (e.g., Luchko 2021–2023) explicitly list the development of a theory on $L^p$ and Hölder weighted spaces as an important open direction. While the theory has been advanced on spaces of continuous functions, on functions with integrable singularity at zero, on a finite interval, and via multi-kernel and operational-calculus extensions, no comprehensive mapping theory analogous to the Riemann–Liouville case on $L^p$ or weighted Hölder spaces appears to have been established.

original_question: How can infinite-state-representation algorithms for numerically solving Caputo-type fractional differential equations be designed and analyzed rigorously rather than heuristically, including the construction of quadrature formulas, the interaction between the ODE solver for the infinite states and the quadrature rule, the effect of algorithmic parameters on the final accuracy, and error bounds whose dependence on the fractional order alpha is understood uniformly over alpha in (0,1)?
self_contained_problem:
For a fractional order $\alpha\in(0,1)$, the Caputo fractional derivative of a sufficiently smooth function $y:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}$ is defined by
$$ ({}^C D^\alpha y)(t) \;=\; \frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}\int_0^t (t-s)^{-\alpha}\, y'(s)\,ds. $$
Consider the initial value problem
$$ ({}^C D^\alpha y)(t) = f(t,y(t)),\qquad t\in[0,T],\qquad y(0)=y_0, $$
with $f$ Lipschitz in its second argument.

A so-called infinite-state representation reformulates this problem by introducing an auxiliary function $\phi(t,\omega)$ on $[0,T]\times(0,\infty)$ such that
$$ y(t) \;=\; y_0 + \int_0^\infty \mu_\alpha(\omega)\,\phi(t,\omega)\,d\omega,\qquad \mu_\alpha(\omega) = \frac{\sin(\alpha\pi)}{\pi}\,\omega^{-\alpha}, $$
where for each $\omega>0$, $\phi(\cdot,\omega)$ satisfies the (classical, integer-order) ordinary differential equation
$$ \partial_t \phi(t,\omega) + \omega\,\phi(t,\omega) \;=\; f(t,y(t)),\qquad \phi(0,\omega)=0. $$
A numerical scheme based on this representation discretizes the $\omega$-integral by a quadrature rule with nodes $\{\omega_j\}_{j=1}^N\subset(0,\infty)$ and weights $\{w_j\}_{j=1}^N$, and integrates each of the $N$ resulting ODEs with a (classical) one-step or multistep method of step size $h>0$.

Develop such an infinite-state-representation algorithm together with a rigorous (non-heuristic) error analysis that establishes all of the following:

1. An explicit construction of the quadrature rule (choice of nodes, weights, and number $N$ of nodes) suited to the singular weight $\mu_\alpha$.

2. A precise specification of the coupling between the chosen ODE solver applied to the auxiliary equations and the quadrature rule, including how the ODE step size $h$ and the quadrature parameters interact.

3. A quantitative description of how the algorithmic parameters $N$, $\{\omega_j\}$, $\{w_j\}$, and $h$ influence the final approximation error $\max_{0\le t_n\le T}|y(t_n)-y_n|$.

4. An error bound of the form
$$ \max_{0\le t_n\le T}\,|y(t_n)-y_n| \;\le\; C(\alpha)\,\bigl(\Phi_1(N) + \Phi_2(h)\bigr), $$
in which the dependence of the constant $C(\alpha)$ on $\alpha$ is made explicit, and the bound is shown to hold uniformly for all $\alpha\in(0,1)$, i.e.\ $\sup_{\alpha\in(0,1)} C(\alpha)<\infty$, so that the constants do not blow up as $\alpha\to 0^+$ or $\alpha\to 1^-$.

Provide such an algorithm and proof, or determine the optimal achievable rates $\Phi_1,\Phi_2$.
status_search_result: The problem of rigorous, non-heuristic analysis of infinite-state-representation (diffusive/oscillatory) algorithms for Caputo fractional ODEs, with quadrature/ODE-solver coupling and $\alpha$-uniform error bounds, is identified as an open program. Recent literature (Diethelm and co-authors, 2021–2024) has begun rigorous analyses of specific Gauss-type and exponentially-convergent quadratures for the kernel, but a complete framework giving uniform-in-$\alpha\in(0,1)$ error bounds for general infinite-state schemes is not established. Status appears open.

original_question: For scalar Caputo terminal value problems of the form CD^alpha_{a+} y(t) = f(t, y(t)) with a terminal condition y(b) = y*, what numerical strategy is best for updating the unknown initial value y(a) inside shooting methods, and how do shooting, collocation, Galerkin, Nystrom, spectral, and spectral-element approaches compare in computational cost, convergence, and the design of basis functions that capture the endpoint singular behaviour of exact solutions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the scalar terminal value problem for a Caputo fractional differential equation of order α ∈ (0,1):
  (CD^α_{a+} y)(t) = f(t, y(t)),  t ∈ [a,b],   y(b) = y*,
where CD^α_{a+} denotes the Caputo fractional derivative based at a, f : [a,b] × ℝ → ℝ is a sufficiently smooth right-hand side, and y* ∈ ℝ is a prescribed terminal value. A shooting method reformulates this problem by guessing the unknown initial value y(a) = η, solving the resulting Caputo initial value problem forward to t = b, and iteratively updating η so that the computed value at b matches y*.

Address the following:

(a) Determine the most efficient and accurate strategy for updating the guess η in the next iteration of such a shooting procedure (in comparison with bisection, secant, Newton, and related root-finding/proportional-type updates), including a rigorous convergence analysis and quantitative comparison of iteration counts and runtime.

(b) The terminal value problem can equivalently be recast as a Fredholm integral equation of the second kind for y on [a,b]. Carry out a systematic comparison of shooting, collocation, Galerkin, Nyström, spectral, and spectral-element methods for solving this equation, addressing computational cost, rates of convergence, and stability.

(c) Design a basis of approximating functions (for use in the Galerkin/collocation/spectral/spectral-element schemes) that simultaneously
   (i) reproduces the typical endpoint singular behaviour of the exact solution and its derivatives as t → a (which generically involves non-integer powers of (t − a)), and
   (ii) yields rapid (ideally spectral) convergence on the smooth component of the solution away from a.
Prove convergence rates for the resulting scheme.
status_search_result: Recent work has made progress on part (a): a "proportional secting" update for the shooting iterate has been proposed and shown numerically to outperform bisection by a factor of roughly 4–10, and shooting–Newton and shooting–secant variants have been studied. However, no consensus optimal strategy with a complete convergence theory has been established, and the broader comparative study of collocation/Galerkin/Nyström/spectral/spectral-element methods for the equivalent Fredholm formulation, together with the construction of singularity-adapted bases capturing the endpoint behaviour as t → a, remains largely open.

original_question: Can one prove the fundamental theorems of fractional calculus for exact fractional differences of non-integer order that arise in lattice fractional calculus and exact-difference approaches to nonlocal continuum and lattice mechanics?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $h>0$ be a fixed lattice spacing and let $f:h\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function defined on the one-dimensional lattice $h\mathbb{Z}=\{hn:n\in\mathbb{Z}\}$. For a real (non-integer) order $\alpha>0$, define the exact fractional difference operator $\Delta^{\alpha}_{h}$ acting on $f$ at the point $x=hn$ by

$$\bigl(\Delta^{\alpha}_{h} f\bigr)(hn)\;=\;\frac{1}{h^{\alpha}}\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty} K_{\alpha}(n-m)\, f(hm),$$

where the kernel $K_{\alpha}:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{R}$ is the "exact" kernel chosen so that the discrete Fourier symbol of $\Delta^{\alpha}_{h}$ on the Brillouin zone $[-\pi/h,\pi/h]$ equals $|k|^{\alpha}$ (or $(ik)^{\alpha}$ in the directed case); explicitly,

$$K_{\alpha}(n)\;=\;\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} |\theta|^{\alpha}\, e^{i n\theta}\,d\theta,$$

and analogously for the Riesz/Caputo-type variants. Let $I^{\alpha}_{h}$ denote the corresponding exact fractional sum operator, defined as the convolution operator on $\ell^{p}(h\mathbb{Z})$ whose Fourier symbol is $|k|^{-\alpha}$ on the Brillouin zone (with appropriate regularization at $k=0$).

Problem. For arbitrary non-integer order $\alpha\in(0,\infty)\setminus\mathbb{N}$, prove (or disprove) the two fundamental theorems of fractional calculus for the pair $(\Delta^{\alpha}_{h},I^{\alpha}_{h})$ on a suitable function class $X\subset\mathbb{R}^{h\mathbb{Z}}$:

(FT1) For every $f\in X$,
$$\Delta^{\alpha}_{h}\bigl(I^{\alpha}_{h} f\bigr)\;=\;f.$$

(FT2) For every $f\in X$,
$$I^{\alpha}_{h}\bigl(\Delta^{\alpha}_{h} f\bigr)(hn)\;=\;f(hn)\;-\;R_{\alpha}[f](hn),$$
where $R_{\alpha}[f]$ is an explicit "boundary/initial-data" remainder that reduces, in the limit $h\to 0$, to the corresponding remainder term of continuum Riemann–Liouville (resp. Caputo, resp. Riesz) fractional calculus, and that vanishes when $f$ satisfies suitable decay/initial conditions.

Identify the maximal natural function class $X$ on which (FT1) and (FT2) hold and give a precise form of the remainder $R_{\alpha}$.
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not return any work explicitly establishing the two fundamental theorems of fractional calculus for the "exact fractional differences" of non-integer order used in lattice fractional calculus. General fractional calculus frameworks have proved fundamental theorems for various integro-differential operators, but a direct proof for the exact-difference (Fourier-symbol $|k|^{\alpha}$) lattice operators of non-integer order does not appear in the indexed literature, so the status is best described as unknown/likely still open.

original_question: What is the most general equation that describes the non-Markovian dynamics of open quantum systems with memory, and how should such a theory be extended to include time-dependent parameters, relativistic quantum systems with memory, path-integral formulations for open systems, uncertainty relations for open systems, and pure stationary states of open systems?
self_contained_problem:
An open quantum system is described by a density operator $\rho(t)$ acting on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$, whose evolution is governed by a (generally non-Markovian) master equation of the form
$$\frac{d\rho(t)}{dt} = \mathcal{L}_t[\rho(t)] + \int_{t_0}^{t} \mathcal{K}(t,s)[\rho(s)]\, ds,$$
where $\mathcal{L}_t$ is a (possibly time-dependent) generator and $\mathcal{K}(t,s)$ is a memory kernel acting on trace-class operators, both required to produce a completely positive trace-preserving family of maps $\{\Phi(t,t_0)\}$ from initial to current states.

Determine the most general admissible form of such an evolution equation describing non-Markovian dynamics of open quantum systems with memory. Specifically:

1. Characterize all pairs $(\mathcal{L}_t, \mathcal{K}(t,s))$ for which the resulting two-parameter family $\Phi(t,t_0)$ is completely positive and trace-preserving for all $t \geq t_0$, generalizing the Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad theorem to the non-Markovian setting with explicit time-dependent parameters.

2. Extend the formulation to relativistic quantum systems with memory, providing a Lorentz-covariant analogue of the master equation above acting on states of a relativistic quantum field or particle.

3. Provide a path-integral representation of the resulting non-Markovian completely positive dynamics, expressing $\Phi(t,t_0)$ as a functional integral with an influence functional encoding the memory kernel.

4. Derive the corresponding generalized uncertainty relations for canonically conjugate observables under non-Markovian evolution, in terms of $\mathcal{L}_t$ and $\mathcal{K}(t,s)$.

5. Classify the pure stationary states $\rho_\infty = |\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$ that are fixed points of the evolution, i.e. satisfy $\mathcal{L}_t[\rho_\infty] + \int_{t_0}^{t}\mathcal{K}(t,s)[\rho_\infty]\,ds = 0$ for all $t$, and give necessary and sufficient conditions on $(\mathcal{L}_t,\mathcal{K})$ for such pure stationary states to exist.
status_search_result: The general form of non-Markovian master equations for open quantum systems remains an active research area without a single agreed-upon canonical form. While Lindblad's theorem fully classifies Markovian generators, the non-Markovian case—especially with time-dependent parameters, relativistic memory effects, path-integral formulations, uncertainty relations, and pure stationary states—is the subject of ongoing investigation, and no comprehensive solution is established.

original_question: What fundamentally new forms of self-organization arise in systems with nonlocality in time and memory, especially when changing memory creates a hierarchy of relaxation times that qualitatively alters the system's behavior?
self_contained_problem:
Consider dynamical systems whose evolution is nonlocal in time, in the sense that the state x(t) at time t is determined not only by its instantaneous value and local derivatives but also by its full past history through a memory kernel K(t,s). Concretely, consider evolution equations of the form

  (D^{α}_{t} x)(t) = F(x(t), t) + ∫_{0}^{t} K(t,s) G(x(s), s) ds,

where D^{α}_{t} denotes a fractional time derivative of order α ∈ (0,1] (e.g. Caputo or Riemann–Liouville), F and G are nonlinear functions, and K(t,s) is a memory kernel that may itself evolve in time, thereby inducing a hierarchy of distinct relaxation times τ_1 < τ_2 < … < τ_n.

Identify and classify the qualitatively new forms of self-organization (e.g. attractors, coherent structures, pattern formation, synchronization regimes, or phase transitions) that can arise in such systems specifically because of the temporal nonlocality and the time-evolving memory, and which do not occur in their memoryless (local-in-time) counterparts. In particular, characterize how a hierarchy of relaxation times generated by a changing memory kernel qualitatively alters the long-time behaviour and emergent collective states of the system, with all other parameters held fixed.
status_search_result: The question is a broad open research direction in nonlinear fractional dynamics concerning self-organization in systems with time nonlocality and evolving memory. No general classification or solution appears in the literature; it is posed as a future research direction rather than a precise conjecture, so the status is best described as open.

paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
original_question: For moduli spaces of supersymmetric gauge theories, Hilbert series (HS) and highest weight generating functions (HWGs) enumerate gauge-invariant operators, while phase diagrams encode the poset structure of symplectic leaves and transverse slices. Can one compute the phase diagrams directly from the corresponding HS or HWGs?
self_contained_problem:
Let X be a symplectic singularity, that is, a normal complex algebraic variety whose smooth locus carries a holomorphic symplectic 2-form that extends to a (possibly degenerate) regular 2-form on any resolution. Such an X admits a finite stratification into symplectic leaves; the closure-ordering on these leaves yields a finite graded poset (the Hasse / phase diagram), and to each covering relation L' < L one associates a transverse slice, itself a symplectic singularity, whose isomorphism type decorates the corresponding edge.

Suppose X is presented as the moduli space (Higgs or Coulomb branch) of a 3d N=4 quiver gauge theory, and that the following data are given:
(a) the Hilbert series HS_X(t,z) = Σ dim(R_n)_λ · t^n · z^λ, the refined generating function counting the graded multiplicities of the global-symmetry irreducible representations appearing in the coordinate ring R = C[X];
(b) the highest weight generating function HWG_X(μ,t), defined by HS_X(t,z) = Σ_{λ dominant} a_λ(t) · χ_λ(z), with HWG_X(μ,t) = Σ a_λ(t) μ^λ, encoding the same information by labeling representations through their highest weights.

Problem. Provide an algorithm that, taking only HS_X(t,z) and/or HWG_X(μ,t) as input, outputs the full phase diagram of X — namely the graded poset of symplectic leaf closures together with the transverse-slice decoration on every covering edge — and prove that the algorithm is correct. Equivalently: determine to what extent the data (HS_X, HWG_X) determine the Hasse diagram of symplectic leaves and its transverse-slice labels of X, and exhibit an explicit reconstruction procedure or an obstruction to one.
status_search_result: No general algorithm extracting Hasse/phase diagrams of symplectic leaves directly from Hilbert series or highest weight generating functions appears in the literature. Phase diagrams are typically computed via quiver subtraction or Kraft–Procesi transitions on the underlying quiver, not from HS/HWG data, and HS/HWG are usually treated as finer/separate invariants. Recent work (e.g. on classifying isolated symplectic singularities via 3d N=4 Coulomb branches) continues to treat the Hasse diagram, Hilbert series and HWG as independent ingredients in the characterization, suggesting the question remains open.

paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
original_question: What is a rigorous mathematical definition of Coulomb branches for 3d N = 4 gauge theories?
self_contained_problem:
Background. A three-dimensional N=4 supersymmetric gauge theory is specified, on the physical side, by a compact (or complex reductive) gauge group G together with a quaternionic (i.e. symplectic) representation M of G. To such a theory physicists associate a hyperkähler moduli space called the Coulomb branch, whose construction in physics involves a quantum-corrected metric and is not a priori algebro-geometric.

Problem. Give a rigorous mathematical definition of the Coulomb branch of a general 3-dimensional N=4 gauge theory as an algebro-geometric object. Concretely, for every pair (G, M) consisting of a complex reductive group G and a finite-dimensional symplectic representation M of G, construct in a functorial way:

(i) a complex affine Poisson variety M_C(G, M),
(ii) equipped with a ℂ^×-action of suitable weight on its coordinate ring,
(iii) whose generic symplectic leaf recovers the expected hyperkähler structure predicted by physics,
(iv) with a natural noncommutative deformation quantization (the quantized Coulomb branch),

such that the construction:
(a) reduces, in the case where M = N ⊕ N^* for some representation N of G, to the affine variety whose coordinate ring is the G((t))-equivariant Borel–Moore homology of the variety of triples (the BFN construction);
(b) is well-defined for arbitrary symplectic representations M (not necessarily of cotangent type);
(c) is compatible with known dualities and expected properties (e.g. symplectic singularities, the expected behaviour under Hamiltonian reduction, gauging, and 3d mirror symmetry).

State and prove a theorem providing such a definition, or determine whether such a uniform mathematical definition exists.
category_tag: Coulomb branches of 3d N=4 gauge theories
status_search_result: For gauge theories whose matter representation is of cotangent type N ⊕ N*, Braverman, Finkelberg and Nakajima gave a rigorous mathematical definition of the Coulomb branch as an affine Poisson variety, using equivariant Borel–Moore homology of a "variety of triples" (the BFN construction, 2015–2016). This has been widely developed since then (e.g. quiver cases related to slices in the affine Grassmannian). However, a fully general mathematical definition for arbitrary symplectic representations M (not of cotangent type), and one that uniformly captures all expected physical properties, is not yet available; the problem is therefore considered partially solved.

paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
original_question: Xie and Yau conjectured that every three-dimensional canonical singularity gives rise to a 5d N = 1 superconformal field theory. Does M-theory on any 3d canonical singularity always define a 5d N = 1 SCFT, and can tools such as dot diagrams and magnetic quivers be used to verify this conjecture?
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. In M-theory, compactification on a local Calabi–Yau threefold with an isolated singularity is expected to engineer a five-dimensional superconformal field theory (5d N=1 SCFT) at the origin of its Coulomb branch. A normal complex threefold singularity (X,0) is called canonical if, for some (equivalently any) resolution π: Y → X with exceptional divisors E_i, one has K_Y = π* K_X + Σ a_i E_i with a_i ≥ 0. Among the structural data attached to a 5d N=1 SCFT one has its Coulomb branch (with prepotential determined by triple intersection numbers on a crepant resolution), its flavor symmetry (read off from the singularity type along the one-dimensional singular locus), and combinatorial/representation-theoretic descriptions such as "dot diagrams" and "magnetic quivers" that compute, for instance, the Higgs branch.

Conjecture (to be assessed). Every three-dimensional canonical singularity (X,0), viewed as a local Calabi–Yau threefold, defines via M-theory a five-dimensional N=1 superconformal field theory.

Problem. Prove or disprove the above conjecture. Equivalently, determine whether for every three-dimensional canonical singularity the M-theory compactification on (X,0) yields an interacting 5d N=1 SCFT, and develop systematic tools — in particular dot diagrams associated with the singularity and magnetic quivers describing the Higgs branch — that allow one to verify the existence of such an SCFT and to compute its physical invariants (Coulomb branch dimension, prepotential, flavor symmetry, Higgs branch) directly from the geometry of the canonical singularity.
status_search_result: The Xie–Yau conjecture (every 3d canonical singularity yields a 5d N=1 SCFT via M-theory) remains an active research program. Subsequent works (e.g., Closset–Del Zotto–Saxena 2020/2021, Closset–Schäfer-Nameki–Wang 2022, and 2024 papers on isolated complete intersection singularities) have verified it in broad classes of cases (toric, hypersurface, ICIS) and developed magnetic-quiver/dot-diagram techniques, but no complete proof for all 3d canonical singularities is known.

paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
original_question: Is there a faster, algorithmic way to determine the generalized s-rule from dot diagrams, suitable for implementation in code without missing admissible tessellations?
self_contained_problem:
In the context of five-dimensional supersymmetric gauge theories engineered by webs of (p,q)-five-branes with 7-branes, one encodes a brane configuration by a "dot diagram" (a planar arrangement of dots inside a polygon together with chosen partitions/colorings indicating how external legs terminate on 7-branes). The "generalized s-rule" is a combinatorial admissibility constraint on tessellations of such a dot diagram into sub-pieces (each corresponding to an irreducible component of the configuration), forbidding configurations in which more than a prescribed number of branes end on the same 7-brane in a way that would break supersymmetry; equivalently, it selects which decompositions of the dot diagram into colored sub-tessellations are physically admissible.

Problem. Design an algorithm that, given as input a dot diagram (the lattice polygon together with its internal/boundary dot data and 7-brane coloring), enumerates all tessellations of the diagram that satisfy the generalized s-rule, with the following properties:

(a) (Completeness) The algorithm must not miss any admissible tessellation.
(b) (Efficiency) The running time should be substantially faster than naive enumerate-and-filter approaches based on listing all tessellations and then checking the s-rule constraint case by case.
(c) (Implementability) The procedure must be explicit enough to be implemented as code, with a precise specification of the data structure for dot diagrams and a precise combinatorial reformulation of the generalized s-rule.

Either exhibit such an algorithm together with a proof of its correctness and a complexity bound, or prove that no algorithm with running time below a specified threshold can exist.
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not return any source presenting an explicit algorithmic enumeration of admissible dot-diagram tessellations under the generalized s-rule, nor a proof of impossibility. No follow-up work claiming to resolve this algorithmic question was located, so the current status is inconclusive.

paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
original_question: Can one define a notion of symplectic duality for affine Grassmannians, analogous to symplectic duality between Higgs and Coulomb branches?
self_contained_problem:
In the framework of three-dimensional N=4 supersymmetric gauge theories, symplectic duality is a conjectural correspondence pairing certain conical symplectic resolutions (X, X^!) with matching algebraic and representation-theoretic structures; canonical examples arise as Higgs and Coulomb branches of a gauge theory and its mirror. Affine Grassmannian slices (closures of intersections of opposite semi-infinite orbits in the affine Grassmannian Gr_G of a complex reductive group G), and more generally generalized affine Grassmannian slices, are known to carry Poisson structures and to admit symplectic resolutions, and in many cases arise as Coulomb branches of quiver gauge theories whose Higgs branches are Nakajima quiver varieties.

Problem: Formulate an intrinsic notion of "symplectic dual" for the affine Grassmannian Gr_G itself (or for its slices and their generalizations), analogous to the symplectic duality relating Higgs and Coulomb branches. Specifically:

(a) Define, in a coordinate-free way, what it should mean for two (ind-)Poisson varieties associated to G and to a possibly different group G^! to be symplectic duals at the level of affine Grassmannians.

(b) Verify that the proposed definition reproduces the known symplectic duality between affine Grassmannian slices for G (or its Langlands dual) and Nakajima quiver varieties in finite ADE type.

(c) Identify the symplectic dual partner of the full affine Grassmannian Gr_G, or prove that no such partner can exist within an appropriate category of (ind-)symplectic varieties.
status_search_result: Recent work (e.g., Kamnitzer's 2022 survey on symplectic resolutions, symplectic duality, and Coulomb branches; Krylov–Perunov; Muthiah–Weekes and others) has established that generalized affine Grassmannian slices arise as Coulomb branches and are symplectic dual to Nakajima quiver varieties in finite ADE type. However, no general intrinsic notion of symplectic duality directly for the affine Grassmannian itself (rather than its slices) appears to have been formulated; the question of an overarching symplectic-dual framework for affine Grassmannians remains open.

paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
original_question: Can one give a rigorous mathematical description of quiver subtraction and quiver addition?
self_contained_problem:
A quiver is a directed multigraph $Q=(Q_0,Q_1,s,t)$, with vertices $Q_0$, arrows $Q_1$, and source/target maps $s,t:Q_1\to Q_0$. In the context of 3d $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric gauge theories, one decorates a quiver with gauge-group data (e.g. unitary or orthosymplectic ranks at each node) and matter content given by the arrows; to such a decorated "magnetic quiver" $Q$ one associates a hyper-Kähler symplectic singularity $\mathcal{C}(Q)$ called its Coulomb branch (defined, e.g., via the monopole formula or as a BFN Coulomb branch). Two heuristic operations on magnetic quivers are used in the physics literature:

(i) "Quiver subtraction": given two decorated quivers $Q$ and $Q'$ such that $\mathcal{C}(Q')$ is realised as a (transverse slice to a) symplectic leaf of $\mathcal{C}(Q)$, a combinatorial procedure produces a new decorated quiver $Q\ominus Q'$ whose Coulomb branch is conjecturally the corresponding transverse slice in the symplectic stratification of $\mathcal{C}(Q)$. Iterating this is supposed to reconstruct the Hasse diagram of symplectic leaves of $\mathcal{C}(Q)$.

(ii) "Quiver addition": a combinatorial procedure that, given a decorated quiver $Q$, produces a new quiver $Q\oplus X$ whose Coulomb branch enlarges $\mathcal{C}(Q)$ in a controlled way (for example, by adjoining a leaf to its Hasse diagram or by enhancing its global symmetry).

Problem. Provide a rigorous mathematical formulation of the operations of quiver subtraction and quiver addition on (an appropriate category of) decorated quivers. In particular:

(a) Define precisely the input data and output decorated quiver in each case.

(b) Prove that the resulting operations realise, on the level of associated symplectic singularities (Coulomb branches), the geometric operations they are conjectured to perform — namely, taking transverse slices in the symplectic stratification (subtraction) and the corresponding inverse operation (addition) — for as wide a class of unitary and orthosymplectic magnetic quivers as possible.
status_search_result: Quiver subtraction and addition remain physics-motivated combinatorial algorithms whose general rigorous mathematical foundations are not established. Recent works (e.g., "Quotient Quiver Subtraction" 2308.05853, "Decay and Fission of Magnetic Quivers" 2312.05304, and "Coulomb branch global symmetry and quiver addition" JHEP 12(2021)127) extend and refine these algorithms and prove case-by-case results, but a uniform rigorous formulation matching the geometry of Coulomb branch symplectic singularities in full generality is still lacking.

paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
context_brief: Maximizers of V_min times Euler number
original_question: For reflexive polytopes, is the maximum of the product V_{n,min} chi attained by fibrations of dP_3, possibly in more than one way?
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. A lattice polytope $\Delta \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ containing the origin in its interior is called reflexive if its polar dual $\Delta^\circ = \{u \in \mathbb{R}^n : \langle u, v\rangle \ge -1 \text{ for all } v \in \Delta\}$ is also a lattice polytope. Each reflexive polytope $\Delta$ determines a Gorenstein toric Fano variety $X_\Delta$ and a corresponding affine toric Calabi–Yau cone $C(Y_\Delta)$ of complex dimension $n+1$ over a Sasaki–Einstein base $Y_\Delta$. Let $V_{n,\min}(\Delta)$ denote the minimum value, taken over Reeb vectors compatible with the toric structure, of the volume function of the Sasaki–Einstein base $Y_\Delta$ (equivalently, the volume minimized via $Z$-minimization over the cone of admissible Reeb vectors associated to $\Delta$), normalized so that $V_{n,\min}$ equals the volume of the round unit sphere $S^{2n+1}$ for the trivial cone. Let $\chi(\Delta)$ denote the Euler number of a smooth crepant resolution of $X_\Delta$ (equivalently, the number of lattice points on the boundary of $\Delta$ minus the appropriate corrections, computed combinatorially from $\Delta$).

Among reflexive polytopes one distinguishes those whose corresponding toric variety admits the structure of a fibration whose generic fiber is the del Pezzo surface $dP_3$ (the blowup of $\mathbb{P}^2$ at three points in general position), realized at the level of polytopes by a projection of $\Delta$ onto a lower-dimensional reflexive polytope whose fibers are the reflexive hexagon associated with $dP_3$.

Question. For each fixed $n$, consider the product $V_{n,\min}(\Delta)\, \chi(\Delta)$ as $\Delta$ ranges over all $n$-dimensional reflexive polytopes. Is the maximum of this product attained by reflexive polytopes corresponding to $dP_3$ fibrations, possibly by more than one such fibration (i.e., not necessarily uniquely)?
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in a list of open questions in quiver gauge theory. A web search did not turn up a subsequent resolution; related work on Calabi–Yau volumes and reflexive polytopes (e.g. the paper "Calabi–Yau Volumes and Reflexive Polytopes" and follow-ups on quiver gauge theories beyond reflexivity) discusses bounds and patterns for $V_{\min}\cdot\chi$ but does not appear to settle the question. Status appears open.

paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
original_question: To determine K-stability of a general variety one must in principle check infinitely many test symmetries. How can one determine a finite set of test symmetries sufficient to decide K-stability for a general variety, and can one identify exactly which test symmetries need to be checked?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X, L)$ be a polarized projective variety over $\mathbb{C}$ (for instance, a $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano variety with $L = -K_X$). Recall that a test configuration of $(X, L)$ is a flat projective family $(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{L}) \to \mathbb{A}^1$ equipped with a $\mathbb{G}_m$-action lifting the standard action on $\mathbb{A}^1$, such that the fiber over $1 \in \mathbb{A}^1$ is isomorphic to $(X, L^{\otimes r})$ for some $r > 0$. To each test configuration one associates the Donaldson–Futaki invariant (or, equivalently in the Fano setting, a normalized generalized Futaki invariant), and $(X, L)$ is said to be K-stable if this invariant is strictly positive for every nontrivial normal test configuration.

Because the space of test configurations is infinite-dimensional, deciding K-stability of a given $(X, L)$ a priori requires checking infinitely many of them. The problem is the following:

(a) Provide a procedure that, given a general polarized variety $(X, L)$, produces a finite collection $\mathcal{T}(X, L)$ of test configurations such that $(X, L)$ is K-stable if and only if the Donaldson–Futaki invariant is positive on every element of $\mathcal{T}(X, L)$.

(b) Identify intrinsically which test configurations must belong to such a finite sufficient set $\mathcal{T}(X, L)$, i.e., describe explicitly the test configurations that need to be checked in order to decide K-stability of $(X, L)$.
status_search_result: The general problem of identifying a finite, explicit set of test configurations whose Donaldson–Futaki invariants determine K-stability of an arbitrary polarized variety appears to remain open. Partial reductions are known: by Li–Xu, for $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties it suffices to check special test configurations; by work of Fujita, Li, Blum, Liu, Xu and others, K-stability can be reformulated via valuations/filtrations and stability thresholds (delta invariant), and finiteness/quasi-monomial reductions are known in special families, but no general algorithmic finite criterion identifying exactly which test configurations must be tested is established.

paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
original_question: Benvenuti and Giacomelli introduced a notion of chiral-ring stability based on dropping certain superpotential terms. Is there a relationship between this notion of stability and the K-stability-based notion of stability for chiral rings?
self_contained_problem:
In four-dimensional N=1 supersymmetric gauge theories, two distinct notions of "stability" have been proposed for chiral rings.

(a) Chiral-ring stability (Benvenuti–Giacomelli): Given a supersymmetric gauge theory with a superpotential W, one declares W to be chiral-ring stable if no monomial term can be dropped from W without enlarging the chiral ring (equivalently, without producing new operators that violate the unitarity bound and must be decoupled). This procedure modifies the superpotential by removing terms whose corresponding operators decouple at the IR fixed point.

(b) K-stability (Collins–Székelyhidi, applied to chiral rings): Given the chiral ring R = C[X] of a graded affine Gorenstein ring associated to a Calabi–Yau cone singularity X with a Reeb (R-symmetry) vector, one tests whether R is K-stable by computing the sign of the Donaldson–Futaki invariant on every nontrivial test configuration (degeneration) of X. K-stability of R is equivalent to the existence of a Ricci-flat Kähler cone metric on X and is used as a criterion for the existence of a superconformal IR fixed point with the prescribed R-charges.

Problem. Determine whether there is a precise mathematical or physical relationship between notion (a) and notion (b). Specifically: does chiral-ring stability of a superpotential W imply, or is it implied by, K-stability of the corresponding chiral ring (after integrating out massive fields and decoupling free operators)? Formulate and prove (or disprove) such an implication, or otherwise exhibit explicit examples relating or distinguishing the two notions.
status_search_result: The two notions of stability (Benvenuti–Giacomelli's chiral-ring stability via decoupling of superpotential terms, and the K-stability criterion applied to chiral rings via Donaldson–Futaki invariants) have been studied separately, but no published work appears to establish a direct relationship between them. The question is posed as an open problem in the survey of open quiver-gauge-theory questions, and no subsequent resolution was located.

paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
context_brief: Generalizing zig-zag paths and perfect matchings
original_question: For brane tilings on the torus T^2, zig-zag paths and perfect matchings are central constructions. What are their mathematical and physical roles for general m in the setting of m-graded quivers and generalized brane tilings on T^{m+1}?
self_contained_problem:
Background. A brane tiling on the two-torus $T^2$ is a bipartite graph embedded in $T^2$ whose faces, edges, and nodes encode the data of a quiver with superpotential associated to a toric Calabi–Yau threefold. Two combinatorial structures play a fundamental role:

(i) Perfect matchings: collections of edges of the bipartite graph such that every node is incident to exactly one chosen edge. Perfect matchings are in correspondence with points of the toric diagram of the underlying Calabi–Yau threefold and parametrize chiral fields entering the master space and the mesonic moduli space.

(ii) Zig-zag paths: oriented closed paths on the bipartite graph that alternately turn maximally right at one color of node and maximally left at the other. Their homology classes in $H_1(T^2,\mathbb Z)$ reproduce the external legs of the $(p,q)$-web dual to the toric diagram, and they control consistency of the tiling.

These notions admit generalizations to $m$-graded quivers with superpotential, which describe the open-string sector of the topological B-model on Calabi–Yau $(m+2)$-folds. In the toric case, such $m$-graded quivers are encoded by generalized brane tilings ("$m$-dimers") realized as cell complexes on the torus $T^{m+1}$, where the case $m=1$ recovers ordinary brane tilings on $T^2$. Generalized perfect matchings and a Kasteleyn-type construction have been formulated for arbitrary $m$.

Problem. For generalized brane tilings on $T^{m+1}$ associated to $m$-graded quivers with superpotential (with $m \geq 1$):

(a) Formulate, in full generality, intrinsic combinatorial/topological definitions of "zig-zag paths" and "perfect matchings" extending the $m=1$ notions, and identify the homological/cohomological invariants on $T^{m+1}$ that they realize.

(b) Determine the mathematical role of these objects: their relation to the toric diagram of the underlying Calabi–Yau $(m+2)$-fold (e.g. as parametrizations of lattice points or of higher-dimensional faces), to the consistency conditions of the generalized tiling, and to mutation classes of $m$-graded quivers.

(c) Determine their physical role in the corresponding $B$-model / gauge-theoretic setting, including their interpretation in terms of moduli spaces, BPS-like states, and any analog of the $(p,q)$-web for higher $m$.

Provide either a complete theory establishing (a)–(c), or precise structural results that determine these roles for all $m \geq 1$.
category_tag: Graded quivers and generalized brane tilings
status_search_result: Generalized perfect matchings for $m$-graded quivers / $m$-dimers have been defined and a Kasteleyn-type algorithm extending the $m=1$ case has been given (Franco–Seong and collaborators, JHEP 11 (2019) 104 and follow-ups), establishing their role in encoding toric data of CY $(m+2)$-folds. A general intrinsic theory of zig-zag paths for arbitrary $m$ on $T^{m+1}$, together with a complete account of their mathematical and physical implications, is not fully developed in the literature found; the question is therefore partially addressed but remains open in its full generality.

paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
original_question: For a brane tiling that is inconsistent in the sense relevant to quiver gauge theories, what is the infrared physics and what is the geometry of the moduli space? Conversely, for consistent brane tilings, can one verify that renormalization-group flow in the field theory reaches the correct geometric moduli space?
self_contained_problem:
A brane tiling is a bipartite graph embedded on a two-dimensional torus that encodes a four-dimensional N=1 supersymmetric quiver gauge theory: vertices (colored black/white) correspond to superpotential terms, faces correspond to U(N) gauge groups, and edges correspond to bifundamental chiral matter fields. The tiling is called consistent (e.g. satisfies the properly-ordered / non-degeneracy conditions, equivalently the associated dimer model has an isoradial embedding and the quiver algebra is a 3-Calabi–Yau algebra) when the resulting gauge theory is expected to flow in the infrared to a superconformal field theory whose mesonic moduli space of vacua reproduces a prescribed toric Calabi–Yau threefold singularity (the one read off from the perfect-matching / characteristic-polynomial data of the tiling). A tiling that fails these consistency conditions is called inconsistent.

(a) For an inconsistent brane tiling, determine the infrared physics of the associated quiver gauge theory (e.g. whether it flows to a nontrivial fixed point, confines, breaks supersymmetry, or develops emergent symmetries) and describe the geometry of its mesonic moduli space of vacua.

(b) For a consistent brane tiling with prescribed toric Calabi–Yau threefold X assigned by the standard combinatorial recipe, prove that the renormalization-group flow of the corresponding quiver gauge theory in the infrared yields a moduli space of vacua isomorphic to X (rather than to some other variety).
category_tag: brane tilings and quiver gauge theories
status_search_result: The question is one of several open problems posed in a 2021 survey on quiver gauge theories. No general classification of the IR behavior of inconsistent brane tilings, nor a general proof that consistent tilings flow to the prescribed toric Calabi–Yau geometry, appears in the literature; partial results exist (e.g. for specific families like Y^{p,q} or via a-maximization), but the general statement remains open.

paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
original_question: What is the physical interpretation of the modular parameter tau_B, obtained from the Belyi pair, in the superconformal field theory described by a brane tiling?
self_contained_problem:
Background. A brane tiling is a bipartite graph drawn on a two-dimensional torus that encodes the data of a four-dimensional N=1 superconformal gauge theory arising on a stack of D3-branes probing a toric Calabi–Yau threefold singularity: faces correspond to gauge groups, edges to bifundamental chiral multiplets, and vertices (black/white) to superpotential terms (with signs given by vertex color). To any brane tiling one can associate a Belyi pair (E_B, β), where E_B is an elliptic curve (a complex torus) and β: E_B → P^1 is a holomorphic map ramified only over {0, 1, ∞}; the bipartite graph is recovered as the preimage β^{-1}([0,1]) with black/white vertices over 0 and 1 and faces over ∞, and the ramification profiles match the valences of the tiling. The complex structure of E_B is specified by a modular parameter τ_B ∈ H/SL(2,Z) (the upper half-plane modulo the modular group), referred to as the Belyi modular parameter of the tiling.

Independently, the superconformal R-charges of the gauge theory (determined by a-maximization) endow the tiling torus with an isoradial embedding, hence with its own complex structure parameter τ_R ∈ H/SL(2,Z) (the "R-charge" or "isoradial" complex structure).

Problem. Give a physical interpretation, intrinsic to the four-dimensional superconformal field theory associated with the brane tiling, of the Belyi modular parameter τ_B. Specifically, identify a physical observable, coupling, or geometric/dynamical quantity of the SCFT (or of its gravity/string-theoretic dual) whose value is determined by τ_B, and explain in what sense τ_B encodes that quantity, distinguishing it from the isoradial parameter τ_R derived from the R-charges.
status_search_result: The relationship between the Belyi complex structure τ_B of a brane tiling and the isoradial/R-charge complex structure τ_R has been studied (notably in works on toric CFTs, permutation triples, and the "beta ansatz"), but a clean, intrinsic physical interpretation of τ_B in the SCFT itself does not appear to have been established. No source located identifies a definitive physical meaning of τ_B; the question appears to remain open.

paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
context_brief: Relations among tau_G, tau_R, and tau_B
original_question: Three modular parameters appear in this setting: tau_G from the geometry of the torus in the Gorenstein singularity, tau_R from the isoradial brane tiling, and tau_B from the Belyi pair. What is the precise relationship among tau_G, tau_R, and tau_B?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $X$ be a toric Calabi–Yau threefold realized as an affine Gorenstein singularity, with associated 4d $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal quiver gauge theory encoded by a brane tiling, i.e. a bipartite graph $\Gamma$ drawn on a real two-torus $T^2$. Three complex-structure (modular) parameters in the upper half-plane $\mathbb{H}$ are naturally attached to this data:

(1) $\tau_G$, the geometric modular parameter. It is the complex structure of the two-torus appearing in the mirror geometry / Sasaki–Einstein description of the Gorenstein singularity $X$, equivalently the complex structure on the torus fibre extracted from the volume/$a$-maximization data of $X$.

(2) $\tau_R$, the isoradial (R-charge) modular parameter. Performing $a$-maximization fixes the superconformal $R$-charges of the bifundamental fields; the bipartite graph $\Gamma$ then admits an isoradial embedding in which the rhombus angle of each edge equals $\pi$ times the corresponding $R$-charge. The fundamental domain of this isoradial embedding is a parallelogram in $\mathbb{C}$ whose modular parameter is $\tau_R\in\mathbb{H}$.

(3) $\tau_B$, the Belyi modular parameter. The brane tiling $\Gamma$ corresponds to a torus Belyi pair: an elliptic curve $E_B=\mathbb{C}/(\mathbb{Z}+\tau_B\mathbb{Z})$ together with a holomorphic map $\beta:E_B\to\mathbb{P}^1$ ramified only over $\{0,1,\infty\}$, whose dessin d'enfant on $E_B$ reproduces $\Gamma$. The complex structure of the source elliptic curve defines $\tau_B\in\mathbb{H}$.

Problem. Determine the precise relationship among the three modular parameters $\tau_G$, $\tau_R$, and $\tau_B$ associated to an arbitrary toric Calabi–Yau Gorenstein singularity and its brane tiling. Specifically, find an explicit (e.g. modular, algebraic, or analytic) map, valid for every such tiling, expressing $\tau_G$, $\tau_R$, and $\tau_B$ in terms of one another (or characterize precisely when they coincide modulo $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$).
status_search_result: The three complex structures τ_G, τ_R, τ_B associated to brane tilings are known to be generically inequivalent; partial work (e.g. on a "modular Mahler flow" and on isoradial/Belyi comparisons in specific examples such as the conifold and Y^{p,q} families) gives equalities of j-invariants in special cases, but no general formula relating all three is established. The question is listed as an open problem in the literature on quiver gauge theory.

paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
original_question: How does Seiberg duality between brane tilings act on the associated dessins d’enfants, and can their duality trees suggest nontrivial Galois invariants?
self_contained_problem:
Background. A brane tiling is a bipartite graph drawn on a 2-torus that encodes the data (quiver with superpotential) of a four-dimensional N=1 supersymmetric gauge theory whose vacuum moduli space is a toric Calabi–Yau threefold. Seiberg duality acts on such gauge theories by a local move (urban renewal / square move on the bipartite graph) and produces, on the level of brane tilings, a tree (the duality tree) of dual phases. A dessin d'enfant is a connected bipartite graph embedded in a compact Riemann surface together with a Belyi map to ℙ¹ ramified only over {0,1,∞}; brane tilings on the torus, viewed as bipartite graphs with a complex structure, can be associated with dessins d'enfants in this way. The absolute Galois group Gal(ℚ̄/ℚ) acts faithfully on the set of dessins, partitioning them into Galois orbits, and a Galois invariant is any function of a dessin that is constant on each orbit (e.g. the passport, the monodromy group, the field of moduli).

Problem. (a) Determine precisely how Seiberg duality between brane tilings (the urban renewal/square move and its iterations) acts on the associated dessins d'enfants: identify the induced transformation on the corresponding Belyi pair (X,β) (or, when the dessin lives on a higher genus curve, on the associated bipartite map) and describe its effect on standard Galois-theoretic data (passport, monodromy, field of moduli, etc.).

(b) Using the structure of Seiberg duality trees (the trees of dual phases of a fixed toric Calabi–Yau threefold), construct nontrivial Galois invariants of dessins d'enfants — i.e. functions of the dessin that (i) are demonstrably constant on Gal(ℚ̄/ℚ)-orbits and (ii) are not implied by the standard known Galois invariants — or prove that no such new invariants arise from this construction.
status_search_result: Related literature establishes partial results: the degree of the number field of definition and the confinement index have been identified as Seiberg duality / Galois invariants, and brane tilings beyond the torus have been linked to dessins. However, no work appears to give a complete description of how Seiberg duality acts on the associated dessins or to derive new Galois invariants from duality trees in the sense asked. The question therefore appears to remain open.
