paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
original_question: Modular surfaces associated with subgroups of PSL(2, Z) can produce Belyi maps and dessins d’enfants. To what extent do modular subgroups connect modular surfaces with dessins d’enfants?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Gamma \le \mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$ be a finite-index subgroup acting on the upper half-plane $\mathbb{H}$, and let $X_\Gamma = \overline{\Gamma\backslash \mathbb{H}}$ denote the associated compactified modular surface (a compact Riemann surface obtained by adjoining the cusps). The natural projection $X_\Gamma \to X_{\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb{Z})} \cong \mathbb{P}^1$ given by the $j$-invariant is a covering ramified only over $\{0, 1728, \infty\}$, and after the normalization $t = j/1728$ becomes a Belyi map $\beta_\Gamma : X_\Gamma \to \mathbb{P}^1$ ramified only over $\{0,1,\infty\}$. By Grothendieck's correspondence, $\beta_\Gamma$ determines a dessin d'enfant $\mathcal{D}_\Gamma = \beta_\Gamma^{-1}([0,1]) \subset X_\Gamma$, a bipartite graph embedded in $X_\Gamma$ whose combinatorial type encodes the permutation representation of $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$ on the cosets $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb{Z})/\Gamma$.

Characterize, as completely as possible, the correspondence
$$\Gamma \;\longmapsto\; (X_\Gamma, \beta_\Gamma, \mathcal{D}_\Gamma).$$
Specifically: determine which Belyi pairs and which dessins d'enfants arise from finite-index subgroups of $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$ in this way; describe how invariants of $\Gamma$ (index, genus, number of cusps, elliptic points, congruence/non-congruence character, conjugacy class) are reflected in invariants of the associated dessin (passport, monodromy group, valency lists, cartographic group); and explain how the action of the absolute Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$ on dessins interacts with this modular construction.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open-ended research problem about the extent to which modular subgroups connect modular surfaces with dessins d'enfants. While the basic correspondence (via the j-line Belyi map) is classical and well-known, and many partial results exist (especially for congruence subgroups and in the work of He, McKay, and others), a complete characterization remains an active and largely open program. No definitive resolution has been published.

paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
context_brief: ReLU tropical functions as quiver theories
original_question: Given the connection between tropical geometry through amoebae and quiver gauge theories, can the tropical functions realized by ReLU neural networks be reformulated as quiver gauge theories?
self_contained_problem:
A ReLU neural network defines a continuous piecewise-linear function f: R^n → R^m by alternating affine maps with the activation ReLU(x) = max(x, 0). Every such function can equivalently be written as a difference of two tropical (max-plus) polynomials, i.e. f = P ⊖ Q where P(x) = max_{i}(⟨a_i, x⟩ + b_i) and Q(x) = max_{j}(⟨c_j, x⟩ + d_j) with integer (or rational) slope vectors a_i, c_j and real constants b_i, d_j; equivalently f is a tropical rational function on R^n. On the other hand, to a quiver gauge theory (a finite directed multigraph Q with a dimension vector and a choice of superpotential / matter content) one can associate, via mirror symmetry and the amoeba/tropicalization of its mirror Newton polynomial, a tropical (piecewise-linear) function on a real vector space describing, for example, the tropical limit of its partition function or the support of its amoeba.

Problem. Construct a procedure that, given an arbitrary tropical function f: R^n → R^m arising from a ReLU neural network (specified by its layer-wise weights and biases, equivalently by its representation as a tropical rational map with integer slopes), produces a quiver gauge theory whose associated tropical/amoeba function coincides with f. More precisely: characterize the class of tropical functions realizable as ReLU networks that admit such a quiver-gauge-theoretic realization, give an explicit dictionary translating the network data (weights, biases, depth, width) into quiver data (nodes, arrows, dimension vector, superpotential), and determine whether every ReLU tropical function can be so realized, or otherwise identify the obstructions.
category_tag: Tropical geometry and quiver gauge theories
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in a list of open questions in quiver gauge theory (2021). No subsequent work appears to provide a quiver-gauge-theoretic reformulation of generic ReLU tropical functions; related literature on tropical geometry of neural networks (Zhang–Naitzat–Lim and follow-ups) and on amoebae of quiver theories has not bridged the two frameworks in the manner asked.

paper_title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics
context_brief: Residual population structure in GWAS and PRS
original_question: How can association and prediction studies of complex human traits fully control residual population structure—the confounding that arises because ancestry or family identity affects both genotype and environmental exposure—without overcorrecting away real genetic signal, so that very large genome-wide association studies and polygenic risk scores do not produce spurious associations or biased predictions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a population of N individuals indexed by i = 1,...,N. For each individual, let g_i ∈ {0,1,2}^M denote a vector of genotypes at M biallelic loci, let y_i ∈ ℝ denote a quantitative trait value, and let a_i denote a (latent) ancestry/family-identity variable taking values in some space A. Assume a generative model

  y_i = Σ_{j=1}^M β_j g_{ij} + e(a_i) + ε_i,

where β = (β_1,…,β_M) is the vector of true causal genetic effects, e: A → ℝ is an unknown environmental effect that depends on ancestry/family identity (because ancestry influences environmental exposures such as climate, nutrition, social context), and ε_i is independent noise. The genotypes also depend on a_i, so that g_i and e(a_i) are statistically dependent through the shared latent ancestry, creating confounding.

A genome-wide association study (GWAS) estimates marginal or joint regressions of y on g; a polygenic risk score (PRS) for a new individual with genotype g* is a linear predictor Σ_j β̂_j g*_j formed from such estimates.

Standard correction methods (e.g., including top principal components of the genotype matrix, linear mixed models with a genetic relatedness matrix, family-based tests, LD-score regression intercepts) reduce but do not eliminate the dependence between estimated effects and a_i; this remaining confounding is called residual population structure. Overcorrection — for example, projecting out too many directions correlated with a_i — can also remove a portion of the true signal Σ_j β_j g_{ij} when β has components aligned with population-differentiated allele-frequency directions.

Problem. Develop a statistical framework and an associated estimator β̂ (and corresponding PRS predictor) such that, under explicit and realistic assumptions on the joint distribution of (g_i, a_i, e(a_i), ε_i) — including very large sample sizes N where biases dominate sampling variance —:

(a) β̂ is a consistent (or provably low-bias) estimator of the causal effects β, controlling all spurious associations induced by residual population structure;

(b) the procedure does not systematically attenuate components of β that are correlated with population-frequency differentiation (i.e., it avoids overcorrection of true genetic signal);

(c) the resulting PRS achieves prediction accuracy in target populations that is unbiased with respect to ancestry, with quantifiable guarantees on transferability across populations a ∈ A.

State precise sufficient conditions on the data-generating process, and either construct such a procedure with rigorous guarantees, or prove an impossibility/identifiability result delineating when consistent unconfounded estimation of β and ancestry-fair PRS prediction is achievable from observational genotype–phenotype data.
status_search_result: Recent literature (2022–2025) continues to document that residual population stratification biases GWAS effect estimates and PRS predictions, particularly in large biobanks, and that current corrections (PCA, LMMs, sib-based designs) only partially address the problem while sometimes overcorrecting. No consensus method or proof of identifiability has been established, so the problem is still considered open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics
original_question: How can gene-environment interactions be rigorously defined, measured, detected, replicated, and incorporated into human complex-trait genetics when environmental factors may modify genetic effects, are difficult to measure consistently across studies, and can change interpretations of heritability and prediction transferability?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantitative human trait Y modeled as a function of a high-dimensional genotype vector G (e.g., genome-wide SNP genotypes) and a vector E of non-genetic ("environmental") determinants, where Y = f(G, E) + noise. A gene-environment interaction (GxE) is said to occur when the partial effect of G on Y depends on E (equivalently, the partial effect of E on Y depends on G), i.e., f is not additively separable into a function of G alone plus a function of E alone.

Develop a rigorous, unified framework that addresses all of the following simultaneously:

1. Definition: Provide a precise mathematical definition of GxE that (a) is invariant under monotone reparameterizations of Y where appropriate, (b) distinguishes scale-dependent from scale-independent interactions, and (c) accommodates both discrete and continuous environmental variables, including imperfectly measured or latent E.

2. Estimation and identification: Specify estimators of GxE effects (at the level of individual variants, polygenic scores, and genome-wide variance components) together with conditions on study design and on the joint distribution of (G, E) under which these estimators are identifiable and consistent, accounting for measurement error in E that may differ across studies.

3. Detection: Provide statistical tests for the presence of GxE with controlled type I error and quantified power in the genome-wide setting, including procedures that remain valid when E is measured with study-specific error or is only partially observed.

4. Replication and meta-analysis: Give a methodology for combining GxE estimates across studies in which environmental variables are defined or measured differently, with formal criteria for when two studies' GxE findings can be considered to replicate one another.

5. Consequences for heritability and prediction: Quantify how the presence of GxE affects (a) the definition and estimation of narrow-sense and broad-sense heritability, and (b) the cross-population and cross-environment transferability of polygenic predictors derived from genome-wide association studies, and provide bounds or correction procedures.

The problem is to construct such a framework, prove its theoretical guarantees, and demonstrate that it resolves the inconsistencies that arise when GxE is defined or measured differently across studies.
status_search_result: Gene-environment interaction methodology in human complex-trait genetics is widely acknowledged as an unresolved methodological challenge, with ongoing work but no comprehensive accepted framework as of 2026. Recent reviews continue to highlight definitional ambiguity, measurement inconsistency, and limited replication as outstanding issues.

paper_title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics
original_question: How can human genetic studies overcome the overrepresentation of European ancestry by collecting diverse cohorts and developing robust trans-ethnic analytical methods, so that genetic associations and polygenic risk scores transfer across populations and causal signals can be distinguished from population-specific confounding or linkage disequilibrium?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the statistical genetics setting in which one collects genome-wide genotype data and a quantitative or binary phenotype from cohorts of individuals drawn from several ancestral populations P_1, ..., P_K (e.g., European, African, East Asian, South Asian, admixed American). For each population P_k one obtains a sample of (X^{(k)}, y^{(k)}) where X^{(k)} \in \{0,1,2\}^{n_k \times M} encodes minor-allele dosages at M variants and y^{(k)} \in \R^{n_k} encodes phenotypes. Genetic association studies typically fit per-variant marginal models or joint linear/logistic models to obtain effect-size estimates \hat{\beta}^{(k)} \in \R^M, and polygenic risk scores (PRS) are defined for an individual with genotype vector x as PRS(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{M} w_j x_j for weights w derived from \hat{\beta}. Empirically, when weights w are estimated from a European-ancestry cohort and applied to individuals of non-European ancestry, predictive accuracy (e.g., R^2 between PRS and phenotype) drops substantially, due to differences in allele frequencies, linkage-disequilibrium (LD) patterns \Sigma^{(k)} = \Cov(X^{(k)}), causal effect heterogeneity, and population-specific confounding.

Formulate and solve the following problem. Develop a framework, together with cohort-design and analytical methodology, that:

(a) Specifies a generative model linking population-specific LD matrices \Sigma^{(k)}, allele frequencies f^{(k)}, and (possibly shared) causal effects \beta^* such that observed marginal effects \hat{\beta}^{(k)} can be related across populations.

(b) Provides an estimator \hat{w} of PRS weights, using multi-ancestry training data, for which the cross-population predictive performance gap
\Delta(k, k') = \E[(y - \mathrm{PRS}_{\hat{w}}(x))^2 \mid \text{ancestry } k'] - \E[(y - \mathrm{PRS}_{\hat{w}}(x))^2 \mid \text{ancestry } k]
is provably bounded under explicit assumptions on the heterogeneity of \beta^*, \Sigma^{(k)}, and f^{(k)}.

(c) Provides a hypothesis-testing procedure that distinguishes, at a given variant or locus, between (i) a genuine shared causal effect, (ii) a population-specific causal effect, and (iii) a spurious association arising from LD tagging or population stratification, with controlled type-I error across all K populations simultaneously.

(d) Quantifies the minimal sample sizes n_1, ..., n_K (in particular for currently underrepresented non-European ancestries) and the required density and ancestry-coverage of haplotype reference panels and genotyping arrays needed to attain a prescribed cross-ancestry transferability of association signals and PRS accuracy.

The goal is a complete, rigorous solution: an analytical methodology with provable guarantees, together with cohort-design recommendations, that achieves trans-ethnic transferability of genetic association results and polygenic risk scores while distinguishing causal signals from population-specific confounding and LD artifacts.
category_tag: trans-ethnic genetic association and polygenic risk scores
status_search_result: This is a broadly recognized open challenge in statistical and human genetics. Recent literature (multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis methods such as MR-MEGA, trans-ethnic PRS methods like PRS-CSx, and ongoing initiatives such as H3Africa, All of Us, and the Global Biobank Meta-analysis Initiative) has produced substantial partial progress, but cross-ancestry PRS portability gaps and the lack of representative reference panels and arrays remain unresolved as of 2026. No comprehensive solution meeting all aspects (a)-(d) exists.

paper_title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics
original_question: How can genetic studies understand, prevent, and correct selection bias or collider bias when voluntary participation, separate case-control recruitment, or survival among cases makes sampled cohorts unrepresentative and can induce spurious genetic associations or biased SNP-heritability estimates?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a population $\mathcal{P}$ of individuals, each characterized by a genotype vector $G \in \{0,1,2\}^M$ (counts of a reference allele at $M$ single-nucleotide polymorphisms, SNPs) and a phenotype $Y$ (either quantitative or a binary case/control status). A genome-wide association study (GWAS) seeks to estimate, for each SNP $j$, the marginal effect $\beta_j$ in a model $Y = \sum_j G_j \beta_j + \varepsilon$, while the SNP-heritability is defined as $h^2_{\text{SNP}} = \mathrm{Var}\!\left(\sum_j G_j \beta_j\right)/\mathrm{Var}(Y)$ (with an appropriate liability-scale transformation in the binary case).

Suppose that the actually observed cohort is not a simple random sample from $\mathcal{P}$ but is drawn according to a sampling indicator $S \in \{0,1\}$ whose distribution depends on $Y$, on $G$, and on unobserved covariates $U$. Three concrete mechanisms are of interest:
(i) voluntary participation, where $\Pr(S=1 \mid Y, G, U)$ depends on health, behavior, or socio-demographic variables correlated with $Y$ and $G$;
(ii) separate case/control ascertainment, where cases ($Y=1$) and controls ($Y=0$) are recruited from different source populations with different distributions of $G$ and $U$;
(iii) survival/prevalence sampling, where among cases only survivors are observed, so that $\Pr(S=1 \mid Y=1, G, U)$ depends on genetic and environmental modifiers of survival.

Conditioning on $S=1$ can open non-causal paths between $G$ and $Y$ (collider bias), producing spurious association signals at SNPs that are not causal, and can systematically distort estimates of $h^2_{\text{SNP}}$ and of genetic correlations between traits.

Develop a rigorous framework that accomplishes all of the following:
(a) Characterize, under explicit and testable assumptions on the selection mechanism $\Pr(S=1 \mid Y, G, U)$, the bias induced in marginal SNP effect estimates $\hat\beta_j$ and in SNP-heritability estimates $\hat h^2_{\text{SNP}}$ obtained from the selected sample.
(b) Provide consistent estimation procedures (using, e.g., external population information, instrumental variables, inverse probability weighting, or auxiliary unselected reference panels) that recover the population-level $\beta_j$ and $h^2_{\text{SNP}}$ from cohorts subject to mechanisms (i)–(iii), together with conditions under which identifiability holds.
(c) Establish best-practice study-design and analysis guidelines (recruitment schemes, weighting, sensitivity analyses) that provably minimize or bound the residual bias when the selection mechanism is only partially known.
category_tag: selection bias in genetic association studies
status_search_result: Several partial solutions have appeared: the PCGC approach estimates SNP-heritability and genetic correlations in case-control studies under non-genetic risk factors; Slope-Hunter and Mendelian-randomization-based estimators correct collider bias in conditional GWAS; and inverse-probability-weighted GWAS (WGWAS) corrects volunteer bias and recovers larger SNP effect sizes and heritability. However, no single framework simultaneously handles voluntary participation, separate case-control ascertainment, and survival bias under weak assumptions, so the broader problem remains active research.

original_question: What explains the gaps between the variance explained by concrete polygenic risk scores, SNP or genotype-based heritability, and twin-based heritability for complex human traits, and can those gaps be resolved by rare variants, non-additive genetic effects, gene-environment interactions, population structure, environmental bias, indirect genetic effects, improved prediction models, or a revised interpretation of heritability itself?

paper_title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics
context_brief: Clinical utility of polygenic risk scores
original_question: What clinical evidence, robustness, reliability, cost-effectiveness, and—where necessary—randomized-trial validation are required before polygenic risk score-guided protocols for complex diseases can be adopted in routine care as supplements to traditional risk-prediction models?
self_contained_problem:
Polygenic risk scores (PRS) are predictors of an individual's susceptibility to a complex disease constructed by aggregating, typically as a weighted sum, the effect-size estimates of many genetic variants (often single-nucleotide polymorphisms) obtained from genome-wide association studies. A PRS-guided clinical protocol is a decision rule that uses an individual's PRS, possibly together with conventional risk factors (age, sex, family history, biomarkers, lifestyle, etc.), to inform screening, prevention, or treatment decisions for a complex disease such as coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes, breast cancer, or schizophrenia.

Formulate and resolve the following question regarding the clinical utility of polygenic risk scores: determine the standards of clinical evidence, predictive robustness across ancestries and populations, reliability and reproducibility of score computation, and cost-effectiveness — together with, where appropriate, randomized controlled trial validation comparing patient outcomes under PRS-augmented protocols versus established risk-prediction models — that are sufficient to justify adopting PRS-guided protocols as supplements to traditional risk-prediction models in routine clinical care for complex diseases. Specifically: identify (i) the disease contexts in which a PRS provides incremental discrimination, calibration, and net reclassification benefit beyond standard clinical risk models; (ii) quantitative thresholds on these performance metrics, on portability across populations, and on cost per quality-adjusted life-year that should be required before deployment; and (iii) the minimal trial designs (e.g., randomized controlled trials with clinical endpoints) needed to establish reliability and robustness of such PRS-guided protocols relative to classical medical protocols.
category_tag: polygenic risk scores and clinical utility
status_search_result: As of recent literature (2023–2025), the clinical utility of polygenic risk scores remains an active and largely unresolved area: while PRS have shown predictive value for several complex diseases (notably coronary artery disease and breast cancer) and pilot implementation studies (e.g., the eMERGE network, Genomics PLC programs) are underway, large-scale randomized controlled trials demonstrating improved patient outcomes, ancestry-portability, and cost-effectiveness sufficient for routine clinical adoption have not yet been completed. Major reviews continue to list these as open challenges.

paper_title: Higher Rank Brill-Noether Theory and Coherent Systems: Open Questions
original_question: Let C be a smooth projective curve over the complex numbers. For which triples (n,d,k) does there exist a stable vector bundle E on C of rank n and degree d with h^0(E) >= k, equivalently for which values is the Brill-Noether locus B(n,d,k) nonempty?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a smooth projective curve of genus $g \geq 2$ over the complex numbers. For integers $n \geq 1$, $d$, and $k \geq 0$, let $M(n,d)$ denote the moduli space of stable vector bundles of rank $n$ and degree $d$ on $C$, and define the higher-rank Brill-Noether locus
$$B(n,d,k) = \{ [E] \in M(n,d) : h^0(C, E) \geq k \}.$$
Determine, for a general curve $C$ of genus $g$ (and more generally for arbitrary $C$), the precise set of triples $(n,d,k)$ with $n \geq 1$, $d \in \mathbb{Z}$, $k \geq 0$ for which $B(n,d,k)$ is non-empty.
status_search_result: The non-emptiness of higher-rank Brill-Noether loci $B(n,d,k)$ for $n\geq 2$ is a long-standing open problem. While many partial results exist (in particular for low rank, small $k$, or specific slope ranges, with contributions by Teixidor i Bigas, Mercat, Brambila-Paz, Newstead and others), no complete classification is known even on a general curve. Recent surveys (2021 and later) continue to list it as an open question.

original_question: Let C be a smooth projective curve over the complex numbers. What are the irreducible components of the Brill-Noether locus B(n,d,k), and in particular for which triples (n,d,k) is B(n,d,k) irreducible?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a smooth projective curve of genus $g \geq 2$ over the field of complex numbers. For positive integers $n$, integers $d$, and non-negative integers $k$, define the higher-rank Brill–Noether locus
$$B(n,d,k) = \{[E] \in M(n,d) : h^0(C,E) \geq k\},$$
where $M(n,d)$ denotes the moduli space of stable vector bundles of rank $n$ and degree $d$ on $C$, and $h^0(C,E) = \dim_{\mathbb C} H^0(C,E)$.

Determine the irreducible components of $B(n,d,k)$. In particular, characterize the triples $(n,d,k)$ (with $n \geq 1$, $k \geq 1$, and $d$ in the appropriate range) for which $B(n,d,k)$ is irreducible.
status_search_result: The general question of identifying irreducible components and characterizing irreducibility of higher-rank Brill–Noether loci $B(n,d,k)$ on smooth projective curves remains open. Recent papers (2023–2025) continue to produce both new irreducibility theorems and new examples of reducible loci, indicating the question is still actively investigated.

paper_title: Higher Rank Brill-Noether Theory and Coherent Systems: Open Questions
original_question: Let C be a smooth projective curve over the complex numbers. Can the Brill-Noether locus B(n,d,k) have singularities outside the smaller locus B(n,d,k+1), and can B(n,d,k) be non-reduced?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a smooth irreducible projective curve of genus $g \geq 2$ over the complex numbers. For integers $n \geq 1$, $d$, and $k \geq 0$, let $M(n,d)$ denote the moduli space of stable vector bundles on $C$ of rank $n$ and degree $d$, and define the Brill–Noether locus
$$B(n,d,k) = \{ E \in M(n,d) : h^0(C,E) \geq k \}.$$
This is a determinantal subscheme of $M(n,d)$ whose closed points parametrize stable bundles with at least $k$ independent global sections. There is a natural chain of closed subschemes
$$\cdots \subseteq B(n,d,k+1) \subseteq B(n,d,k) \subseteq M(n,d).$$
Address the following two questions:
(a) Can $B(n,d,k)$ have singular points lying outside $B(n,d,k+1)$? That is, does there exist a triple $(n,d,k)$ with $n \geq 2$ and a stable bundle $E \in B(n,d,k) \setminus B(n,d,k+1)$ at which $B(n,d,k)$ is singular as a scheme?
(b) Can $B(n,d,k)$ be non-reduced as a scheme?
In particular, exhibit explicit examples or prove that no such examples exist.
status_search_result: The questions are listed as open problems in a recent survey of higher rank Brill–Noether theory. While a Riemann–Kempf style singularity theorem and tangent cone descriptions for higher rank Brill–Noether loci have been established (Hitching, 2020), these results do not resolve whether singularities can occur outside $B(n,d,k+1)$ or whether $B(n,d,k)$ can be non-reduced. No published resolution was found.

paper_title: Higher Rank Brill-Noether Theory and Coherent Systems: Open Questions
original_question: Suppose B(n,d,k) is nonempty and its Brill-Noether number beta(n,d,k) is positive. Must the Brill-Noether locus B(n,d,k) be connected?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a smooth irreducible projective curve of genus $g \geq 2$ over the complex numbers. For integers $n \geq 1$, $d$, and $k \geq 1$, let $M(n,d)$ denote the moduli space of stable vector bundles of rank $n$ and degree $d$ on $C$, and define the Brill–Noether locus
$$B(n,d,k) := \{ E \in M(n,d) : h^0(C,E) \geq k \},$$
endowed with its natural scheme structure. The (higher rank) Brill–Noether number is
$$\beta(n,d,k) := n^2(g-1) + 1 - k(k - d + n(g-1)).$$

paper_title: Higher Rank Brill-Noether Theory and Coherent Systems: Open Questions
original_question: What should count as a mathematically useful and robust definition of a curve being Brill-Noether general in higher rank n, given that the rank-1 notion does not transfer directly?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a smooth irreducible projective curve of genus $g \geq 2$ over an algebraically closed field. For integers $n \geq 1$, $d$, and $k \geq 0$, denote by $\mathcal{U}_C(n,d)$ the moduli space of stable vector bundles of rank $n$ and degree $d$ on $C$, and by
$$B_C(n,d,k) = \{[E] \in \mathcal{U}_C(n,d) : h^0(C,E) \geq k\}$$
the higher-rank Brill–Noether locus. The expected (Brill–Noether) dimension of $B_C(n,d,k)$ is
$$\beta(n,d,k) = n^2(g-1) + 1 - k(k - d + n(g-1)).$$

In rank $n=1$, a curve $C$ is called Brill–Noether general if for every $d, k$ the locus $W^{k-1}_d(C) = B_C(1,d,k)$ has dimension equal to $\max(\beta(1,d,k), -1)$ (in particular, it is empty when $\beta(1,d,k) < 0$); equivalently, $C$ is a Petri curve. This characterization does not transfer directly to rank $n \geq 2$: there are pairs $(n,d,k)$ with $\beta(n,d,k) < 0$ for which $B_C(n,d,k)$ is nonempty for every smooth curve $C$ of genus $g$, so the rank-$1$ definition fails to single out a meaningful generic locus in the moduli space of curves.

Problem. Formulate a definition of "Brill–Noether general in rank $n$" for a smooth projective curve of genus $g$ that
(i) is satisfied by a nonempty (preferably dense) open subset of the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_g$,
(ii) reduces to the classical (Petri) notion when $n=1$,
(iii) controls the dimensions and nonemptiness of the loci $B_C(n,d,k)$ in a uniform way across all admissible triples $(n,d,k)$, and
(iv) is robust enough to support analogues of the Brill–Noether existence, connectedness, irreducibility, and smoothness theorems in higher rank.
status_search_result: The question of finding a "good" definition of Brill–Noether general in higher rank is explicitly listed as an open question in surveys of higher-rank Brill–Noether theory and coherent systems. Recent works (e.g., on higher-rank Brill–Noether loci on nodal curves, and a 2026 preprint on Brill–Noether generality of curves and K3 surfaces) continue to investigate variants of the notion, but no consensus definition meeting all the desired properties has emerged.

paper_title: Higher Rank Brill-Noether Theory and Coherent Systems: Open Questions
original_question: For twisted Brill-Noether loci B(n,d,k)(F), can the additional numerical hypotheses imposed in Hitching-Hoff-Newstead for proving non-emptiness and the existence of a generically smooth component of dimension beta(n,d,k)(F) be weakened?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a smooth irreducible complex projective curve of genus $g \geq 2$. For positive integers $n$, $d$, $k$ and a vector bundle $F$ on $C$, let $M(n,d)$ denote the moduli space of stable vector bundles of rank $n$ and degree $d$ on $C$, and define the twisted Brill–Noether locus
$$B(n,d,k)(F) = \{ E \in M(n,d) : h^0(C, F \otimes E) \geq k \}.$$
Its expected dimension is the twisted Brill–Noether number
$$\beta(n,d,k)(F) = n^2(g-1) + 1 - k\bigl(k - \chi(F \otimes E)\bigr),$$
where $\chi(F\otimes E) = \deg(F\otimes E) + \operatorname{rk}(F\otimes E)(1-g)$.

Known sufficient conditions (involving numerical inequalities on $n$, $d$, $k$, $g$ and the rank and degree of $F$) guarantee that $B(n,d,k)(F)$ is non-empty and has an irreducible component which is generically smooth of dimension $\beta(n,d,k)(F)$. The problem is to determine whether these numerical hypotheses can be weakened: specifically, find weaker (preferably sharp) sufficient conditions on the parameters $(n,d,k,g)$ and on $F$ under which $B(n,d,k)(F)$ remains non-empty and admits a generically smooth irreducible component of the expected dimension $\beta(n,d,k)(F)$.
status_search_result: Subsequent work (e.g., "New examples of twisted Brill-Noether loci I and II", arXiv:2212.05573 and arXiv:2601.11855) has constructed new examples of nonempty twisted Brill-Noether loci, expanding the known region. However, I found no result claiming a definitive weakening of the full set of hypotheses for non-emptiness together with the existence of a generically smooth component of the expected dimension. The question appears to remain open in general.

paper_title: Higher Rank Brill-Noether Theory and Coherent Systems: Open Questions
original_question: For which ranks n >= 2 and for which smooth curves C does Mercat's Conjecture Cliff_n(C) = Cliff_1(C) hold, and more generally what good lower bounds can one prove for Cliff_n(C)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a smooth irreducible projective curve of genus $g \geq 2$ over the complex numbers. For an integer $n \geq 1$, define the rank-$n$ Clifford index of $C$ by
$$\mathrm{Cliff}_n(C) = \min\left\{ \frac{1}{n}\bigl(\deg E - 2(h^0(E) - n)\bigr) \;\Big|\; E \text{ a vector bundle on } C \text{ of rank } n,\ h^0(E) \geq n+1,\ \mu(E) \leq g-1 \right\},$$
where $\mu(E) = \deg(E)/\mathrm{rk}(E)$. For $n=1$ this recovers the classical Clifford index $\mathrm{Cliff}_1(C)$ of the curve.

Mercat's Conjecture asserts that $\mathrm{Cliff}_n(C) = \mathrm{Cliff}_1(C)$ for every $n \geq 2$.

Determine for which integers $n \geq 2$ and for which smooth projective curves $C$ Mercat's Conjecture holds. More generally, establish good lower bounds for $\mathrm{Cliff}_n(C)$ valid for all $n \geq 2$ and all such curves $C$.
category_tag: Higher rank Brill-Noether theory / Mercat's conjecture
status_search_result: Mercat's conjecture is known to hold in rank 2 for generic curves of every genus (Bakker–Farkas), but fails on a divisor in M_g for odd g. For ranks n ≥ 3 (and n ≥ 4), explicit counterexamples have been constructed using Lazarsfeld–Mukai bundles on curves lying on K3 surfaces. The general problem of characterizing for which n and which C the conjecture holds, and finding sharp lower bounds for Cliff_n(C), remains open.

original_question: For a general smooth curve C, what are the higher-rank gonalities gon_{n,k} and gon^s_{n,k}, and for which pairs (n,k) do the semistable and stable versions coincide?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a general smooth projective curve of genus $g \geq 2$ over the complex numbers. For integers $n \geq 1$ and $k \geq 1$, define the higher-rank gonalities of $C$ as follows:

- $\mathrm{gon}_{n,k}(C)$ is the minimal degree $d$ such that there exists a semistable vector bundle $E$ on $C$ of rank $n$ and degree $d$ with $h^0(C,E) \geq n + k$.
- $\mathrm{gon}^{s}_{n,k}(C)$ is the minimal degree $d$ such that there exists a stable vector bundle $E$ on $C$ of rank $n$ and degree $d$ with $h^0(C,E) \geq n + k$.

(For $n=1$ both invariants reduce to the classical $k$-th gonality of $C$.)

Problems:

(a) Determine, as functions of $g$, $n$, and $k$, the values of $\mathrm{gon}_{n,k}(C)$ and $\mathrm{gon}^{s}_{n,k}(C)$ for a general curve $C$ of genus $g$.

(b) Characterize the pairs $(n,k)$ (depending on $g$) for which $\mathrm{gon}_{n,k}(C) = \mathrm{gon}^{s}_{n,k}(C)$.
status_search_result: The problem of computing higher-rank gonalities $\mathrm{gon}_{n,k}$ and $\mathrm{gon}^s_{n,k}$ on a general curve, and identifying when the semistable and stable versions agree, is listed as an open question in the survey on higher-rank Brill–Noether theory and coherent systems. While related higher-rank Brill–Noether results (e.g., for low genus or fixed classical gonality) have appeared, no general formula determining these invariants for all $(n,k)$ on a general curve has been published.

paper_title: Higher Rank Brill-Noether Theory and Coherent Systems: Open Questions
context_brief: Rank-3 Clifford index on general curves
original_question: For a general smooth curve C of genus g, what is the value of Cliff_3(C), and which vector bundles compute that rank-3 Clifford index?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a smooth projective curve of genus $g$ over $\mathbb{C}$. For a vector bundle $E$ on $C$ of rank $r \geq 1$ and degree $d$, define the (rank-$r$) Clifford index of $E$ by
$$\gamma(E) = \frac{1}{r}\bigl(\deg(E) - 2(h^0(E) - r)\bigr) = \mu(E) - \frac{2}{r}(h^0(E) - r),$$
where $\mu(E) = d/r$ is the slope. The rank-$r$ Clifford index of $C$ is
$$\mathrm{Cliff}_r(C) = \min\{\gamma(E) : E \text{ a semistable bundle of rank } r \text{ on } C \text{ with } h^0(E) \geq 2r,\ \mu(E) \leq g-1\}.$$
A bundle $E$ is said to compute $\mathrm{Cliff}_r(C)$ if it is semistable, satisfies $h^0(E) \geq 2r$ and $\mu(E) \leq g-1$, and $\gamma(E) = \mathrm{Cliff}_r(C)$.

For a general smooth curve $C$ of genus $g$, determine the value of $\mathrm{Cliff}_3(C)$ as a function of $g$, and classify the vector bundles $E$ on $C$ that compute $\mathrm{Cliff}_3(C)$.
status_search_result: The problem is open in general. Partial results are known: for a general curve, $\mathrm{Cliff}_3(C)$ has been computed in specific genera (e.g., $g=9$: $10/3$; $g=10$: $4$; $g=11$: $14/3$), and Mercat's conjecture for rank 3 has been established for $g \leq 8$ and $g \geq 13$ when $C$ has classical Clifford index 3. A complete formula for general $g$ and full classification of computing bundles do not appear in the literature.

original_question: Suppose C is a non-hyperelliptic curve of genus 3 and (E,V) is a general generated linear series in G(1,2k,k) with k >= 6. Is the dual-span bundle D_{E,V} stable?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a smooth non-hyperelliptic projective curve of genus $3$ over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. A coherent system of type $(n,d,k)$ on $C$ is a pair $(E,V)$ where $E$ is a vector bundle of rank $n$ and degree $d$ on $C$ and $V \subseteq H^0(C,E)$ is a $k$-dimensional subspace. The coherent system $(E,V)$ is said to be generated if the evaluation map $\mathrm{ev}\colon V\otimes \mathcal{O}_C \to E$ is surjective. When this holds, its kernel, twisted by a sign, gives the dual span bundle $D_{E,V}$, defined by the exact sequence
$$0 \longrightarrow D_{E,V}^{\vee} \longrightarrow V\otimes \mathcal{O}_C \xrightarrow{\;\mathrm{ev}\;} E \longrightarrow 0,$$
so that $D_{E,V}$ is a vector bundle of rank $k-n$ on $C$. Let $G(1,2k,k)$ denote the moduli space of coherent systems $(E,V)$ on $C$ with $n=1$, $d=2k$, and $\dim V = k$, restricted to those that are generated. Fix an integer $k \geq 6$ and consider a general such generated coherent system $(E,V) \in G(1,2k,k)$.

Question: Is the dual span bundle $D_{E,V}$ slope-stable with respect to the canonical slope on $C$?

original_question: For a general smooth curve C, do there exist nonempty Brill-Noether loci B(n,d,n+1) whose bundles all fail to be generated, so that the locus contains no generated bundles at all?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a general smooth projective curve of genus $g\ge 2$ over $\mathbb{C}$. For positive integers $n,d,k$, let $B(n,d,k)$ denote the Brill–Noether locus parametrizing isomorphism classes of stable vector bundles $E$ on $C$ of rank $n$ and degree $d$ with $h^0(C,E)\ge k$. A vector bundle $E$ on $C$ is called generated (or globally generated) if the natural evaluation map $H^0(C,E)\otimes \mathcal{O}_C \to E$ is surjective.

Question: Do there exist integers $n,d$ with $g,n,d$ such that the Brill–Noether locus $B(n,d,n+1)$ is non-empty and yet every bundle $E$ representing a point of $B(n,d,n+1)$ fails to be globally generated (i.e., $B(n,d,n+1)$ contains no generated bundles)?
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in surveys on higher-rank Brill–Noether theory. While examples of non-empty B(n,d,n+1) without generated elements exist on special curves (e.g., smooth plane curves of degree 7 give B(2,15,3) non-empty with no generated bundles), no analogous example or non-existence proof on a general curve appears to have been established. Recent work on coherent systems of type (n,d,n+1) and dual span bundles addresses related stability/birationality questions but does not resolve this specific existence question on a general curve.

original_question: For coherent systems of type (n,d,k) on the projective line P^1, when is the interval I(n,d,k)={alpha | G(alpha;n,d,k) is nonempty} itself nonempty, and if I(n,d,k)=(alpha_m,alpha_M) with alpha_M possibly infinite, what are the endpoint values alpha_m and alpha_M?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{P}^1$ denote the projective line over an algebraically closed field. A coherent system of type $(n,d,k)$ on $\mathbb{P}^1$ is a pair $(E,V)$ where $E$ is a vector bundle on $\mathbb{P}^1$ of rank $n$ and degree $d$, and $V \subseteq H^0(E)$ is a linear subspace of dimension $k$. For a positive real parameter $\alpha > 0$, the $\alpha$-slope of a coherent system $(E,V)$ is defined by
$$\mu_\alpha(E,V) = \frac{d}{n} + \alpha\,\frac{k}{n}.$$
A coherent system $(E,V)$ is $\alpha$-stable if for every proper coherent subsystem $(E',V')$ (with $E' \subset E$ a subbundle and $V' \subseteq V \cap H^0(E')$),
$$\mu_\alpha(E',V') < \mu_\alpha(E,V).$$
Let $G(\alpha;n,d,k)$ denote the moduli space of $\alpha$-stable coherent systems of type $(n,d,k)$ on $\mathbb{P}^1$, and define
$$I(n,d,k) = \{\alpha > 0 \mid G(\alpha;n,d,k) \neq \emptyset\}.$$
It is known that $I(n,d,k)$, when nonempty, is an open interval $(\alpha_m, \alpha_M)$, where $\alpha_M$ may equal $+\infty$.

(a) necessary and sufficient conditions on $(n,d,k)$ for $I(n,d,k)$ to be nonempty;
(b) the explicit value of the lower endpoint $\alpha_m$;
(c) the explicit value of the upper endpoint $\alpha_M$ (allowing $+\infty$).

context_brief: Flip loci and cohomology on P^1
original_question: Can one explicitly determine the flip loci for coherent systems of type (n,d,k) on P^1 and use them to compute the Hodge and Poincare polynomials of the chamber moduli spaces G_i(n,d,k)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{P}^1$ be the complex projective line. A coherent system of type $(n,d,k)$ on $\mathbb{P}^1$ is a pair $(E,V)$ where $E$ is a holomorphic vector bundle of rank $n$ and degree $d$ on $\mathbb{P}^1$ and $V \subseteq H^0(\mathbb{P}^1,E)$ is a $k$-dimensional linear subspace of global sections. For a real parameter $\alpha > 0$, the $\alpha$-slope of $(E,V)$ is defined by
$$\mu_\alpha(E,V) = \frac{d}{n} + \alpha \frac{k}{n},$$
and $(E,V)$ is called $\alpha$-(semi)stable if for every proper coherent subsystem $(E',V') \subset (E,V)$ with $0 < \operatorname{rk}(E') < n$ one has $\mu_\alpha(E',V') < \mu_\alpha(E,V)$ (resp. $\le$). The moduli space of $\alpha$-stable coherent systems of type $(n,d,k)$ on $\mathbb{P}^1$ is denoted $G_\alpha(n,d,k)$.

As $\alpha$ varies over $(0,\infty)$, there is a finite set of critical values $0 < \alpha_1 < \alpha_2 < \cdots < \alpha_L$ at which the moduli space changes; on each open chamber $(\alpha_{i-1},\alpha_i)$ the moduli space is constant, denoted $G_i(n,d,k)$. At each critical value $\alpha_i$, the difference between the moduli spaces on adjacent chambers is concentrated on the so-called flip loci, the subvarieties parametrizing coherent systems that are stable on one side of $\alpha_i$ but unstable on the other.

Problem. For all admissible triples $(n,d,k)$ with $n \ge 2$, $k \ge 1$, give an explicit description of the flip loci at every critical value $\alpha_i$ for coherent systems of type $(n,d,k)$ on $\mathbb{P}^1$, and use this description to compute the Hodge polynomial and the Poincaré polynomial of each chamber moduli space $G_i(n,d,k)$.
category_tag: moduli of coherent systems on curves
status_search_result: The case $k=1$ has been carried out: Lange–Newstead ("Coherent systems of genus 0, III: Computation of flips for $k=1$", arXiv:0707.1466) determine the flip loci and compute Hodge polynomials of $G_i(n,d,1)$ explicitly for ranks 2 and 3 and in certain cases for arbitrary rank. For general $k \ge 2$ on $\mathbb{P}^1$, no complete explicit determination of the flip loci or the resulting Hodge/Poincaré polynomials of $G_i(n,d,k)$ appears in the literature, so the problem is only partially solved.

original_question: Can one write an explicit formula for the change in the Hodge-Deligne polynomial, or equivalently in favorable cases the Poincare polynomial, when crossing a critical value alpha_i in the wall-crossing of coherent-system moduli spaces?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a smooth irreducible complex projective curve of genus $g \geq 2$. A coherent system of type $(n,d,k)$ on $C$ is a pair $(E, V)$ where $E$ is a vector bundle on $C$ of rank $n$ and degree $d$, and $V \subseteq H^0(C, E)$ is a linear subspace of dimension $k$. For a real parameter $\alpha > 0$, the $\alpha$-slope of $(E,V)$ is
$$\mu_\alpha(E,V) = \frac{d}{n} + \alpha \frac{k}{n},$$
and $(E,V)$ is called $\alpha$-(semi)stable if for every proper coherent subsystem $(E',V') \subset (E,V)$ one has $\mu_\alpha(E',V') < \mu_\alpha(E,V)$ (resp. $\leq$). Let $G(\alpha; n,d,k)$ denote the moduli space of $\alpha$-stable coherent systems of type $(n,d,k)$. As $\alpha$ varies over the positive reals, the parameter range is divided by a finite (or in some ranges discrete) set of critical values $\alpha_1 < \alpha_2 < \cdots$ at which the moduli space changes; on the open intervals between consecutive critical values, the moduli space is constant up to isomorphism, denoted $G_i := G(\alpha; n,d,k)$ for $\alpha \in (\alpha_i, \alpha_{i+1})$.

For a quasi-projective complex variety $X$, let $E(X; u, v) = \sum_{p,q,k} (-1)^k h^{p,q}(H^k_c(X,\mathbb{C})) u^p v^q$ denote its Hodge–Deligne (E-) polynomial; in cases where $X$ has pure cohomology and is smooth projective, this specializes (up to substitution) to its Poincaré polynomial.

$$E(G_i; u, v) - E(G_{i-1}; u, v)$$
arising from crossing a critical value $\alpha_i$ in the wall-crossing of moduli spaces of $\alpha$-stable coherent systems of type $(n,d,k)$ on $C$.

paper_title: Higher Rank Brill-Noether Theory and Coherent Systems: Open Questions
original_question: How are the Segre stratifications of the moduli space M(n,d), defined via maximal degrees of rank-r subbundles, related to the stratification induced by the Brill-Noether loci inside M(n,d)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a smooth irreducible projective curve of genus $g \geq 2$ over an algebraically closed field, and let $M(n,d)$ denote the moduli space of stable vector bundles of rank $n$ and degree $d$ on $C$.

For an integer $r$ with $1 \leq r \leq n-1$ and a stable bundle $E \in M(n,d)$, define the $r$-th Segre invariant by
$$s_r(E) \;=\; rd - n \cdot \max\{\deg F : F \subset E \text{ is a subbundle of rank } r\}.$$
For each integer $s$, let
$$M(n,d;r,s) \;=\; \{E \in M(n,d) : s_r(E) = s\}.$$
The locally closed subsets $M(n,d;r,s)$ (and their closures, the loci where $s_r(E) \leq s$) define the Segre stratifications of $M(n,d)$.

On the other hand, the Brill–Noether loci are defined, for integers $k \geq 1$, by
$$B(n,d,k) \;=\; \{E \in M(n,d) : h^0(C,E) \geq k\}.$$
These give the Brill–Noether stratification of $M(n,d)$.

Determine the precise relationship between the Segre stratifications $\{M(n,d;r,s)\}_{r,s}$ and the Brill–Noether stratification $\{B(n,d,k)\}_k$ of $M(n,d)$: describe how the strata of one are positioned with respect to the strata of the other (in terms of containments, intersections, dimensions, irreducible components, and generic behavior), and characterize the loci on which the two stratifications refine, coincide with, or are transverse to each other.
status_search_result: The relationship between Segre and Brill–Noether stratifications of M(n,d) is the subject of ongoing research. Partial results exist for low rank (notably rank 2 on curves and on P^2) and for moduli of coherent systems, where Segre invariants are used to stratify and to detect components of Brill–Noether loci, but no general structural answer relating the two stratifications in arbitrary rank is known. The question is presented as an open question in surveys on higher rank Brill–Noether theory.

self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a smooth irreducible projective curve of genus $g \geq 2$ over the complex numbers. For integers $n \geq 1$, $d$, and $k \geq 1$, recall the following moduli-theoretic objects associated to $C$:

(a) The Brill–Noether locus $B^{k}_{n,d}(C) \subset M_{n,d}(C)$ inside the moduli space $M_{n,d}(C)$ of (semi)stable vector bundles of rank $n$ and degree $d$ on $C$, defined as the locus of bundles $E$ with $h^{0}(C,E) \geq k$.

(b) The moduli space $G(\alpha; n,d,k)$ of $\alpha$-(semi)stable coherent systems $(E,V)$ of type $(n,d,k)$ on $C$, where $E$ is a vector bundle of rank $n$ and degree $d$ on $C$, $V \subseteq H^{0}(C,E)$ is a linear subspace of dimension $k$, and $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ is a stability parameter.

Formulate and resolve Torelli-type statements for these moduli spaces. Specifically: determine the extent to which the isomorphism class of $C$ is recovered from the data of one (or several) of the moduli spaces $B^{k}_{n,d}(C)$ or $G(\alpha;n,d,k)(C)$, as an abstract variety. That is, identify ranges of parameters $(n,d,k,\alpha)$ for which an isomorphism
$$B^{k}_{n,d}(C) \cong B^{k}_{n,d}(C') \quad \text{or} \quad G(\alpha;n,d,k)(C) \cong G(\alpha;n,d,k)(C')$$
of complex varieties implies $C \cong C'$, and conversely characterize cases where the moduli space fails to determine $C$.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction in higher-rank Brill–Noether theory. While classical Torelli theorems are known for moduli of stable bundles (Mumford–Newstead, Narasimhan–Ramanan, Kouvidakis–Pantev) and partial Torelli-type results exist for some Brill–Noether loci, a comprehensive answer covering the full range of Brill–Noether loci and coherent system moduli spaces does not appear in the literature. No source found resolves this in general.

paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
context_brief: QCD critical point existence and location
original_question: Does the QCD critical point exist in the temperature-density phase diagram of QCD, and if it does, what are its critical temperature and density coordinates? Equivalently, can a first-principles finite-density QCD calculation establish either the existence or the non-existence of a critical endpoint separating crossover and first-order behavior in baryonic matter?
self_contained_problem:
Consider Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the SU(3) gauge theory of quarks and gluons, at nonzero temperature T and nonzero baryon chemical potential μ_B. As a function of (T, μ_B), the theory exhibits a phase structure separating a hadronic phase from a quark–gluon plasma phase. At μ_B = 0, lattice QCD with physical quark masses establishes that the transition is an analytic crossover at a pseudocritical temperature T_pc ≈ 155 MeV. Model studies and effective theories suggest that at sufficiently large μ_B the transition becomes first order, in which case the line of first-order transitions must terminate at a second-order critical endpoint (the "QCD critical point") in the (T, μ_B) plane.

Resolve the following from first principles within full QCD (e.g., via a controlled finite-density lattice calculation that overcomes the fermion sign problem):

(a) Determine whether a critical endpoint exists in the QCD phase diagram in the (T, μ_B) plane, i.e., a point at which a line of first-order chiral/deconfinement transitions terminates in a second-order transition.

(b) If such a critical endpoint exists, determine its location, i.e., the values (T_c, μ_B^c).
status_search_result: As of 2025–2026, the existence and location of the QCD critical endpoint remain unresolved. Recent continuum-extrapolated lattice QCD work (using entropy-contour extrapolations from imaginary chemical potential) excludes a critical point at μ_B < 450 MeV at the 2σ level but cannot establish its existence; the methodology itself is debated. Experimental searches (RHIC Beam Energy Scan / STAR) continue. No first-principles proof of existence or non-existence has been established.

paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
original_question: What breakthrough is required to obtain a successful, quantitatively reliable first-principles approach to finite-density baryonic matter from QCD? In particular, since existing phenomenological descriptions have substantial model dependence and there is currently no established successful method for finite-density baryonic matter, what new conceptual or computational development would allow QCD itself to describe such matter quantitatively?
self_contained_problem:
In Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the Euclidean lattice path integral at nonzero baryon chemical potential μ has a complex action: the fermion determinant det M(μ) satisfies [det M(μ)]* = det M(−μ*), so for real μ ≠ 0 the integrand of the partition function

  Z(μ) = ∫ DU e^{−S_g[U]} det M(U,μ)

is not real-positive. This obstructs standard importance-sampling Monte Carlo and is known as the sign problem of finite-density lattice QCD. Existing techniques (reweighting, Taylor expansion in μ/T, imaginary-μ analytic continuation, complex Langevin dynamics, Lefschetz thimble methods, density-of-states approaches, tensor-network and quantum-computing approaches) are restricted to small μ/T, suffer from uncontrolled systematic errors, fail to converge correctly in physically relevant regimes, or are not yet scalable to four-dimensional QCD with physical quark masses.

Problem. Provide a quantitatively reliable, first-principles method for evaluating expectation values

  ⟨O⟩ = (1/Z(μ)) ∫ DU e^{−S_g[U]} det M(U,μ) O[U]

in lattice QCD with Nf = 2+1 flavors at physical quark masses for baryon chemical potentials μ_B in the cold, dense regime (T ≪ μ_B, with μ_B of order the nucleon mass), with controlled and systematically improvable errors, sufficient to compute the equation of state and phase structure of finite-density baryonic matter directly from QCD. Equivalently, exhibit a conceptual or computational development that overcomes the finite-density sign problem in this regime and demonstrate its quantitative reliability against known benchmarks.
status_search_result: The finite-density QCD sign problem remains an open problem. Recent reviews and ongoing contributions to the Lattice 2025 symposium continue to discuss complex Langevin, Lefschetz thimble, density-of-states, machine-learning, and quantum-computing approaches, but none has been established as a quantitatively reliable first-principles method for cold, dense baryonic matter at physical quark masses.

paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
original_question: How can one determine, in a robust and practically usable way, when a finite-density QCD method that is formally correct in principle is actually failing in practice and producing unphysical answers? This includes identifying diagnostics that distinguish trustworthy results from artifacts caused by pitfalls such as hidden overlap problems, uncontrolled phase fluctuations, or other failures of methods that are mathematically sound but numerically unreliable.
status_search_result: No general solution is known. Reviews on the lattice QCD sign problem (2021–2025) consistently describe the diagnosis of silent failures in formally-correct methods (overlap problem, complex-Langevin boundary terms, missed thimbles) as an active and unresolved research area, with only partial, method-specific criteria available (e.g., Aarts–Seiler–Stamatescu boundary-term and drift-distribution criteria for complex Langevin). A unified, robust diagnostic framework remains open.

paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
original_question: Can Taylor expansion around zero chemical potential determine the QCD equation of state and, more importantly, identify phase transitions or the QCD critical point when only low-order coefficients are practically accessible and the convergence near the transition region is slow? This includes the open issue of whether sufficiently accurate higher-order coefficients can be computed to make the method reliable beyond very small chemical potential.
self_contained_problem:
Consider lattice quantum chromodynamics (QCD) on a four-dimensional Euclidean lattice with quark chemical potential $\mu$, and let $p(T,\mu)$ denote the pressure (equation of state) as a function of temperature $T$ and $\mu$. Because the fermion determinant becomes complex for $\mu 
eq 0$, direct Monte Carlo sampling suffers from a sign problem. The Taylor expansion method approximates the equation of state via
$$\frac{p(T,\mu)}{T^4} \;=\; \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_{n}(T)\,\Big(\frac{\mu}{T}\Big)^{n},$$
where the coefficients $c_n(T)$ are computed at $\mu=0$ as expectation values of products of derivatives of $\ln\det M(\mu)$ (with $M$ the lattice Dirac operator). In practice only low-order coefficients $c_n$ (currently up to about $n=8$) can be evaluated, since the statistical variance of the stochastic estimators of $c_n$ grows rapidly with $n$, and the radius of convergence of the series is expected to shrink near a phase transition or a putative QCD critical point in the $(T,\mu)$ plane.

Problem. Determine whether the Taylor expansion of the QCD equation of state around $\mu=0$ can, with only practically accessible low-order coefficients $\{c_n\}_{n\le N}$ (for moderate $N$), reliably (i) reconstruct the equation of state $p(T,\mu)/T^4$ in a neighborhood of the chiral/deconfinement transition, and (ii) detect and locate phase transitions and the QCD critical point. In particular, establish whether sufficiently accurate higher-order Taylor coefficients $c_n(T)$ can be computed by lattice methods so as to extend the reliable range of the expansion beyond the regime $\mu/T \ll 1$, or alternatively prove obstructions (e.g., from the location of Lee–Yang singularities and the finite radius of convergence) that preclude such reconstruction near the transition region.
status_search_result: The Taylor expansion approach to finite-density lattice QCD remains an active area of research as of 2025–2026. Higher-order coefficients (through eighth order) have been computed by the HotQCD and Wuppertal–Budapest collaborations, and methods based on Padé/conformal resummations and Lee–Yang zero analyses are being developed, but a definitive determination of the QCD critical point or the equation of state at moderate-to-large $\mu/T$ has not been achieved. The fundamental obstruction—rapid growth of statistical error in higher-order coefficients and a possibly limited radius of convergence near the transition—is unresolved.

paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
original_question: What is the continuum-limit behavior of the Roberge-Weiss endpoint and related critical temperatures for Wilson-fermion lattice QCD, and can the continuum extrapolation be achieved there? This asks whether the qualitative picture known from staggered-fermion studies survives quantitatively when Wilson fermions are pushed to the continuum limit.
self_contained_problem:
Consider lattice QCD with Nf=2 mass-degenerate Wilson fermions at finite temperature in the presence of an imaginary quark chemical potential μ = iμ_I. The grand-canonical partition function is periodic in θ = μ_I/T with period 2π/3, and along the lines θ = (2k+1)π/3 there is a first-order Roberge–Weiss (RW) transition associated with the spontaneous breaking of charge-conjugation symmetry above a critical temperature T_RW. The RW endpoint at T = T_RW depends on the quark mass m: it is first-order (triple point) for sufficiently small or sufficiently large m, and second-order (Ising) for intermediate masses, with two tricritical mass values m_tric^(light) and m_tric^(heavy) separating these regimes.

(a) Determine the continuum-limit values of the RW endpoint temperature T_RW and of the tricritical quark masses m_tric^(light), m_tric^(heavy) for Nf=2 Wilson-fermion lattice QCD, by performing a controlled continuum extrapolation Nτ → ∞ (with aspect ratio fixed and Nτ a = 1/T).

(b) Determine the continuum-limit value of the pseudocritical/critical temperature T_c at zero chemical potential for Nf=2 Wilson fermions, and verify whether the qualitative phase-structure picture established with staggered fermions (location of the RW endpoint, mass dependence of its order, position of the tricritical points) is reproduced quantitatively by Wilson fermions in the continuum limit.
status_search_result: Lattice studies of the Roberge–Weiss endpoint with Nf=2 Wilson fermions have been carried out at Nτ=4 and Nτ=6, with exploratory Nτ=8 results. These studies report that the tricritical masses shift toward smaller values as the lattice is refined and explicitly state that significantly finer lattices are needed before a continuum extrapolation becomes feasible. No continuum-extrapolated result for T_RW or T_c with Wilson fermions at finite (imaginary) chemical potential is reported in the available literature, indicating the problem is still open.

paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
original_question: Can the canonical method determine the QCD critical point and first-order transition structure on substantially larger lattices with controlled errors, rather than only on the small volumes used in existing successful studies? This includes whether canonical calculations can overcome the growing sign problem and computational cost enough to make their current critical-point claims robust in larger-volume regimes.
self_contained_problem:
Consider lattice Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) at finite baryon density studied via the canonical ensemble method. In this approach one fixes the net quark (or baryon) number N and computes the canonical partition function Z_C(N,T,V) by Fourier-transforming the grand-canonical partition function in the imaginary chemical potential μ = iθT:
   Z_C(N,T,V) = (1/2π) ∫_{-π}^{π} dθ e^{-iNθ} Z_GC(iθT, T, V),
where Z_GC is evaluated by standard Monte Carlo simulation at imaginary chemical potential (where the fermion determinant is real and the sign problem is absent). Observables at real chemical potential μ_B are reconstructed via fugacity expansion Z_GC(μ_B,T,V) = Σ_N Z_C(N,T,V) e^{N μ_B/T}. By searching for an S-shaped structure (Maxwell construction) in the chemical-potential–density relation, one attempts to locate the QCD critical end point and the first-order chiral/deconfinement transition line in the (T, μ_B) plane.

Existing successful canonical-method studies that have reported a QCD critical point have all used small spatial lattice volumes. The question is the following:

Can the canonical method determine the QCD critical end point and the structure of the first-order transition line on substantially larger spatial lattices (taking the thermodynamic limit under control) with quantitatively controlled statistical and systematic errors? In particular, can the canonical-method computation overcome:
(i) the residual/oscillatory sign problem arising from rapid phase fluctuations of the integrand e^{-iNθ} Z_GC(iθT) at large N, especially in the hadronic/confined phase, and
(ii) the growing computational cost of accurately determining Z_C(N,T,V) for the range of N relevant to the first-order transition,
to the extent that current critical-point claims become robust as the lattice volume is increased toward the thermodynamic limit?
status_search_result: Recent literature (through 2025) continues to treat the QCD critical point search via the canonical method as an active, unresolved problem. Existing canonical-method critical-point studies remain on small lattices, and known phase-fluctuation issues in the canonical approach (a residual sign problem at large N) and computational cost still limit reliable extension to larger volumes. Recent work (e.g., 2025 lattice constraints on the critical point via improved equations of state) addresses related questions but does not establish a controlled-error canonical determination of the critical point on substantially larger lattices.

paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
original_question: For the regime mπ/2 < µ < mN/3 at low temperature, how do complex phase cancellations operate so that physically the quark-number expectation value can remain zero even though individual gauge configurations can already give nonzero quark number? Equivalently, what is the detailed phase-distribution mechanism that enforces the Silver-Blaze behavior in this interval?
self_contained_problem:
Consider lattice QCD with $N_f$ light quark flavors at nonzero baryon chemical potential $\mu$ and low temperature $T \to 0$. Let $m_\pi$ denote the pion mass and $m_N$ the nucleon mass. The grand-canonical partition function is

$$Z(\mu) = \int \mathcal{D}U\, e^{-S_g[U]}\, \det M(U,\mu),$$

where $S_g[U]$ is the gauge action and $M(U,\mu)$ is the quark Dirac operator on a gauge background $U$. For $\mu \neq 0$, $\det M(U,\mu)$ is in general complex; write $\det M(U,\mu) = |\det M(U,\mu)|\, e^{i\theta(U,\mu)}$. The expectation value of the quark number operator $\hat{n}$ on a single gauge configuration is generally nonzero, $\hat{n}[U,\mu] \neq 0$, yet the Silver-Blaze property requires that the full ensemble expectation value $\langle \hat{n}\rangle$ vanish for $\mu$ below the physical onset $\mu < m_N/3$.

In the interval $m_\pi/2 < \mu < m_N/3$, where the phase-quenched theory has already undergone pion condensation but full QCD has not yet reached baryon onset, determine the precise mechanism by which the distribution of the phase $\theta(U,\mu)$ over the gauge ensemble produces cancellations that enforce

$$\langle \hat{n}\rangle = \frac{1}{Z(\mu)}\int \mathcal{D}U\, e^{-S_g[U]}\, \det M(U,\mu)\, \hat{n}[U,\mu] = 0.$$

Specifically, characterize the joint distribution of $\theta(U,\mu)$ and $\hat{n}[U,\mu]$ on configurations weighted by $e^{-S_g[U]}|\det M(U,\mu)|$ that is responsible for the exact cancellation of the quark-number contributions, and show how this distribution evolves with $\mu$ across the interval $(m_\pi/2,\, m_N/3)$.
status_search_result: Recent reviews and lattice studies (including a 2026 review on the Silver Blaze problem in QCD and complex Langevin equation-of-state work in 2022) indicate that, while the Silver Blaze phenomenon is widely observed and discussed, the detailed mechanism by which phase cancellations enforce vanishing quark number in the interval m_π/2 < μ < m_N/3 remains unresolved. The mechanism leading to such cancellations is described in the literature as still unknown.

paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
context_brief: future reach and reliability of current results
original_question: Can the parts of the QCD phase diagram that are currently out of reach become accessible in the future, and are some of the results currently believed to be correct actually still vulnerable to revision? This is the paper’s broad meta-level open question about the long-term reliability and eventual completeness of present finite-density lattice QCD knowledge.
self_contained_problem:
Consider lattice quantum chromodynamics (QCD) at finite baryon density, formulated on a Euclidean spacetime lattice with quark chemical potential μ ≠ 0. Because the Euclidean fermion determinant det M(μ) is in general complex for μ ≠ 0, direct importance sampling Monte Carlo simulation is obstructed by the so-called sign problem, and large regions of the (T, μ) phase diagram — in particular the conjectured QCD critical end point and the cold, dense regime relevant to neutron-star matter — are currently inaccessible to fully controlled first-principles lattice computations. Existing partial results rely on techniques such as Taylor expansion around μ = 0, analytic continuation from imaginary chemical potential, reweighting, the complex Langevin equation, Lefschetz-thimble methods, and dual/worldline reformulations, each with its own systematic uncertainties.

Address the following meta-level question regarding the long-term completeness and reliability of finite-density lattice QCD:

(a) Determine whether the regions of the QCD phase diagram in the (T, μ) plane that are presently out of reach of controlled lattice simulations — including a rigorous determination of the existence and location of the conjectured critical end point and of the phase structure at low temperature and large baryon chemical potential — can in principle be made accessible by some future algorithmic or theoretical development that fully resolves the sign problem (or by a proof that no polynomial-time resolution exists, as for example under standard complexity-theoretic assumptions).

(b) Determine whether any of the finite-density lattice QCD results currently believed to be correct (such as the curvature of the pseudo-critical line near μ = 0, equation-of-state expansions, and bounds on the location of the critical end point obtained from Taylor coefficients or from imaginary-μ analytic continuation) are subject to revision when their as-yet-uncontrolled systematic errors (truncation of the Taylor series, ambiguities of analytic continuation, finite-volume and continuum-limit effects) are eventually brought under full control.

Provide either a rigorous resolution of (a) and (b), or a precise framework in which such a resolution can be formulated.
category_tag: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem
status_search_result: The sign problem in finite-density lattice QCD remains an outstanding open problem; no general controlled method exists for the cold, dense regime, and the existence/location of the QCD critical end point is still unresolved as of recent reviews and lattice conference proceedings. Complexity-theoretic results (Troyer–Wiese) suggest a generic resolution is unlikely, but partial progress continues via complex Langevin, Lefschetz thimbles, and Taylor/imaginary-μ methods.

paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
original_question: Can quantum entanglement or tensor-network-based descriptions provide a genuinely new route to solving or sharply characterizing the sign problem in finite-density QCD? More specifically, can entanglement serve as the right measure of the effective degrees of freedom and computational cost in a way that leads to new numerical strategies for dense QCD?
self_contained_problem:
Consider lattice quantum chromodynamics (lattice QCD) at nonzero baryon chemical potential μ ≠ 0. The Euclidean fermion determinant det M(μ) is generally complex, so the standard Boltzmann weight e^{-S_g} det M(μ) cannot be interpreted as a probability density. This obstruction—the sign problem—prevents direct importance-sampling Monte Carlo simulation of dense QCD, including the quark–gluon plasma, nuclear matter, and neutron-star regimes.

A tensor-network state on a lattice is a variational ansatz (e.g. matrix product state, projected entangled pair state, MERA) for the wavefunction or path-integral tensor, parametrized by local tensors whose bond dimension D controls the maximal bipartite entanglement entropy S ≤ log D that the ansatz can represent. Tensor-network methods are formulated directly in Hilbert space (or as exact tensor contractions of the partition function) and therefore do not rely on probabilistic sampling of complex weights, so they are not afflicted by the sign problem in the Monte Carlo sense.

Question. Determine whether quantum entanglement and tensor-network representations can provide a genuinely new route to solving or sharply characterizing the sign problem of finite-density lattice QCD in 3+1 dimensions. In particular:

(a) Does the bipartite entanglement entropy of the ground state (or thermal state) of finite-density QCD serve as a faithful measure of the effective number of degrees of freedom and of the computational cost required by any tensor-network algorithm that targets that state? Make this notion precise and prove or disprove it.

(b) Construct, or prove the impossibility of constructing, a tensor-network algorithm whose computational cost (as a function of system size, lattice spacing, and chemical potential) is polynomial in the relevant entanglement measure and which yields controlled approximations to expectation values of gauge-invariant observables in 3+1-dimensional lattice QCD at nonzero baryon density.
category_tag: lattice QCD sign problem and tensor networks

Whether entanglement provides the correct measure of computational cost for dense QCD is still an open research direction.

paper_title: On a general Syracuse problem with conjectures
context_brief: Divergent trajectories in generalized Syracuse maps
original_question: Let a and b be odd integers with a > −b and a + b = 2^ν₀, and let T(n)=n/2 for even n and T(n)=(a n+b)/2 for odd n. Let G(∞) be the set of positive starting values n for which T^k(n) tends to infinity. Which conditions on a and b make G(∞) empty, and which conditions make G(∞) nonempty? Equivalently, for which such maps does every trajectory eventually enter a finite cycle rather than diverge?
self_contained_problem:
Let $a$ and $b$ be odd integers satisfying $a > -b$ and $a + b = 2^{\nu_0}$ for some positive integer $\nu_0$. Define the map $T : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ by
$$T(n) = \begin{cases} n/2 & \text{if } n \text{ is even},\\ (an+b)/2 & \text{if } n \text{ is odd}. \end{cases}$$
For each starting value $n \in \mathbb{N}$, consider the trajectory $\{T^{(k)}(n)\}_{k \geq 0}$ obtained by iterating $T$. Define
$$G(\infty) = \{\, n \in \mathbb{N} : \lim_{k \to \infty} T^{(k)}(n) = \infty \,\}.$$
Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the pair $(a,b)$ (subject to the standing assumptions above) under which $G(\infty)$ is empty, and conditions under which $G(\infty)$ is nonempty. Equivalently, characterize those parameters $(a,b)$ for which every positive integer trajectory of $T$ eventually enters a finite cycle, as opposed to diverging to infinity.
status_search_result: This is a generalization of the Collatz (Syracuse) conjecture. Even the classical case $a=3$, $b=1$ remains famously open (Lagarias, Tao 2019 partial result on almost-bounded trajectories). No general characterization of $(a,b)$ producing only bounded trajectories is known, and the question is widely regarded as open.

paper_title: On a general Syracuse problem with conjectures
original_question: Let a and b be odd integers with a > −b and a + b = 2^ν₀, and let T(n)=n/2 for even n and T(n)=(a n+b)/2 for odd n. Under which conditions on a and b does T have exactly one cycle, #C(a,b)=1? In that case, is the unique cycle necessarily the trivial cycle Ω(1), and, if G(∞)=∅ as well, does every positive integer n satisfy T^k(n)=1 for some k, so that all positive integers lie in G(1)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $a$ and $b$ be odd integers satisfying $a > -b$, and write $a + b = 2^{\nu_0}$ for some nonnegative integer $\nu_0$. Define the map $T : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ by
$$T(n) = \begin{cases} n/2 & \text{if } n \text{ is even}, \\ (an+b)/2 & \text{if } n \text{ is odd}. \end{cases}$$
A cycle of $T$ is a finite set $\Omega \subset \mathbb{N}$ on which some iterate $T^{(k)}$ acts as the identity, with length $k$ being the smallest such positive integer. Let $\mathcal{C}(a,b)$ denote the set of all cycles of $T$ in $\mathbb{N}$. For $\omega \in \mathbb{N}$ define
$$G(\omega) = \{ n \in \mathbb{N} : \exists\, k \in \mathbb{N},\ T^{(k)}(n) = \omega \}, \qquad G(\infty) = \{ n \in \mathbb{N} : \lim_{k \to \infty} T^{(k)}(n) = \infty \}.$$
The "trivial cycle" $\Omega(1)$ is the cycle containing $1$ that arises naturally from the iteration of $T$ starting at $1$ (using $a+b = 2^{\nu_0}$, so that $T^{(\nu_0)}(1) = 1$).

(a) Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the pair $(a,b)$ under which $\#\mathcal{C}(a,b) = 1$.

(b) Show that whenever $\#\mathcal{C}(a,b) = 1$, the unique cycle of $T$ is $\Omega(1)$.

(c) Assuming both $\#\mathcal{C}(a,b) = 1$ and $G(\infty) = \emptyset$, prove that for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ there exists $k \in \mathbb{N}$ with $T^{(k)}(n) = 1$, i.e.\ $\mathbb{N} = G(1)$.
status_search_result: The classical Syracuse/Collatz conjecture (the case $a=3,b=1$) remains open, and broader generalizations of the form $T(n)=(an+b)/2$ have been studied (e.g.\ by Matthews and others) without a general resolution; Kurtz–Simon even showed certain natural generalizations are undecidable. No source verifies a complete characterization of when $\#\mathcal{C}(a,b)=1$ or a proof that all trajectories reach $1$ under the stated hypotheses, so the problem is regarded as open.

context_brief: Cycle classification for the 5n+3 Syracuse variant

Define the map T : ℤ_{>0} → ℤ_{>0} by
   T(n) = n/2          if n is even,
   T(n) = (5n+3)/2     if n is odd.

Consider the seven explicit cycles
  Ω(1)  = (1 → 4 → 2 → 1),
  Ω(3)  = (3 → 9 → 24 → 12 → 6 → 3),
  Ω(39) = (39 → 99 → 249 → 624 → 312 → 156 → 78 → 39),
  Ω(43) = (43 → 109 → 274 → 137 → 344 → 172 → 86 → 43),
  Ω(51) = (51 → 129 → 324 → 162 → 81 → 204 → 102 → 51),
  Ω(53) = (53 → 134 → 67 → 169 → 424 → 212 → 106 → 53),

paper_title: On a general Syracuse problem with conjectures
context_brief: Cycle classification for the 3n+5 Syracuse variant
original_question: For the map T(n)=n/2 when n is even and T(n)=(3n+5)/2 when n is odd, is C(3,5) exactly the six cycles with least elements 1, 5, 19, 23, 187, and 347, of respective lengths 3, 2, 5, 5, 27, and 27? Equivalently, do the positive integers decompose as N=G(1)∪G(5)∪G(19)∪G(23)∪G(187)∪G(347), with no divergent trajectories G(∞)=∅?
self_contained_problem:
Define the map $T:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ by
$$T(n)=\begin{cases}n/2 & \text{if }n\text{ is even},\\ (3n+5)/2 & \text{if }n\text{ is odd}.\end{cases}$$
For a positive integer $m$, let $\Omega(m)$ denote a cycle of $T$ whose least element is $m$, and let $G(m)$ denote the set of positive integers whose forward $T$-orbit eventually enters $\Omega(m)$. Let $G(\infty)$ denote the set of positive integers with divergent $T$-orbit (orbit unbounded), and let $\mathcal{C}(3,5)$ be the set of all cycles of $T$ on $\mathbb{N}$.

The following six cycles of $T$ are known:
- $\Omega(1):\ 1\to 4\to 2\to 1$ (length $3$),
- $\Omega(5):\ 5\to 10\to 5$ (length $2$),
- $\Omega(19):\ 19\to 31\to 49\to 76\to 38\to 19$ (length $5$),
- $\Omega(23):\ 23\to 37\to 58\to 29\to 46\to 23$ (length $5$),
- $\Omega(187)$ of length $27$,
- $\Omega(347)$ of length $27$.

Prove or disprove: $\mathcal{C}(3,5)=\{\Omega(1),\Omega(5),\Omega(19),\Omega(23),\Omega(187),\Omega(347)\}$, $G(\infty)=\emptyset$, and consequently
$$\mathbb{N}=G(1)\cup G(5)\cup G(19)\cup G(23)\cup G(187)\cup G(347).$$
status_search_result: The 3n+5 variant of the Collatz/Syracuse map is a well-known generalized Collatz problem. The six cycles with least elements 1, 5, 19, 23, 187, 347 are documented in the literature, but no proof exists that these are the only cycles or that no divergent trajectory exists. Like the standard Collatz conjecture, this remains an open conjecture.
