paper_title: Causal Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: Review and Open Problems
original_question: How can graphical causal methods be explicitly integrated with multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), where multiple learning agents interact in a shared environment, so that causal reinforcement-learning methods that already support off-policy learning, data fusion, and counterfactual reasoning can address the additional complexities introduced by interacting agents?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) setting formalized as a Markov game (S, {A_i}_{i=1}^n, P, {R_i}_{i=1}^n, γ), in which n agents simultaneously choose actions a_i ∈ A_i in state s ∈ S, the environment transitions according to P(s' | s, a_1, …, a_n), and each agent i receives reward R_i(s, a_1, …, a_n, s') and seeks to maximize its discounted return E[Σ_t γ^t R_i,t]. Augment this setting with a structural causal model (SCM) M = (U, V, F, P(U)) whose endogenous variables V include the states, the joint actions, and the rewards across time, whose exogenous variables U represent unobserved confounders that may simultaneously influence multiple agents' policies and the environment, and whose structural equations F induce a causal graph G over V.

Develop a unified framework that explicitly integrates graphical causal inference (interventions do(·), counterfactuals, identifiability of causal effects from observational and interventional data via the do-calculus, and data fusion across heterogeneous sources) with MARL, such that the following are simultaneously addressed:

(1) Off-policy evaluation and learning: given trajectories generated by behavior joint policies that may differ from the target joint policies and that may be confounded by U, derive estimators of each agent's target-policy value that are consistent under the causal graph G.

(2) Data fusion: given a collection of datasets D_1, …, D_k arising from different experimental or observational regimes (e.g., interventions on subsets of agents, partial observability, simulator vs. real environment), give graphical conditions on G under which the joint-policy value or per-agent counterfactual quantities are identifiable from {D_j} and provide an algorithm to compute them.

(3) Counterfactual reasoning with interacting agents: define and identify counterfactual best-response and counterfactual regret quantities of the form E[R_i(s, a_1, …, a_{i-1}, a'_i, a_{i+1}, …, a_n) | observed trajectory] in the presence of unobserved confounders shared across agents, and characterize when such quantities are identifiable from available data.

State and prove identifiability theorems and provide provably convergent learning algorithms that solve (1)–(3) jointly in the n ≥ 2 agent case, recovering known single-agent causal RL results in the limit n = 1.
status_search_result: The integration of graphical causal inference with multi-agent reinforcement learning remains an active and largely open research program. While individual components (off-policy evaluation, counterfactual policy evaluation, and data fusion) have been studied in single-agent causal RL, no comprehensive framework providing identifiability theorems and convergent algorithms for the full multi-agent case has been established as of the search date. Recent works explore pieces of the problem (e.g., causal influence in MARL, counterfactual credit assignment), but the overall problem of explicitly bridging graphical causal methods with MARL is acknowledged as an open direction.

paper_title: Causal Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: Review and Open Problems
original_question: How can the causal-game concept of a causal Nash equilibrium, in which cooperative agents jointly optimize their actions while maintaining probabilistic beliefs about possible causal models of the environment, be applied to multi-agent reinforcement-learning problems?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a multi-agent reinforcement-learning setting in which a finite set of cooperative agents repeatedly interact with an unknown environment. The environment is modeled by an unknown structural causal model drawn from a class M of candidate causal models over the variables describing states, actions, and rewards. Each agent i maintains a (possibly shared) Bayesian posterior belief b ∈ Δ(M) over which causal model in M generates the environment's transitions and rewards, updated from observed trajectories.

A causal game is defined as the tuple (N, M, b, {A_i}, {U_i}), where N is the set of agents, A_i is agent i's action space, and U_i(a, m) is agent i's expected utility under joint action a = (a_1, …, a_n) when the true causal model is m ∈ M. A joint (possibly mixed) strategy π* = (π_1*, …, π_n*) is called a causal Nash equilibrium with respect to b if, for every agent i and every alternative strategy π_i,
    E_{m ∼ b} E_{a ∼ (π_i, π_{-i}*)}[U_i(a, m)] ≤ E_{m ∼ b} E_{a ∼ π*}[U_i(a, m)],
i.e. no agent gains by unilaterally deviating, where expectations are taken jointly over the belief over causal models and the induced action distributions. In the cooperative case, U_i ≡ U is shared, and agents jointly optimize the belief-averaged utility.

Problem: Develop a multi-agent reinforcement-learning framework that operationalizes the causal Nash equilibrium concept above. Specifically:
(a) Define a learning protocol under which cooperative agents interact with an environment whose causal model is unknown, update a posterior b_t over M, and adapt joint policies π_t.
(b) Provide conditions on M, the exploration mechanism, and belief-updating rule under which π_t converges (in an appropriate sense) to a causal Nash equilibrium with respect to the limiting belief.
(c) Quantify how the resulting equilibrium policies differ — in sample complexity, robustness to model misspecification, and achieved cooperative utility — from policies learned by standard MARL algorithms that ignore causal structure.
status_search_result: A literature search for "causal Nash equilibrium" applied to multi-agent reinforcement learning returns only general work on Nash equilibria in MARL and on causality-aware single-agent or cooperative MARL methods; no published framework instantiates the Bayesian-causal-game causal Nash equilibrium concept as a learning algorithm with convergence guarantees in MARL. The direction appears to remain an open research problem.

paper_title: Causal Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: Review and Open Problems
original_question: How can causal inference be used to model and reduce non-stationarity in decentralized MARL when an individual agent has limited information about other agents' adapting policies and must treat their unknown behavior as a source of uncertainty or observation noise?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) setting formalized as a partially observable stochastic game with $N$ agents indexed by $i \in \{1,\dots,N\}$. The environment has state space $\mathcal{S}$, joint action space $\mathcal{A} = \prod_i \mathcal{A}_i$, transition kernel $T(s' \mid s, a_1,\dots,a_N)$, individual observation functions $O_i: \mathcal{S} \to \mathcal{O}_i$, and individual reward functions $R_i(s, a_1,\dots,a_N)$. Each agent $i$ chooses a (possibly time-varying) policy $\pi_i^t: \mathcal{O}_i \to \Delta(\mathcal{A}_i)$ based only on its own observation history, without access to the other agents' policies $\{\pi_j^t\}_{j\neq i}$ or their internal states.

From the perspective of a single agent $i$, the effective transition and reward dynamics induced by marginalizing over the unknown behaviour policies of the other agents are non-stationary: as the other agents adapt $\{\pi_j^t\}_{j\neq i}$ over time in response to observed outcomes, the conditional distribution $P^t(o_i', r_i \mid o_i, a_i)$ that agent $i$ faces changes with $t$. Assume agent $i$ has access to structural causal knowledge of the form of a directed acyclic graph $\mathcal{G}_i$ on variables $(O_i, A_i, U_{-i}, O_i', R_i)$, where $U_{-i}$ is an unobserved variable summarizing the joint policy/action of the other agents, together with the qualitative information that certain components of $U_{-i}$ are present (e.g., the agent knows another agent is in its vicinity).

Provide a principled framework, grounded in causal inference (e.g., structural causal models, do-calculus, counterfactual reasoning, or causal effect identification under unobserved confounding), that allows agent $i$ to:

(a) model the non-stationarity in $P^t(o_i', r_i \mid o_i, a_i)$ as a causal effect of the latent confounder $U_{-i}$ on its observed transitions and rewards;

(b) attribute observed observation/reward noise to the unknown behaviour policies of the other agents in a way that is consistent with $\mathcal{G}_i$;

(c) quantitatively reduce the non-stationarity-induced bias or variance in agent $i$'s policy learning, with provable guarantees (e.g., regret bounds, identifiability conditions, or sample complexity improvements) compared to a non-causal decentralized learner that treats the environment as a stationary single-agent POMDP.

Specify the assumptions on $\mathcal{G}_i$ and on the other agents' adaptation dynamics under which such guarantees can be obtained.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction in the causal MARL literature. No published work appears to provide a complete, principled causal-inference framework with provable guarantees for reducing decentralized MARL non-stationarity from limited information about other agents' policies; partial progress exists on causal models for confounded bandits and single-agent RL, but a general solution remains open.

paper_title: Causal Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: Review and Open Problems
context_brief: Causal imitation and transfer in MARL
original_question: In multi-agent knowledge sharing, when can causal imitation learning, causal transfer learning, and data fusion determine whether one agent can imitate or learn from a more knowledgeable teacher agent, which variables are important for imitation, and what performance should be expected?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a multi-agent decision-making setting modeled as a Markov game with $n$ agents. Each agent $i$ has its own observation space $\mathcal{O}_i$, action space $\mathcal{A}_i$, and policy $\pi_i$. Suppose one designated agent (the "teacher") $T$ has access to a policy $\pi_T$ that achieves expected return $V^{\pi_T}$ in some environment described by a structural causal model (SCM) $\mathcal{M}_T = (U_T, V_T, F_T, P(U_T))$, where $V_T$ are endogenous variables (states, actions, rewards), $U_T$ are exogenous variables, and $F_T$ are structural assignments. A second agent (the "learner") $L$ operates in an environment described by an SCM $\mathcal{M}_L$ that may differ from $\mathcal{M}_T$ in observation availability, intervention set, or causal mechanisms. The learner observes only demonstration trajectories $\{(o_t^T, a_t^T)\}_{t\ge 0}$ from $\pi_T$ together with possibly heterogeneous datasets $\mathcal{D}_1,\dots,\mathcal{D}_k$ collected from related environments under different interventions.

Provide a formal framework, drawing on causal imitation learning, causal transfer learning, and causal data fusion, that answers all of the following:

(a) Imitability criterion. Give necessary and sufficient graphical/structural conditions on $(\mathcal{M}_T, \mathcal{M}_L)$ and on the learner's observable variables under which there exists a learner policy $\pi_L$ such that the imitation gap $V^{\pi_T} - V^{\pi_L}$ can be made zero (or bounded) using only the demonstrations and auxiliary datasets.

(b) Variable selection. Characterize the minimal subset $S \subseteq V_T$ of variables that the learner must observe and condition on so that imitating $\pi_T$ via $S$ is sound, identifying when latent confounders between $S$ and the teacher's action prevent valid imitation.

(c) Performance guarantees. Derive expected-return bounds on $V^{\pi_L}$ as a function of (i) the discrepancy between $\mathcal{M}_T$ and $\mathcal{M}_L$, (ii) the sample sizes of the demonstration and fusion datasets, and (iii) identifiability of the relevant causal effects across environments.

The problem is to formulate this framework, state and prove the corresponding identifiability and feasibility theorems, and produce matching upper and lower bounds on the achievable imitation performance in the multi-agent setting.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction in causal multi-agent reinforcement learning. While single-agent causal imitation learning (e.g., work by Zhang, Kumor, and Bareinboim) provides graphical criteria for imitability and variable selection in the single-agent case, no comprehensive multi-agent framework unifying causal imitation, causal transfer, and causal data fusion with matching performance guarantees appears to have been established as of 2026. The problem remains open.

context_brief: stochastic mirror descent rates for conjugate MAP on barrier objectives
original_question: View conjugate MAP estimation in an exponential family as stochastic mirror descent on the negative log-likelihood, with mirror map induced by the log-partition function A and decreasing step sizes γ_n = 1/(n_0 + n). Find a convergence-rate theorem for stochastic mirror descent that is strong enough to cover the MAP iterates arising from standard exponential-family models, including Gaussian examples such as N(m, σ^2) or the barrier-type case N(0, σ^2), despite the fact that existing relative-smoothness analyses fail on these barrier objectives. In particular, the desired result should explain the observed O(1/n) behavior for MAP-like updates in settings where current SMD bounds do not apply.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ be a regular exponential family on a sample space $\mathcal{X}$ with natural parameter $\theta\in\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$, sufficient statistic $T:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^d$, base measure $\nu$, and log-partition function $A(\theta)=\log\int_{\mathcal{X}} e^{\langle\theta,T(x)\rangle}\,d\nu(x)$, so that the density is $p_\theta(x)=\exp(\langle\theta,T(x)\rangle - A(\theta))$. The function $A$ is strictly convex and smooth on the interior of $\Theta$, and serves as a Legendre-type mirror map; let $D_A(\theta,\theta')=A(\theta)-A(\theta')-\langle\nabla A(\theta'),\theta-\theta'\rangle$ denote the associated Bregman divergence.

Given i.i.d.\ observations $X_1,X_2,\dots$ from $P_{\theta^\star}$ and a conjugate prior with hyperparameters $(\chi,n_0)$, the conjugate MAP recursion can be written as the stochastic mirror descent iteration
$$\nabla A(\theta_{n+1}) = \nabla A(\theta_n) - \gamma_n\,\widehat{g}_n,\qquad \gamma_n=\frac{1}{n_0+n},$$
where $\widehat{g}_n=\nabla A(\theta_n)-T(X_{n+1})$ is an unbiased stochastic (sub)gradient of the negative log-likelihood objective $F(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P_{\theta^\star}}[-\log p_\theta(X)]$.

Problem. Establish a non-asymptotic convergence-rate theorem for stochastic mirror descent with mirror map $A$, step sizes $\gamma_n=1/(n_0+n)$, and unbiased stochastic gradients of $F$, that
(i) applies to conjugate MAP iterates for standard exponential families, including Gaussian models such as $\mathcal{N}(m,\sigma^2)$ with unknown mean and the barrier-type model $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$ with unknown variance, in regimes where $F$ is not relatively smooth with respect to $A$ on the closure of the iterates' domain (so that existing relative-smoothness based SMD analyses do not apply); and
(ii) yields a rate of the form $\mathbb{E}[F(\theta_n)-F(\theta^\star)]=O(1/n)$ (or $\mathbb{E}[D_A(\theta^\star,\theta_n)]=O(1/n)$), matching the empirically observed behavior of MAP estimators in these models.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an explicit open problem. Existing stochastic mirror descent analyses rely on uniform relative-smoothness assumptions that fail for barrier-type objectives such as the negative log-likelihood of $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$, where iterates can approach the boundary of the domain. Recent related works on SMD and natural-gradient variational inference have made partial progress (e.g., geometric convergence to a neighborhood, or rates under stronger assumptions) but no published result yet establishes a general $O(1/n)$ rate covering MAP iterates in all standard exponential-family/Gaussian barrier examples.

paper_title: New results and open problems on subgraph centrality
original_question: Let A be a non-diagonalizable n × n matrix with nonnegative algebraic entries, regarded as the adjacency matrix of a weighted directed graph G, and let β ≠ 0 be an algebraic number. If two vertices i and j satisfy [e^{βA}]_{ii} = [e^{βA}]_{jj}, must i and j be cospectral? Equivalently, prove or disprove that the cospectrality conclusion from the diagonalizable case still holds without assuming diagonalizability or special restrictions on the Jordan form.
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ matrix all of whose entries are nonnegative algebraic numbers, viewed as the adjacency matrix of a weighted directed graph $G$ on vertex set $\{1,\dots,n\}$, and assume that $A$ is not diagonalizable. Let $\beta$ be a nonzero algebraic number, and consider the matrix exponential $e^{\beta A} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(\beta A)^k}{k!}$.

Two vertices $i$ and $j$ of $G$ are called cospectral (with respect to $A$) if the principal submatrices obtained by deleting row and column $i$ and by deleting row and column $j$ have the same characteristic polynomial; equivalently, the closed-walk generating functions $[A^k]_{ii} = [A^k]_{jj}$ for every nonnegative integer $k$.

Prove or disprove: if $[e^{\beta A}]_{ii} = [e^{\beta A}]_{jj}$ for two vertices $i,j$, then $i$ and $j$ are cospectral.

A web search did not turn up any subsequent paper resolving this case; the diagonalizable case (Estrada's conjecture) has been proven, but the non-diagonalizable extension appears unresolved.

paper_title: New results and open problems on subgraph centrality
original_question: Given a graph with n vertices, determine the largest possible number of interlacing values for subgraph centrality that a pair of its vertices can have. In particular, determine whether there are graph classes for which the upper bound d − 1 is attained, where d denotes the number of distinct eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix.
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a simple undirected graph on n vertices with adjacency matrix A, and let A = sum_{k=1}^{d} mu_k E_k be its spectral decomposition, where mu_1 > mu_2 > ... > mu_d are the d distinct eigenvalues of A and E_k denotes the orthogonal projector onto the eigenspace of mu_k. For a vertex v of G, the subgraph centrality of v is defined as

   SC(v) = sum_{j>=0} (A^{2j})_{vv} / (2j)!  =  (e^A)_{vv}  =  sum_{k=1}^{d} (E_k)_{vv} cosh(sqrt(|mu_k|) * ... )  

equivalently SC(v) = sum_{k=1}^{d} (E_k)_{vv} e^{mu_k}. More generally one can consider, for a parameter t > 0, the quantity SC_t(v) = (e^{tA})_{vv} = sum_{k=1}^{d} (E_k)_{vv} e^{t mu_k}.

Given two vertices u, v of G, an "interlacing value" for the pair (u, v) is a positive real number t > 0 at which SC_t(u) = SC_t(v); equivalently, a positive zero of the function

   f_{u,v}(t) = sum_{k=1}^{d} ((E_k)_{uu} - (E_k)_{vv}) e^{t mu_k},

provided f_{u,v} is not identically zero. Since f_{u,v} is a real linear combination of d distinct exponentials, it has at most d - 1 positive zeros.

Questions:
(a) Determine, as a function of n, the maximum possible number of interlacing values that any pair (u, v) of vertices of an n-vertex graph G can have.
(b) Decide whether there exist classes of graphs in which the upper bound d - 1 is attained for some pair of vertices, and if so describe such classes.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem about the maximal number of interlacings of subgraph centralities between two vertices of a graph, and whether the natural upper bound d-1 (with d the number of distinct adjacency eigenvalues) can be attained. Web searches returned only general references on subgraph centrality and eigenvalue interlacing; no source resolving this specific extremal question was found, so it appears to remain open.

paper_title: New results and open problems on subgraph centrality
original_question: Does the bound from Theorem 2.9 for subgraph centrality interlacing continue to hold for directed graphs with positive weights? In other words, if A is the adjacency matrix of a positively weighted directed graph and i, j are two vertices, must the number of β > 0 for which [e^{βA}]_{ii} = [e^{βA}]_{jj} still satisfy the same finiteness bound proved in the undirected case?
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a finite directed graph on n vertices with positive edge weights, and let A ∈ R^{n×n} denote its (in general non-symmetric) weighted adjacency matrix, where A_{uv} > 0 if there is an arc from u to v and A_{uv} = 0 otherwise. For β > 0 the matrix exponential e^{βA} is well defined, and its diagonal entry [e^{βA}]_{ii} = Σ_{k≥0} β^k [A^k]_{ii}/k! is a generalized notion of subgraph centrality of vertex i (counting weighted closed walks at i).

In the undirected case (A symmetric with nonnegative entries), the following is known: for any two distinct vertices i and j, the set
   S_{ij} = { β > 0 : [e^{βA}]_{ii} = [e^{βA}]_{jj} }
is finite, with an explicit upper bound on |S_{ij}| depending only on n (the analogue of an interlacing-type bound for the entire functions β ↦ [e^{βA}]_{ii} and β ↦ [e^{βA}]_{jj}).

Question: Does the same finiteness bound continue to hold for every positively weighted directed graph? That is, for every directed graph G with positive weights, every adjacency matrix A as above, and every pair of distinct vertices i, j, must the set S_{ij} = { β > 0 : [e^{βA}]_{ii} = [e^{βA}]_{jj} } satisfy the same upper bound that is valid in the undirected case?

A web search did not surface any subsequent work resolving the directed (positively weighted) extension; later literature on subgraph centrality and Estrada-style indices does not appear to settle it.

paper_title: New results and open problems on subgraph centrality
context_brief: Extremal interlacing counts for subgraph centrality
original_question: For a graph G with adjacency matrix A, define the subgraph centrality of a vertex i by SC(i, β) = [e^{βA}]_{ii}. Two non-cospectral vertices i and j interlace at β when SC(i, β) = SC(j, β); such a β is called an interlacing value. Given k ∈ N, characterize the smallest graph or graphs that contain a pair of vertices with at least k interlacing values for subgraph centrality. Conversely, for a graph on n vertices, determine the largest possible number of subgraph-centrality interlacing values that one pair of vertices can have, and in particular decide whether there are graph classes for which the general upper bound d − 1, where d is the number of distinct eigenvalues of A, is attained.
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a finite simple graph with vertex set V(G) and adjacency matrix A. For a real parameter β, the subgraph centrality of a vertex i ∈ V(G) is defined by

  SC(i, β) = [e^{βA}]_{ii} = Σ_{k≥0} β^k [A^k]_{ii} / k!.

Two vertices i, j ∈ V(G) are called cospectral if [A^k]_{ii} = [A^k]_{jj} for every nonnegative integer k (equivalently, SC(i, β) = SC(j, β) for all β). Two non-cospectral vertices i and j are said to interlace at β if SC(i, β) = SC(j, β); such a value β is called an interlacing value of the pair (i, j). Let d denote the number of distinct eigenvalues of A; it is known that the number of interlacing values of any non-cospectral pair is at most d − 1.

Address the following:

(a) For each k ∈ ℕ, characterize the graph(s) of smallest order containing a pair of non-cospectral vertices with at least k interlacing values of the subgraph centrality.

(b) For each n ∈ ℕ, determine the maximum, over all graphs G on n vertices and all non-cospectral pairs (i, j) of vertices of G, of the number of interlacing values of (i, j).

(c) Decide whether there exist classes of graphs for which the upper bound d − 1 on the number of interlacing values of a non-cospectral pair is attained, and if so describe such classes.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open problem in the literature on subgraph centrality. Search results indicate that only partial examples are known (e.g., minimal graphs with up to two interlacing values, and a 60-vertex example with three interlacing values), and obtaining sharper bounds for specific graph classes and characterizing extremal graphs remain open.

paper_title: New results and open problems on subgraph centrality
original_question: The paper proves that if G is a possibly weighted undirected graph with adjacency matrix A and d distinct eigenvalues, then any two non-cospectral vertices have at most d − 1 interlacing values for subgraph centrality. Does the same conclusion remain true for directed graphs, allowing positive edge weights? In other words, for a directed graph with positive weights, must every pair of non-cospectral vertices have at most d − 1 positive parameters β such that [e^{βA}]_{ii} = [e^{βA}]_{jj}?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a directed graph on $n$ vertices with positive edge weights, and let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be its (in general non-symmetric) weighted adjacency matrix, where $A_{ij} > 0$ if there is a directed edge from $i$ to $j$ and $A_{ij}=0$ otherwise. For a real parameter $\beta > 0$, define the subgraph centrality of vertex $i$ as
$$ SC_i(\beta) := \bigl[e^{\beta A}\bigr]_{ii} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{\beta^k}{k!}\,[A^k]_{ii}. $$
Two vertices $i,j$ are called cospectral if $SC_i(\beta) = SC_j(\beta)$ for all $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$; otherwise they are non-cospectral. A value $\beta > 0$ is called an interlacing value for the pair $(i,j)$ if $SC_i(\beta) = SC_j(\beta)$. Let $d$ denote the number of distinct eigenvalues of $A$ (over $\mathbb{C}$).

Question: Is it true that for every such weighted directed graph $G$ and every pair of non-cospectral vertices $i,j$, the number of positive interlacing values is at most $d-1$?

(The corresponding statement is known to hold for possibly weighted undirected graphs, where $A$ is symmetric.)

paper_title: Research Problems on Relations Between Nijenhuis Geometry and Integrable Systems
original_question: Can two distinct third-order Poisson structures be compatible when at least one of them is non-Darboux–Poisson, and more generally how large can a pencil of first-order geometric Poisson structures compatible with a non-Darboux–Poisson third-order structure be?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider a smooth manifold $M$ with local coordinates $u^1,\dots,u^n$. A homogeneous differential-geometric Poisson structure of order $k$ is a Poisson bracket on the loop space of $M$ given, on local functionals, by an operator of the form
$$P^{ij} = \sum_{s=0}^{k} A^{ij}_s(u,u_x,u_{xx},\dots)\,\partial_x^{\,k-s},$$
whose leading coefficient and lower-order coefficients depend polynomially on the jets in such a way that $P$ is homogeneous of weight $k$ (with $\deg \partial_x = 1$ and $\deg u^i_{(\ell)} = \ell$) and skew-symmetric, and such that the associated bracket $\{F,G\} = \int \frac{\delta F}{\delta u^i} P^{ij} \frac{\delta G}{\delta u^j}\,dx$ satisfies the Jacobi identity. Two such structures $P_1, P_2$ are called compatible if every linear combination $\lambda P_1 + \mu P_2$ is again a Poisson structure; the family $\{\lambda P_1+\mu P_2\}$ is then called a (Poisson) pencil. A third-order Poisson structure is said to be Darboux–Poisson if there exist local coordinates in which all of its coefficients are constant (so it reduces to $c^{ij}\partial_x^3$ with $c^{ij}$ constant skew-symmetric).

Problems.
(a) Do there exist two distinct (i.e., non-proportional) compatible third-order homogeneous differential-geometric Poisson structures on some manifold $M$ such that at least one of them is not Darboux–Poisson? If yes, classify such pairs; if no, prove that compatibility of two third-order structures forces both to be Darboux–Poisson (up to a common change of coordinates).

(b) Given a third-order homogeneous differential-geometric Poisson structure $P_3$ on $M$ that is not Darboux–Poisson, describe all first-order homogeneous differential-geometric Poisson structures $P_1$ (i.e., Hamiltonian operators of hydrodynamic type) that are compatible with $P_3$. In particular, determine the maximal possible dimension of a linear pencil of such first-order structures compatible with $P_3$.
status_search_result: A web search did not surface any publication resolving the compatibility question for higher-order (specifically third-order) homogeneous differential-geometric Poisson structures with at least one being non-Darboux–Poisson, nor a classification of first-order Poisson pencils compatible with a non-Darboux–Poisson third-order structure. The problems appear to remain open as posed in the broader Nijenhuis-geometry/integrable-systems literature.

original_question: Let (W1,S1) and (W2,S2) be Coxeter systems, and let u,v in W1 and w,z in W2 be such that the Bruhat intervals [u,v] and [w,z] are isomorphic as posets. Must the corresponding Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials agree, i.e. must P_{u,v}(q) = P_{w,z}(q)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(W_1, S_1)$ and $(W_2, S_2)$ be two Coxeter systems. Recall that for a Coxeter system $(W, S)$, the Bruhat order $\le$ on $W$ is the partial order generated by declaring $u \le v$ whenever some reduced expression for $v$ contains a reduced expression for $u$ as a subword; for $u \le v$ in $W$, the Bruhat interval $[u,v]$ is the poset $\{x \in W : u \le x \le v\}$. To each pair $u \le v$ in a Coxeter system one associates the Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial $P_{u,v}(q) \in \mathbb{Z}[q]$, the unique polynomial of degree at most $(\ell(v) - \ell(u) - 1)/2$ (with $P_{u,u}=1$) defined by the recursion arising from the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis of the Hecke algebra of $(W,S)$.

Suppose $u, v \in W_1$ and $w, z \in W_2$ satisfy $u \le v$, $w \le z$, and there is an isomorphism of posets $[u,v] \cong [w,z]$. Prove or disprove: under these hypotheses one always has
$$P_{u,v}(q) = P_{w,z}(q).$$
status_search_result: The statement is the Combinatorial Invariance Conjecture of Lusztig and Dyer, formulated in the 1980s. It remains open in general. Significant progress has been made in special cases (e.g., for lower intervals in the symmetric group via hypercube decompositions, including work motivated by DeepMind collaborations), but no proof for arbitrary Coxeter systems has been established.

original_question: Let W be a Weyl group of type A and let u <= v in W. Suppose [u,z] is a hypercube decomposition of the Bruhat interval [u,v] in the sense defined in the paper. Does the Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomial P_{u,v}(q) always equal the polynomial P~_{u,v,z}(q) produced from that hypercube decomposition?
self_contained_problem:
Let $W$ be a Weyl group of type $A$ (i.e. a symmetric group $S_n$) with its standard set of simple reflections, length function $\ell$, and Bruhat order $\le$. For $u\le v$ in $W$, let $[u,v]=\{w\in W : u\le w\le v\}$ denote the Bruhat interval, and let $P_{u,v}(q)\in\mathbb Z[q]$ denote the Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial.

Recall the following combinatorial constructions, defined purely in terms of the poset $[u,v]$:

1. (Diamond completeness) An interval $[u,z]\subseteq[u,v]$ is called diamond complete if, whenever $w\in[u,z]$ and $w'\in[u,v]$ cover $w$ in Bruhat order with $w'\notin[u,z]$, certain "diamond" completion conditions force the existence of corresponding elements in $[u,z]$.

2. (Hypercube cluster) For $w\in[u,v]$, let $U(w)$ denote the set of atoms above $w$ in $[u,v]$ (the elements covering $w$). One says that $U(w)$ spans a hypercube cluster if the order ideal generated by $U(w)$ in $[w,v]$ is isomorphic to the Boolean lattice $2^{|U(w)|}$ (a hypercube), with the Hasse diagram structure inherited from Bruhat order.

3. (Hypercube decomposition) An interval $[u,z]\subseteq[u,v]$ is called a hypercube decomposition of $[u,v]$ if $[u,z]$ is diamond complete and $U(w)$ spans a hypercube cluster for every $w\in[u,z]$.

Given a hypercube decomposition $[u,z]$ of $[u,v]$, one defines a polynomial $\widetilde P_{u,v,z}(q)\in\mathbb Z[q]$ by an explicit recursion that uses only the Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials of strictly smaller subintervals together with the combinatorial data of the hypercube decomposition.

Question: Is it true that for every $u\le v$ in $W$ and every hypercube decomposition $[u,z]$ of $[u,v]$,
$$P_{u,v}(q)=\widetilde P_{u,v,z}(q)\,?$$

It has been verified for the standard hypercube decomposition via geometric representation theory, and a 2024–2025 preprint proves it for lower intervals $[e,v]$, described as the first non-trivial class of intervals for which it is established. The full conjecture for arbitrary Bruhat intervals in type $A$ remains open.

original_question: For n >= 5, let L(sigma) be the odd inversion number of a permutation sigma in S_n, and let L_n(x) = sum_{sigma in S_n} x^{L(sigma)}. Is the polynomial L_n(x) always symmetric and unimodal?
self_contained_problem:
For an integer n ≥ 1, let S_n denote the symmetric group of all permutations of {1, 2, …, n}. For σ ∈ S_n, define the odd inversion number
  L(σ) := |{ (i, j) ∈ [n]² : i < j, σ(i) > σ(j), and i ≢ j (mod 2) }|,
i.e. the number of inversions (i, j) of σ such that i and j have opposite parities. Define the odd inversion enumerator
  L_n(x) := Σ_{σ ∈ S_n} x^{L(σ)} ∈ ℤ[x].

Prove or disprove: for every integer n ≥ 5, the polynomial L_n(x) is symmetric (i.e. its coefficient sequence reads the same forwards and backwards) and unimodal (i.e. its coefficient sequence is weakly increasing up to some index and weakly decreasing thereafter).
status_search_result: The conjecture appears in a 2024 collection of open problems on Coxeter groups and unimodality by F. Brenti. No published resolution was found in a web search; related work characterizes odd inversion sets via orientations of Turán graphs but does not establish symmetry/unimodality of L_n(x) for all n ≥ 5.

original_question: For a graph G, let tau(G; x) be the polynomial defined by tau(G; x) = sum_{pi in Pi(V)} a(G[pi]) x^{|pi|}. Does tau(G; x) have only real roots for every graph G?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph with $|V|=n$. Recall that the chromatic polynomial $\chi(G;x)$ counts the proper colorings of $G$, and can be uniquely written in the basis of falling factorials $\langle x\rangle_i := x(x-1)(x-2)\cdots(x-i+1)$ as
$$\chi(G;x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}(-1)^{n-i}c_i(G)\,\langle x\rangle_i,$$
where the coefficients $c_i(G)$ are nonnegative integers. Define the $\tau$-polynomial of $G$ by
$$\tau(G;x):=\sum_{i=0}^{n}c_i(G)\,x^{i}.$$

For a subset $B\subseteq V$, let $G[B]$ denote the subgraph of $G$ induced by $B$, and for a set partition $\pi=\{B_1,\ldots,B_k\}\in\Pi(V)$ of $V$, let $G[\pi]$ denote the disjoint union $G[B_1]\sqcup\cdots\sqcup G[B_k]$. For any finite graph $H$, let $a(H)$ denote the number of acyclic orientations of $H$ (so $a(G[\pi])=\prod_{j=1}^{k}a(G[B_j])$). It is known that
$$\tau(G;x)=\sum_{\pi\in\Pi(V)}a(G[\pi])\,x^{|\pi|},$$
where $|\pi|$ is the number of blocks of $\pi$.

Question: Does $\tau(G;x)$ have only real roots for every finite simple graph $G$?

original_question: Let sum_{i=0}^d h_i t^i be a polynomial with only real roots such that h_0 = 1 and h_0 < h_1 < ... < h_k for some 0 <= k <= d. Must there exist a simplicial complex whose f-vector is (h_0, h_1 - h_0, ..., h_k - h_{k-1})?

$$h_0<h_1<\cdots<h_k.$$
Define the vector
$$f=(h_0,\; h_1-h_0,\; h_2-h_1,\; \dots,\; h_k-h_{k-1}).$$
Must there exist a (finite abstract) simplicial complex $\Delta$ whose $f$-vector equals $f$? context_brief: Uniform random generation of fullerene isomers
original_question: A fullerene is a convex, 3-regular polytope consisting only of pentagonal and hexagonal facets. For a feasible integer n, meaning a positive even integer n >= 20 with n != 22, let C_n denote the set of all fullerenes with exactly n vertices, considered up to graph isomorphism as fullerene isomers. Can one design a computationally efficient procedure that samples uniformly from the fullerene isomers in C_n, so that every isomer in C_n is selected with the same probability?
self_contained_problem:
A fullerene is a convex 3-regular polytope whose facets are all pentagons or hexagons; equivalently (via its 1-skeleton), a 3-regular planar graph all of whose faces have length 5 or 6. By Euler's formula such a graph must have exactly 12 pentagonal faces, and the number n of vertices satisfies: n is even, n ≥ 20, and n ≠ 22. Call such an integer n feasible. For each feasible n, let C_n denote the set of all fullerenes with exactly n vertices, considered up to graph isomorphism (i.e., the equivalence classes are the C_n-isomers).

Design a computationally efficient algorithm (running in time polynomial in n, or otherwise demonstrably tractable) that, for any feasible input n, outputs a fullerene isomer in C_n drawn uniformly at random — i.e., such that every isomorphism class in C_n is produced with probability exactly 1/|C_n|.
status_search_result: The problem of efficiently generating fullerene isomers uniformly at random is stated as an open problem. Existing algorithms (face spiral, growth/Stone–Wales operations, Buckygen) can enumerate fullerenes — Buckygen being the fastest known full enumerator — but exhaustive enumeration becomes infeasible for large n (e.g., n > 400) due to the rapid growth of |C_n|, and no known efficient algorithm samples uniformly from C_n for all feasible n.

original_question: A fullerene is a convex, 3-regular polytope consisting only of pentagonal and hexagonal facets. For a feasible n, meaning a positive even integer n >= 20 with n != 22, let T_n be the unique dual graph of such a fullerene. If A is the adjacency matrix of T_n and D is its degree matrix, define the (alpha, beta)-character by ch_{alpha,beta}(T_n) := tr(exp(alpha A + beta D)). original_question: In the high-temperature cluster expansion of a homogeneous two-component Fermi gas at unitarity, can one prove the conjectured general formula for every mixed sector (n↑,n↓) ≠ (1,1), expressing the cluster coefficient b_{n↑,n↓} as a mass prefactor times an integral over the logarithmic derivative of the Efimov function Λ_{n↑,n↓}(iS), plus the quantum-statistical correction from indistinguishable non-monoatomic subclusters? The formula is established for N = 3 and numerically supported in a special N = 4 equal-mass case, but a general proof requires control of the analytic properties of Λ_{n↑,n↓} in the complex plane.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a homogeneous two-component (spin ↑, spin ↓) Fermi gas in three dimensions with zero-range s-wave interactions tuned to the unitary limit (inverse scattering length a^{-1}=0). At high temperature, the grand-canonical pressure admits a virial/cluster expansion in the fugacities z_↑, z_↓ of the form

  P/(k_B T) = λ_T^{-3} Σ_{n_↑,n_↓ ≥ 0, (n_↑,n_↓)≠(0,0)} b_{n_↑,n_↓} z_↑^{n_↑} z_↓^{n_↓},

where λ_T is the thermal de Broglie wavelength and b_{n_↑,n_↓} are the (mixed) cluster coefficients. For each sector (n_↑,n_↓) with N = n_↑+n_↓ ≥ 2, let Λ_{n_↑,n_↓}(s) denote the Efimov-type spectral function defined as the regularized product (or appropriate analytic determinant) over the eigenvalues of the scale-invariant N-body unitary problem in a harmonic trap, viewed as an entire/meromorphic function of the complex variable s.

Conjecture to prove: For every mixed sector (n_↑,n_↓) with (n_↑,n_↓) ≠ (1,1) (and N ≥ 2), the unitary cluster coefficient is given by

  b_{n_↑,n_↓} = C_{n_↑,n_↓} ∫_0^∞ S · (d/dS) log Λ_{n_↑,n_↓}(iS) dS  +  Δ_{n_↑,n_↓},

where C_{n_↑,n_↓} is an explicit prefactor depending only on the masses and particle numbers, and Δ_{n_↑,n_↓} is the explicit quantum-statistical correction accounting for indistinguishable non-monoatomic subclusters (built from lower-order cluster coefficients in the standard Ursell/Mayer way).

The formula is known to hold for N = 3 (proved) and is numerically supported in a particular equal-mass N = 4 case. Establish the formula for all (n_↑,n_↓) ≠ (1,1); a complete proof requires control of the analytic properties (zeros, poles, growth) of Λ_{n_↑,n_↓}(s) in the complex plane.

The formula is established for N=3 and supported numerically for a special equal-mass N=4 case; the general proof requires analytic control of the Efimov spectral functions Λ_{n↑,n↓} in the complex plane and remains unresolved in the literature located.

original_question: In a weakly polarized pair-condensed Fermi gas, where the excess majority-spin fermions appear as gapped fermionic quasiparticles χ and the low-energy sound quanta are phonons φ, what are the correct low-energy φ–χ and χ–χ interactions? In particular, what is the correct low-energy φ–χ scattering amplitude, given that existing calculations disagree?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a three-dimensional pair-condensed (BCS-BEC crossover) Fermi gas of two spin species with a small population imbalance. In the weakly polarized regime, the excess majority-spin fermions form a dilute population of gapped fermionic quasiparticles, denoted χ, while the low-energy collective excitations of the paired condensate are gapless phonons, denoted φ, with a linear dispersion at long wavelength.

Working within a low-energy effective field theory built from the order-parameter (phonon) field and the gapped Bogoliubov quasiparticle field on top of the BCS ground state, derive the correct low-energy effective interactions between these degrees of freedom, namely:

(i) the φ–χ coupling vertex and the resulting on-shell phonon–quasiparticle scattering amplitude in the limit of small phonon momentum and quasiparticle momentum near the gap minimum, and

(ii) the χ–χ effective interaction (induced direct quasiparticle–quasiparticle scattering, including phonon-mediated contributions).

In particular, determine the unambiguous expression for the leading low-energy φ–χ scattering amplitude as a function of the equation-of-state parameters of the unpolarized superfluid (e.g., the chemical potential, sound velocity, and gap, together with their derivatives with respect to density), reconciling the conflicting results that have appeared in the literature.

original_question: Can Landau-Khalatnikov four-phonon damping φφ → φφ be observed and quantitatively measured in a superfluid whose acoustic branch is concave at low wave number, γ < 0, such as a strongly interacting Fermi gas in a box trap or superfluid helium-4 under pressure? The target is the low-temperature regime where phonon decay into multiple phonons is kinematically forbidden and four-phonon scattering is predicted to dominate over three-phonon Beliaev-Landau damping.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a three-dimensional superfluid at low temperature whose elementary excitations include an acoustic (phonon) branch with dispersion relation ω(q) = c q [1 + (γ/8)(ℏq/mc)^2 + O(q^4)] for small wave number q, where c is the sound velocity, m a characteristic mass, and γ the dimensionless curvature parameter. Assume γ < 0 (concave start of the dispersion), so that one-phonon decay into two phonons (Beliaev process) and merging of two phonons into one (Landau process) are kinematically forbidden at low q, and the leading damping mechanism is the Landau–Khalatnikov four-phonon process φφ → φφ. The corresponding damping rate Γ_q^{γ<0}(T) at temperature T has been predicted theoretically (in the regime ℏcq, k_B T much smaller than the characteristic gap or roton scale).

Two physical realizations satisfy γ < 0: (i) a unitary (or strongly interacting) Fermi gas of paired atoms confined in a uniform box trap, in the collisionless low-temperature regime; (ii) bulk superfluid helium-4 under sufficiently high pressure.

Problem: Devise an experimental protocol in one of these two systems that allows the four-phonon damping rate Γ_q^{γ<0}(T) of a phonon mode of wave number q to be observed and quantitatively measured at low temperature, where three-phonon Beliaev–Landau processes are kinematically forbidden, and compare the measured rate against the theoretical prediction.
status_search_result: Theoretical predictions for the four-phonon Landau–Khalatnikov damping rate exist for strongly interacting Fermi gases and high-pressure superfluid helium-4 (concave acoustic branch, γ < 0), but available sources indicate that this four-phonon damping has not yet been observed experimentally in any system; its measurement remains an open experimental challenge.

context_brief: Nonperturbative phonon damping in low dimensions
original_question: In lower-dimensional superfluids where the Born-Markov approximation fails for phonon damping—especially the two-dimensional convex acoustic branch and the one-dimensional low-temperature fixed-density regime—what controlled nonperturbative self-energy or kinetic theory correctly predicts the decay rate or decay law of a phonon mode? The desired theory should replace naive Fermi-golden-rule/Born-Markov power counting when the perturbative expansion in the cubic phonon interaction is not valid.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a low-dimensional superfluid (in either two or one spatial dimensions) at temperature T, with mass density ρ, sound velocity c, and healing length ξ, whose long-wavelength low-energy excitations are phonons of momentum q with a dispersion ω_q. Suppose the leading nonlinearity in the effective phonon Hamiltonian is a cubic three-phonon coupling, and consider the retarded phonon self-energy Σ_q(ζ) (so that the damping rate Γ_q is, formally, −Im Σ_q(ω_q+i0⁺)/ℏ).

In the following two regimes, the Born–Markov / Fermi golden-rule power counting based on the cubic interaction breaks down (the perturbative series in the cubic coupling is no longer controlled):

(i) A two-dimensional superfluid whose acoustic branch ω_q is convex (curving upward away from the linear part) at low momentum.

(ii) A one-dimensional superfluid in the low-temperature, fixed dimensionless density regime k_B T/(mc²) → 0 with ρξ held fixed.

Construct, in either or both of these regimes, a controlled (i.e., nonheuristic and systematic) nonperturbative approximation scheme for the phonon self-energy Σ_q(ζ) — for instance via a self-consistent Dyson-type equation, a resummation of an identifiable infinite class of diagrams, or a kinetic-theory framework beyond Born–Markov — and derive from it the leading low-momentum and/or low-temperature decay rate Γ_q (or, where appropriate, a non-exponential decay law) of a single phonon mode. The result must be shown to agree, in its regime of validity, with the true asymptotic damping observed in classical-field or microscopic simulations, and must reduce to the Fermi golden rule in regimes where perturbation theory is valid.
status_search_result: Recent work (e.g., arXiv:2307.12705) confirms that Fermi's golden rule fails for the 2D convex acoustic branch and resorts to a heuristic nonperturbative regularization, while 1D low-temperature damping still relies on self-consistent approximations rather than a controlled scheme. No fully controlled nonperturbative self-energy/kinetic theory for these regimes appears established in the literature, so the problem is open.

paper_title: Open questions for strongly interacting Fermi gases with zero-range interactions
context_brief: Phase diffusion for concave acoustic branch
original_question: For a pair-condensed Fermi gas with a concave acoustic branch γ < 0, what is the true finite phase-diffusion coefficient Dλ, if any, once all relevant phonon collision channels are included? A four-phonon small-angle Landau-Khalatnikov treatment conserves the total number of phonons and gives an infinite Dλ with superdiffusive phase spreading, so the unresolved task is to include subdominant five-phonon processes φφ ↔ φφφ and large-angle four-phonon processes consistently.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a three-dimensional homogeneous pair-condensed Fermi gas at very low temperature T (with k_B T much less than the pairing gap), so that its low-energy excitations are bosonic phonons with linear dispersion ω_q ≃ c q at small wave number q, where c is the sound velocity and m is the fermion mass. Assume the next-to-linear correction to the acoustic branch is concave, i.e.

  ω_q = c q [1 + (γ/8)(ħ q/(m c))^2 + o(q^2)],   with γ < 0.

Let λ(t) denote the global phase of the order parameter; in a canonical-like ensemble its variance grows in time, and one defines the phase-diffusion coefficient

  D_λ = lim_{t→∞} (1/(2t)) Var[λ(t) − λ(0)],

assuming this limit exists and is finite.

For γ < 0, restricting the phonon collision integral to the small-angle Landau–Khalatnikov four-phonon processes φφ → φφ (which conserve the total phonon number N_φ and have a typical rate ∝ (k_B T/(m c^2))^7 · m c^2/(ħ|γ|) ∝ T^7) yields a divergent D_λ and superdiffusive spreading of λ(t).

Determine the true, finite value of D_λ (or prove its finiteness/infiniteness) when one consistently includes, in addition, the subdominant five-phonon processes φφ ↔ φφφ that do not conserve N_φ (rate ∝ T^9) together with the large-angle four-phonon processes φφ → φφ of comparable order, for a pair-condensed Fermi gas with concave acoustic branch γ < 0.
category_tag: Phonon kinetics in pair-condensed Fermi gases
status_search_result: Existing analyses of phonon interactions in pair-condensed Fermi gases (Kurkjian–Castin–Sinatra and follow-ups) treat only the small-angle Landau–Khalatnikov 2↔2 channel for γ<0, which yields a divergent phase-diffusion coefficient. No published computation appears to incorporate both the five-phonon φφ↔φφφ processes and the large-angle four-phonon processes needed to obtain a finite D_λ; the question is described in the literature as remaining largely open.

paper_title: Open questions for strongly interacting Fermi gases with zero-range interactions
original_question: How should the microscopic finite-wave-number collective-mode equation for a pair-condensed Fermi gas, det M(q,z)=0 and its analytic continuation through the broken-pair continuum, be extended to nonzero temperature beyond a simple time-dependent-BCS or Gaussian-fluctuation mean-field treatment? A satisfactory finite-temperature theory should include the phonon-phonon coupling that mean-field linearization misses, while still describing coupling to broken-pair fermionic quasiparticles.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a three-dimensional pair-condensed Fermi gas of spin-1/2 fermions with a zero-range s-wave interaction in the BCS–BEC crossover. At zero temperature, the linear-response collective modes of wave vector q and complex energy z are encoded by an eigenvalue equation

   det M(q, z) = 0,

where M(q, z) is the 3×3 matrix obtained by linearizing the time-dependent BCS (equivalently, the Gaussian-fluctuation) equations around the BCS ground state. The matrix elements involve integrals over fermionic quasiparticle energies E_k = sqrt((ε_k − μ)^2 + Δ^2) (with ε_k = ℏ²k²/2m, chemical potential μ, and order parameter Δ), and the dispersion relation z(q) is to be analytically continued from the upper half-plane through the branch cut associated with the broken-pair fermionic continuum [2Δ, ∞), thereby capturing both undamped phonon-like solutions and complex modes that describe coupling of the order-parameter phase mode φ to broken-pair excitations χ.

Writing the order-parameter fluctuations in terms of a phase field φ and a modulus field χ, the linearized (mean-field / Gaussian) theory captures the φ–χ coupling but omits the φ–φ self-interaction (phonon–phonon coupling) that becomes relevant at nonzero temperature, where a thermal population of phonons is present.

Problem. Construct a microscopic finite-wave-number collective-mode equation

   det M_T(q, z) = 0,

valid at nonzero temperature T > 0 in the superfluid phase, that

  (i) reduces to det M(q, z) = 0 in the limit T → 0,
  (ii) goes beyond the simple BCS / Gaussian-fluctuation mean-field linearization by incorporating phonon–phonon (φ–φ) coupling induced by thermally excited collective modes,
  (iii) still incorporates the coupling of collective modes to broken-pair fermionic quasiparticles, including the analytic continuation of det M_T(q, z) through the broken-pair continuum so that complex mode energies z(q, T) can be extracted,

and determine the resulting dispersion relation and damping of the high-frequency (pair-breaking) collective modes as functions of q and T.
category_tag: BCS pair-condensed Fermi gases / collective modes
status_search_result: The question is explicitly identified as open in the source survey of open problems for strongly interacting Fermi gases. No published microscopic finite-temperature extension that incorporates phonon–phonon coupling alongside coupling to broken-pair quasiparticles appears to be available.

paper_title: Open questions for strongly interacting Fermi gases with zero-range interactions
context_brief: Pair-breaking energy, order parameter, and Higgs interpretation
original_question: Beyond BCS theory and in experiments, what is the relation between the pair-breaking energy Epair, the order-parameter amplitude |Δ|, and the Higgs or amplitude branch of a pair-condensed Fermi gas? In particular, does Epair = 2|Δ| remain true at zero temperature in more accurate theories or measurements, and how should zero-wave-number order-parameter oscillation experiments be interpreted when their decay exponent, possible exponential damping, and lack of frequency softening near Tc do not match the simplest zero-temperature Higgs-oscillation picture?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a three-dimensional pair-condensed Fermi gas with two equally populated spin components and zero-range (s-wave) interactions, tunable through a Feshbach resonance and described, at the simplest level, by BCS mean-field theory. Within BCS theory at zero temperature, the minimum energy required to break a Cooper pair, denoted E_pair, satisfies the identity

  E_pair = 2|Δ|,

where Δ is the complex order-parameter (gap) amplitude. Small fluctuations of |Δ| about its equilibrium value support an amplitude (Higgs) collective branch which, in the BCS approximation at T = 0 and at zero wave number, produces undamped oscillations whose frequency tends to 2|Δ|/ℏ and whose amplitude decays as a power law t^{-α} with α = 1/2 at the unitary limit.

Address the following:

(a) Does the equality E_pair = 2|Δ| continue to hold at zero temperature in theories that go beyond BCS mean field (for instance theories that include pairing fluctuations or correlations beyond mean field) and/or in laboratory measurements on strongly interacting Fermi gases? Provide a proof, a counterexample, or a precise quantitative correction.

(b) For experiments performed at nonzero temperature in the unitary regime that probe the zero-wave-number oscillations of the order-parameter amplitude, give a theoretical interpretation that accounts simultaneously for: (i) a measured power-law decay exponent α ≈ 1 (rather than the BCS value 1/2 at unitarity); (ii) the possibility that the decay is in fact exponential rather than power-law; and (iii) the absence of any observable softening (reduction) of the oscillation angular frequency as the temperature approaches the superfluid critical temperature T_c. Determine whether such observations are compatible with a Higgs amplitude-mode interpretation and, if not, identify the dominant physical mechanism responsible for the oscillations and their decay.
category_tag: Strongly interacting Fermi gases / Higgs mode
status_search_result: Recent theoretical and experimental works (2019–2025) on Higgs oscillations in unitary Fermi superfluids confirm a resonance near 2|Δ| and qualitative agreement with time-dependent BCS theory but do not rigorously establish E_pair = 2|Δ| beyond mean field, and the discrepancies in decay exponent, possible exponential damping, and the lack of frequency softening near T_c remain unresolved. The status is therefore open.

original_question: For a strictly separating intermediate cone C_i in the filtration between the sum-of-squares cone Σ_{n+1,2d} and the cone P_{n+1,2d} of positive semidefinite forms, explicitly describe its dual cone C_i^∨ = {L in Hom(R[X], R) | L(f) ≥ 0 for all f in C_i}.
self_contained_problem:
Let $n,d\ge 1$ be integers and let $\mathbb{R}[X]_{2d}=\mathbb{R}[X_0,\dots,X_n]_{2d}$ denote the vector space of real homogeneous forms of degree $2d$ in $n+1$ variables, of dimension $k(n,d)=\binom{n+2d}{2d}$. Let
$$P_{n+1,2d}=\{f\in\mathbb{R}[X]_{2d}:f(x)\ge 0\text{ for all }x\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\}$$
be the cone of positive semidefinite forms, and let
$$\Sigma_{n+1,2d}=\Big\{\sum_{j} g_j^2 : g_j\in\mathbb{R}[X]_d\Big\}$$
be the cone of sums of squares. Let $\nu_d:\mathbb{P}^n\to\mathbb{P}^{N}$, $N=\binom{n+d}{d}-1$, denote the $d$-th Veronese embedding, and for a real projective variety $V\subseteq\mathbb{P}^N$ containing the Veronese variety $\nu_d(\mathbb{P}^n)$ let
$$C(V)=\{f\in\mathbb{R}[X]_{2d}: \exists\text{ a positive semidefinite Gram matrix for }f\text{ supported on }V\},$$
i.e.\ the set of forms admitting a Gram representation by a positive semidefinite quadratic form on the ambient space of $\mathbb{P}^N$ that vanishes on $V$ modulo the form. Choosing a chain of real projective varieties
$$\nu_d(\mathbb{P}^n)=V_{k(n,d)-n}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq V_1\subseteq V_0=\mathbb{P}^N$$
one obtains a filtration
$$\Sigma_{n+1,2d}=C_0\subseteq C_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq C_{k(n,d)-n}=P_{n+1,2d},$$
where $C_i:=C(V_i)$. Assume the chain is strictly separating, i.e.\ $C_i\subsetneq C_{i+1}$ for each $i$. For each such intermediate cone $C_i$, give an explicit description of its dual cone
$$C_i^{\vee}:=\{L\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{R}[X]_{2d},\mathbb{R}):L(f)\ge 0\text{ for all }f\in C_i\}$$
in terms of the variety $V_i$ (e.g.\ as moment-type functionals associated with measures, Hankel/moment matrix positivity conditions on $V_i$, or otherwise intrinsic geometric data).
category_tag: Real algebraic geometry / SOS and PSD cones
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an explicit open problem ("Give an explicit description of $C_i^\vee$") in the source preprint from November 2024, and no follow-up work resolving it was located in a web search.

original_question: For each i in {0, ..., k-n}, let Λ_i := {α_s + α_t | 0 ≤ s, t ≤ n+i} ⊆ I_{n+1,2d} ⊆ N_0^{n+1}. Determine how the dual cone C_i^∨ is related to the Λ_i-truncated moment problem, where one asks whether a truncated multisequence indexed by Λ_i admits a non-negative Borel representing measure.
self_contained_problem:
Fix integers $n \geq 0$, $d \geq 1$, and $k \geq n$. Let $I_{n+1,2d} = \{\alpha \in \mathbb{N}_0^{n+1} : |\alpha| = 2d\}$ be the set of exponents of monomials of degree $2d$ in $n+1$ variables, and enumerate the elements of $I_{n+1,d} = \{\alpha \in \mathbb{N}_0^{n+1} : |\alpha| = d\}$ as $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots$ in some fixed order, where $|I_{n+1,d}| = \binom{n+d}{d}$.

For a finite set $\Lambda \subseteq \mathbb{N}_0^{n+1}$, the $\Lambda$-truncated moment problem asks: given a real multisequence $(y_\alpha)_{\alpha \in \Lambda}$, when does there exist a non-negative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ (or on a prescribed support set) such that
$$y_\alpha = \int X^\alpha \, d\mu(X) \qquad \text{for all } \alpha \in \Lambda?$$

Suppose that, in a fixed Gram-matrix style construction, one has a nested family of closed convex cones
$$\mathrm{SOS}_{n+1,2d} = C_{k-n} \subseteq C_{k-n-1} \subseteq \cdots \subseteq C_0 \subseteq \mathrm{PSD}_{n+1,2d}$$
inside the space of real forms of degree $2d$ in $n+1$ variables, together with their dual cones $C_i^\vee$ (with respect to the standard apolar/coefficient pairing).

For each $i \in \{0, 1, \ldots, k-n\}$, define
$$\Lambda_i := \{\alpha_s + \alpha_t : 0 \leq s, t \leq n+i\} \subseteq I_{n+1,2d} \subseteq \mathbb{N}_0^{n+1}.$$

Problem: Describe explicitly the relationship between the dual cone $C_i^\vee$ and the $\Lambda_i$-truncated moment problem; in particular, characterize membership of a multisequence $(y_\alpha)_{\alpha \in \Lambda_i}$ in (a suitable projection of) $C_i^\vee$ in terms of the existence of a representing non-negative Borel measure for $(y_\alpha)_{\alpha \in \Lambda_i}$.
category_tag: truncated moment problem and SOS cones
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an explicitly listed open problem in a 2024 work titled "Separating Cones defined by Toric Varieties: Some Properties and Open Problems." No subsequent work resolving the specific link between the cone filtration $C_i^\vee$ and the $\Lambda_i$-truncated moment problem was found.

original_question: Let G be a 3-connected cubic graph with a blue-red vertex coloring. Write B and R for the subgraphs induced by the blue and red vertices. A crumby coloring is one with maximum degree Delta(B) <= 1, minimum degree delta(R) >= 1, and no path with 3 edges in R. Since the original conjecture asserting that every 3-connected cubic graph has such a coloring is false, what relaxation of the conditions imposed on the red induced subgraph R is sufficient to guarantee that every 3-connected cubic graph admits a blue-red coloring of this type?
status_search_result: The original Thomassen-style crumby coloring conjecture for 3-connected cubic graphs was disproved by Bellitto, Klimošová, Merker, Witkowski and Yuditsky, who constructed an infinite counterexample family. The follow-up question of finding the right relaxation of the conditions on the red subgraph that holds for all 3-connected cubic graphs remains open; partial positive results are known only for restricted classes (e.g., 2-connected outerplanar graphs, subdivisions of K_4, 1-subdivisions of cubic graphs).

original_question: For every graph G, is the list packing number chi*_l(G) always at most twice the list-chromatic number chi_l(G)? Equivalently, if chi_l(G) is the least k such that every k-list-assignment admits a proper coloring and chi*_l(G) is the least k such that every k-list-assignment admits k pairwise-disjoint proper colorings, must chi*_l(G) <= 2 chi_l(G) hold for all graphs G?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite simple graph. A list-assignment for $G$ is a function $L$ that assigns to every vertex $v\in V(G)$ a set $L(v)$ of allowed colors; it is called a $k$-list-assignment if $|L(v)|=k$ for all $v$. An $L$-coloring of $G$ is a proper coloring $c$ of $G$ such that $c(v)\in L(v)$ for every $v$. The list-chromatic number (choosability) $\chi_\ell(G)$ is the least integer $k$ such that every $k$-list-assignment $L$ of $G$ admits an $L$-coloring.

Given a $k$-list-assignment $L$, an $L$-packing of size $k$ is a collection of $k$ proper $L$-colorings $c_1,\dots,c_k$ such that for every vertex $v$ the colors $c_1(v),\dots,c_k(v)$ are pairwise distinct (equivalently, $\{c_1(v),\dots,c_k(v)\}=L(v)$). The list packing number $\chi_\ell^\star(G)$ is the least integer $k$ such that for every $k$-list-assignment $L$ of $G$ there exists an $L$-packing of size $k$.

Determine whether the inequality
$$\chi_\ell^\star(G)\;\le\; 2\,\chi_\ell(G)$$
holds for every finite simple graph $G$.
status_search_result: Recent works on list packing (Cambie–Cames van Batenburg–Davies–Kang and follow-ups) treat bounding $\chi_\ell^\star(G)$ in terms of $\chi_\ell(G)$ as an open direction; only partial results (e.g., the fractional analogue, bounded-degree and degeneracy bounds $\chi_\ell^\star\le 2\Delta$ or $2d$, and special graph classes) are known. No proof or counterexample to the general inequality $\chi_\ell^\star(G)\le 2\chi_\ell(G)$ appears in the literature retrieved.

original_question: Let G be a cubic planar graph and let L be a 3-list-assignment on G. Is it always possible to choose three pairwise-disjoint proper L-colorings, that is, three proper colorings from the given vertex lists such that each vertex receives three different colors across the three colorings?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a cubic planar graph (a planar graph in which every vertex has degree exactly 3). A list-assignment on $G$ is a function $L$ that assigns to each vertex $v \in V(G)$ a set $L(v)$ of permissible colors; it is a 3-list-assignment if $|L(v)| = 3$ for every $v$. An $L$-coloring of $G$ is a map $c: V(G) \to \mathbb{N}$ with $c(v) \in L(v)$ for every $v$; it is proper if $c(u) \neq c(v)$ whenever $u$ and $v$ are adjacent. Two $L$-colorings $c_i, c_j$ are called disjoint if $c_i(u) \neq c_j(u)$ for every vertex $u \in V(G)$.

Question: For every cubic planar graph $G$ and every 3-list-assignment $L$ on $G$, do there always exist three pairwise-disjoint proper $L$-colorings of $G$?
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open question in workshop problem collections on cycles and colorings. Related work (Cambie, Cames van Batenburg, Davies, Kang and others on "disjoint list-colorings for planar graphs") shows that for general planar graphs with 3-list-assignments three disjoint proper L-colorings cannot always be guaranteed, but the cubic planar case remains a posed open problem; no resolution was found in the search.

original_question: For a graph G with maximum degree Delta(G), is the list packing number always at most Delta(G) + 1? In other words, must chi*_l(G) <= Delta(G) + 1 hold for every graph G?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph. A list-assignment for $G$ is a function $L$ that assigns to each vertex $v\in V$ a set $L(v)$ of allowed colors; $L$ is called a $k$-list-assignment if $|L(v)|=k$ for every $v\in V$. A proper $L$-coloring of $G$ is a function $c:V\to\bigcup_{v}L(v)$ with $c(v)\in L(v)$ for all $v$ and $c(u)\ne c(v)$ whenever $uv\in E$. An $L$-packing of size $k$ is a collection $(c_1,c_2,\dots,c_k)$ of proper $L$-colorings of $G$ such that for every vertex $v\in V$ the values $c_1(v),c_2(v),\dots,c_k(v)$ are pairwise distinct (equivalently, $\{c_1(v),\dots,c_k(v)\}=L(v)$). The list packing number $\chi^{*}_{\ell}(G)$ is the least integer $k$ such that for every $k$-list-assignment $L$ of $G$, an $L$-packing of size $k$ exists. Let $\Delta(G)$ denote the maximum degree of $G$.

Prove or disprove: for every finite simple graph $G$,
$$\chi^{*}_{\ell}(G)\le \Delta(G)+1.$$
status_search_result: The conjecture that $\chi^{*}_{\ell}(G) \le \Delta(G)+1$ for every graph $G$ is an active open problem in list packing. Partial results exist: the bound is known for graphs of small maximum degree, and the fractional relaxation $\chi^{*}_{c}(G) \le \Delta(G)+1$ has been studied, with $\chi^{*}_{c}(G) \le 2\Delta-2$ established for $\Delta\ge 4$. No general proof or counterexample is reported.

original_question: Is the list packing number of every planar graph at most 7? That is, does chi*_l(G) <= 7 hold for every planar graph G?
self_contained_problem:
Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple graph. A list assignment for G is a function L that assigns to each vertex v ∈ V a set L(v) of admissible colors. Given a positive integer k, L is called a k-list-assignment if |L(v)| = k for every v ∈ V. An L-coloring of G is a proper coloring c such that c(v) ∈ L(v) for every v ∈ V (i.e., c(u) ≠ c(v) whenever uv ∈ E and c(v) ∈ L(v) for all v).

An L-packing of size k of G is a collection (c_1, c_2, …, c_k) of k proper L-colorings of G that are pairwise permutation-disjoint at every vertex; more precisely, for every vertex v ∈ V, the multiset {c_1(v), c_2(v), …, c_k(v)} equals L(v) (so each color in L(v) is used exactly once at v across the k colorings).

The list packing number χ*_ℓ(G) of G is the least integer k such that for every k-list-assignment L of G, G admits an L-packing of size k.

Question: Does every planar graph G satisfy χ*_ℓ(G) ≤ 7?

The question appears to remain open.

original_question: Let v be a vertex of a graph G. Is the list packing number of G always at most two more than the list packing number of the vertex-deleted graph G \ v? Equivalently, must chi*_l(G) <= chi*_l(G \ v) + 2 hold for every graph G and every vertex v of G?

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a (finite, simple) graph. A list-assignment of $G$ is a function $L$ that assigns to each vertex $v\in V$ a set $L(v)$ of colors. For a positive integer $k$, $L$ is called a $k$-list-assignment if $|L(v)|=k$ for every $v\in V$.

Given a $k$-list-assignment $L$, an $L$-packing of size $k$ is a collection $(\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_k)$ of $k$ proper colorings of $G$ such that:
(i) $\varphi_i(v)\in L(v)$ for every vertex $v$ and every $i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$, and
(ii) for every vertex $v\in V$, the colors $\varphi_1(v),\ldots,\varphi_k(v)$ are pairwise distinct (i.e. they form the entire list $L(v)$).

The list packing number $\chi_\ell^\star(G)$ is the smallest integer $k$ such that for every $k$-list-assignment $L$ of $G$, there exists an $L$-packing of size $k$.

$$\chi_\ell^\star(G) \;\le\; \chi_\ell^\star(G\setminus v) + 2$$
hold for every graph $G$ and every vertex $v$ of $G$, where $G\setminus v$ denotes the graph obtained from $G$ by deleting the vertex $v$ together with its incident edges?

self_contained_problem:
Let G=(V,E) be a finite simple graph. A list assignment on G is a function L assigning to each vertex v∈V a finite set L(v) of allowed colors. For an integer k≥1, an L-packing of size k is a collection {f_1,…,f_k} of proper L-colorings of G such that for all 1≤i<j≤k and all v∈V, f_i(v)≠f_j(v). The list packing number χ*_ℓ(G) is the least integer k such that for every list assignment L with |L(v)|=k for all v∈V, an L-packing of size k exists.

Fix an integer k>2. Consider the decision problem: given a graph G as input, decide whether χ*_ℓ(G)≤k. Determine whether this problem is complete for the complexity class Π^P_2 (the class of languages decidable by a co-nondeterministic polynomial-time machine with access to an NP oracle, i.e., the second universal level of the polynomial hierarchy).

original_question: Does there exist a constant c >= 0 such that every non-complete graph G of order n with minimum degree delta(G) >= n/2 + c has rainbow connection number rc(G) = 2? In particular, does the weaker threshold delta(G) >= n/2 already imply rc(G) = 2?
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a finite, simple, connected graph. An edge-coloring of G (not necessarily proper) is called rainbow connected if for every pair of distinct vertices u, v of G there exists a u-v path all of whose edges receive pairwise distinct colors. The rainbow connection number rc(G) is the minimum number of colors in a rainbow connected edge-coloring of G. For a graph G of order n, let δ(G) denote the minimum degree.

(a) Does there exist an absolute constant c ≥ 0 such that every non-complete graph G of order n with δ(G) ≥ n/2 + c satisfies rc(G) = 2?

(b) In particular, does δ(G) ≥ n/2 already imply that rc(G) = 2 for every non-complete graph G of order n?
status_search_result: The best known result, due to Caro, Lev, Roditty, Tuza, and Yuster, is that δ(G) ≥ n/2 + log n implies rc(G) = 2 for non-complete graphs, with subsequent refinements involving lower-order logarithmic terms. Removing the logarithmic gap—i.e., obtaining a constant c (or c = 0) such that δ(G) ≥ n/2 + c forces rc(G) = 2—appears to remain unresolved in the literature.

original_question: An r-graph is an r-regular graph G such that every odd vertex set X subseteq V(G) is joined to its complement by at least r edges. Such a graph is poorly matchable if any two of its perfect matchings intersect. Is there a poorly matchable 5-edge-connected 5-graph?
self_contained_problem:
Define an r-graph (for a positive integer r) to be an r-regular multigraph G on a finite even-order vertex set such that for every odd-cardinality vertex subset X ⊆ V(G), the number of edges with one endpoint in X and the other in V(G)∖X is at least r. A perfect matching of G is a set of edges that covers every vertex exactly once; by parity and the r-graph condition, every r-graph has perfect matchings. Call an r-graph poorly matchable if any two of its perfect matchings share at least one edge.

Question: Does there exist a 5-graph G that is 5-edge-connected (i.e., every edge cut of G has at least 5 edges) and poorly matchable?

original_question: Let v1, ..., vn be a linear ordering of the vertices of a graph G, and for each vertex vi define d-(vi) = |{j < i : vivj in E(G)}| and d+(vi) = |{j > i : vivj in E(G)}|. A Type-A order is one in which every vertex v satisfies that d-(v) is odd or 0. Can it be decided in polynomial time whether a graph G admits a Type-A order or a Type-B order, where a Type-B order requires that each vertex either has d-(v) odd or 0, or else has d-(v) even and d+(v) = 0?
self_contained_problem:
Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple graph on n vertices. Given a linear ordering v_1, v_2, …, v_n of V, define for each vertex v_i:
  d^-(v_i) = |{ j < i : v_i v_j ∈ E(G) }|,
  d^+(v_i) = |{ j > i : v_i v_j ∈ E(G) }|.

Call such an ordering a Type-A order if every vertex v satisfies
  d^-(v) is odd, or d^-(v) = 0.

Call it a Type-B order if every vertex v satisfies one of:
  (i) d^-(v) is odd, or d^-(v) = 0; or
  (ii) d^-(v) is even and d^+(v) = 0.

Question: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, given an input graph G, decides whether G admits a Type-A order? Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that decides whether G admits a Type-B order?
status_search_result: No published resolution of the recognition complexity for Type-A or Type-B orders in this sense was found through web search; the question is posed as an open problem and no follow-up establishing polynomial-time algorithms or hardness was located.

original_question: Let S be a semigroup and let X be any set. A semigroup conjugacy relation on S is partition-covering if, for every partition of X, one can put a semigroup structure on X whose conjugacy classes are exactly the blocks of that partition. For the standard semigroup conjugacy relations ∼o, defined by a ∼o b when there exist g,h in S with ag = gb and bh = ha; ∼p, defined by a ∼p b when there exist u,v in S with a = uv and b = vu; and ∼tr, the epigroup relation defined using idempotent powers a^ω and b^ω together with elements g,h satisfying ghg = g, hgh = h, hg = a^ω, gh = b^ω, and ga^(ω+1)h = b^(ω+1), must every partition arise as the set of conjugacy classes of some semigroup?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be an arbitrary nonempty set. For a semigroup $S$, define the following equivalence relations on $S$ (called semigroup conjugacy relations):

(1) $a \sim_o b$ iff there exist $g,h \in S^1$ with $ag = gb$ and $bh = ha$.

(2) $a \sim_p b$ iff there exist $u,v \in S^1$ with $a = uv$ and $b = vu$.

(3) (Defined on epigroups, where each element $a$ has a power $a^n$ lying in a subgroup of $S$, with idempotent $a^\omega$ denoting the identity of that subgroup, and $a^{\omega+1} = a \cdot a^\omega$.) $a \sim_{tr} b$ iff there exist $g, h \in S$ such that $ghg = g$, $hgh = h$, $hg = a^\omega$, $gh = b^\omega$, and $g\, a^{\omega+1}\, h = b^{\omega+1}$.

A semigroup conjugacy relation $\sim$ is called partition-covering if for every partition $\mathcal{P}$ of $X$ there exists a semigroup structure on $X$ whose $\sim$-classes are exactly the blocks of $\mathcal{P}$.

Question: Are each of $\sim_o$, $\sim_p$, and $\sim_{tr}$ partition-covering?
status_search_result: The question is answered affirmatively: each of the standard semigroup conjugacy relations $\sim_o$, $\sim_p$, and $\sim_{tr}$ (along with $\sim_c$, $\sim_n$, $\sim_{p^*}$) is shown to be partition-covering, resolving the cited Problem 6.10.

original_question: Define Otto conjugacy on a semigroup S by a ∼o b if there exist elements u and v in S such that au = ub and va = bv. Is there a finite semigroup S for which ∼o is a congruence and the quotient semigroup S/∼o is not cancellative?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S$ be a semigroup. Define the Otto conjugacy relation $\sim_o$ on $S$ by declaring $a \sim_o b$ if and only if there exist elements $u, v \in S$ such that
$$au = ub \quad \text{and} \quad va = bv.$$
A semigroup $T$ is said to be cancellative if for all $x, y, z \in T$, both $xy = xz \Rightarrow y = z$ and $yx = zx \Rightarrow y = z$.

Determine whether there exists a finite semigroup $S$ such that:
(i) $\sim_o$ is a congruence on $S$ (i.e., an equivalence relation compatible with multiplication on both sides), and
(ii) the quotient semigroup $S/\!\sim_o$ is not cancellative.

original_question: Does there exist an infinite family of semigroup conjugacy relations that are first-order definable, that agree with ordinary group conjugacy on every group, and that form an antichain under inclusion, so that no one of the relations contains another?
self_contained_problem:
Background. A semigroup conjugacy is a binary relation $\sim$ on semigroups, defined uniformly across the class of all semigroups, such that:
(i) for every semigroup $S$, the relation $\sim_S$ on $S$ is an equivalence relation;
(ii) whenever $S$ is a group, $\sim_S$ coincides with the usual group-theoretic conjugacy relation $\{(a,b) : \exists g\in S,\ b = g^{-1}ag\}$.
Such a conjugacy is called first-order definable if there is a first-order formula $\varphi(x,y)$ in the language of semigroups (a single binary operation symbol) such that for every semigroup $S$ and all $a,b\in S$,
$$ a \sim_S b \iff S \models \varphi(a,b). $$
The collection of all first-order definable semigroup conjugacies is partially ordered by inclusion: $\sim \,\le\, \approx$ means that $a\sim_S b$ implies $a\approx_S b$ for every semigroup $S$ and all $a,b\in S$.

Question. Does there exist an infinite antichain in this partial order? That is, does there exist an infinite family $\{\sim^{(i)} : i\in I\}$ of first-order definable semigroup conjugacies such that for all distinct $i,j\in I$ neither $\sim^{(i)} \,\le\, \sim^{(j)}$ nor $\sim^{(j)} \,\le\, \sim^{(i)}$?
status_search_result: Recent work constructs an infinite chain of first-order definable semigroup conjugacies, giving a partial answer to the original two-part problem (chain or antichain). The antichain part of the question does not appear to have been resolved in the located sources, so it remains open.
