context_brief: recoverable sets in Gabor phase retrieval
original_question: In the Gaussian-window setting for Gabor phase retrieval from lattice samples, is there a dense set of functions in L^2(R) beyond the known examples that can be recovered up to global phase from their sampled Gabor magnitudes, and if so is that set meagre or comeagre in the sense of Baire category?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G f(x,\omega) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(t)\, \overline{w(t-x)}\, e^{-2\pi i \omega t}\, dt$ denote the Gabor transform of $f \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$ with window $w$, and take $w(t) = e^{-\pi t^2}$ to be the standard Gaussian. Fix lattice parameters $a, b > 0$ and let $\Omega = a\mathbb{Z} \times b\mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{R}^2$. Two functions $f, g \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$ are said to be equal up to a global phase if there exists $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ with $g = e^{i\alpha} f$. Define
$$ \mathcal{R}_\Omega = \{\, f \in L^2(\mathbb{R}) : \text{if } g \in L^2(\mathbb{R}) \text{ satisfies } |Gg(x,\omega)| = |Gf(x,\omega)| \text{ for all } (x,\omega) \in \Omega, \text{ then } g = e^{i\alpha} f \text{ for some } \alpha \in \mathbb{R}\,\}, $$
the set of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ functions that can be recovered up to a global phase from the sampled Gabor magnitudes on $\Omega$. It is known that the Gaussian itself lies in $\mathcal{R}_\Omega$ while there is a dense subset of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ disjoint from $\mathcal{R}_\Omega$.

Determine whether $\mathcal{R}_\Omega$ contains a dense subset of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ beyond the currently known examples, and if so decide whether $\mathcal{R}_\Omega$ is of the first category (meagre) or of the second category (comeagre) in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ in the sense of Baire.
status_search_result: A 2025 preprint ("On a dense set of functions determined by sampled Gabor magnitude", arXiv:2507.14556) establishes that phase retrieval from sampled Gabor magnitudes is possible for a dense class of signals (those whose Bargmann transforms are entire functions of exponential type, sampled on uniformly discrete sets of sufficient lower Beurling density), thereby answering the existence part affirmatively for a broad class. However, this work does not appear to settle the Baire category (meagre vs. comeagre) question for the recoverable set in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$. The full question therefore appears only partially resolved.

original_question: Let T be a rooted labelled tree with n parking spaces and let f be an n-mapping on [n]. For m drivers, write S(T, m) for the number of parking sequences that successfully park on T and S(f, m) for the analogous number for f. Is there a simple general characterization of the counting functions S(T, m) and S(f, m), rather than only case-by-case formulas or bounds?
self_contained_problem:
Let $T$ be a rooted labelled tree on the vertex set $[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, regarded as a parking structure: each vertex is a parking space, and each non-root edge is oriented toward the root, giving each non-root vertex a unique outgoing edge. A sequence of $m\le n$ drivers arrives one by one; driver $j$ has a preferred space $s_j\in[n]$ and proceeds as follows: starting at vertex $s_j$, the driver parks there if it is unoccupied; otherwise the driver follows the directed edges toward the root, parking at the first unoccupied vertex encountered. If the driver reaches the root and it is occupied, the driver fails. The sequence $(s_1,\dots,s_m)\in[n]^m$ is called a parking sequence for $T$ with $m$ drivers if all $m$ drivers successfully park. Let
$$S(T,m)=\#\{(s_1,\dots,s_m)\in[n]^m:\text{all }m\text{ drivers park on }T\}.$$

Analogously, let $f:[n]\to[n]$ be a mapping (an $n$-mapping), with functional digraph having an edge from $i$ to $f(i)$ for each $i$. A driver with preference $s\in[n]$ starts at $s$ and follows the directed edges $i\mapsto f(i)$, parking at the first unoccupied vertex; if the driver returns to a previously visited (occupied) vertex without finding a free space, the driver fails. Define $S(f,m)$ as the number of sequences in $[n]^m$ for which all $m$ drivers successfully park.

Problem: Give a simple, general structural characterization of the counting functions $S(T,m)$ (for arbitrary rooted labelled trees $T$) and $S(f,m)$ (for arbitrary $n$-mappings $f$), beyond case-by-case formulas, bounds, or treatments of extremal cases.
category_tag: Parking functions on trees and mappings
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in a recent survey of parking problems on random trees. Existing literature (Kenyon–Yin, Panholzer and collaborators, Yan et al.) provides characterizations and bounds in extremal or specific cases, but no general simple characterization of $S(T,m)$ or $S(f,m)$ for arbitrary trees and mappings appears in the literature as of 2026.

original_question: For increasing and decreasing tree families, especially recursive trees viewed as unordered increasing trees, can one determine the total number of parking functions or related aggregate quantities such as sums of parking functions, despite the fact that the differential equations produced by the current approach do not appear to have tractable solutions?
self_contained_problem:
Background. A simple tree family on the vertex set $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$ is called an increasing tree family if every tree is rooted, the labels along any root-to-leaf path are strictly increasing, and the family is specified by a degree-weight generating function $\varphi(x)=\sum_{k\ge 0}\varphi_k x^k$ that assigns weight $\varphi_{d(v)}$ to a node of out-degree $d(v)$. Decreasing tree families are defined analogously with strictly decreasing labels. Recursive trees are the special case obtained by viewing increasing trees as unordered (i.e. children of a node form an unordered set), corresponding to $\varphi(x)=e^x$ in the exponential framework.

A parking function for a rooted labelled tree $T$ on $n$ vertices with $m\le n$ cars is a sequence $(s_1,\dots,s_m)\in V(T)^m$ of preferred parking spots such that the following process succeeds: car $i$ drives from $s_i$ toward the root, parking at the first unoccupied vertex it encounters; if all vertices on its path to the root are occupied, the process fails. The sequence is a parking function on $T$ when every car parks successfully. Let $P_{n,m}(T)$ denote the number of parking functions of length $m$ on $T$, and define the aggregate
$$ \mathcal{P}_{n,m}^{\mathcal{T}} \;=\; \sum_{T \in \mathcal{T}_n} w(T)\, P_{n,m}(T), $$
where $\mathcal{T}_n$ is the set of trees of size $n$ in a given increasing or decreasing tree family $\mathcal{T}$ and $w(T)$ is its combinatorial weight. One may also consider the sum-of-parking-function statistic $\sum_{(s_1,\dots,s_m)} (s_1+\cdots+s_m)$ summed over all parking functions of $T$, then averaged/summed over $\mathcal{T}_n$.

Problem. For increasing and decreasing tree families—and in particular for recursive trees (unordered increasing trees)—obtain a tractable determination of:
(a) the total number $\mathcal{P}_{n,m}^{\mathcal{T}}$ of parking functions, and
(b) related aggregate statistics such as the sums of parking-function values $\sum_T \sum_{(s_1,\dots,s_m)\in \mathrm{PF}(T)} (s_1+\cdots+s_m)$,
either by closed-form expressions, exact recursions, or asymptotic formulas (including possible phase-transition thresholds in $m/n$), despite the fact that the natural generating-function / differential-equation approach for recursive trees does not appear to yield directly solvable equations.
status_search_result: A recent survey on parking problems on random trees explicitly lists determining the total number of parking functions (and related aggregates such as sums of parking functions) for increasing/decreasing tree families—especially recursive trees—as an open problem, noting that the differential equations arising from the natural generating-function approach for recursive trees do not appear to have tractable solutions. No subsequent work resolving this question was located.

original_question: For trees T and mappings f with parking sequence s, can one enumerate or otherwise analyze defective parking functions, meaning pairs (T, s) or (f, s) in which exactly k drivers fail to park successfully?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let n and m be positive integers with m ≤ n. Consider one of the following two combinatorial structures on the vertex set [n] = {1,2,…,n}:

(A) Tree model. T is a rooted labelled tree on [n] with edges oriented toward the root. Each non-root vertex is regarded as a parking space, and the unique outgoing edge from a vertex points to the next space a driver tries upon finding the current space occupied.

(B) Mapping model. f : [n] → [n] is an arbitrary function, encoded by its functional digraph whose vertices are parking spaces and whose edges v → f(v) indicate where a driver moves when the current space is occupied.

Parking process. There are m drivers, and a "parking sequence" s = (s_1, …, s_m) ∈ [n]^m specifies, for each driver i, the preferred initial vertex s_i. Drivers arrive one by one. Driver i first attempts to park at s_i; if that vertex is already occupied, the driver moves along the directed edge to the next vertex, and continues until either finding an empty vertex (in which case the driver parks there) or returning to a vertex already visited / reaching a dead end without finding an empty space (in which case the driver is unsuccessful and leaves).

Defective parking functions. For a fixed nonnegative integer k, call a pair (T, s) (in model A) or (f, s) (in model B) a k-defective parking function if exactly k of the m drivers fail to park successfully.

Problem. Develop an enumerative theory of k-defective parking functions in these two settings. Specifically:

1. Determine the number T_{n,m,k} of pairs (T, s), where T ranges over rooted labelled trees on [n] and s ∈ [n]^m, such that exactly k drivers are unsuccessful.

2. Determine the analogous number M_{n,m,k} of pairs (f, s) with f : [n] → [n] and s ∈ [n]^m, in which exactly k drivers are unsuccessful.

3. Derive generating-function identities for these quantities, and obtain exact closed-form and asymptotic expressions, including a description of any phase transition occurring near m ≈ n/2.
category_tag: Defective parking functions on trees and mappings
status_search_result: The problem is posed as a direction for further study: while defective (overflow) parking functions on a line have been enumerated (Cameron–Johannsen–Prellberg–Tetali, 2008) and parking functions on trees and mappings have been analyzed (e.g., Kuba and collaborators, 2015–2016), the enumeration and analytic-combinatorial treatment of k-defective parking functions in the tree and mapping settings has not been carried out in the literature found. It is listed as a preliminary/open direction in a recent survey on parking problems on random trees.

original_question: Let X_n be the random variable equal to the number of parking sequences with n drivers that succeed on a uniformly chosen labelled unordered tree T of size n. Beyond the known first-moment asymptotic E(X_n) = F_n / T_n, can one determine higher moments of X_n or obtain nontrivial information about the full distribution of X_n?
self_contained_problem:
Let $T$ be a labelled unordered (rooted) tree of size $n$, chosen uniformly at random from the set of all such trees, and let $T_n$ denote the total number of these trees. A parking sequence on $T$ with $n$ drivers is a sequence $s=(s_1,\dots,s_n)$ of preferred nodes of $T$ such that the following parking procedure succeeds: drivers arrive one by one; driver $i$ goes to node $s_i$ and, if it is empty, parks there; otherwise the driver moves toward the root and parks at the first empty node encountered; if the driver reaches past the root without finding an empty node, parking fails. The sequence is successful if all $n$ drivers park. Let $X_n$ be the random variable counting the number of successful parking sequences on the random tree $T$, and let $F_n$ be the total number of pairs $(T,s)$ where $T$ is a labelled unordered tree of size $n$ and $s$ is a successful parking sequence with $n$ drivers on $T$. It is known that
$$\mathbb{E}(X_n) = \frac{F_n}{T_n}.$$
Determine higher moments $\mathbb{E}(X_n^k)$ for $k\ge 2$ of $X_n$, or otherwise obtain nontrivial information (e.g.\ variance, concentration, limit law) about the full distribution of $X_n$ as $n\to\infty$.
status_search_result: The question is stated as an open problem in a recent (2025) survey on parking problems on random trees. A web search returns the survey itself and related work (Lackner–Panholzer, Contat et al., recent papers on parking on random recursive trees and tree parking distributions), but no source establishing higher moments or the limiting distribution of X_n for uniform random labelled unordered trees. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: For parking problems on random trees, especially in regimes involving heavy-tailed car-arrival distributions and frozen modifications of the Erdos-Renyi process, can one prove scaling-limit results in Gromov-weak or Gromov-Hausdorff-Prokhorov type metric topologies, and do the resulting limits relate to additive and multiplicative coalescents or to inhomogeneous continuum random trees?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the parking process on a random tree, defined as follows. Let $T_n$ be a random rooted tree on $n$ vertices (for example, a uniform Cayley tree, a critical Galton–Watson tree with a prescribed offspring law, or more generally a random tree with a given degree sequence). At each vertex $v\in T_n$, an independent number $A_v$ of cars arrives, where the $A_v$ are i.i.d. with common law $\mu$ on $\{0,1,2,\dots\}$. Cars are then processed sequentially: each car tries to park at its arrival vertex; if that vertex is already occupied, the car drives along the unique path toward the root until it finds the first empty vertex and parks there, or exits the tree from the root if no empty vertex is found. Write $\mathcal{C}_1(n)\ge\mathcal{C}_2(n)\ge\dots$ for the connected components of parked cars, equipped with the induced graph metric and the counting measure on parked cars.

Consider in addition the frozen Erdős–Rényi process, a variant of the Erdős–Rényi random graph process in which connected components carrying cycles are "frozen" and no longer participate in further mergers, coupled to the parking process in the critical window.

Address the following:

(a) When the car-arrival distribution $\mu$ has a heavy tail (say $\mu(\{k\})\sim c\, k^{-\alpha-1}$ for some $\alpha\in(1,2)$), and at criticality for the parking phase transition, do the components $(\mathcal{C}_i(n))_{i\ge 1}$, suitably rescaled, converge in the Gromov-weak topology and in the Gromov–Hausdorff–Prokhorov topology to a sequence of random compact measured metric spaces?

(b) If such scaling limits exist, can they be described in terms of (the entrance boundary of) the additive coalescent, the multiplicative coalescent, or a hybrid coalescent obtained from the frozen modification of the Erdős–Rényi process; and are the limiting metric spaces realized as inhomogeneous continuum random trees of the kind constructed in connection with the additive coalescent and critical inhomogeneous random graphs?

Prove or disprove the existence of these scaling limits and identify the limiting objects.
status_search_result: Recent work by Contat–Curien and Contat–Laulin (2023–2025) has established scaling limits for parking on critical Galley/Galton–Watson trees toward the Brownian growth-fragmentation tree and analyzed parking on the random recursive tree, but a general scaling-limit theory in Gromov-weak / Gromov–Hausdorff–Prokhorov topologies for heavy-tailed car-arrival laws together with the frozen Erdős–Rényi coupling, with limits identified in terms of additive/multiplicative coalescents and inhomogeneous continuum random trees, has not been established and is explicitly listed as an open research direction.

paper_title: Descriptions of Cantor Sets: A Set-Theoretic Survey and Open Problems
original_question: Find an explicit set-theoretic formula or a recursive set-theoretic formula for deterministic Cantor subsets of [0,1] that are generated by an iterated-function system with K ≥ 2 maps and that do not preserve bilateral symmetry.
self_contained_problem:
Let K ≥ 2 be an integer and let Φ = {φ_1, …, φ_K} be an iterated function system on the unit interval [0,1], where each φ_i : [0,1] → [0,1] is a contraction (for concreteness, an affine contraction φ_i(x) = r_i x + t_i with 0 < r_i < 1 and 0 ≤ t_i ≤ 1 − r_i) chosen so that the images φ_i([0,1]) are pairwise disjoint or meet only at endpoints. Let C(Φ) ⊆ [0,1] denote the unique nonempty compact set satisfying

  C(Φ) = ⋃_{i=1}^{K} φ_i(C(Φ)).

paper_title: Descriptions of Cantor Sets: A Set-Theoretic Survey and Open Problems
original_question: Given a sequence (α_n)_{n≥1} with 0 < α_n < 1 for all n and satisfying 1 - ∑_{n=1}^∞ 2^{n-1}α_n ≥ 0, find a recursive set-theoretic description for the Cantor set produced by a stage-by-stage middle-deletion construction in which the open middle interval of length α_n is removed at stage n.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(\alpha_n)_{n \ge 1}$ be a sequence of real numbers with $0 < \alpha_n < 1$ for every $n \ge 1$, satisfying the admissibility condition
$$1 - \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 2^{n-1}\alpha_n \ge 0.$$
Construct a Cantor-type subset $C \subseteq [0,1]$ by the following stage-by-stage middle-deletion procedure:
- Stage 0: Set $C_0 = [0,1]$.
- Stage $n$ (for $n \ge 1$): $C_{n-1}$ is a disjoint union of $2^{n-1}$ closed intervals, each of the same length. From each of these intervals remove the open middle subinterval of length $\alpha_n$ (relative to $[0,1]$, i.e., the absolute length removed from each of the $2^{n-1}$ intervals equals $\alpha_n$). Let $C_n$ be the resulting union of $2^n$ closed intervals.
- Set $C = \bigcap_{n \ge 0} C_n$.

The admissibility condition guarantees that this construction is well-defined and yields a nonempty compact totally disconnected perfect subset of $[0,1]$ (a Cantor set) of Lebesgue measure $1 - \sum_{n=1}^\infty 2^{n-1}\alpha_n$.

Problem: Provide an explicit recursive set-theoretic description (a closed-form formula expressing $C$ in terms of the sequence $(\alpha_n)$, e.g., as the set of points in $[0,1]$ whose coordinates satisfy an explicit recursion in $n$ depending on $(\alpha_n)$) for the Cantor set $C$.

paper_title: Descriptions of Cantor Sets: A Set-Theoretic Survey and Open Problems
original_question: Establish conditions under which the Cantor-set families arising from the asymmetric-construction problem, the irrational-endpoint problem, the variable-gap deletion problem, and the symmetry-variation problem have a non-empty mutual intersection.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following four families of Cantor-type subsets of the unit interval [0,1], each obtained as the limit of an iterative interval-removal procedure:

(F1) Asymmetric IFS Cantor sets. For an integer K ≥ 2, let Φ = {φ_1, …, φ_K} be a finite system of contracting affine maps φ_i(x) = r_i x + s_i with 0 < r_i < 1, whose images φ_i([0,1]) are pairwise disjoint subintervals of [0,1] and such that the configuration {φ_i([0,1])}_{i=1}^K is not invariant under the reflection x ↦ 1−x. Let C(Φ) denote the unique non-empty compact set satisfying C(Φ) = ⋃_{i=1}^K φ_i(C(Φ)).

(F2) Irrational-endpoint Cantor sets. The subfamily of (F1) (with K ≥ 2) for which at least one endpoint of some interval φ_i([0,1]) is irrational.

(F3) Variable-gap middle-deletion Cantor sets. Given a sequence (α_n)_{n≥1} with 0 < α_n < 1 and 1 − ∑_{n=1}^∞ 2^{n−1} α_n ≥ 0, construct C((α_n)) by setting C_0 = [0,1] and, given C_{n−1} as a disjoint union of 2^{n−1} closed intervals of equal length, removing from each the open middle interval of relative length α_n; let C((α_n)) = ⋂_{n≥0} C_n.

(F4) Symmetry-controlled Cantor sets. The subfamily of (F3) further parameterized by whether each stage's removed middle interval is required to be centrally symmetric within its parent component or is allowed to be off-center by a prescribed offset.

Let 𝓕_1, 𝓕_2, 𝓕_3, 𝓕_4 denote the four families above, viewed as collections of subsets of [0,1].

Problem. Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the parameters defining the four families under which the intersection 𝓕_1 ∩ 𝓕_2 ∩ 𝓕_3 ∩ 𝓕_4 is non-empty; that is, characterize when there exists a Cantor set C ⊂ [0,1] simultaneously realizable as a member of all four families.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as a synthesis of four open problems concerning descriptive formulas for Cantor sets generated by asymmetric IFSs, irrational endpoints, variable middle-gap deletions, and symmetry variations. No published resolution of the joint intersection question was located; the constituent problems are stated as open.

original_question: For a real x, define Ω^x = Σ_{σ∈2^{<ω}} 2^{-K^x(σ)}, where K^x(σ) = min{|τ| : U^x(τ) = σ}. Is there an x such that Ω^x computes 0''?

original_question: Let T ⊆ 2^{<ω} be a positive tree, meaning that [T] has positive measure. Let P^− be the statement that every positive tree has infinitely many distinct paths, and let P be the statement that every positive tree has a perfect subtree. Over RCA_0, does P^− imply P?

\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathsf{P}$: Every positive tree $T \subseteq 2^{<\omega}$ has a perfect subtree $S \subseteq T$.

original_question: Suppose L is a finitely generated group with Π^0_1 word problem that is effectively residually finite in the sense of Theorem 14. Investigate the following: (a) can such a group have unsolvable word problem; (b) is there a finitely generated residually finite Π-group that is not effectively residually finite; and (c) Morozov constructed a Π-group not isomorphic to a subgroup of S_rec, and can one build such a group so that it is also residually finite?

Work in the free group F_k of rank k with the standard generating set. For a normal subgroup N ⊴ F_k, call the finitely generated group S = F_k/N a Π-group if N is a Π^0_1 (co-recursively enumerable) subset of F_k, equivalently if the set of words representing the identity has a co-r.e. presentation.

Call a finitely generated group S = F_k/N effectively residually finite (e.r.f.) if there exists an algorithm which, on input a word w ∈ F_k with w ∉ N, computes a finite group Q and a homomorphism r : F_k → Q such that r(N) = {e_Q} and r(w) ≠ e_Q. (a) Does there exist a finitely generated group L which is a Π-group and effectively residually finite (in the above sense) but whose word problem is undecidable?

(b) Does there exist a finitely generated residually finite Π-group that is not effectively residually finite?

original_question: For a first-order sentence φ in the language of groups, determine the descriptive or algorithmic complexity of the class {G : G |= φ} when G ranges over profinite groups.

Determine the possible descriptive set-theoretic and algorithmic complexities of classes of the form $\mathrm{Mod}(\varphi)$, as $\varphi$ ranges over first-order sentences in the language of groups. In particular, characterize which levels of the Borel/projective hierarchy (and, in computability-theoretic terms, which levels of the arithmetical or analytical hierarchy on suitable codes) can be attained by such classes, and identify natural upper bounds valid for all first-order $\varphi$ together with sentences witnessing that those bounds are sharp.

paper_title: Open Problems in Computability Theory and Descriptive Set Theory
original_question: Nies, Schlicht, and Tent showed that topological isomorphism of oligomorphic groups is Borel reducible to E_∞. Is that isomorphism relation actually smooth?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S_\infty$ denote the Polish group of all permutations of $\mathbb{N}$ with the pointwise convergence topology. A closed subgroup $G \le S_\infty$ is called oligomorphic if for every $n \ge 1$ the natural action of $G$ on $\mathbb{N}^n$ has only finitely many orbits. The space of closed subgroups of $S_\infty$ is a standard Borel space, on which topological isomorphism $\cong_{\mathrm{top}}$ is an analytic equivalence relation.

Given Borel equivalence relations $E, F$ on standard Borel spaces $X, Y$, one says $E$ is Borel reducible to $F$, written $E \le_B F$, if there exists a Borel map $f : X \to Y$ such that $x \mathrel{E} x'$ iff $f(x) \mathrel{F} f(x')$. An equivalence relation $E$ is called smooth if $E \le_B \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}}$ (equivalently, classes can be separated by a Borel function into a standard Borel space). The equivalence relation $E_\infty$ is the universal countable Borel equivalence relation, i.e., the $\le_B$-maximum among Borel equivalence relations all of whose classes are countable.

It is known that the restriction of $\cong_{\mathrm{top}}$ to oligomorphic closed subgroups of $S_\infty$ is Borel reducible to $E_\infty$. Determine whether this restricted topological isomorphism relation on oligomorphic closed subgroups of $S_\infty$ is smooth.
status_search_result: The Nies–Schlicht–Tent result (2019/2021) establishes that topological isomorphism of oligomorphic closed subgroups of $S_\infty$ is Borel reducible to a countable Borel equivalence relation (hence to $E_\infty$). Subsequent literature, including Kechris–Nies–Tent, leaves open whether this relation is smooth; no later source found that resolves the question.

paper_title: Open Problems in Computability Theory and Descriptive Set Theory
original_question: Is there a Borel invariant class C of closed subgroups of S_∞ such that the isomorphism relation on C is not Borel reducible below graph isomorphism? More strongly, can one get an analytic-complete isomorphism relation in this way? The paper asks this in particular for the class of pro-countable groups.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S_\infty$ denote the Polish group of all permutations of $\mathbb{N}$, equipped with the topology of pointwise convergence. The closed subgroups of $S_\infty$ form a standard Borel space (e.g., via the Effros Borel structure on $F(S_\infty)$), on which $S_\infty$ acts by conjugation; topological group isomorphism between closed subgroups of $S_\infty$ coincides on this space with the orbit equivalence relation of an associated $S_\infty$-action, and is in general an analytic equivalence relation. A class $\mathcal{C}$ of closed subgroups of $S_\infty$ is called Borel and invariant if it is Borel as a subset of this standard Borel space and is closed under topological group isomorphism. The graph isomorphism equivalence relation $\cong_{\mathrm{Gr}}$ is the isomorphism relation on the Polish space of countable graphs on $\mathbb{N}$; it is known to be Borel complete among isomorphism relations of countable structures.

Questions:
(a) Does there exist a Borel invariant class $\mathcal{C}$ of closed subgroups of $S_\infty$ such that the topological group isomorphism relation restricted to $\mathcal{C}$ is not Borel reducible to $\cong_{\mathrm{Gr}}$?
(b) Can such a class $\mathcal{C}$ be chosen so that the isomorphism relation on $\mathcal{C}$ is analytic-complete (i.e., every analytic equivalence relation Borel reduces to it)?

paper_title: Open Problems in Computability Theory and Descriptive Set Theory
original_question: Every degree of decidable categoricity is a degree of categoricity. Is the converse true: must every degree of categoricity also occur as a degree of decidable categoricity? The paper notes in particular the cases of degrees at or above 0^(α) for large computable ordinals α, and asks what happens for d.c.e. degrees.
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions.

Work in the setting of computable structure theory. A countable structure $\mathcal{A}$ in a computable language is called computable if its domain is $\omega$ and all its atomic relations and functions are uniformly computable; it is called decidable if its elementary diagram is computable. For a Turing degree $\mathbf{d}$, a structure $\mathcal{A}$ is $\mathbf{d}$-computably categorical if for any two computable copies $\mathcal{B}, \mathcal{C}$ of $\mathcal{A}$ there is a $\mathbf{d}$-computable isomorphism $\mathcal{B} \to \mathcal{C}$; similarly, $\mathcal{A}$ is $\mathbf{d}$-decidably categorical if for any two decidable copies $\mathcal{B}, \mathcal{C}$ of $\mathcal{A}$ there is a $\mathbf{d}$-computable isomorphism between them.

The degree of categoricity of a computable structure $\mathcal{A}$ is, when it exists, the least Turing degree $\mathbf{d}$ such that $\mathcal{A}$ is $\mathbf{d}$-computably categorical. The degree of decidable categoricity of a decidable structure $\mathcal{A}$ is, when it exists, the least Turing degree $\mathbf{d}$ such that $\mathcal{A}$ is $\mathbf{d}$-decidably categorical. A Turing degree is called a degree of categoricity (respectively, a degree of decidable categoricity) if it arises in this way from some computable (respectively, decidable) structure.

It is known that every degree of decidable categoricity is a degree of categoricity.

Questions.

(1) Is the converse true? That is, does every degree of categoricity arise as the degree of decidable categoricity of some decidable structure?

(2) In particular, for a "sufficiently large" computable ordinal $\alpha$ (for instance $\alpha = \omega$), is it true that every Turing degree $\mathbf{d} \geq \mathbf{0}^{(\alpha)}$ which is a degree of categoricity is also a degree of decidable categoricity?

(3) What is the answer when one restricts attention to d.c.e. degrees $\mathbf{d}$ (Turing degrees of differences of two computably enumerable sets)?
category_tag: Computable structure theory: degrees of categoricity
status_search_result: A web search returns only general results on degrees of categoricity and decidable categoricity (Csima et al., Goncharov, Downey–Kach–Lempp, and related works), but no source establishing the converse — that every degree of categoricity is a degree of decidable categoricity — either in general, for cones above $\mathbf{0}^{(\alpha)}$, or for d.c.e. degrees. The question appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Computability Theory and Descriptive Set Theory
original_question: Does Baire space have a degree of topological categoricity?
self_contained_problem:
Background. Let $\mathcal{N} = \omega^\omega$ denote the Baire space, i.e. the set of all functions from $\omega$ to $\omega$ equipped with the product topology (with $\omega$ discrete). A computable (Polish) presentation of a Polish space $X$ is a pair consisting of a countable dense sequence $(x_i)_{i\in\omega}$ in $X$ together with a complete compatible metric $d$ such that the function $(i,j)\mapsto d(x_i,x_j)$ is computable as a real-valued function (uniformly in $i,j$). Given a Turing degree $\mathbf{d}$, two computable presentations of $X$ are said to be $\mathbf{d}$-homeomorphic if there is a homeomorphism between the underlying spaces that, regarded as a map between Cauchy-name representations, is computable relative to an oracle of degree $\mathbf{d}$.

A Turing degree $\mathbf{d}$ is called a degree of topological categoricity of a Polish space $X$ if:
(i) for any two computable presentations of $X$ there is a $\mathbf{d}$-computable homeomorphism between them; and
(ii) $\mathbf{d}$ is the least such degree (i.e. every degree $\mathbf{e}$ satisfying (i) also satisfies $\mathbf{d}\le_T \mathbf{e}$).

Question. Does the Baire space $\mathcal{N} = \omega^\omega$ admit a degree of topological categoricity?
category_tag: computable Polish spaces, degrees of categoricity
status_search_result: The question of whether Polish spaces (and in particular the Baire space) admit degrees of topological categoricity is part of an actively investigated but largely unresolved area. Surveys on computable categoricity of Polish spaces describe this as a "wide open area," and no published resolution for the Baire-space case was located. Status appears to be open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Computability Theory and Descriptive Set Theory
original_question: Let M satisfy RCA_0 + BΣ_n + ¬IΣ_n. Fix a Π_n subset X of M, and let ⟨A_s : s ∈ M⟩ be a sequence of pairwise disjoint M-finite sets with A_s ∩ X nonempty for every s. Must there exist a function definable in M that chooses an element of A_s ∩ X for each s?
self_contained_problem:
Work in the language of second-order arithmetic. Recall the following axiom schemes over the base theory $\mathrm{RCA}_0$:
- $\mathrm{I}\Sigma_n$ (induction for $\Sigma_n$ formulas): for every $\Sigma_n$ formula $\varphi(x)$, $(\varphi(0)\wedge\forall x(\varphi(x)\to\varphi(x+1)))\to\forall x\,\varphi(x)$.
- $\mathrm{B}\Sigma_n$ (bounding/collection for $\Sigma_n$ formulas): for every $\Sigma_n$ formula $\varphi(x,y)$ and every $a$, $\forall x<a\,\exists y\,\varphi(x,y)\to\exists b\,\forall x<a\,\exists y<b\,\varphi(x,y)$.

Let $M$ be a model of $\mathrm{RCA}_0+\mathrm{B}\Sigma_n+\neg\mathrm{I}\Sigma_n$ (with $n\ge 1$). Recall that a subset $X\subseteq M$ is $\Pi_n$ (over $M$) if it is definable by a $\Pi_n$ formula with parameters from $M$, and a set is $M$-finite if it is coded by an element of $M$ in the usual sense. A function $f:M\to M$ is said to be definable in $M$ if its graph is definable by a formula (of arbitrary complexity) with parameters from $M$.

Fix a $\Pi_n$ set $X\subseteq M$ and a sequence $\langle A_s : s\in M\rangle$ of pairwise disjoint $M$-finite sets such that $A_s\cap X\neq\emptyset$ for every $s\in M$.

Question: Must there exist a function $f$ definable in $M$ such that $f(s)\in A_s\cap X$ for every $s\in M$?
status_search_result: The problem is listed among open problems in computability theory and descriptive set theory (2025). A 2025 preprint by Chong and Wong on definability over $\mathrm{B}\Sigma_2$-models addresses closely related definable-choice questions but does not appear to resolve the general $\mathrm{B}\Sigma_n+\neg\mathrm{I}\Sigma_n$ case. No published resolution was found.

paper_title: Open Problems in Computability Theory and Descriptive Set Theory
original_question: For countable graphs G on ω, consider the property that G is isomorphic to its complement G^c. Is the set {G ∈ 2^{ω×ω} : G is a graph on ω and G ≅ G^c} Borel?
self_contained_problem:
Identify a graph on the natural numbers ω with its edge set, viewed as an element of the Cantor space 2^{ω×ω} (with the product topology), where G ⊆ ω×ω is required to be symmetric and irreflexive. For such a graph G, let G^c denote its complement, i.e. the graph on ω whose edge set is {(i,j) ∈ ω×ω : i ≠ j and (i,j) ∉ G}. Write G ≅ G^c to mean that there exists a bijection π : ω → ω such that for all i,j ∈ ω, (i,j) ∈ G if and only if (π(i),π(j)) ∈ G^c. Consider the set
   S = { G ∈ 2^{ω×ω} : G is a graph on ω and G ≅ G^c }.
Determine the descriptive-set-theoretic complexity of S. In particular, is S a Borel subset of 2^{ω×ω}?
status_search_result: According to the workshop record where this question was posed, the problem was resolved during the workshop: the set of self-complementary countable graphs (coded in 2^{ω×ω}) is Σ¹₁-complete, and therefore not Borel.

paper_title: Open Problems in Computability Theory and Descriptive Set Theory
original_question: Call a countable Borel equivalence relation E hyperfinite-over-hyperfinite (hf/hf) if there is a Borel partial order ≤ on its space X such that x ≤ y implies x E y, and the restriction of ≤ to each E-class is a suborder of Z^2. If E is hf/hf, must E be hyperfinite?
self_contained_problem:
A countable Borel equivalence relation on a standard Borel space X is an equivalence relation E ⊆ X × X that is Borel as a subset of X × X and each of whose equivalence classes is countable. Such an E is called hyperfinite if it can be written as an increasing union E = ⋃_n F_n of Borel equivalence relations F_n with all classes finite.

Let ≤_{Z^2} denote the coordinatewise partial order on Z × Z, i.e. (a,b) ≤_{Z^2} (c,d) iff a ≤ c and b ≤ d.

Call a countable Borel equivalence relation E on X hyperfinite-over-hyperfinite (hf/hf) if there exists a Borel partial order ≤ on X such that:
(i) x ≤ y implies x E y, and
(ii) for every x ∈ X, the restriction of ≤ to the E-class [x]_E is order-isomorphic to a suborder of (Z × Z, ≤_{Z^2}).

Question: Must every hyperfinite-over-hyperfinite countable Borel equivalence relation be hyperfinite?

Recent work (arXiv:2404.17516, "An order analysis of hyperfinite Borel equivalence relations") explicitly states it is unknown whether hyperfinite-over-hyperfinite equivalence relations are hyperfinite, and obtains only partial results (e.g., hyperfiniteness under an additional self-compatibility assumption on the Z^2-ordering).

paper_title: Open Problems in Computability Theory and Descriptive Set Theory
original_question: Is every orbit equivalence relation arising from a Borel action of a countable amenable group hyperfinite?
self_contained_problem:
A Borel equivalence relation on a standard Borel space $X$ is a subset $E \subseteq X \times X$ that is an equivalence relation and is Borel as a subset of $X \times X$. Such an $E$ is called countable if every $E$-equivalence class is countable. A countable Borel equivalence relation $E$ on $X$ is called hyperfinite if there is an increasing sequence $E_0 \subseteq E_1 \subseteq E_2 \subseteq \cdots$ of Borel equivalence relations on $X$ such that each $E_n$ has all classes finite and $E = \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} E_n$.

A countable discrete group $G$ is amenable if there exists a finitely additive, left-invariant probability measure on the power set of $G$ (equivalently, $G$ admits a F\o lner sequence). A Borel action of $G$ on a standard Borel space $X$ is an action $G \times X \to X$ that is Borel as a function, and its orbit equivalence relation $E_G^X$ is defined by $x \, E_G^X \, y \iff \exists g \in G\; g \cdot x = y$; this $E_G^X$ is a countable Borel equivalence relation.

Question: Is it true that for every countable amenable group $G$ and every Borel action of $G$ on a standard Borel space $X$, the orbit equivalence relation $E_G^X$ is hyperfinite?
status_search_result: Weiss's question remains open in full generality. It has been resolved positively for many classes of countable amenable groups: abelian groups (Gao–Jackson), polycyclic groups, locally nilpotent groups, and more recently (via Borel asymptotic dimension techniques of Conley–Jackson–Marks–Seward–Tucker-Drob and others) for all virtually polycyclic groups, lamplighter-type groups, and virtually solvable groups of finite Prüfer rank. The general case for arbitrary countable amenable groups is still unresolved as of 2025.

context_brief: Measurable perfect matchings in Schreier graphs
original_question: Let Act(F_∞,([0,1], λ)) be the space of measure-preserving actions of the free group F_∞ on the Lebesgue probability space, and for x in this space let Sch(x) be the Schreier graph of the action. Is the set of actions whose Schreier graph admits a measurable perfect matching Σ^1_1-complete?
self_contained_problem:
Let $F_\infty$ denote the free group on countably infinitely many generators, with a fixed free generating set $S = \{s_1, s_2, \dots\}$. Let $([0,1], \lambda)$ denote the unit interval with Lebesgue measure, and let $\mathrm{Act}(F_\infty, ([0,1], \lambda))$ denote the Polish space of measure-preserving actions of $F_\infty$ on $([0,1], \lambda)$ (with the usual weak topology inherited from the Polish group of measure-preserving transformations).

For an action $x \in \mathrm{Act}(F_\infty, ([0,1], \lambda))$, define the Schreier graph $\mathrm{Sch}(x)$ to be the (labeled) graph on vertex set $[0,1]$ whose edges are the pairs $\{t, s_i \cdot_x t\}$ with $t \in [0,1]$ and $s_i \in S$. A measurable perfect matching of $\mathrm{Sch}(x)$ is a Borel (equivalently, $\lambda$-measurable) set $M$ of edges of $\mathrm{Sch}(x)$ such that, modulo a $\lambda$-null set, every vertex $t \in [0,1]$ is incident to exactly one edge in $M$.

Consider the set
$$A = \{x \in \mathrm{Act}(F_\infty, ([0,1], \lambda)) : \mathrm{Sch}(x) \text{ admits a measurable perfect matching}\}.$$

Determine whether $A$ is $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^1_1$-complete (i.e., analytic and complete for the class of analytic subsets of Polish spaces under Borel reducibility).

paper_title: Open Problems in Computability Theory and Descriptive Set Theory
original_question: For every Borel ideal I on ω, does there exist a closed I-MED, that is, a closed maximal eventually different family relative to I?
self_contained_problem:
Let ω denote the set of natural numbers and ω^ω the set of functions from ω to ω. Let I be an ideal on ω containing all finite sets, and write I^+ = P(ω) \ I for its coideal. A family ε ⊆ ω^ω is called an I-maximal eventually different family (I-MED) if:
(i) for all distinct f, g ∈ ε, the set {n ∈ ω : f(n) = g(n)} belongs to I, and
(ii) for every h ∈ ω^ω there exists f ∈ ε such that {n ∈ ω : f(n) = h(n)} ∈ I^+.

Equip ω^ω with the product (Baire space) topology. Question: for every Borel ideal I on ω, does there exist an I-MED family ε ⊆ ω^ω that is closed in ω^ω?

original_question: Let X = (X_1, ..., X_d) have independent components with unit variances, with at most one Gaussian component, and suppose the representation Y_0 = X^T beta_0 is minimal in the sense that there is no proper sub-vector of X whose linear span already represents Y_0. Is the regression parameter beta_0 in unlinked linear regression identifiable up to sign flips and permutations of its components?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X = (X_1, \dots, X_d)$ be a $d$-dimensional random vector ($d \geq 2$) whose components $X_1, \dots, X_d$ are independent, each with unit variance, and such that at most one of the $X_i$ has a Gaussian distribution. Fix $\beta_0 \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and define the random variable $Y_0 = X^\top \beta_0$. Assume that the representation of $Y_0$ as a linear combination of the components of $X$ is minimal in the following sense: there is no proper sub-vector $X_S = (X_i)_{i \in S}$ (with $S \subsetneq \{1, \dots, d\}$) and no vector of coefficients $\gamma \in \mathbb{R}^{|S|}$ such that $Y_0 \stackrel{d}{=} X_S^\top \gamma$.

In the unlinked linear regression setting, one observes only the marginal distribution of $Y_0$ (equivalently, the marginal distributions of $X$ and of $Y_0$, but not the joint distribution linking responses to covariates). Two parameters $\beta_0, \beta_0' \in \mathbb{R}^d$ are considered equivalent if $X^\top \beta_0 \stackrel{d}{=} X^\top \beta_0'$.

Question: Under the assumptions above, is $\beta_0$ identifiable from the distribution of $Y_0 = X^\top \beta_0$ up to sign flips and permutations of its components? That is, must any $\beta_0' \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with $X^\top \beta_0' \stackrel{d}{=} X^\top \beta_0$ satisfy $\beta_0' = (\epsilon_{\pi(1)} \beta_{0,\pi(1)}, \dots, \epsilon_{\pi(d)} \beta_{0,\pi(d)})$ for some permutation $\pi$ of $\{1, \dots, d\}$ and signs $\epsilon_i \in \{-1, +1\}$?
status_search_result: The question is stated as an informal broad conjecture on weak identifiability for unlinked linear regression with independent (non-i.i.d.) covariates having at most one Gaussian component. Available literature establishes identifiability up to sign flips and permutations only in special cases: when components are i.i.d. (analogous to ICA-type results), under additional parametric assumptions for general $d$, or under fourth-moment conditions when $d=2$. No source verifies the full conjecture in the general independent (non-identically distributed) setting, so it appears to remain open.

paper_title: Resolving Open Problems on the Euler Sombor Index
context_brief: maximum Euler Sombor index for connected graphs with fixed order and girth
original_question: Let EUS(G) = sum over all edges v_i v_j in E(G) of sqrt(d_i^2 + d_j^2 + d_i d_j), where d_i and d_j are the degrees of the endpoints. For connected graphs G with a fixed order n, where order means the number of vertices, and a fixed girth g, where girth means the length of the shortest cycle, determine the maximum possible value of the Euler Sombor index EUS(G) and characterize all connected graphs that attain that maximum.
self_contained_problem:
For a simple graph $G=(V,E)$, let $d_v$ denote the degree of vertex $v$. Define the Euler Sombor index of $G$ by
$$\mathrm{EUS}(G) \;=\; \sum_{v_iv_j \in E(G)} \sqrt{d_i^{\,2} + d_j^{\,2} + d_i d_j}.$$
The order of $G$ is $|V(G)|$, and the girth of $G$ is the length of a shortest cycle in $G$ (defined for graphs containing at least one cycle).

paper_title: Open problems in ageing science: A roadmap for biogerontology
original_question: In ageing science, do fundamental ageing processes exist and, if they do, how do those processes synchronize age-related changes and promote age-related diseases?
self_contained_problem: Determine whether there exist fundamental biological processes of ageing — that is, a set of underlying mechanisms common to ageing organisms that drive the progressive functional decline observed with age. If such fundamental ageing processes exist, characterize how they coordinate and synchronize the diverse age-related changes that occur across different tissues and organ systems, and explain by what mechanisms they promote the onset and progression of age-related diseases (e.g., cardiovascular disease, neurodegeneration, cancer, metabolic dysfunction). A complete answer should (i) identify candidate fundamental processes (or rigorously argue for their nonexistence), (ii) provide a framework explaining their coupling to multi-system age-related phenotypes, and (iii) describe causal pathways linking these processes to specific age-related pathologies.
status_search_result: This is a foundational open question in biogerontology. While candidate frameworks such as the "hallmarks of ageing" (López-Otín et al., 2013, 2023) and "pillars of ageing" have been proposed, there is no consensus that fundamental ageing processes exist as unified drivers, nor a definitive mechanistic account of how they synchronize age-related changes and produce disease. The question remains actively debated in current ageing-research roadmaps.

paper_title: Open problems in ageing science: A roadmap for biogerontology
original_question: During ageing, in which contexts are senescent cells beneficial and in which contexts are they detrimental?
self_contained_problem:
A senescent cell is a somatic cell that has entered a stable cell-cycle arrest while remaining metabolically active, typically exhibiting markers such as elevated p16^INK4a and p21^CIP1 expression, persistent DNA-damage response signalling, lysosomal senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity, and the secretion of a characteristic senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) consisting of cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, and matrix-remodelling proteases. Senescent cells accumulate in mammalian tissues with chronological ageing and have been implicated in both physiological processes (such as embryonic patterning, wound healing, and tumour suppression) and pathological processes (such as chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and age-related tissue dysfunction).

Identify and characterize, across mammalian tissues and life stages, the precise biological contexts — specifying cell type of origin, inducing stimulus (e.g. replicative exhaustion, oncogene activation, oxidative or genotoxic stress, developmental cue), tissue microenvironment, duration of persistence, and composition of the SASP — under which the presence of senescent cells confers a net beneficial effect on organismal health, and the contexts under which the presence of senescent cells confers a net detrimental effect. In particular, determine: (i) which subtypes of senescent cells (defined by molecular signature and origin) are beneficial versus detrimental; (ii) at which temporal windows during development, adulthood, and ageing each role predominates; and (iii) the mechanistic determinants (intrinsic or microenvironmental) that switch a senescent cell between beneficial and detrimental functions.
status_search_result: The roles of senescent cells in ageing — beneficial (development, wound healing, tumour suppression) versus detrimental (chronic inflammation, fibrosis, age-related pathology) — remain an actively investigated open question in biogerontology. Current reviews continue to emphasize context-dependence and heterogeneity of senescent cells, and the precise contextual mapping is not resolved.

original_question: Which ageing-related changes observed in model organisms also occur in a similar way in humans?
self_contained_problem: Identify and characterize which ageing-associated biological changes documented in standard laboratory model organisms (such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila melanogaster, and Mus musculus) occur in humans in a qualitatively and quantitatively similar manner. Specifically: (i) enumerate the cellular, molecular, physiological, and organismal changes that accompany ageing in each model organism; (ii) for each such change, determine whether an analogous change is observed during human ageing, and specify the criteria (e.g., shared molecular pathway, comparable kinetics, comparable phenotypic consequence) under which the two are deemed "similar"; (iii) classify the changes into those that are conserved across species, those that are model-specific, and those whose conservation status is currently undetermined.
status_search_result: This is an open biological research question rather than a mathematical problem. The comparison of ageing-related changes between model organisms and humans is an active area of biogerontology research; while certain hallmarks of ageing (e.g., genomic instability, telomere attrition, cellular senescence, mitochondrial dysfunction) are widely regarded as conserved, a comprehensive and validated mapping remains incomplete and is the subject of ongoing investigation.

original_question: How can cell function that is lost during ageing be reversed or restored?

paper_title: Open problems in ageing science: A roadmap for biogerontology
original_question: Which interventions for ageing should be prioritized for human clinical trials, and by what criteria should they be prioritized?
self_contained_problem: Consider the set of candidate interventions proposed to slow, halt, or reverse biological ageing in humans — including pharmacological agents (e.g., rapamycin and other mTOR inhibitors, metformin, senolytics such as dasatinib + quercetin, NAD+ precursors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors), dietary and lifestyle interventions (caloric restriction, intermittent fasting, exercise regimens), hormonal and growth-factor modulators, cellular reprogramming approaches (partial reprogramming via Yamanaka factors), gene therapies (e.g., telomerase, follistatin), and plasma- or stem-cell-based therapies. Formulate a principled framework that answers the following: (a) Which subset of these interventions should be prioritized for human clinical trials targeting ageing as an endpoint? (b) What explicit, justifiable criteria should determine that prioritization — for example, strength and reproducibility of preclinical evidence across model organisms, mechanistic plausibility with respect to recognized hallmarks of ageing, magnitude and breadth of effect on healthspan/lifespan endpoints, safety profile and existing human exposure data, feasibility of trial design (availability of biomarkers, required sample size, duration, cost), translational gap between model organisms and humans, equity and accessibility considerations, and expected public-health impact? Provide a weighting or decision-theoretic procedure (e.g., multi-criteria decision analysis or a formal expected-value model) that aggregates these criteria into a ranking, and demonstrate the resulting prioritized list under the proposed framework.
status_search_result: The question is a roadmap-level open problem in biogerontology. No consensus framework or agreed-upon prioritized list of ageing interventions for human clinical trials currently exists; ongoing efforts (e.g., the TAME trial for metformin, PEARL for rapamycin, various senolytic trials) reflect competing prioritizations rather than a settled answer. The problem is considered open in the field.

paper_title: Open problems in ageing science: A roadmap for biogerontology
original_question: Can stem-cell therapy based on a person's own young stem cells, such as cells preserved from cord blood, be used to modulate ageing?
self_contained_problem: Consider an individual human organism that has undergone the biological process of ageing, characterized by progressive functional decline of tissues, accumulated cellular and molecular damage, and increased risk of age-related disease. Suppose that at an earlier developmental stage (for example, at birth) a sample of that individual's own stem cells — such as hematopoietic and other progenitor cells obtained from umbilical cord blood — has been collected, cryopreserved, and maintained in a biologically viable, "young" state (i.e., with low replicative history, intact telomeres, and a youthful epigenetic profile). Determine whether an autologous stem-cell therapy that reintroduces these preserved young stem cells into the same individual at an older age can be designed so as to measurably modulate the ageing process of that individual. Concretely: does there exist a delivery protocol (cell type selection, dosage, route of administration, conditioning, and timing) such that the intervention produces a statistically significant and clinically meaningful change in established biomarkers of biological ageing (e.g., epigenetic age clocks, immune system rejuvenation indices, tissue regenerative capacity, frailty indices, healthspan endpoints) relative to matched untreated controls, while remaining safe? Characterize the mechanisms by which such young autologous stem cells could exert systemic rejuvenating effects, and identify the biological constraints (engraftment, niche compatibility, paracrine signalling, immune interactions) that determine whether such modulation of ageing is achievable.
status_search_result: The question of whether autologous young stem cells (e.g., banked cord-blood-derived cells) can be used therapeutically to modulate human ageing remains an open research question in biogerontology. While stem-cell-based interventions and parabiosis-inspired approaches have shown rejuvenating effects in preclinical models, no clinical evidence to date establishes that autologous young stem cell reinfusion modulates human ageing, and the topic is identified as an outstanding open problem in recent biogerontology roadmaps.

paper_title: Open problems in ageing science: A roadmap for biogerontology

paper_title: Some open questions and conjectures about visibility and iteration in bounded convex domains in ℂ^N
original_question: Let Ω ⊂ ℂ^N be a bounded convex domain, and let {γ_k} be a sequence of non-visible geodesic segments, meaning that γ_k([0,1]) eventually avoids every compact subset of Ω while the endpoints satisfy γ_k(0) → p and γ_k(1) → q for two distinct boundary points p,q ∈ ∂Ω. Define the boundary cluster set Γ({γ_k}) = {x ∈ ∂Ω : there exist indices k_n and parameters t_{k_n} ∈ [0,1] such that γ_{k_n}(t_{k_n}) → x}. If p and q are two distinct points of Γ({γ_k}), must one of the following two alternatives always hold: either the open real segment {tp + (1−t)q : 0 < t < 1} lies in Ω, or the closed real segment {tp + (1−t)q : 0 ≤ t ≤ 1} lies in ∂Ω and the complex affine line through p and q, namely (ℂ(p−q)+q), does not meet Ω?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^N$ be a bounded convex domain, equipped with its standard structure as an open convex subset of $\mathbb{C}^N$. A geodesic segment in $\Omega$ is a continuous map $\gamma:[0,1]\to\Omega$ (for instance, a real geodesic for the Kobayashi distance, or any reasonable curve; the statement below is intended for arbitrary geodesic segments). Consider a sequence $\{\gamma_k\}$ of such geodesic segments $\gamma_k:[0,1]\to\Omega$ that is non-visible in the following sense: for every compact subset $K\subset\Omega$ there exists $k_0$ such that, for all $k\ge k_0$, the image $\gamma_k([0,1])$ is disjoint from $K$, while the endpoints converge, $\gamma_k(0)\to p$ and $\gamma_k(1)\to q$, to two distinct points $p,q\in\partial\Omega$.

Define the boundary cluster set
$$\Gamma(\{\gamma_k\}) := \{x\in\partial\Omega : \exists\, k_n\to\infty,\ \exists\, t_{k_n}\in[0,1]\ \text{with}\ \gamma_{k_n}(t_{k_n})\to x\}.$$

Prove or disprove: for every two distinct points $p,q\in\Gamma(\{\gamma_k\})$, at least one of the following two alternatives must hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item the open real segment $\{tp+(1-t)q : 0<t<1\}$ is contained in $\Omega$; or
\item the closed real segment $\{tp+(1-t)q : 0\le t\le 1\}$ is contained in $\partial\Omega$, and the complex affine line through $p$ and $q$, namely $\mathbb{C}(p-q)+q$, does not intersect $\Omega$.
\end{enumerate}

paper_title: Some open questions and conjectures about visibility and iteration in bounded convex domains in ℂ^N
original_question: For a bounded convex domain Ω ⊂ ℂ^N, call Ω complex visible if for every pair of distinct boundary points p,q ∈ ∂Ω there exists a compact set K ⊂⊂ Ω such that whenever z_k → p and w_k → q, every sequence of complex geodesics φ_k with z_k,w_k ∈ φ_k(𝔻) satisfies φ_k(𝔻) ∩ K ≠ ∅ for all sufficiently large k. Is this notion actually equivalent to ordinary visibility? In other words, is a bounded convex domain visible if and only if it is complex visible?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^N$ be a bounded convex domain, and let $\mathbb{D} \subset \mathbb{C}$ denote the open unit disk. A holomorphic map $\varphi: \mathbb{D} \to \Omega$ is called a complex geodesic if it is an isometry between the Poincaré distance on $\mathbb{D}$ and the Kobayashi distance on $\Omega$. The domain $\Omega$ is said to be visible if for every pair of distinct boundary points $p, q \in \partial \Omega$ there exists a compact set $K \subset\subset \Omega$ and neighborhoods $U_p, U_q$ of $p, q$ in $\overline{\Omega}$ such that every real Kobayashi geodesic in $\Omega$ joining a point of $U_p$ to a point of $U_q$ meets $K$.

Call $\Omega$ complex visible if for every pair of distinct boundary points $p, q \in \partial \Omega$ there exists a compact set $K \subset\subset \Omega$ such that whenever sequences $z_k \to p$ and $w_k \to q$ are given, every sequence of complex geodesics $\varphi_k: \mathbb{D} \to \Omega$ with $z_k, w_k \in \varphi_k(\mathbb{D})$ satisfies $\varphi_k(\mathbb{D}) \cap K \neq \emptyset$ for all sufficiently large $k$.

Prove or disprove: a bounded convex domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^N$ is visible if and only if it is complex visible.

One direction (visibility implies complex visibility) is generally known; the converse remains unestablished, and no resolution appears in the literature found.

paper_title: Some open questions and conjectures about visibility and iteration in bounded convex domains in ℂ^N
original_question: Fix z_0 ∈ Ω for a bounded convex domain Ω ⊂ ℂ^N, and let G_{z_0} be the family of all geodesic segments and geodesic rays starting from z_0, parametrized by hyperbolic arc-length. Is visibility of Ω equivalent to uniform equicontinuity of this family G_{z_0} as maps from [0,+∞) with its Euclidean topology into ℂ^N with its Euclidean topology?

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^N$ be a bounded convex domain, equipped with its Kobayashi distance $k_\Omega$. A geodesic segment (respectively, geodesic ray) in $\Omega$ is an isometric map $\gamma\colon I \to (\Omega, k_\Omega)$ where $I \subset \mathbb{R}$ is a compact interval (respectively, $I=[0,+\infty)$), parametrized by hyperbolic arc-length. The domain $\Omega$ is said to be visible if for every pair of distinct boundary points $p, q \in \partial\Omega$ there exist neighborhoods $U_p$ of $p$ and $U_q$ of $q$ in $\mathbb{C}^N$ with $\overline{U_p}\cap\overline{U_q}=\emptyset$ and a compact subset $K \subset \Omega$ such that every geodesic segment in $\Omega$ joining a point of $U_p\cap\Omega$ to a point of $U_q\cap\Omega$ intersects $K$.

Fix a basepoint $z_0 \in \Omega$, and let $\mathcal{G}_{z_0}$ denote the family of all geodesic segments and geodesic rays of $(\Omega, k_\Omega)$ starting at $z_0$, each parametrized by hyperbolic arc-length and extended (if necessary) so that its domain is contained in $[0,+\infty)$. Regard each element of $\mathcal{G}_{z_0}$ as a map from $[0,+\infty)$ (with its Euclidean topology) into $\mathbb{C}^N$ (with its Euclidean topology).

Determine whether $\Omega$ is visible if and only if the family $\mathcal{G}_{z_0}$ is uniformly equicontinuous.

paper_title: Some open questions and conjectures about visibility and iteration in bounded convex domains in ℂ^N
original_question: For a bounded convex domain Ω ⊂ ℂ^N, is visibility equivalent to the Denjoy–Wolff property for holomorphic self-maps without fixed points? That is, does Ω enjoy the Denjoy–Wolff property if and only if Ω is visible?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^N$ be a bounded convex domain. Equip $\Omega$ with its Kobayashi distance $k_\Omega$.

Definitions.
(a) $\Omega$ is said to be *visible* if for every pair of distinct boundary points $p, q \in \partial\Omega$ there exist neighborhoods $U_p, U_q$ in $\mathbb{C}^N$ with $\overline{U_p}\cap\overline{U_q}=\emptyset$ and a compact set $K\subset\Omega$ such that every $(1,\kappa)$-quasi-geodesic (for some fixed $\kappa\geq 0$) for $k_\Omega$ joining a point of $U_p\cap\Omega$ to a point of $U_q\cap\Omega$ intersects $K$.

(b) $\Omega$ is said to enjoy the *Denjoy–Wolff property* if for every holomorphic self-map $F:\Omega\to\Omega$ without fixed points in $\Omega$, the iterates $F^{\circ n}$ converge, uniformly on compact subsets of $\Omega$, to a constant map $z\mapsto p$ for some point $p\in\partial\Omega$.

Question. Is it true that $\Omega$ enjoys the Denjoy–Wolff property if and only if $\Omega$ is visible?
status_search_result: One direction is known: visibility of a bounded (convex) domain implies the Denjoy–Wolff property (Bharali–Maitra and related works). The converse — that the Denjoy–Wolff property forces visibility for bounded convex domains in ℂ^N — remains an open conjecture, with recent work (e.g., on failure of Denjoy–Wolff in smooth convex domains without analytic discs in the boundary) clarifying related constraints but not resolving the equivalence.

context_brief: Sarkozy Problem 67 on ternary sums from dense prime subsets
original_question: If Q = {q1, q2, ...} is an infinite set of primes satisfying lim inf_{x -> infinity} (log x / x) |{qi : qi <= x, qi in Q}| > 1/2, does every sufficiently large odd integer 2n + 1 admit a representation qi + qj + qk = 2n + 1 with qi, qj, qk in Q?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{P}$ denote the set of all prime numbers. For a set $Q = \{q_1, q_2, \dots\} \subseteq \mathcal{P}$, define the lower relative prime density of $Q$ as
$$\underline{d}(Q) = \liminf_{x \to \infty} \frac{\log x}{x}\,\bigl|\{q \in Q : q \le x\}\bigr|.$$
(Note that by the prime number theorem, $\underline{d}(\mathcal{P}) = 1$.)

Question: Is it true that whenever $Q \subseteq \mathcal{P}$ is an infinite set of primes satisfying
$$\underline{d}(Q) > \tfrac{1}{2},$$
every sufficiently large odd integer $2n+1$ can be written as
$$q_i + q_j + q_k = 2n+1$$
with $q_i, q_j, q_k \in Q$ (not necessarily distinct)?

Decide whether the implication holds, or exhibit a counterexample.
category_tag: ternary Goldbach in dense prime subsets
status_search_result: The problem has been resolved negatively. A construction produces an infinite set of primes with upper relative prime density 1 and lower relative prime density 5/8 such that infinitely many odd integers cannot be written as a sum of three primes from the set, refuting the conjectured implication.

paper_title: Open Questions about Time and Self-reference in Living Systems
context_brief: non-iterative search of biological possibility space
original_question: Are there non-iterative physical mechanisms, other than generate-and-test evolution or growth and development, that can effectively explore the vast combinatorial state space of viable living forms—for example by quantum collapse to a viable candidate in a single step—or is an iterative process still required to prepare a state whose collapse has non-negligible probability of yielding a viable candidate?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{S}$ denote the combinatorial state space of all candidate physical configurations of a living organism (for example, all sequences of biopolymers up to some bounded length, together with their spatial arrangements). Let $V \subset \mathcal{S}$ be the subset of configurations that are "viable" in the sense of corresponding to a self-maintaining living system, and assume $|\mathcal{S}|$ is "Vast" (e.g.\ super-exponential in the size of the organism) while $|V|/|\mathcal{S}|$ is exponentially small.

A \emph{search procedure} for $V$ is a physical process that, starting from resources (matter, energy, information) whose preparation cost is polynomial in the description length of an organism, outputs an element of $\mathcal{S}$. Call the procedure \emph{iterative} if it consists of a sequence of generate-and-test steps (as in Darwinian variation and selection) or of a developmental/growth trajectory whose length scales at least polynomially with the description length. Call it \emph{non-iterative} if it produces a candidate in $\mathcal{S}$ in $O(1)$ physical steps after preparation.

Question: Does there exist a physical (in particular, possibly quantum-mechanical) non-iterative search procedure that, with non-negligible probability, outputs an element of $V$? Concretely, can one prepare a quantum state $|\psiangle$ on a Hilbert space whose computational basis is indexed by $\mathcal{S}$, using only resources polynomial in the description length, such that a single projective measurement in that basis yields an outcome in $V$ with probability bounded below by an inverse polynomial? Or must any physical procedure achieving non-negligible success probability necessarily include an iterative preparation stage of length growing with the description length of viable organisms?
category_tag: quantum search of biological state spaces
status_search_result: The question is posed as an explicitly open conceptual problem at the interface of quantum physics, theoretical biology, and search complexity. No published mathematical or physical result is known to settle whether viable biological configurations can be reached by a genuinely non-iterative quantum process; standard quantum search lower bounds (e.g.\ BBBV) suggest unstructured search of a Vast space cannot be done non-iteratively, but no formal model of biological viability has been shown to fall under such bounds. Status remains open.

paper_title: Achievement sets – current results and open problems
original_question: Do there exist fast convergent sequences (x_n) such that the adjoint Cantorval E\(x_n) associated with E(x_n) is itself achievable?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. For a sequence $(x_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ of positive real numbers with $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} x_n < \infty$, the achievement set (set of subsums) is
$$E(x_n) = \Bigl\{\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \varepsilon_n x_n : (\varepsilon_n) \in \{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\Bigr\}.$$
Such a set $E(x_n)$ is always one of the following: a finite union of closed intervals, homeomorphic to the Cantor set, or a Cantorval (a nonempty compact set $C \subset \mathbb R$ such that $C$ is the closure of its interior, and both endpoints of every nontrivial component of the complement of $C$ are accumulation points of trivial components of the complement). 

The sequence $(x_n)$ is called fast convergent if $x_n \ge \sum_{k>n} x_k$ for every $n$. 

For a fast convergent sequence $(x_n)$ such that $E(x_n)$ is a Cantorval, the adjoint Cantorval $E\setminus(x_n)$ is defined as the set of all sums $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \varepsilon_n x_n$ taken with the "complementary" choice rule that swaps the role of $0$ and $1$ at indices where $x_n = \sum_{k>n} x_k$ (equivalently, the Cantorval obtained from $(x_n)$ by reflecting the digit conventions at equality positions, which produces another Cantorval associated with the same sequence). A set $A \subset \mathbb R$ is called achievable if there exists an absolutely summable sequence $(y_n)$ of positive reals with $A = E(y_n)$.

Question. Does there exist a fast convergent sequence $(x_n)$ such that the adjoint Cantorval $E\setminus(x_n)$ associated with $E(x_n)$ is itself an achievable set?
status_search_result: The problem is listed as an open problem in the recent survey on achievement sets (arXiv:2512.17285), where it appears as Problem 36 in the open problems section. No publication resolving it was found in the search.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Let u be a ﬁxed point of a primitive morphism. Then the language of u is closed under reversal if and only if u is palindromic.
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and $\varphi : A^* \to A^*$ a morphism. Recall that $\varphi$ is called primitive if there exists an integer $k \ge 1$ such that, for every pair of letters $a, b \in A$, the letter $a$ occurs in $\varphi^k(b)$. An infinite word $u \in A^{\mathbb{N}}$ is a fixed point of $\varphi$ if $\varphi(u) = u$. The language $\mathcal{L}(u)$ of $u$ is the set of all finite factors (contiguous subwords) of $u$. The reversal of a finite word $w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_n$ is $\widetilde{w} = w_n \cdots w_2 w_1$, and a word $w$ is a palindrome if $w = \widetilde{w}$. The language $\mathcal{L}(u)$ is said to be closed under reversal if $\widetilde{w} \in \mathcal{L}(u)$ whenever $w \in \mathcal{L}(u)$. Finally, the infinite word $u$ is called palindromic if $\mathcal{L}(u)$ contains infinitely many distinct palindromes.

Prove or disprove: if $u$ is a fixed point of a primitive morphism, then $\mathcal{L}(u)$ is closed under reversal if and only if $u$ is palindromic.
status_search_result: This is closely related to the Hof–Knill–Simon (HKS) question on palindromic substitutive sequences. One implication (palindromic ⇒ closed under reversal) is straightforward, while the converse is the subject of active research. Labbé (2014) provided a counterexample to a related question of Hof, Knill and Simon, indicating that statements of this kind require additional hypotheses. The exact equivalence as stated remains open in full generality, with positive results known in restricted settings (e.g. binary alphabet, marked morphisms).

original_question: Given a tournament T, an integer k, and vertices x and y of T, must T contain two arc-disjoint spanning branchings: an in-arborescence rooted at x and an out-arborescence rooted at y, with each branching having at most k leaves? Equivalently, characterize or decide when a tournament admits arc-disjoint in- and out-branchings with prescribed roots and with both branchings having at most k leaves.
self_contained_problem:
A tournament is a directed graph $T=(V,A)$ obtained by orienting each edge of a complete undirected graph; equivalently, for every pair of distinct vertices $u,v\in V$ exactly one of the arcs $(u,v)$ or $(v,u)$ belongs to $A$. A spanning out-arborescence (out-branching) of $T$ rooted at a vertex $y$ is a spanning subdigraph $B^+\subseteq T$ that is a tree when its arcs are regarded as undirected edges, and in which every vertex except $y$ has exactly one entering arc (so there is a unique directed path from $y$ to every other vertex). A spanning in-arborescence (in-branching) of $T$ rooted at a vertex $x$ is defined analogously but with every vertex except $x$ having exactly one outgoing arc (so there is a unique directed path from every vertex to $x$). A leaf of a branching is a vertex whose out-degree (in the out-branching) or in-degree (in the in-branching) within the branching is zero. Two branchings are arc-disjoint if they share no arc.

Problem. Determine the computational complexity, and provide a structural characterization, of the following decision problem:

Input: a tournament $T$, two (not necessarily distinct) vertices $x,y\in V(T)$, and a non-negative integer $k$.

Question: does $T$ contain a spanning in-arborescence $B^-$ rooted at $x$ and a spanning out-arborescence $B^+$ rooted at $y$ such that $B^-$ and $B^+$ are arc-disjoint and each of $B^-$ and $B^+$ has at most $k$ leaves?
status_search_result: Without the leaf restriction, the existence of arc-disjoint in- and out-branchings with prescribed roots in a tournament (and more generally in semicomplete digraphs) is known to admit a polynomial-time decision algorithm (Bang-Jensen's conjecture, established for tournaments and extended to semicomplete digraphs in 2023). However, no characterization or complexity result was found for the variant where each branching is additionally required to have at most $k$ leaves; related parameterized problems (k-distinct branchings, branchings with many leaves) have been studied but do not resolve this specific question. The status therefore appears to be unresolved based on available sources.

context_brief: Logical definability of orders in tournaments
original_question: Fix a class of tournaments of bounded clique-width. Is there a constant number of colors and a CMSO-definable binary formula φ(x, y) such that, for every tournament T in the class, one can choose a coloring λ of the vertices so that φ interprets a total order on V(T), meaning that for all vertices x and y, x < y holds in that order exactly when the colored structure (T, λ) satisfies φ(x, y)?
self_contained_problem:
Let CMSO denote counting monadic second-order logic over relational structures. A tournament is a directed graph T=(V(T),E(T)) such that for every pair of distinct vertices x,y exactly one of (x,y) or (y,x) belongs to E(T). The clique-width of a tournament is defined analogously to the undirected case, using the operations of introducing a single-labeled vertex, taking disjoint union, adding all arcs in one direction between vertices of two given labels, and relabeling.

Given a finite set C of colors, a C-coloring of T is a map λ:V(T)→C; the resulting structure (T,λ) is regarded as a relational structure equipping the tournament with unary predicates indexed by C. A CMSO formula φ(x,y) with two free first-order variables and access to the predicates of (T,λ) interprets a total order on V(T) if the binary relation

  { (x,y) ∈ V(T)×V(T) : (T,λ) ⊨ φ(x,y) }

is a strict total order on V(T).

Question: Fix a class 𝒞 of tournaments of bounded clique-width. Do there exist a finite set of colors C and a CMSO formula φ(x,y) such that, for every tournament T ∈ 𝒞, one can choose a coloring λ:V(T)→C with the property that φ interprets a total order on V(T) inside (T,λ)?
status_search_result: Recent work (Geniet, Ghasemi, Kanté, "Transducing Linear Decompositions of Tournaments", 2026) establishes that linear clique-decompositions of bounded width can be produced by a first-order transduction on tournaments of bounded linear clique-width, which yields CMSO-definable orderings in that linear setting and gives an equivalence between CMSO and existential MSO there. The general bounded clique-width (non-linear) case for tournaments does not appear to be settled in the located sources, so the status is reported as unknown.

context_brief: Forward paths across multiple vertex orderings
original_question: For a digraph D and a vertex ordering L, call a directed path forward in L if its vertices appear in the same order as the orientation of the path. What is the smallest integer k such that every digraph D admits k vertex orderings L_1, ..., L_k with the property that for every two distinct vertices v_i and v_j, either some ordering L_ℓ contains a forward path from v_i to v_j or some ordering L_ℓ contains a forward path from v_j to v_i?
self_contained_problem:
Let $D=(V,A)$ be a finite digraph. A linear ordering (enumeration) $L$ of $V$ is a bijection from $V$ to $\{1,2,\dots,|V|\}$. A directed path $v_{i_1}\to v_{i_2}\to\cdots\to v_{i_r}$ in $D$ is said to be forward in $L$ if $L(v_{i_1})<L(v_{i_2})<\cdots<L(v_{i_r})$, i.e., its vertices appear in $L$ in the same order as the orientation of the path.

A family of orderings $L_1,\dots,L_k$ of $V(D)$ is called a forward cover of $D$ if for every pair of distinct vertices $u,v\in V(D)$ there exists an index $\ell\in\{1,\dots,k\}$ such that $L_\ell$ contains a forward path from $u$ to $v$, or there exists an index $\ell'\in\{1,\dots,k\}$ such that $L_{\ell'}$ contains a forward path from $v$ to $u$.

Determine the smallest integer $k$ (if any) such that every digraph $D$ admits a forward cover of size $k$.
status_search_result: Recent work on "forward covers" of digraphs poses this exact question and conjectures that every strong digraph on n vertices admits a forward cover of size O(log n); the conjecture is established for bi-oriented graphs, but the general problem (and in particular whether a constant k suffices, or any tight bound) appears to remain open.

context_brief: Dichromatic number of a recursively built class
original_question: Let C be the class of digraphs generated by the following rules: the oriented graph K_2 belongs to C; adding a twin of a vertex of a graph in C keeps the graph in C; and gluing two members of C along at most two non-adjacent vertices again produces a member of C. Does every digraph in C have bounded dichromatic number, or can the dichromatic number in this class grow arbitrarily large?

original_question: Given a digraph D, can its arc set be partitioned into two linear forests in such a way that the connected components of one of the two forests all have bounded length?
self_contained_problem:
Let D = (V, A) be a finite digraph. A directed linear forest in D is a subdigraph whose connected components are pairwise vertex-disjoint directed paths; the length of such a component is its number of arcs. For a positive integer k, a directed linear forest is called k-bounded if every one of its directed path components has length at most k.

Determine, as a function of the structural parameters of D (for example its maximum in-degree and out-degree), the smallest integer k = k(D), if any, with the following property: the arc set A can be partitioned into two directed linear forests F_1 and F_2 such that F_1 is k-bounded (while no length restriction is placed on F_2).

In particular, characterize the class of digraphs whose arc set admits such a decomposition into two directed linear forests one of which has all components of bounded length, and decide the algorithmic complexity, for each fixed pair (k, ℓ) of nonnegative integers, of testing whether A can be partitioned into a k-bounded directed linear forest and an ℓ-bounded directed linear forest.
status_search_result: A 2024 paper "Decompositions into two linear forests of bounded lengths" (Discrete Mathematics) and a follow-up HAL preprint settle the complexity of the (k,ℓ)-bounded directed linear forest decomposition problem for all fixed k,ℓ: it is polynomial-time solvable when k+ℓ ≤ 3 and NP-complete otherwise. Thus the existence/complexity version of the question is essentially resolved, while structural/extremal versions (e.g., the smallest k that always suffices in terms of degree parameters) appear to remain open in general.
