paper_title: Open Questions in CMR Manganites, Relevance of Clustered States, and Analogies with other Compounds
original_question: Are the mesoscopic clusters observed in LPCMO by electron diffraction representative of bulk and single-crystal behavior, do manganites require two distinct forms of phase separation at nanoscale and microscale lengths, and can one evolve smoothly into the other as the Curie temperature decreases?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the family of doped perovskite manganite compounds (La_{1-y}Pr_y)_{1-x}Ca_xMnO_3 (LPCMO), a colossal magnetoresistance (CMR) material in which competing ferromagnetic metallic and charge-ordered antiferromagnetic insulating phases coexist below a characteristic Curie temperature T_C. Experimental electron-diffraction studies have reported "mesoscopic" (sub-micron to micron scale) cluster textures, while other probes have reported "nanoscale" (a few nanometers to tens of nanometers) inhomogeneities in the same and related manganite families.

Address the following theoretical/experimental questions in a unified framework:

(a) Determine whether the mesoscopic clusters observed in LPCMO via electron-diffraction techniques are intrinsic representations of the bulk thermodynamic state and of single-crystal samples (as opposed to artifacts of thin-film geometry, surface effects, or sample preparation).

(b) Decide whether a correct microscopic description of phase separation in manganites requires the simultaneous presence of two distinct kinds of inhomogeneity — one at the nanoscale and one at the mesoscopic/microscale — or whether a single mechanism suffices.

(c) Construct a theoretical model (or provide experimental evidence) showing whether, as T_C is varied (for instance by tuning the Pr fraction y or by other means that lower T_C), the nanoscale cluster state can evolve continuously and smoothly into the mesoscopic cluster state, or whether the crossover is sharp.

Provide a definitive resolution of (a)–(c), including identification of the physical mechanism (elastic strain, long-range Coulomb interactions, disorder correlations, quenched chemical inhomogeneity) responsible for the chosen length scale(s).
status_search_result: Substantial experimental and theoretical progress has been made since the question was posed. Studies have confirmed that LPCMO exhibits genuine bulk phase separation with coexisting nanoscale (ferromagnetic) and micrometer-scale (paramagnetic / charge-ordered) regions, and have identified chemical (Pr) ordering, quenched disorder, and elastic strain as central mechanisms controlling the length scale. Size-dependent studies show the crossover between regimes as particle size and T_C are varied. However, a unified, predictive theory that fully accounts for the smooth evolution between nanoscale and mesoscopic textures across the full LPCMO phase diagram is not yet established, so the question remains only partially resolved.

paper_title: Open Questions in CMR Manganites, Relevance of Clustered States, and Analogies with other Compounds
original_question: Are the glassy states observed in some manganites ordinary spin glasses or a distinct class of phase-separated glasses or cluster glasses, how should such glasses be classified, and what time-dependent phenomena are essential for determining their nature?
self_contained_problem:
Consider hole-doped manganite compounds of the form R_{1-x}A_x MnO_3 (with R a trivalent rare-earth ion and A a divalent alkaline-earth ion) in regimes where neutron, transport, and magnetization measurements reveal coexisting ferromagnetic metallic and antiferromagnetic/charge-ordered insulating regions on nanometer to micrometer length scales. At low temperatures, many such systems exhibit "glassy" magnetic behavior: history dependence, memory and aging effects, slow non-exponential relaxation of the magnetization, frequency-dependent peaks in the ac susceptibility, and a divergence of relaxation times resembling that of canonical spin glasses (e.g., dilute magnetic alloys such as CuMn) or cluster glasses (interacting frozen ferromagnetic clusters).

Formulate and resolve the following:

(a) Establish criteria, based on equilibrium and non-equilibrium magnetic observables (e.g., scaling of the nonlinear susceptibility chi_3 near a freezing temperature T_f, critical exponents of a putative spin-glass transition, aging and memory protocols, thermo-remanent and isothermal remanent magnetization decay, and noise/fluctuation–dissipation behavior), that distinguish a canonical atomic spin glass from a phase-separated glass whose elementary degrees of freedom are mesoscopic clusters of correlated spins/charges.

(b) Determine whether the glassy low-temperature states observed in representative phase-separated manganites (in particular near half-doping x ≈ 0.5, where charge/orbital ordering competes with ferromagnetism) fall into the universality class of standard Heisenberg/Ising spin glasses, or whether they constitute a genuinely distinct class — to be called "phase-separated glasses" or "cluster glasses" — characterized by frozen-in inhomogeneity of coexisting electronic phases rather than by frustrated atomic exchange interactions.

(c) Provide a classification of magnetic glassy states that includes (i) canonical spin glasses, (ii) cluster glasses with well-defined ferromagnetic clusters, and (iii) phase-separated electronic glasses with competing ordered phases, specifying which time-dependent phenomena (aging, rejuvenation, memory, sub-aging exponents, waiting-time dependence of relaxation, breakdown of the fluctuation–dissipation theorem) are essential diagnostics for assigning a given material to one of these classes.
status_search_result: Recent literature continues to debate whether glassy manganite states are canonical spin glasses or distinct cluster/phase-separated glasses. Studies on Nd2/3Ca1/3MnO3, Eu0.5Ba0.5MnO3, and La2/3Sr1/3-based systems report cluster-glass and Griffiths-phase signatures with both similarities and contradictions to conventional spin glasses, and a general classification has not been settled.

paper_title: Open Questions in CMR Manganites, Relevance of Clustered States, and Analogies with other Compounds
original_question: For charge-ordered manganite states below half doping, such as Pr1−xCaxMnO3 with x<0.5, what are the actual spin and orbital arrangements, how is the excess electronic charge distributed relative to the CE pattern, and do these charge-ordered states possess enough entropy to be thermodynamically stable at high temperature?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the perovskite manganite family Pr_{1-x}Ca_xMnO_3 in the hole-doping regime x < 1/2 (below half doping). At x = 1/2, the well-known CE-type ordering is realized: a checkerboard arrangement of Mn^{3+} and Mn^{4+} cations in the ab-plane (charge order), a zigzag pattern of ferromagnetic chains coupled antiferromagnetically (spin order), and an associated alternating pattern of occupied e_g orbitals (orbital order), stacked antiferromagnetically along the c-axis. For x < 1/2, the system contains an excess of electrons (more Mn^{3+} sites than Mn^{4+}) relative to the x = 1/2 CE reference state, yet exhibits charge-ordered phases that are commonly said to "resemble" the CE state.

(a) Determine the actual long-range spin arrangement (magnetic unit cell, ordering wavevector, and sublattice moments) and the orbital arrangement (which e_g orbitals are occupied at which Mn sites) of the charge-ordered ground state for generic x in the interval (0, 1/2), and in particular near x = 1/4 and x = 1/3.

(b) Decide how the excess electronic charge, relative to the x = 1/2 CE pattern, is spatially distributed: is it placed randomly on the Mn^{4+} sites of the CE structure, distributed uniformly (e.g., as a homogeneous reduction of the disproportionation amplitude), organized into a distinct superlattice (such as stripes or Wigner-crystal-like arrangements), or accommodated through phase separation into CE-ordered and electron-rich (e.g., ferromagnetic) regions?

(c) Estimate the configurational, magnetic, and orbital entropy of these charge-ordered states at x < 1/2 and determine whether it is sufficiently large to make them thermodynamically stable (i.e., to give them a free energy lower than competing uniform or phase-separated states) up to the experimentally observed charge-ordering transition temperatures.
status_search_result: Partial answers exist. Experimental and theoretical work (neutron scattering, x-ray scattering, imaging, and model calculations) indicates that for 0.3 ≲ x < 0.5 a CE-like charge/orbital order persists with short-range orbital correlations and coexisting incommensurate spin correlations, while near x ≈ 0.25 long-range orbital order without sharp charge order is reported. A critical doping near x ≈ 0.35 has been proposed separating phase-separated site-centered from bond-centered/charge-disproportionated CO ground states. However, a unified, quantitatively confirmed picture of the spin/orbital pattern, the distribution of excess charge, and the entropy stabilizing these phases across all x < 1/2 has not been established, so the question remains only partially resolved.

paper_title: Open Questions in CMR Manganites, Relevance of Clustered States, and Analogies with other Compounds
original_question: Can the temperature dependence of d.c. resistivity in metallic manganites be understood in enough detail to determine whether non-Fermi-liquid transport is present?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the family of doped perovskite manganite compounds of the form R_{1-x}A_x MnO_3, where R is a trivalent rare-earth cation (e.g., La, Pr, Nd) and A is a divalent alkaline-earth cation (e.g., Ca, Sr, Ba), in the doping range and temperature regime where the bulk material is in a metallic phase (i.e., the d.c. resistivity ρ(T) decreases with decreasing temperature). In a conventional Fermi liquid one expects, at low temperatures, ρ(T) = ρ_0 + A T^2, where ρ_0 is the residual resistivity and the T^2 term arises from electron–electron scattering. A non-Fermi-liquid metal is, by contrast, characterized by an anomalous power-law or other non-analytic low-temperature dependence, e.g., ρ(T) - ρ_0 ∝ T^α with α ≠ 2 (commonly α between 1 and 5/3) over a wide temperature window, signaling the breakdown of Landau quasiparticle transport.

Problem. Provide a sufficiently detailed quantitative analysis of the temperature dependence of the d.c. resistivity ρ(T) of metallic manganites — including the identification of the dominant scattering mechanisms (electron–phonon, electron–magnon, electron–electron, polaronic, spin-cluster, etc.), the functional form of ρ(T) over the accessible temperature range, and the low-temperature exponent α — to decide unambiguously whether the metallic phase of manganites exhibits non-Fermi-liquid transport, as observed in various other strongly correlated metals.
status_search_result: This is an open-ended physics question about whether metallic manganites exhibit non-Fermi-liquid d.c. transport. The question was posed as an open issue in the early 2000s manganite literature, and while many subsequent experimental and theoretical studies have analyzed ρ(T) in metallic manganites (often fitting T^2 or T^{4.5} forms), no community-wide consensus identifying a definitive non-Fermi-liquid regime appears to have been established. Status is therefore taken as unknown/open.

paper_title: Open Questions in CMR Manganites, Relevance of Clustered States, and Analogies with other Compounds
original_question: What is the full phase diagram of realistic three-dimensional and bilayer two-orbital manganite models, including whether they host additional competing ordered phases beyond the known A-type antiferromagnetic state near x=0, ferromagnetic metal near x≈0.3, CE-type order near x=0.5, C-type order near x≈0.75, and G-type order near x=1?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the two-orbital double-exchange model for manganites on a three-dimensional cubic lattice and on a bilayer (two coupled square-lattice planes) geometry. The Hamiltonian includes: (i) hopping of e_g electrons between nearest-neighbor Mn sites in the two-orbital basis {d_{x^2-y^2}, d_{3z^2-r^2}} with the standard orbital- and direction-dependent hopping amplitudes; (ii) a large Hund coupling J_H between the e_g spin and a localized t_{2g} core spin S=3/2 (often treated as a classical unit vector); (iii) antiferromagnetic superexchange J_AF between nearest-neighbor t_{2g} spins; (iv) cooperative Jahn–Teller coupling λ between the e_g orbitals and the Q_2, Q_3 lattice distortions, together with their elastic energy; and (v) optionally on-site Hubbard U and inter-orbital U' Coulomb interactions. Let x denote the hole doping (fraction of Mn^{4+}).

Determine the complete ground-state phase diagram of this model as a function of x and the model parameters (J_AF, λ, U, U', bandwidth, and, in the bilayer case, the interlayer coupling). The following ordered phases are already known to appear in appropriate regions: A-type antiferromagnetic order near x=0, ferromagnetic metallic order near x≈0.3, CE-type charge/orbital/spin order near x=0.5, C-type antiferromagnetic order near x≈0.75, and G-type antiferromagnetic order near x=1. The question is to identify all additional competing ordered or inhomogeneous phases (e.g. further charge-, orbital-, spin- or stripe-ordered states, phase-separated regions, or novel orbital liquids) that appear in the full 3D and bilayer phase diagrams, and to delineate the regions of (x, parameter) space where each occurs.
status_search_result: The full phase diagram of realistic 3D and bilayer two-orbital manganite models is still not completely characterized. Partial results exist (e.g., established A-type, FM, CE, C-type, and G-type regions; CE/A-AF phase competition in bilayer La2-2xSr1+2xMn2O7; bi-stripe orbital order near x≈0.59; nanoscale phase coexistence in La0.25Sr0.75MnO3), but a complete classification of all competing phases across the full doping range and parameter space has not been achieved, with new ordered/phase-separated states continuing to be reported.

paper_title: Open Questions in CMR Manganites, Relevance of Clustered States, and Analogies with other Compounds
original_question: How important is the antiferromagnetic Heisenberg coupling JAF between localized t2g spins for stabilizing A-type, CE-type, and charge-stacked states in manganites, and are there alternative microscopic mechanisms that can stabilize those phases if JAF is not the whole explanation?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a two-orbital double-exchange model for manganites of the form
H = -∑⟨ij⟩,αβ,σ t^{αβ}_{ij} c†_{iασ} c_{jβσ} - J_H ∑_i s_i · S_i + J_AF ∑_⟨ij⟩ S_i · S_j + H_{JT}+ H_{Coul},
where c_{iασ} annihilates an e_g electron of orbital α∈{d_{x²-y²}, d_{3z²-r²}} and spin σ at site i on a cubic lattice, S_i is a localized t_{2g} spin (treated classically, |S_i|=3/2), s_i is the e_g spin density at i, J_H ≫ |t| is the Hund coupling, J_AF > 0 is the nearest-neighbour antiferromagnetic Heisenberg coupling between localized t_{2g} spins, H_{JT} is the cooperative Jahn–Teller coupling of e_g electrons to Q_2, Q_3 distortions of the MnO_6 octahedra, and H_{Coul} contains on-site and nearest-neighbour Coulomb repulsions.

The "A-type" antiferromagnetic state (ferromagnetic xy planes stacked antiferromagnetically along z), the "CE-type" state at hole density x=1/2 (zigzag ferromagnetic chains with checkerboard charge order, antiferromagnetically stacked), and "charge-stacked" states (planes of identical charge density alternating along z) are well-known ordered phases observed in manganites such as La_{1-x}Ca_xMnO_3 and related compounds.

Address the following:

(a) Within the above model, is a nonzero antiferromagnetic Heisenberg coupling J_AF between localized t_{2g} spins necessary to stabilize the A-type, CE-type, and charge-stacked phases as ground states in the appropriate doping ranges? Determine, as quantitatively as possible, the minimal J_AF/t required (or prove that J_AF can be set to zero) for each of these three phases to be the ground state in the relevant region of the phase diagram.

(b) Identify alternative microscopic mechanisms — for example, cooperative Jahn–Teller distortions, nearest-neighbour Coulomb repulsion V, orbital ordering, or electron–phonon couplings beyond the breathing mode — that, in the limit J_AF → 0, can by themselves stabilize each of the A-type, CE-type, and charge-stacked phases. For each phase, decide whether such an alternative mechanism exists and, if so, exhibit it.
category_tag: strongly correlated electron models for manganites
status_search_result: Subsequent work has shown that Jahn–Teller distortions and nearest-neighbour Coulomb repulsion can play a major role in stabilizing CE-type charge ordering at half doping, and Monte Carlo studies of one- and two-orbital models with cooperative phonons explore the interplay with J_AF. However, no consensus quantitative answer specifying the minimal J_AF needed for A-, CE- and charge-stacked phases, nor a complete classification of alternative mechanisms, appears to have been established; the question remains an open modeling problem.

paper_title: Open Questions in CMR Manganites, Relevance of Clustered States, and Analogies with other Compounds
original_question: For explaining colossal magnetoresistance, is there a fundamental physical distinction between theories where the competing phases originate mainly from Jahn-Teller electron-phonon interactions and theories where they originate mainly from Coulomb interactions, and can realistic many-body models produce a large magnetoresistance effect without relying only on phenomenological descriptions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider strongly correlated electron systems modeling doped manganites of the form R_{1-x}A_x MnO_3 (with R a rare earth and A an alkaline earth), in which the competition between a ferromagnetic metallic phase and an insulating (charge/orbital/antiferromagnetically ordered) phase is believed to underlie the colossal magnetoresistance (CMR) phenomenon — namely a dramatic decrease of electrical resistivity upon application of an external magnetic field near the Curie temperature.

Two broad classes of microscopic many-body Hamiltonians are commonly proposed to generate such competing phases:

(A) Jahn-Teller (JT) electron-phonon models. The Hamiltonian has the schematic form
   H_JT = -Σ_{ij,αβ,σ} t^{αβ}_{ij} c^†_{iασ} c_{jβσ} - J_H Σ_i s_i·S_i + λ Σ_{i,αβ} Q_i^{αβ} c^†_{iα} c_{iβ} + (1/2) Σ_i (P_i^2 + K Q_i^2) + J_{AF} Σ_{⟨ij⟩} S_i·S_j,
 where α,β ∈ {d_{x^2-y^2}, d_{3z^2-r^2}} are e_g orbitals on a Mn lattice, S_i are localized t_{2g} core spins, J_H is the Hund coupling, and Q_i are JT phonon modes coupling to the orbital pseudospin with coupling λ.

(B) Coulomb-interaction-based models. The Hamiltonian has the schematic form
   H_C = -Σ_{ij,αβ,σ} t^{αβ}_{ij} c^†_{iασ} c_{jβσ} - J_H Σ_i s_i·S_i + U Σ_{iα} n_{iα↑} n_{iα↓} + U' Σ_{i,α<β} n_{iα} n_{iβ} + J Σ_{i,α<β} S_{iα}·S_{iβ} + V Σ_{⟨ij⟩} n_i n_j + J_{AF} Σ_{⟨ij⟩} S_i·S_j,
 with on-site and inter-orbital Coulomb repulsions U, U', Hund exchange J, and nearest-neighbour repulsion V, but with no explicit electron-phonon coupling.

Questions:
(1) In the regime of parameters relevant to manganites and near a first-order transition between a ferromagnetic metallic and an insulating phase, is there a fundamental, qualitative, experimentally distinguishable distinction between the low-energy physics produced by Hamiltonians of type (A) and those of type (B)? Equivalently, do these two families belong to the same universality class of phase competition at the relevant scales, or do they yield essentially different predictions for the structure of the inhomogeneous (clustered) states and for transport in a magnetic field?

(2) Can a sharp, large colossal magnetoresistance — i.e. an order-of-magnitude or greater drop in resistivity in response to a magnetic field of order a few Tesla near the magnetic ordering temperature — be derived directly from one of these realistic many-body Hamiltonians (A) or (B), without recourse to purely phenomenological random-resistor / percolation / coexistence postulates, but instead as an emergent consequence of the model's intrinsic dynamics?
status_search_result: The two questions remain open in the condensed matter community. Reviews and subsequent literature on CMR manganites continue to debate whether JT phonon-based and Coulomb-based scenarios are fundamentally distinct or operationally equivalent, and obtaining a large CMR effect directly from realistic microscopic many-body Hamiltonians (rather than from phenomenological percolative/coexistence models) is still considered an unresolved challenge.

paper_title: Open Questions in CMR Manganites, Relevance of Clustered States, and Analogies with other Compounds
original_question: Do some manganites exhibit two genuinely different mechanisms for colossal magnetoresistance, one associated with the standard transition into a ferromagnetic metal near higher temperature and another associated with a low-temperature first-order field-induced metal-insulator transition, and can theory explain both within a unified phase-competition framework?
self_contained_problem:
Consider hole-doped manganite perovskites of the form R_{1-x}A_x MnO_3 (with R a rare-earth and A an alkaline-earth cation), modeled by competing ferromagnetic metallic (FM) and charge/orbital-ordered insulating (CO/OO) phases, with degrees of freedom including itinerant e_g electrons coupled via double-exchange to localized t_{2g} spins, Jahn–Teller phonons, and superexchange antiferromagnetic interactions. Experimentally, some such compounds display two distinct colossal magnetoresistance (CMR) regimes as functions of temperature T and applied magnetic field H:

(a) a high-temperature CMR near the paramagnetic-to-ferromagnetic-metal transition at T = T_C, where resistivity drops continuously with field; and

(b) a low-temperature CMR associated with a first-order, field-induced metal–insulator transition out of a charge/orbital-ordered (or otherwise insulating) state, exhibiting hysteresis as a function of H.

Question: Do these two CMR regimes correspond to genuinely distinct physical mechanisms, and can a single theoretical framework based on phase competition and intrinsic inhomogeneity (electronic phase separation between FM-metallic and insulating phases on nanometer-to-mesoscopic scales, with percolation-type transport) account for both (a) and (b) simultaneously, including the qualitative dependence of the two CMR signatures on temperature, magnetic field, bandwidth, and quenched disorder?
status_search_result: Subsequent theoretical and experimental work supports a phase-competition / electronic phase-separation picture in which both the high-T CMR near T_C and the low-T field-induced first-order metal-insulator transition in CO/OO manganites arise from competition between FM-metallic and insulating phases, with quenched disorder enabling nanoscale coexistence and percolative transport. A fully unified, quantitative microscopic theory covering both regimes across all relevant manganite families is not established, so the question is best characterized as partially resolved.

paper_title: Open Questions in CMR Manganites, Relevance of Clustered States, and Analogies with other Compounds
original_question: Should superconductivity be excluded in manganites, or can a doped or pressure-tuned manganite near a metal-insulator or quantum-critical regime support superconductivity; and if superconductivity still never appears, does that imply the spin-1/2 character of cuprates is essential in a way that higher-spin manganites are not?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the family of perovskite manganite compounds of the form R₁₋ₓAₓMnO₃, where R is a trivalent rare-earth ion (e.g., La, Pr, Nd, Sm) and A is a divalent alkaline-earth ion (e.g., Ca, Sr, Ba). These materials exhibit a rich phase diagram including ferromagnetic metallic, antiferromagnetic insulating, charge-ordered, and orbital-ordered phases, and colossal magnetoresistance near magnetic-ordering transitions. The Mn ions carry spins S ≥ 1 (e.g., S = 3/2 for Mn⁴⁺ and S = 2 for Mn³⁺), in contrast with the spin-1/2 Cu²⁺ ions of the cuprate superconductors.

Address the following questions:

(a) Does there exist a choice of cations R, A and a hole-doping fraction x (preferably in a large-bandwidth manganite family) such that the resulting compound remains metallic and paramagnetic down to arbitrarily low temperatures, without ordering into any magnetic, charge-ordered, or orbital-ordered phase?

(b) Alternatively, can such a metallic, non-ordering low-temperature state be reached in some manganite by tuning a non-thermal control parameter (for example, hydrostatic pressure or chemical substitution) toward a metal–insulator transition or a magnetic quantum critical point?

(c) In any such regime, can a bulk superconducting phase emerge in a manganite at low temperatures, or must superconductivity be rigorously excluded from the manganite phase diagram on general grounds?

(d) If the conclusion of (c) is that no manganite supports bulk superconductivity, determine whether this absence necessarily implies that the spin-1/2 nature of the magnetic ions in the cuprates plays an essential role in the mechanism of high-temperature superconductivity that cannot be replicated by higher-spin (S > 1/2) transition-metal oxides.
category_tag: Strongly correlated electron systems / manganite superconductivity
status_search_result: No established bulk superconducting manganite has been reported. Some studies report fragmentary or filamentary signatures of superconductivity in frustrated manganites such as La₁₋ySmyMnO₃₊δ at low temperatures, but these are not confirmed as bulk superconductivity. Whether a paramagnetic-metallic manganite near a quantum-critical or metal–insulator regime can host superconductivity, and the implied role of spin-1/2 character in cuprates, remain open.

paper_title: Open Questions in CMR Manganites, Relevance of Clustered States, and Analogies with other Compounds
original_question: Can cuprates exhibit colossal or other percolative competition-driven effects analogous to manganites because small superconducting, antiferromagnetic, or charge-ordered regions coexist and can be aligned by weak perturbations, and what is the actual order of the antiferromagnet–superconductor transition in clean cuprates: first-order, bicritical, tricritical, or tetracritical?
self_contained_problem:
Consider hole-doped cuprate compounds, modeled as a strongly correlated electron system on a two-dimensional CuO2 lattice in which several types of order may coexist locally: d-wave superconductivity (SC), antiferromagnetism (AF), and charge order (e.g. stripes or checkerboards). Suppose that, as in a phase-separated landscape, the system in some doping range supports nanoscale clusters of distinct competing orders that can be reoriented or grown by weak external perturbations (small magnetic, electric, or strain fields).

(a) Determine whether such a clean cuprate system can exhibit "colossal" responses analogous to the colossal magnetoresistance observed in manganites, i.e. whether weak perturbations can align or percolate the competing nanoscale clusters so as to produce dramatic (orders-of-magnitude) changes in transport, magnetic, or superconducting properties. Provide either (i) a microscopic mechanism and quantitative estimate showing under what conditions such percolative colossal effects can occur in cuprates, or (ii) an argument ruling them out.

(b) For an idealized clean cuprate (without quenched disorder) at zero temperature, determine the nature of the quantum phase transition between the antiferromagnetic insulating phase and the d-wave superconducting phase as a function of hole doping. Specifically, decide which of the following scenarios is realized in the global phase diagram (in the temperature–doping plane):
   1. a single direct first-order transition,
   2. a bicritical point at finite temperature where two second-order lines merge tangentially into a first-order line,
   3. a tricritical point at which a line of second-order transitions becomes first-order, or
   4. a tetracritical point at which an intermediate coexistence (AF + SC) phase is bounded by two distinct second-order lines.
category_tag: strongly correlated electrons and competing orders in cuprates
status_search_result: The questions remain open. The order of the AF–SC transition in clean cuprates is still debated: SO(5) and related theoretical analyses predict a bicritical point for repulsive biquadratic AF–SC couplings and a tetracritical (biconical) point for attractive ones, with no consensus from experiment in clean systems. Recent work (e.g. 2023 Nature Communications on disorder-removed lightly-doped cuprates) and 2022 analyses of bi/tetracritical phase diagrams continue to investigate the issue without a definitive resolution. Whether percolative "colossal" effects analogous to manganites occur in cuprates is also still an open phenomenological question.

paper_title: Open Questions in CMR Manganites, Relevance of Clustered States, and Analogies with other Compounds
original_question: Do diluted magnetic semiconductors such as Ga1−xMnxAs have a manganite-like clustered regime above the Curie temperature associated with a temperature scale T*, and can the resulting insulating behavior and other similarities to manganites be established quantitatively enough to show that both classes of materials share the same basic phenomenology?
self_contained_problem:
Consider diluted magnetic semiconductors of the form Ga$_{1-x}$Mn$_x$As (and related III–V or II–VI Mn-doped semiconductors) in which carrier-mediated (Zener-type) ferromagnetism appears below a Curie temperature $T_C$. By analogy with colossal-magnetoresistance manganites, one may postulate the existence of a higher characteristic temperature $T^* > T_C$ below which short-range ferromagnetic correlations produce nanoscale magnetic/charge clusters embedded in a paramagnetic, electronically inhomogeneous matrix, leading to insulating-like transport, a resistivity peak near $T_C$, large negative magnetoresistance, and other transport and thermodynamic signatures characteristic of manganites.

The problem is to determine whether such a clustered regime exists quantitatively in diluted magnetic semiconductors, namely:

1. Establish, theoretically and/or experimentally, the existence of a temperature scale $T^*(x)$ in Ga$_{1-x}$Mn$_x$As above $T_C(x)$ that marks the onset of nanoscale ferromagnetic cluster formation.
2. Show that the insulating (or bad-metallic) behavior observed in the regime $T_C < T < T^*$, together with the resistivity peak near $T_C$ and the associated colossal magnetoresistance, can be derived from a model of percolating/competing ferromagnetic clusters analogous to those used for manganites.
3. Provide quantitative criteria (e.g. cluster size distributions, scaling of $T^*/T_C$ with carrier density and Mn concentration, transport exponents, optical-conductivity spectral weight transfer) that demonstrate that diluted magnetic semiconductors and manganites share the same underlying phase-separation phenomenology.

status_search_result: Literature on Ga$_{1-x}$Mn$_x$As reports a resistivity peak near $T_C$, crossover critical behavior, and qualitative similarities with manganite transport, and several works explicitly stress analogies between DMS and manganites. However, no source unambiguously establishes a quantitative manganite-like clustered regime with a well-defined $T^*$ scale and the full phase-separation phenomenology in DMS; the question remains a topic of ongoing investigation rather than a definitively settled result.

paper_title: Open Questions in CMR Manganites, Relevance of Clustered States, and Analogies with other Compounds
original_question: Do the similarities between manganites and other correlated materials such as organic superconductors and heavy-fermion compounds—especially phase competition, first-order transitions or coexistence, and a higher crossover scale T*—reflect a shared underlying phenomenology rather than accidental analogy?
self_contained_problem:
Consider three families of strongly correlated electronic materials: (i) colossal-magnetoresistance manganites of the form R_{1-x}A_x MnO_3 (with R a rare earth and A a divalent alkaline earth), (ii) quasi–two-dimensional organic superconductors of the (BEDT-TTF) and (TMTSF) families, and (iii) heavy-fermion intermetallic compounds based on Ce, U or Yb. Across these families one observes the following common low-temperature phenomenology near a control parameter g (chemical doping, pressure, or magnetic field) that tunes between two competing electronic phases A and B (for example ferromagnetic-metallic versus charge/orbital-ordered insulating in manganites, antiferromagnetic-insulating versus superconducting in organics, antiferromagnetic versus heavy Fermi-liquid or superconducting in heavy fermions):

1. A first-order transition line, or an extended regime of mesoscopic phase coexistence between A and B, in the (g, T) phase diagram at low temperature.
2. A crossover temperature T*(g) substantially larger than the ordering temperatures of either pure phase, below which non-trivial short-range correlations, pseudogap features, or precursor inhomogeneities appear.
3. Strong sensitivity of bulk response functions (resistivity, susceptibility, specific heat) to quenched disorder near the boundary between A and B.

Question. Formulate and decide the following: does there exist a single universal effective theory — for instance a Ginzburg–Landau–Wilson functional with two competing order parameters φ_A, φ_B coupled to elastic strain and to quenched random-field disorder — whose phase diagram and finite-temperature crossovers simultaneously reproduce features (1)–(3) in all three families, with material-dependent parameters but family-independent universal exponents and scaling functions governing the coexistence region and the crossover scale T*? Equivalently, are the observed similarities (first-order transitions / phase coexistence and the higher crossover scale T*) manifestations of one shared underlying phenomenology of competing orders with disorder, or do they arise from microscopically distinct mechanisms that only superficially mimic each other?
status_search_result: The question of whether competing-phase phenomenology with first-order transitions, mesoscopic coexistence, and a higher crossover scale T* in manganites, organic superconductors, and heavy-fermion compounds reflects a single universal framework remains a topic of active debate. While substantial theoretical work (e.g., Dagotto and collaborators on competing-phase scenarios with quenched disorder, and the quantum-critical-point / competing-order paradigm for heavy fermions and organics) supports broad analogies, no rigorous universal effective theory has been established and accepted across all three families. The status is best described as open.

paper_title: Some results and open problems in research on low dimensional organic conductors
original_question: Which effective theoretical description should be used for the electron gas in Bechgaard salts: a Luttinger-liquid description, a Fermi-liquid description, or a regime-dependent combination of the two? The paper notes that standard statistical mechanics predicts failure of the Fermi-liquid picture in strictly one-dimensional systems and favors the Luttinger-liquid model, while Bechgaard salts are physically quasi one-dimensional rather than exactly one-dimensional. The open problem is therefore to determine, with clear physical criteria, which model correctly describes these materials in which experimental situations.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Bechgaard salts, a family of quasi-one-dimensional organic charge-transfer compounds of the form (TMTSF)$_2$X (with X an inorganic anion such as PF$_6$ or ClO$_4$). These materials consist of stacks of TMTSF molecules forming highly anisotropic conducting chains with intra-chain transfer integral $t_\parallel$ much larger than the inter-chain transfer integrals $t_\perp, t_{\perp\perp}$, so the electronic motion is strongly one-dimensional but not strictly so.

Two competing low-energy effective descriptions exist for the interacting electron gas in such a system:

(a) The Tomonaga–Luttinger liquid (TLL), the generic non-Fermi-liquid fixed point of interacting fermions in one spatial dimension, characterized by spin-charge separation, the absence of a coherent quasiparticle pole in the single-particle Green's function, and power-law decay of correlation functions with non-universal exponents controlled by a Luttinger parameter $K_\rho$.

(b) The Landau Fermi liquid (FL), the standard description in dimension $d\ge 2$, characterized by long-lived quasiparticles near the Fermi surface with a finite quasiparticle residue $Z>0$ and the usual analytic structure of the Green's function.

Formulate clear, quantitative physical criteria (in terms of temperature $T$, frequency $\omega$, wavevector, applied pressure, magnetic field, and the microscopic parameters $t_\parallel$, $t_\perp$, $t_{\perp\perp}$, on-site/extended Coulomb couplings, and the Luttinger parameter $K_\rho$) that determine in which experimentally accessible regimes the electron gas of the Bechgaard salts is correctly described by:

  (i) a pure Tomonaga–Luttinger liquid,
  (ii) a Landau Fermi liquid (possibly anisotropic), or
  (iii) a crossover/coexistence regime between the two,

and identify the dimensional-crossover scale $T^*$ (and the associated single-particle deconfinement scale) above which interchain coherence is lost and TLL behavior dominates, versus below which a higher-dimensional Fermi-liquid description becomes appropriate. Provide the criteria in a form that can be tested against transport, optical conductivity, NMR, and angle-resolved photoemission measurements.
category_tag: Luttinger vs Fermi liquid in quasi-1D conductors
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made: optical and photoemission experiments support Tomonaga–Luttinger liquid behavior at high temperatures/energies in Bechgaard salts, and chain-DMFT and renormalization-group treatments capture a dimensional crossover at a scale T* (∼100 K for (TMTSF)$_2$PF$_6$, ≥200 K for (TMTSF)$_2$ClO$_4$) from a high-T Luttinger liquid to a low-T (anisotropic) Fermi liquid. However, a complete, quantitatively predictive theory unifying all experimental regimes (transport anomalies, pseudogap, role of interchain coupling and pressure) is still not fully settled, so the problem is best classified as partially solved.

paper_title: Some results and open problems in research on low dimensional organic conductors
original_question: For Bechgaard salts modeled from the one-dimensional Hubbard Hamiltonian, what is the dependence of the electrical conductivity on band filling? Here band filling means the ratio of the number of electrons to the number of lattice sites, and experimentally it can be changed by doping with electron donors or acceptors. The open problem is to carry out the conductivity calculation and determine how conductivity varies as the filling changes, especially in relation to the thermodynamic behavior near half filling.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the one-dimensional Hubbard Hamiltonian on a chain of L sites,
   H = -t \sum_{i,\sigma} (c_{i,\sigma}^\dagger c_{i+1,\sigma} + h.c.) + U \sum_i n_{i,\uparrow} n_{i,\downarrow},
with hopping amplitude t > 0, on-site repulsion U > 0, fermionic operators c_{i,\sigma}, c_{i,\sigma}^\dagger, and number operators n_{i,\sigma} = c_{i,\sigma}^\dagger c_{i,\sigma}. Define the band filling n = N_e / L, where N_e is the total number of electrons.

Using the Kubo formula, the (temperature- and frequency-dependent) electrical conductivity \sigma(\omega, T; n, U/t) is determined by current-current correlation functions of the current operator
   J = -i t e \sum_{i,\sigma} (c_{i,\sigma}^\dagger c_{i+1,\sigma} - c_{i+1,\sigma}^\dagger c_{i,\sigma}).

Determine analytically (or to the extent possible) the dependence of the conductivity \sigma(\omega, T; n, U/t)—including the Drude weight, the regular part, and the dc limit—on the band filling n for 0 < n < 2 at fixed U/t. In particular, describe the qualitative and quantitative behaviour of \sigma as n approaches the half-filled point n = 1, and relate the resulting filling dependence to the thermodynamic properties (e.g., charge compressibility and spin/charge gaps obtained from the Bethe-ansatz solution) of the model in the vicinity of half filling.
status_search_result: The optical/Drude conductivity of the 1D Hubbard model has been studied extensively via Bethe-ansatz, bosonization, and numerical (DMRG, Bethe-ansatz-based) methods. Results exist for the Drude weight as a function of filling and U/t, and for the optical conductivity at and away from half filling, including dimerized/extended variants relevant to Bechgaard salts. A complete closed-form expression of the full conductivity as a function of filling, frequency, and temperature is, however, not available, so the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: Some results and open problems in research on low dimensional organic conductors
context_brief: Q2D conductivity with lattice and pressure
original_question: How should one construct a theoretical conductivity model for quasi-two-dimensional organic conductors based on BEDT-TTF (ET) salts that includes as many real material parameters as possible, explicitly incorporates the crystal lattice, and can therefore be used to analyze how high external pressure affects conductivity? The paper frames this as a natural next step given the large body of conductivity measurements on Q2D salts and the expectation that doping changes the chemical potential and thereby influences transport.
self_contained_problem:
Consider quasi-two-dimensional (Q2D) organic charge-transfer salts based on the donor molecule BEDT-TTF (commonly denoted ET), whose crystal structure consists of weakly coupled conducting layers of ET molecules separated by anion layers. The single-particle electronic structure near the Fermi level is dominated by the highest occupied molecular orbitals of the ET dimers, giving rise to a quarter- or half-filled (depending on the salt) tight-binding band on an anisotropic two-dimensional lattice (typically of κ-, β-, θ- or α-type), with weak interlayer hopping t_⊥ ≪ t_∥. External hydrostatic pressure modifies the intermolecular distances and hence the transfer integrals t_ij and the on-site/intersite Coulomb couplings.

Construct a microscopic theoretical model for the electrical conductivity σ(T, P, μ) of such Q2D ET salts as a function of temperature T, hydrostatic pressure P, and chemical potential μ, satisfying the following requirements:

(i) The model must be defined on the actual three-dimensional crystal lattice of the salt (rather than on a featureless 2D continuum), with transfer integrals {t_ij(P)} and interaction parameters obtained from, or parametrized by, real material data.

(ii) It must incorporate as many physically relevant parameters as possible: the anisotropic intralayer hopping pattern, interlayer hopping, on-site and nearest-neighbor Coulomb interactions, electron–phonon coupling to the relevant lattice modes, and disorder.

(iii) It must give an explicit, pressure-dependent prescription t_ij = t_ij(P), so that σ(T, P, μ) can be computed and compared with measured pressure dependences of the conductivity.

(iv) It must allow the chemical potential μ to vary (modeling doping or band filling) and predict the resulting changes in transport coefficients.

Within this framework, derive a closed expression (or a controlled computational scheme) for the in-plane and out-of-plane conductivity tensor components, and analyze the qualitative and quantitative effect of increasing pressure on σ for representative κ-(ET)_2X salts.
status_search_result: The question is an open-ended modeling program rather than a precisely posed conjecture. While there is an extensive literature on tight-binding and Hubbard-type models for BEDT-TTF salts (including DFT-parametrized hoppings and pressure-induced changes), no single, universally accepted lattice-based microscopic conductivity theory incorporating all listed material parameters and reproducing the pressure dependence of σ in Q2D ET salts has been established. The problem therefore appears to remain open in its full form.

paper_title: Some results and open problems in research on low dimensional organic conductors
original_question: What is the origin of high-temperature superconductivity? In the context of this review, the question is whether insights from low-dimensional organic conductors, fulleride-based conductors, and high-Tc materials can be integrated into a definitive explanation of the mechanism responsible for high-temperature superconductivity.
self_contained_problem: Identify the microscopic pairing mechanism responsible for high-temperature superconductivity. Specifically, formulate a unified theoretical framework — for instance, a many-body Hamiltonian on a lattice together with an effective pairing interaction — that simultaneously accounts for the superconducting phases observed in (i) quasi-low-dimensional organic conductors (such as Bechgaard and Fabre salts of the (TMTSF)_2X and (TMTTF)_2X families and BEDT-TTF based κ-phase salts), (ii) alkali-doped fulleride conductors A_3C_60, and (iii) cuprate and related high-Tc superconductors. The framework should predict the symmetry of the superconducting order parameter, the dependence of the critical temperature T_c on control parameters (pressure, doping, dimensionality, bandwidth), and the proximity of the superconducting phase to competing instabilities (antiferromagnetic, charge-density-wave, spin-density-wave, or Mott-insulating phases). Determine whether a single non-phononic (e.g. electronic, magnetic) pairing mechanism, a conventional electron–phonon mechanism, or a combination thereof can quantitatively reproduce the observed phenomenology across all three classes of materials.
status_search_result: The mechanism of high-temperature superconductivity remains a celebrated open problem in condensed matter and mathematical physics. Despite decades of intensive theoretical and experimental work, no consensus microscopic theory has been established that uniformly explains pairing in cuprates, organic conductors, and fullerides.

paper_title: Selected results and open problems in a semiclassical theory of dense matter
original_question: The SK theory currently yields, for a celestial object, only a physically allowed interval for the angular speed of rotation rather than a single predicted value. What additional theoretical structure, constraints, or calculational procedure would allow the theory to determine a unique angular speed of rotation for a given celestial object, instead of only an admissible interval?
self_contained_problem:
Within the semiclassical (SK) theory of dense matter, a self-gravitating celestial body in steady rotation is modelled as a fluid configuration whose mass density, pressure, and gravitational potential satisfy the SK equations of state together with the equilibrium (Euler/Poisson) equations in a frame rotating uniformly with angular speed ω. For a body of given total mass and chemical composition, requiring the existence of a regular, bounded, axisymmetric equilibrium with a free boundary determines not a unique value of ω, but a nonempty interval [ω_min, ω_max] of admissible angular speeds (as confirmed numerically when applied to Earth and several planets, where the observed rotation rate falls inside the predicted interval).

Problem. Formulate additional theoretical structure—extra physical principles, variational or stability criteria, boundary or matching conditions, or a constructive calculational procedure—within the SK framework that singles out exactly one element ω* ∈ [ω_min, ω_max] as the predicted angular speed of rotation of the body, and prove that the resulting prescription:
(i) yields a unique ω* for every celestial body to which the SK theory applies;
(ii) reduces the admissible interval to this single value in a manner consistent with all SK equilibrium equations; and
(iii) reproduces, in the cases where comparison is possible (such as Earth and the planets previously treated), the empirically observed rotation rates.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an explicitly open issue in the semiclassical (SK) theory of dense matter. A web search did not surface any subsequent work claiming to single out a unique angular speed of rotation from the SK-admissible interval; the question appears to remain open.

paper_title: Selected results and open problems in a semiclassical theory of dense matter
original_question: The current SK theory explains phase-transition pressures using only a simplified electrostatic interaction and neglects additional contributions to the intermolecular or interparticle potential energy. How should the theory be refined so that more components of the interparticle potential energy are included, and does incorporating those missing potential terms materially reduce the discrepancy between predicted and measured high-pressure phase-transition pressures?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a semiclassical model (the Siringo–Kocik / SK-type framework) for predicting structural phase-transition pressures in dense molecular or atomic matter, in which each particle is treated as a polarizable charge distribution and the only interaction energy retained is a simplified electrostatic (Coulomb / multipole-screened) potential V_es(r) between particles. Within this model, the predicted high-pressure phase-transition pressures P_th differ systematically from experimentally measured values P_exp.

Let the full pair interparticle potential admit a decomposition

    V_total(r) = V_es(r) + V_exch(r) + V_disp(r) + V_ind(r) + V_rep(r) + ...,

where V_exch is the exchange (Pauli) contribution, V_disp the dispersion (van der Waals) contribution, V_ind the induction (polarization) contribution, and V_rep the short-range repulsive core, each treated at an appropriate semiclassical level.

Problem. 
(a) Formulate an extension of the semiclassical theory in which the equation of state and the criterion determining structural phase-transition pressures are derived from V_total rather than from V_es alone. Specify how each non-electrostatic component should be modeled (functional form, parameters, and how it enters the free energy / stability criterion) so that the resulting theory remains semiclassical and tractable.
(b) Determine quantitatively whether the inclusion of the non-electrostatic components V_exch, V_disp, V_ind, V_rep materially reduces the discrepancy |P_th − P_exp| for a representative set of high-pressure phase transitions; in particular, identify which of these components dominate the correction and obtain bounds or estimates for the improved theoretical pressures.
status_search_result: No specific follow-up work was located that systematically refines the SK semiclassical theory by incorporating exchange, dispersion, induction, and short-range repulsive contributions and demonstrates a quantitative reduction of the discrepancy with measured high-pressure phase-transition pressures. The problem appears to remain an open research direction.

paper_title: Selected results and open problems in a semiclassical theory of dense matter
original_question: A preliminary comparison is said to connect parameters of the SK theory with those of Landau theory. Can the SK theory be reformulated in terms of modern theories of quantum phase transitions, so that its phase structure, control parameters, and predicted transitions are expressed using the language and methods of contemporary quantum critical phenomena rather than the original semiclassical presentation?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the semiclassical (SK) theory of dense matter, formulated as an expansion of the many-body free energy functional F[ρ] in powers of ℏ around the Thomas–Fermi limit, with order parameters describing density inhomogeneities, pairing, or magnetic ordering in a strongly interacting fermion system at high density. Suppose that the parameters of this SK theory (e.g. gradient coefficients, effective coupling constants, and chemical-potential-dependent susceptibilities) have already been put into correspondence with those of a Landau-type free-energy expansion F_L[φ] = a(g) φ² + b φ⁴ + c (∇φ)² + … in an order parameter φ with a control parameter g.

Problem: Reformulate the SK theory within the framework of modern theories of quantum phase transitions. Concretely, identify
(i) a quantum order parameter field φ(x, τ) on d+1-dimensional space–time (with imaginary time τ ∈ [0, β]),
(ii) an effective quantum action S[φ] of Hertz–Millis type, including its dynamical exponent z, correlation-length exponent ν, and tuning parameter (e.g. density, pressure, or coupling) that drives the system through a quantum critical point at zero temperature,
(iii) the resulting phase diagram in the (T, g)-plane, including quantum critical, quantum disordered, and thermally disordered regimes,
such that the predictions of the SK theory for the phase structure of dense matter (locations of transitions, scaling of order parameters, and low-temperature thermodynamic anomalies) are reproduced by the universal scaling behavior of this quantum critical action.

State explicitly the dictionary between SK parameters and (a, b, c, g, z, ν), and determine the universality class of the implied quantum phase transition(s).

status_search_result: No specific published reformulation of the SK semiclassical theory of dense matter in the language of modern quantum phase transitions (Hertz–Millis type actions, dynamical exponents, quantum critical scaling) could be verified. The question appears to remain a programmatic open direction rather than a settled result.

paper_title: Selected results and open problems in a semiclassical theory of dense matter
original_question: Under static compression, metallic hydrogen had been predicted by the SK theory to appear near 300 GPa, but experiments up to 342 GPa had not shown metallization at the time of this paper, and disorder was suggested as one possible explanation for the mismatch. At what pressure and under what physical conditions, if any, does hydrogen actually undergo metallization under high pressure, and why had the experimentally accessible static-compression regime up to 342 GPa not yet exhibited the metallization expected from theory?
self_contained_problem: Consider solid molecular hydrogen subjected to static high pressure at low temperature. Semiclassical electronic-structure theory predicts a transition to a metallic state at a pressure near 300 GPa, yet diamond-anvil-cell experiments performed at static pressures up to 342 GPa have not observed metallization. Determine the actual pressure (and accompanying thermodynamic conditions—temperature, crystalline vs. fluid phase, ordered vs. disordered configuration) at which hydrogen undergoes a transition to a metallic state under static compression, and provide a physical explanation for why metallization has not been observed in the experimentally accessible static-compression regime up to 342 GPa. In particular, assess whether structural disorder, molecular dissociation barriers, or other mechanisms account for the discrepancy between the theoretical prediction and experiment.
status_search_result: Dynamic (shock) compression experiments have demonstrated metallization of fluid hydrogen, and some diamond-anvil-cell studies have reported signatures of metallic behavior at very high static pressures (around 400–500 GPa), but a fully reproduced, room-temperature solid metallic hydrogen phase under static compression remains contested. Recent reviews (2024) describe ongoing challenges, with theory now placing solid-phase metallization above ~500 GPa, beyond the 342 GPa range cited as not yet showing metallization. The question is thus partially resolved: metallization is observed in dynamic/fluid regimes, while solid static metallization at room temperature is still an active experimental problem.

paper_title: Spin-density-functional theory: some open problems and application to inhomogeneous Heisenberg models
original_question: What is the full physical and formal relationship between spin-density-functional theory and current-density-functional theory for magnetic systems, given that spin currents of the form spin current equals the curl of the spin magnetization connect the spin degrees of freedom described by SDFT with the current variables used in CDFT, but the relationship between the two formalisms is described as only partly understood?
self_contained_problem:
Consider two density-functional formulations for nonrelativistic interacting electron systems in the presence of magnetic fields:

(a) Spin-density-functional theory (SDFT). The basic variables are the particle density n(r) and the spin magnetization density m(r). The Hohenberg–Kohn-type theorem asserts that the ground-state energy is a universal functional E_SDFT[n, m] coupled to an external scalar potential v(r) and external magnetic field B(r) that couples only through the Zeeman term −∫ m·B dr.

(b) Current-density-functional theory (CDFT) (Vignale–Rasolt). The basic variables are the particle density n(r) and the paramagnetic current density j_p(r). The universal functional E_CDFT[n, j_p] is coupled to an external scalar potential and to a vector potential A(r) entering through both the minimal-coupling kinetic term and the diamagnetic term.

For a fully magnetic system (with both Zeeman coupling to spin and orbital coupling to A), define the total spin current density by
   j_s(r) = ∇ × m(r),
so that the magnetization contributes a divergence-free current that is simultaneously a manifestation of the spin degrees of freedom (and hence should be encoded in SDFT) and a genuine current density (and hence should be encoded in CDFT).

Problem. Establish the complete physical and formal relationship between SDFT and CDFT in the presence of both spin and orbital magnetic couplings. In particular:

1. Give a precise mathematical map (or pair of maps) connecting the universal functionals E_SDFT[n, m] and E_CDFT[n, j_p], and identify the class of external (v, A, B) configurations for which such a map is exact, approximate, or fails.

2. Characterize the role played by the identity j_s = ∇ × m in linking the two formalisms, including how the divergence-free part of the current carried by the spin magnetization is to be partitioned between j_p and m in a consistent variational principle.

3. Determine whether the combined spin–current density-functional theory taking (n, m, j_p, j_s) as basic variables yields functionals from which both E_SDFT and E_CDFT can be recovered by suitable constrained-search projection, and prove or disprove a corresponding Hohenberg–Kohn-type uniqueness theorem.
category_tag: density functional theory for magnetic systems
status_search_result: Partial progress exists: spin-current density-functional theory (SCDFT) has been developed (e.g., gauge-invariant formulation, exact-exchange SCDFT, adiabatic-connection SCDFT, and applications to quantum spin-Hall phases), unifying spin and current variables and providing concrete functional connections. However, a complete and rigorous physical/formal mapping between SDFT and CDFT, including a full Hohenberg–Kohn-type uniqueness result for arbitrary magnetic systems, does not appear to be fully settled in the literature, so the problem is best characterized as partially solved.

original_question: What is the best theoretically consistent and computationally practical way to treat noncollinear spin configurations in spin-density-functional theory beyond the local-spin-density approximation, given that standard noncollinear SDFT implementations assume the exchange-correlation magnetic field is parallel to the spin magnetization, while generalized-gradient-type functionals can make that field nonparallel and alternatives such as staggered-density formulations require new functionals and more complicated Kohn-Sham equations?
status_search_result: Considerable progress has been made since the problem was posed. Source-free xc magnetic field constructions (Sharma et al., 2018), the "signed canonical" GGA formulation with screening of unstable terms (Pittalis et al. and later Bulik–Scalmani–Frisch developments), orbital-dependent / EXX noncollinear functionals (2018), and recent reformulations (Phys. Rev. Research 5, 013036, 2023) provide consistent noncollinear GGA schemes with nonvanishing local torque, proper collinear limit, and improved numerical stability. However, no single formulation is universally accepted as optimal: each existing scheme trades off rotational invariance, treatment of longitudinal vs. transverse gradients, torque properties, and stability differently. The question of the "best" theoretically consistent and practical scheme therefore remains partially solved rather than settled.

paper_title: Spin-density-functional theory: some open problems and application to inhomogeneous Heisenberg models
context_brief: Exact treatment of inhomogeneous Heisenberg models
original_question: Can analytical or comparably scalable exact methods be developed for Heisenberg models outside the homogeneous spin-one-half linear-chain case, especially for higher spin, higher-dimensional lattices, or inhomogeneous situations such as a substitutional spin with value different from the background spin, where only small-system numerical exact solutions are known?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Lambda$ be a finite or countably infinite lattice (e.g., a $d$-dimensional hypercubic lattice with $d \ge 1$). For each site $i \in \Lambda$, let $S_i \in \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ be a fixed spin quantum number, and let $\mathbf{\hat S}_i = (\hat S_i^x, \hat S_i^y, \hat S_i^z)$ denote the corresponding spin-$S_i$ operators acting on the local Hilbert space $\mathbb{C}^{2S_i+1}$, with the standard $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ commutation relations $[\hat S_i^a, \hat S_j^b] = i\,\delta_{ij}\,\epsilon^{abc}\hat S_i^c$. Given a (possibly site-dependent) real coupling $J_{ij}$ for each pair $i,j \in \Lambda$, define the inhomogeneous Heisenberg Hamiltonian
$$
\hat H \;=\; \sum_{i<j} J_{ij}\,\mathbf{\hat S}_i \cdot \mathbf{\hat S}_j
$$
acting on the tensor-product Hilbert space $\bigotimes_{i\in\Lambda} \mathbb{C}^{2S_i+1}$.

It is known that when $\Lambda$ is a one-dimensional chain, $S_i = \tfrac12$ for all $i$, and $J_{ij}=J\,\delta_{|i-j|,1}$ (homogeneous nearest-neighbour spin-$\tfrac12$ chain), the model admits an exact analytical solution via the Bethe ansatz.

Develop an exact analytical solution method, or an exact algorithm whose computational cost scales subexponentially in $|\Lambda|$, for $\hat H$ in at least one of the following regimes that lies strictly outside the solved homogeneous spin-$\tfrac12$ linear-chain case:

(i) homogeneous nearest-neighbour Heisenberg chains with $S_i = S$ for all $i$ and a fixed $S > \tfrac12$;

(ii) homogeneous nearest-neighbour Heisenberg models on a lattice $\Lambda$ of dimension $d \ge 2$;

(iii) inhomogeneous Heisenberg chains with a single substitutional impurity, i.e.\ $S_i = S$ for all $i \neq i_0$ and $S_{i_0} = S' \neq S$, with otherwise homogeneous nearest-neighbour couplings.

Either produce such a method (with a proof of correctness and a complexity or closed-form analysis), or prove an obstruction showing that no such exact analytical or scalable exact method can exist within a precisely specified framework.
status_search_result: No exact analytical solution is known for general higher-spin Heisenberg chains, higher-dimensional Heisenberg models, or single-impurity inhomogeneous chains beyond the integrable spin-1/2 chain solved by Bethe ansatz. Standard references on the Bethe ansatz and on quantum integrability (Baxter; Faddeev; Takhtajan) confirm that integrable cases are highly restricted; spin-S chains are integrable only via Takhtajan–Babujian-type higher-spin generalizations with specific (non-Heisenberg) Hamiltonians, and 2D Heisenberg models and impurity-perturbed chains remain unsolved analytically. No subsequent breakthrough has been reported, so the problem is regarded as open.

paper_title: Euclidean random matrices: solved and open problems
original_question: For low-density Euclidean random matrices in three dimensions, how can one construct a single approximation scheme that combines the strengths of the leading low-density expansion and the Gaussian variational approximation, so that it captures both the overall spectral shape and the peak produced by small clusters?
self_contained_problem:
Consider Euclidean random matrices in three dimensions defined as follows. Let $x_1,\dots,x_N$ be $N$ points distributed independently and uniformly at random in a cubic box of volume $V \subset \mathbb{R}^3$, with number density $\rho = N/V$, and consider the thermodynamic limit $N,V\to\infty$ with $\rho$ fixed. Given a real-valued function $f:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}$, form the $N\times N$ symmetric random matrix $M$ with entries $M_{ij}=f(x_i-x_j)$ (the diagonal may be set to a prescribed value such as $\sum_{k\neq i} f(x_i-x_k)$ depending on the convention), and let $g(\lambda)=\lim_{N\to\infty} N^{-1}\mathbb{E}\sum_{i=1}^N \delta(\lambda-\lambda_i)$ denote the limiting average spectral density.

In the low-density regime ($\rho\to 0$), two standard approximations exist:

(A) The leading term of the low-density expansion, in which $g(\lambda)$ is approximated by the average spectral density of small finite clusters (pairs, triples, …) of points; this scheme captures sharp peaks in the spectrum generated by tightly bound small clusters but fails to reproduce the overall shape and bulk of the spectrum.

(B) The Gaussian variational (or self-consistent Gaussian) approximation, which captures the overall spectral shape and the leading orders of magnitude of $g(\lambda)$ but is unable to reproduce the cluster-induced peaks.

Construct a single, mathematically well-defined approximation scheme for $g(\lambda)$ in the low-density limit that simultaneously
(i) reproduces, to leading order, the bulk spectral shape predicted by the Gaussian variational approximation, and
(ii) reproduces the small-cluster peaks predicted by the leading low-density expansion,
and prove (or argue in a controlled way) that it converges to $g(\lambda)$ in the appropriate low-density asymptotic sense.
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not return any work proposing a unified approximation scheme for low-density three-dimensional Euclidean random matrices that combines the leading low-density (cluster) expansion with the Gaussian variational approximation. No clear resolution of this construction problem could be identified from publicly available sources, so the status is recorded as unknown.

paper_title: Euclidean random matrices: solved and open problems
original_question: For the phonon problem in Euclidean random matrices, how can one compute the very-low-momentum spectral properties correctly by analyzing the two-loop contribution to the self-energy, beyond the one-loop result that gives the asymptotic linewidth scaling?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Euclidean random matrix model for scalar phonons defined as follows. Let $x_1,\dots,x_N$ be $N$ points drawn independently and uniformly from a box of volume $V=N/\rho$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ at density $\rho$, and let $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ be a smooth, rapidly decaying potential. Define the $N\times N$ random matrix
$$M_{ij}\;=\;\delta_{ij}\sum_{k=1}^{N} f(x_i-x_k)\;-\;f(x_i-x_j),$$
which is the Hessian of a pairwise potential and plays the role of a dynamical (mass) matrix for scalar vibrations. The phonon Green's function is
$$G(p,\omega)\;=\;\Big\langle\Big[\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i,j} e^{ip\cdot(x_i-x_j)}\big(\omega^2-M+i0^+\big)^{-1}_{ij}\Big]\Big\rangle,$$
and the self-energy $\Sigma(p,\omega)$ is defined by the Dyson decomposition
$$G(p,\omega)^{-1}\;=\;\omega^2-\varepsilon_0(p)-\Sigma(p,\omega),$$
where $\varepsilon_0(p)=\rho\,(\widehat f(0)-\widehat f(p))$ is the bare dispersion. Expand $\Sigma$ in powers of $1/\rho$ (the loop expansion): the one-loop term $\Sigma^{(1)}$ yields, in the regime of small external momentum $p\ll 1$, an asymptotic phonon linewidth (imaginary part of $\Sigma$ on shell) obeying a known power-law scaling in $p$.

Problem. Compute the two-loop contribution $\Sigma^{(2)}(p,\omega)$ to the self-energy of this model in the very-low-momentum regime $p\to 0$, and use it to determine the correct leading behavior of the phonon spectral function (in particular the linewidth and dispersion relation) at very low momentum, going beyond the one-loop asymptotic result.
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not return specific results on the explicit two-loop self-energy computation for very-low-momentum phonons in the Euclidean random matrix model. General references on Euclidean random matrices and phonon localization exist, but no authoritative source confirming a complete two-loop calculation and the resulting low-p spectral properties was located, so the current status is not determinable from available evidence.

paper_title: Euclidean random matrices: solved and open problems
original_question: For Euclidean random matrices built from correlated random points, how can one treat the general case in which many-point correlations are present, rather than only the two-point correlations handled by existing approaches?
self_contained_problem:
Let $V \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a bounded region and let $\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_N$ be random points in $V$ drawn from a joint probability distribution $P(\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_N)$ whose marginal correlation functions
$$\rho_k(\mathbf{y}_1, \dots, \mathbf{y}_k) \;=\; \frac{N!}{(N-k)!}\int P(\mathbf{y}_1,\dots,\mathbf{y}_k,\mathbf{x}_{k+1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_N)\, d\mathbf{x}_{k+1}\cdots d\mathbf{x}_N$$
are nontrivial for arbitrary $k \geq 2$ (i.e. the points are not independent and exhibit genuine many-body correlations that do not factorize into pair correlations).

Given a deterministic measurable function $f : \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{C}$), define the associated Euclidean random matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$ by
$$A_{ij} \;=\; f(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j), \qquad 1 \le i,j \le N.$$

Develop a general method to compute, in the thermodynamic limit $N \to \infty$ with $N/\mathrm{vol}(V)$ fixed, the spectral properties of $A$ — in particular the limiting eigenvalue density and the resolvent $\langle (z - A)^{-1}\rangle$ — that incorporates the full hierarchy of correlation functions $\{\rho_k\}_{k\ge 2}$ of the underlying point process, rather than only the two-point correlation $\rho_2$.
status_search_result: Recent works (2024–2026) on long-range correlated random matrices and interaction-correlated random matrices study spectral consequences of entry correlations, but a general framework for Euclidean random matrices built on point processes with arbitrary many-point correlations remains incomplete; existing analytical approaches still primarily treat the two-point (pair) correlation level.

paper_title: Euclidean random matrices: solved and open problems
original_question: How can one determine whether Euclidean random matrix models have a phase in which supersymmetry is spontaneously broken, and what are the physical effects of such breaking if that phase exists?
self_contained_problem:
Consider Euclidean random matrix models defined as follows. Let $\{x_1,\dots,x_N\}$ be $N$ points drawn independently and uniformly at random from a region of $\mathbb{R}^d$ of volume $V$, with fixed density $\rho=N/V$. Given a (deterministic) pair function $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$, form the $N\times N$ Euclidean random matrix $M$ with entries
$$M_{ij}=\delta_{ij}\sum_{k\ne i}f(x_i-x_k)-(1-\delta_{ij})f(x_i-x_j),$$
or more general variants whose entries are functions of the relative positions $x_i-x_j$. Such models possess a hidden supersymmetric structure that can be exposed by representing their resolvent and spectral observables as integrals over commuting and anticommuting (Grassmann) variables, yielding a graded action invariant under a supersymmetry that rotates bosonic and fermionic replicas into each other.

Problem. Determine whether, in the thermodynamic limit $N,V\to\infty$ with $\rho$ fixed, there exists a region of parameter space (i.e., a choice of density $\rho$, dimension $d$, and pair function $f$) in which this supersymmetry is spontaneously broken, in the sense that the supersymmetric Ward identities fail and the order parameter associated with the symmetry acquires a nonzero expectation value. If such a broken-supersymmetry phase exists, identify its physical consequences for the spectral density, the localization properties of eigenvectors, and the low-frequency behavior of dynamical correlation functions of the model.
status_search_result: A web search returns related work on spontaneous supersymmetry breaking in matrix models and on the supersymmetry method in random matrix theory (e.g., Kanamori–Sugino, Kuroki–Sugino, Zirnbauer), but no source was found that conclusively establishes or rules out the existence of a spontaneously broken-supersymmetry phase specifically for Euclidean random matrix ensembles defined by random points in $\mathbb{R}^d$. The question therefore appears to remain open / unresolved in the literature accessible via search.

original_question: For the antiferromagnetic spin-1/2 Heisenberg XXX spin chain, consider ground-state correlation functions of local spin operators on sequential lattice sites, including quantities such as the emptiness formation probability. These correlation functions are known to be expressible as polynomials in ln 2 and in values of the Riemann zeta function, or equivalently the alternating zeta series, at odd arguments with rational coefficients. Find an efficient and tractable description of the rational coefficients that appear in these polynomial expressions.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the antiferromagnetic spin-1/2 Heisenberg XXX chain on the infinite one-dimensional lattice, with Hamiltonian
H = J ∑_{k∈ℤ} ( S^x_k S^x_{k+1} + S^y_k S^y_{k+1} + S^z_k S^z_{k+1} ),  J > 0,
where S^α_k = (1/2)σ^α_k act on the k-th copy of ℂ^2. Let |GS⟩ denote the (unique, in the thermodynamic limit) ground state at zero temperature and zero external magnetic field, and let ⟨·⟩ denote the ground-state expectation value.

For any positive integer n, consider the ground-state correlation functions of products of local spin operators acting on n consecutive sites, e.g. ⟨S^{α_1}_1 S^{α_2}_2 ⋯ S^{α_n}_n⟩, and in particular the emptiness formation probability
P(n) = ⟨ ∏_{k=1}^n ( 1/2 + S^z_k ) ⟩,
which is the probability that the first n consecutive sites are all in the spin-up state.

It is known (and assumed throughout) that every such n-site ground-state correlation function can be written as a polynomial, with rational coefficients, in ln 2 and in the values ζ(2m+1), m ≥ 1, of the Riemann zeta function at odd integer arguments (equivalently, in values of the alternating zeta series ζ_a(s) = ∑_{k≥1} (−1)^{k−1}/k^s at odd s).

Problem: Provide an efficient and tractable closed-form description of the rational coefficients appearing in these polynomial expressions, valid for arbitrary n and for arbitrary choices of the local spin operators on the n consecutive sites.
category_tag: Heisenberg XXX spin chain correlation functions
status_search_result: Literature searches indicate that while explicit polynomial expressions in ln 2 and odd zeta values have been computed for short-range correlators (up to about n=6 or 7 sites) using the qKZ equation, hidden Grassmann structure, and fermionic basis approaches, no efficient general closed-form description of the rational coefficients for arbitrary n-site XXX correlators is known. The problem of an efficient description of these rational coefficients remains open.

original_question: For the XXZ spin chain in the critical regime -1 ≤ Δ < 1, study time- and temperature-dependent correlation functions at large separation in space and time, including the correlation function g(n,t) discussed in the paper. Derive an explicit analytic formula for the asymptotic exponential decay of these correlation functions in the joint large-distance, large-time limit.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the spin-1/2 XXZ Heisenberg chain on the infinite line with Hamiltonian
  H = J ∑_{n∈ℤ} ( σ^x_n σ^x_{n+1} + σ^y_n σ^y_{n+1} + Δ ( σ^z_n σ^z_{n+1} − 1 ) ),
where σ^{x,y,z}_n are Pauli matrices acting at site n and Δ is the anisotropy parameter, in the critical (massless) regime −1 ≤ Δ < 1. At inverse temperature β > 0 and in thermal equilibrium, define the dynamical two-point correlation function
  g(n,t) = ⟨ σ^-_0(0) σ^+_n(t) ⟩_β = Tr( e^{-β H} σ^-_0 e^{i t H} σ^+_n e^{-i t H} ) / Tr( e^{-β H} ),
together with the analogous longitudinal correlator ⟨ σ^z_0(0) σ^z_n(t) ⟩_β.

Derive an explicit analytic closed-form expression for the leading asymptotic behavior of these correlation functions in the joint limit of large spatial separation n → ∞ and large time t → ∞ (with n/t fixed or in a specified scaling regime). In particular, exhibit the conjectured exponential decay rate as an explicit function of Δ, β, n and t, including the prefactor.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made since the problem was posed. Dugave, Göhmann, and Kozlowski (2013, arXiv:1305.0118) developed a thermal form factor expansion for the XXZ chain and obtained the large-distance asymptotics of static finite-temperature correlation functions. For the free-fermion XX point, the long-time large-distance asymptotics of dynamical transverse correlators at finite temperature were derived (arXiv:1908.11555, 2020). Subsequent works treat dynamical asymptotics in the massless XXZ regime via thermal form factors, but a fully explicit closed-form formula for the joint large-distance, large-time exponential decay of g(n,t) throughout −1 ≤ Δ < 1 at general temperature is not yet established in complete generality, so the problem remains only partially resolved.
